# 1. Why This Chapter Matters

Up to this point, we have mostly discussed MLOps in platform-neutral terms:

```text
training

pipelines

model registry

feature systems

serving

monitoring

GPU infrastructure
```

Now we map those responsibilities onto Google Cloud.

The goal is **not** to memorize Google product names.

The goal is to understand:

```text
Requirement
   |
   v
MLOps Capability
   |
   v
Possible GCP Service
```

For example:

```text
Need:
large analytical training dataset

Capability:
data warehouse

Possible GCP service:
BigQuery
```

Or:

```text
Need:
managed model training

Capability:
training execution

Possible GCP service:
Vertex AI Custom Training
```

That thinking is much stronger in interviews than listing twenty Google services.

---

# 2. The Big Google Cloud MLOps Picture

A simplified architecture:

```text
                    DATA SOURCES
                         |
          +--------------+--------------+
          |                             |
          v                             v
       Pub/Sub                       Databases
          |                             |
          v                             |
       Dataflow                         |
          |                             |
          +--------------+--------------+
                         |
                         v
                  DATA PLATFORM
               BigQuery / GCS
                         |
                         v
                  VERTEX AI PIPELINES
                         |
         +---------------+---------------+
         |                               |
         v                               v
   DATA PROCESSING                  MODEL TRAINING
                                         |
                                         v
                                  EXPERIMENTATION
                                         |
                                         v
                                   MODEL REGISTRY
                                         |
                    +--------------------+--------------------+
                    |                                         |
                    v                                         v
            Vertex AI Endpoint                              GKE
                    |                                  KServe / vLLM /
                    |                                  Triton / custom
                    +--------------------+--------------------+
                                         |
                                         v
                                   MONITORING
```

This is not the only design.

But it is a useful mental framework.

---

# 3. Vertex AI Mental Model

Think of Vertex AI as:

> Google's managed machine-learning platform on Google Cloud.

It provides capabilities across much of the ML lifecycle.

Broad categories include:

```text
experimentation

training

pipelines

model management

deployment

prediction

evaluation

governance
```

Architecturally, Vertex AI can reduce how much ML control-plane infrastructure your team needs to operate itself.

---

# 4. Managed Platform vs Self-Built Platform

Suppose your team needs:

```text
training

pipelines

registry

serving
```

Option A:

```text
Kubernetes
+
Kubeflow
+
MLflow
+
KServe
+
custom IAM
+
custom monitoring
```

Option B:

```text
Vertex AI managed services
```

Option A gives:

```text
control

customization

portability
```

Option B gives:

```text
less operational overhead

tighter GCP integration

faster platform adoption
```

The correct choice depends on requirements.

---

# 5. When Managed Vertex AI Is Attractive

Imagine:

```text
20 ML teams

all workloads on GCP

small platform engineering team

strong BigQuery usage

standard training workloads

moderate customization needs
```

Vertex AI may be very attractive because you can avoid building and maintaining large parts of the ML control plane.

---

# 6. When GKE May Be More Attractive

Suppose:

```text
custom GPU scheduling

specialized LLM runtime

multi-cloud requirement

deep Kubernetes expertise

custom inference routing

custom distributed systems
```

Then GKE may provide the control you need.

Examples:

```text
vLLM

Triton

Ray Serve

custom KServe runtime
```

may run there.

---

# 7. Hybrid Is Often the Best Answer

You do not have to choose:

```text
Vertex AI
OR
GKE
```

You can combine them.

Example:

```text
BigQuery
   |
   v
Vertex AI Pipelines
   |
   v
Vertex AI Training
   |
   v
Vertex AI Model Registry
   |
   v
GKE Custom Serving
   |
   v
vLLM
```

This is often a very practical enterprise design.

---

# 8. BigQuery in MLOps

BigQuery is highly relevant for ML because many organizations already keep:

```text
customer data

transaction data

product data

event data
```

there.

It can serve as:

```text
analytical data warehouse

training dataset source

feature computation platform

evaluation data store
```

---

# 9. Why BigQuery Works Well for Training Data

Training often requires queries such as:

```text
join billions of transactions

aggregate historical behavior

create labeled datasets

build time-window features
```

These are analytical workloads.

BigQuery is designed for large-scale analytical processing.

---

# 10. Example Training Data Flow

```text
Production Systems
      |
      v
BigQuery
      |
      v
SQL Feature Engineering
      |
      v
Training Table
      |
      v
Vertex AI Training
```

Simple.

Powerful.

Often enough for many business ML workloads.

---

# 11. BigQuery Is Not Usually Your Low-Latency Feature Store

Suppose fraud prediction requires:

```text
P99 feature lookup < 10 ms
```

BigQuery is not generally the architecture you would choose for synchronous per-request feature serving.

Instead:

```text
BigQuery
-> offline feature computation

low-latency store
-> online feature access
```

Same principle as Chapter 9.

---

# 12. Cloud Storage in MLOps

Google Cloud Storage, or GCS, is frequently used for:

```text
training data files

model artifacts

checkpoints

pipeline outputs

LLM weights

evaluation artifacts
```

Think:

> durable object storage for large ML artifacts.

---

# 13. Why Object Storage Matters

ML artifacts can be enormous.

Example:

```text
dataset = 10 TB

checkpoint = 500 GB

LLM weights = 140 GB
```

Putting these in relational databases is usually inappropriate.

Object storage provides:

```text
durability

large-object support

lifecycle management
```

---

# 14. Artifact Separation

A good architecture may use:

```text
BigQuery
-> structured analytical data

GCS
-> files / artifacts / checkpoints

metadata DB / managed service
-> run metadata
```

Different storage systems for different workloads.

---

# 15. Pub/Sub

Pub/Sub provides managed messaging/event infrastructure.

Mental model:

```text
Producer
   |
   v
Topic
   |
   +---- Consumer A
   |
   +---- Consumer B
```

MLOps uses may include:

```text
event ingestion

feature pipelines

training triggers

prediction events

monitoring pipelines
```

---

# 16. Example Fraud Architecture

```text
Payment Service
      |
      v
Pub/Sub
      |
      +---- Fraud Feature Pipeline
      |
      +---- Analytics Pipeline
      |
      +---- Audit Pipeline
```

Pub/Sub decouples the payment service from downstream ML/data consumers.

---

# 17. Dataflow

Dataflow is Google's managed data-processing service based on Apache Beam concepts.

Useful for:

```text
batch processing

stream processing
```

In MLOps it can compute:

```text
streaming features

data transformations

training datasets

prediction-event processing
```

---

# 18. Pub/Sub + Dataflow Pattern

Real-time features:

```text
Application Events
      |
      v
Pub/Sub
      |
      v
Dataflow
      |
      v
Feature Store / Low-Latency DB
```

This is a common cloud-native streaming architecture.

---

# 19. Event Time in Dataflow

Recall:

```text
event time
vs
processing time
```

Streaming frameworks need to handle:

```text
late events

windows

watermarks
```

Those matter for features such as:

```text
transactions_last_10_minutes
```

Google services do not remove the need to understand streaming semantics.

---

# 20. Vertex AI Workbench

Workbench provides managed environments for interactive ML development.

Think:

```text
data scientist
     |
     v
notebook environment
     |
     v
BigQuery / GCS / Vertex AI
```

Useful for:

```text
exploration

experimentation

development
```

But notebooks should not become the production deployment mechanism.

---

# 21. Notebook to Production

A mature path:

```text
Notebook Exploration
      |
      v
Reusable Python Code
      |
      v
Git
      |
      v
CI
      |
      v
Training Pipeline
```

The notebook is for experimentation.

Production logic belongs in:

```text
versioned

reviewed

tested
```

code.

---

# 22. Vertex AI Custom Training

Custom Training lets you run your own training code on managed infrastructure.

Mental model:

```text
Training Container
       |
       v
Vertex AI Training Job
       |
       v
Managed Compute
       |
       v
Model Artifact
```

You provide:

```text
training code

container/runtime

machine requirements
```

Google manages much of the execution infrastructure.

---

# 23. Why Custom Training Is Useful

You may need:

```text
PyTorch

TensorFlow

XGBoost

custom Python training
```

but do not want to operate Kubernetes jobs directly.

Managed training provides an execution abstraction.

---

# 24. Training Container Pattern

Strong pattern:

```text
Git
 |
 v
CI
 |
 v
Build Training Container
 |
 v
Artifact Registry
 |
 v
Vertex AI Training Job
```

Now:

```text
training runtime
```

is immutable and reproducible.

---

# 25. Artifact Registry

Artifact Registry can store artifacts such as:

```text
container images

software packages
```

For MLOps, this commonly means:

```text
training images

serving images
```

It plays the same role as an enterprise container/package registry.

---

# 26. Training Image Provenance

Record:

```text
Git commit

container digest

build pipeline

dependency versions
```

Then Vertex AI job can reference:

```text
immutable image digest
```

rather than:

```text

```

Same DevOps discipline.

---

# 27. Managed GPUs

Training jobs may use accelerator-backed compute.

Architect still needs to decide:

```text
GPU type

GPU count

job topology

cost
```

Managed infrastructure reduces operations.

It does not eliminate capacity and cost engineering.

---

# 28. Distributed Training on Vertex AI

Large training jobs may use multiple workers.

Conceptually:

```text
Vertex AI Training
       |
       +---- Worker 0
       +---- Worker 1
       +---- Worker N
```

Your framework may still implement:

```text
DDP

distributed TensorFlow

other distributed strategies
```

Managed cloud schedules the machines.

Framework handles training semantics.

---

# 29. Managed Does Not Mean You Ignore Networking

If distributed workers communicate heavily:

```text
all-reduce

gradient synchronization
```

performance still depends on:

```text
machine topology

network performance

framework configuration
```

The cloud service simplifies operations, not physics.

---

# 30. Vertex AI Pipelines

Vertex AI Pipelines provides managed ML workflow orchestration.

Example:

```text
Validate Data
      |
      v
Create Features
      |
      v
Train
      |
      v
Evaluate
      |
      v
Register
```

This maps directly to our pipeline concepts from Chapter 5.

---

# 31. Why Pipelines Are Valuable on GCP

A pipeline may connect:

```text
BigQuery

Dataflow

Vertex AI Training

Model Registry

Endpoints
```

into one repeatable workflow.

This provides:

```text
automation

lineage

reproducibility

scheduling
```

---

# 32. Pipeline Components

A component should still have:

```text
defined inputs

defined outputs

isolated execution

versioned code
```

Managed orchestration does not change good software design.

---

# 33. Pipeline Example

```text
BigQuery Table
      |
      v
Data Validation
      |
      v
Feature Engineering
      |
      v
Vertex Training Job
      |
      v
Evaluation
      |
      +---- Fail -> Stop
      |
      +---- Pass
             |

```

This is the classic managed MLOps workflow.

---

# 34. Pipeline Caching

If immutable inputs have not changed:

```text

```

may reduce:

```text

latency

cost
```

But as discussed earlier:

> Cache correctness depends on input identity.

Mutable tables can make caching dangerous.

---

# 35. Pipeline Identity

A pipeline run should ideally capture:

```text
pipeline version

container version

model parameters

training output

evaluation output
```

This builds reproducibility.

---

# 36. Vertex AI Experiments

Experiment tracking capabilities help compare:

```text
runs

parameters

```

Conceptually:

```text
Experiment
   |
   +---- Run A
   +---- Run B
   +---- Run C
```

Same mental model as MLflow.

---

# 37. Managed vs MLflow Tracking

Why might you use managed Vertex capabilities?

```text
tighter GCP integration

less infrastructure

unified IAM
```

Why MLflow?

```text
portability

existing ecosystem

custom workflows
```

Again:

requirements first.

---

# 38. Vertex AI Model Registry

The Model Registry provides a managed catalog for model versions.

Conceptually:

```text
FraudModel
   |
   +---- v1
   +---- v2
   +---- v3
```

It supports lifecycle management around models.

---

# 39. Registry Responsibilities

A registry should help answer:

```text
Which version exists?

Which training run produced it?

Which artifact is associated?

Which version is deployed?
```

The same model-governance principles from Chapter 4 still apply.

---

# 40. Registry Is Not Runtime

Very important:

```text
Model Registry
```

should not need to be queried for every prediction.

Deployment retrieves/pins an approved version.

Runtime serves independently.

Control plane vs data plane.

---

# 41. Vertex AI Endpoints

Managed endpoints provide online model serving.

Conceptually:

```text
Client
  |
  v
Vertex AI Endpoint
  |
  v
Model Deployment
  |
  v
Managed Compute
```

The platform handles much of:

```text
infrastructure

routing

scaling

deployment lifecycle
```

---

# 42. Managed Online Prediction

Good fit when:

```text
standard model serving

GCP-native workloads

limited desire to manage Kubernetes

supported runtime requirements
```

You trade lower operational burden for less low-level control.

---

# 43. Online vs Batch Prediction

Online:

```text
request
-> immediate prediction
```

Batch:

```text
large dataset
-> bulk predictions
-> output dataset/file
```

Choose based on latency needs.

Do not deploy an online service for a job that runs once nightly if batch is sufficient.

---

# 44. Batch Prediction Example

```text
BigQuery
   |
   v
10 million customers
   |
   v
Batch Prediction
   |
   v
BigQuery Output
```

This can be much more cost-efficient than maintaining always-on replicas.

---

# 45. Endpoint Autoscaling

Managed endpoints can provide autoscaling capabilities.

But you still need to understand:

```text
minimum replicas

maximum replicas

traffic

model startup
```

For very large models, startup time can still make reactive scaling problematic.

---

# 46. Managed Endpoint vs GKE Serving

Managed endpoint:

```text
less operations

standardized lifecycle

integrated IAM
```

GKE:

```text
custom runtime

custom autoscaling

custom GPU topology

custom routing
```

That is the central trade-off.

---

# 47. When vLLM Pushes You Toward GKE

Suppose you need:

```text
open-source 70B LLM

continuous batching

specialized KV-cache tuning

custom routing

multi-GPU topology control
```

A custom GKE-based vLLM deployment may offer greater flexibility.

This is exactly why a hybrid architecture can make sense.

---

# 48. GKE as Custom ML Execution Plane

You can use:

```text
Vertex AI
```

for:

```text
training

pipelines

registry
```

and:

```text
GKE
```

for:

```text
specialized serving
```

Example:

```text
Vertex Registry
      |
      v
Deployment Pipeline
      |
      v
GKE
      |
      v
KServe
      |
      v
vLLM
```

Very realistic architecture.

---

# 49. GKE + Triton

Traditional GPU models:

```text
GKE
 |
 v
KServe
 |
 v
Triton
 |
 v
GPU
```

Useful when standardizing high-performance inference for mixed model types.

---

# 50. GKE + Ray

Ray can run on Kubernetes to support:

```text
distributed training

batch compute

serving
```

If your organization has complex distributed Python workloads, this may be useful.

But running Ray yourself means operating another distributed platform.

---

# 51. Vertex AI vs GKE Is Not Binary

An architect may decide:

```text
Standard workloads
-> Vertex AI

Specialized workloads
-> GKE
```

This is often a stronger strategy than forcing everything into one runtime.

---

# 52. IAM in Google Cloud MLOps

IAM is central to production design.

Different workloads should have different permissions.

Example:

```text
Training Job
-> read training bucket
-> write artifacts

Deployment Pipeline
-> read approved model
-> deploy endpoint

Inference Runtime
-> read online features
```

Principle:

```text
least privilege
```

---

# 53. Service Accounts

Cloud workloads generally operate under service identities.

Example:

```text
vertex-training-sa
```

with:

```text
read BigQuery dataset

write GCS artifacts
```

Avoid using broad project-wide admin identities.

---

# 54. IAM Boundary Example

Data scientist:

```text
can submit training
```

but cannot:

```text
directly modify production endpoint
```

Production deployment pipeline:

```text
can deploy only approved models
```

This implements separation of duties.

---

# 55. VPC and Private Networking

ML workloads may need to remain inside private network boundaries.

Architecture may require:

```text
private access

controlled egress

internal endpoints
```

for:

```text
sensitive training

financial data

enterprise inference
```

Do not assume every ML endpoint should be public internet-facing.

---

# 56. Data Exfiltration Risk

Training workloads often have broad access to valuable data.

If they also have unrestricted internet egress:

```text
data could potentially leave the environment
```

Architects may use:

```text
network restrictions

IAM

private access

audit
```

to reduce risk.

---

# 57. CMEK / Encryption Considerations

Enterprise workloads may require control over encryption keys.

Architect-level discussions can include:

```text
encryption at rest

encryption in transit

key management

rotation
```

Especially for:

```text
regulated

financial

sensitive
```

workloads.

---

# 58. Secret Manager

Secrets such as:

```text
API credentials

external database credentials
```

should be stored in a managed secret system.

Do not bake them into:

```text
training container

notebook

pipeline code
```

Same DevOps principle.

---

# 59. Cloud Build / CI

A GCP-native CI flow may conceptually look like:

```text
Git
 |
 v
CI Build
 |
 +---- lint
 +---- test
 +---- scan
 |
 v
Build Container
 |
 v
Artifact Registry
```

Then:

```text
pipeline
```

launches the image.

Specific CI technology can vary.

The architecture principle matters more.

---

# 60. Terraform for GCP MLOps

Terraform may manage:

```text
GKE

service accounts

IAM roles

GCS buckets

networking

Artifact Registry

BigQuery resources
```

Potentially some ML platform configuration as well.

Infrastructure should be:

```text
reviewable

versioned

reproducible
```

---

# 61. Terraform Boundary

Do not put every dynamic model lifecycle operation into Terraform.

Terraform is excellent for:

```text
long-lived infrastructure
```

Model promotion is often better handled through:

```text
ML deployment pipelines
```

rather than constantly changing Terraform state for every model run.

Use the right control mechanism for the right lifecycle.

---

# 62. Cloud Monitoring

Infrastructure and service monitoring on GCP can be centralized through Google's managed observability ecosystem.

But ML-specific metrics still need to be designed.

Examples:

```text
model version

prediction distribution

feature freshness

TTFT

tokens/sec
```

Managed monitoring does not automatically know what business/model health means.

---

# 63. Logging

Prediction and pipeline logs may go into centralized cloud logging infrastructure.

But remember:

```text
prompts

features

predictions
```

can contain sensitive information.

Logging policy must include:

```text
redaction

retention

access
```

---

# 64. Google Cloud LLM Architecture

A custom LLM platform might look like:

```text
Clients
   |
   v
Global Load Balancer / Gateway
   |
   v
GKE
   |
   v
LLM Router
   |
   +---- vLLM Pool A
   |
   +---- vLLM Pool B
   |
   v
GPU Nodes
```

Supporting services:

```text
GCS
-> model weights

Artifact Registry
-> images

Cloud Monitoring
-> telemetry
```

---

# 65. RAG on Google Cloud — Conceptual Architecture

```text
Documents
   |
   v
Ingestion Pipeline
   |
   v
Chunking
   |
   v
Embedding
   |
   v
Vector Search / Index
   |
   v

User Query
   |
   v
Retriever
   |
   v
Relevant Chunks
   |
   v
LLM
```

The exact vector/search product can vary.

The architectural responsibilities remain the same.

---

# 66. BigQuery for RAG Metadata

Even if vector retrieval happens elsewhere, BigQuery may hold:

```text
document metadata

evaluation results

usage analytics

retrieval logs
```

Architects combine systems rather than expecting one product to solve every layer.

---

# 67. LLM Release Pipeline on GCP

```text
Prompt / Retrieval / Model Change
             |
             v
             CI
             |
             v
       Offline Evaluation
             |
             v
      Register Artifacts
             |
             v
       Deploy Canary
             |
             v
         Observe
             |
       +-----+-----+
       |           |
      Fail        Pass
       |           |
   Rollback     Promote
```

This should look familiar now.

---

# 68. Multi-Region Architecture

Global inference:

```text
Global Users
     |
     v
Global Traffic Layer
     |
   +-----+-----+
   |           |
   v           v
Region A     Region B
   |           |
 Model       Model
 Serving     Serving
```

Need to consider:

```text
model replication

artifact locality

feature locality

failover

data residency
```

---

# 69. Regional Artifact Replication

If a 100GB model lives only far away from the target region:

```text
cold-start time increases
```

Possible strategy:

```text
replicate artifacts regionally
```

so local serving nodes can load faster.

This matters greatly for LLM fleets.

---

# 70. Regional Training

Training should generally run near:

```text
training data

available accelerator capacity
```

Cross-region data movement may cause:

```text
latency

cost

governance concerns
```

Data locality still matters in managed cloud.

---

# 71. Multi-Region Model Consistency

Question:

> How do you ensure every region serves the correct model?

Possible architecture:

```text
central approved model version
        |
        v
regional deployment pipelines
        |
        v
version verification
```

Monitor:

```text
model version by region
```

to detect drift.

---

# 72. Active-Active Inference

Both regions serve production traffic.

Advantages:

```text
low latency

high availability
```

Challenges:

```text
capacity duplication

state synchronization

feature consistency
```

This is common for high-availability global systems.

---

# 73. Active-Passive Inference

Primary region serves.

Secondary waits for disaster recovery.

Advantages:

```text
simpler

lower steady complexity
```

Challenges:

```text
failover delay

cold secondary capacity
```

Again:

cost vs recovery.

---

# 74. Data Residency

Example:

```text
EU data must remain in EU
```

Then architecture may require:

```text
EU training

EU features

EU model serving
```

with only allowed metadata crossing regions.

Global ML architecture must respect data boundaries.

---

# 75. Managed Endpoint DR Question

Always ask:

```text
What happens if the regional managed endpoint is unavailable?
```

Possible answers:

```text
route to another region

serve fallback

degrade functionality
```

Availability architecture exists above the managed service too.

Managed does not mean "no architecture needed."

---

# 76. Google Cloud Fraud Reference Architecture

```text
Payment System
      |
      v
Pub/Sub
      |
      v
Dataflow
      |
      +----> Real-Time Feature Store
      |
      +----> BigQuery / GCS
                    |
                    v
             Vertex AI Pipeline
                    |
                    v
                Training
                    |
                    v
             Model Registry
                    |
                    v
         Managed Endpoint / GKE
                    |
                    v
              Fraud Decision
```

This covers:

```text
online path

offline path

retraining path
```

---

# 77. Real-Time Fraud Request Path

```text
Transaction Request
      |
      v
Fraud API
      |
      v
Online Features
      |
      v
Inference Service
      |
      v
Risk Score
```

The historical/training path should not sit inside this synchronous critical path.

---

# 78. Recommendation Architecture

Batch-oriented design:

```text
User Events
    |
    v
BigQuery
    |
    v
Feature Computation
    |
    v
Vertex AI Training
    |
    v
Batch Predictions
    |
    v
BigQuery / Cache
    |
    v
Application
```

This may be much simpler than real-time inference.

Never over-engineer.

---

# 79. Real-Time Recommendation Design

If real-time personalization is genuinely required:

```text
Events
  |
  v
Pub/Sub
  |
  v
Dataflow
  |
  v
Online Features
  |
  v
Model Endpoint
  |
  v
Recommendation
```

Now latency and feature freshness become first-class concerns.

---

# 80. Enterprise MLOps Architecture

For many teams:

```text
                       ML DEVELOPERS
                            |
                            v
                   Notebook / IDE / Git
                            |
                            v
                           CI
                            |
                            v
                  Artifact Registry
                            |
                            v
                   Vertex AI Pipelines
                            |
          +-----------------+-----------------+
          |                                   |
          v                                   v
      BigQuery / GCS                    Vertex Training
                                              |
                                              v
                                       Model Registry
                                              |
                 +----------------------------+---------------------------+
                 |                                                        |
                 v                                                        v
        Managed Vertex Endpoint                                      GKE Platform
                                                                  KServe / vLLM /
                                                                  Triton / Ray
                 |                                                        |
                 +----------------------------+---------------------------+
                                              |
                                              v
                                         Monitoring
```

This is a strong interview reference model.

---

# 81. Platform Team Responsibility in Managed Cloud

Even with Vertex AI, platform engineers still own:

```text
IAM

network design

templates

CI/CD

governance

cost

developer experience

observability standards
```

Managed ML platforms do not eliminate platform engineering.

They change what the platform team manages.

---

# 82. Golden Training Template on Vertex

Internal platform could expose:

```text
dataset

training image

machine type

GPU count

hyperparameters
```

Then automatically configure:

```text
IAM

logging

experiment tracking

checkpoint path

cost labels
```

This is platform engineering on top of managed services.

---

# 83. Golden Deployment Template

Teams provide:

```text
approved model

latency class

traffic level
```

Platform decides:

```text
managed endpoint
or
GKE specialized runtime
```

This hides complexity from most users.

---

# 84. Workload Classification

A sophisticated internal platform may classify workloads:

```text
Small CPU Model
-> managed endpoint

Standard GPU Model
-> managed endpoint

Large LLM
-> GKE + vLLM

Complex inference graph
-> GKE + Ray Serve
```

This is a very architect-level platform idea.

---

# 85. Cost Optimization — Training

Strategies:

```text
choose appropriate accelerators

use smaller test runs

checkpoint long jobs

avoid data movement

track GPU-hours
```

Managed services make resources easier to provision.

That can make overspending easier too.

---

# 86. Cost Optimization — Serving

Ask:

```text
online or batch?

minimum replicas needed?

CPU sufficient?

smaller GPU sufficient?

can quantization help?

can caching help?
```

The most expensive service is often one that is always running but barely used.

---

# 87. Cost Attribution

Every training/deployment should ideally carry:

```text
team

project

model

environment
```

metadata.

Then you can build:

```text
team-level cost dashboards
```

Without attribution, optimization becomes political guesswork.

---

# 88. Quota and Capacity

Cloud accelerators are not infinitely available.

A production architecture should consider:

```text
GPU quotas

regional availability

capacity reservations

fallback GPU classes
```

Do not assume you can instantly provision hundreds of GPUs during an incident.

---

# 89. Accelerator Availability as Architecture Constraint

Suppose architecture requires:

```text
200 H100 GPUs in one region
```

but that capacity is not realistically available.

The architecture is invalid.

Infrastructure design must account for real capacity.

---

# 90. Security: Data Scientist Notebook

Workbench/notebook environment can access powerful data.

Protect with:

```text
IAM

private networking

restricted service accounts

audit logging
```

Interactive environments are often a major security boundary.

---

# 91. Production vs Research Projects

A strong organization may separate:

```text
research project

staging project

production project
```

This helps enforce:

```text
IAM isolation

billing

blast-radius control
```

Production should not be merely another notebook environment.

---

# 92. Cross-Project Architecture

Central platform may exist in:

```text
platform project
```

while teams operate in:

```text
team projects
```

Architect questions:

```text
Who owns networks?

Who owns IAM?

Where are artifacts?

How does deployment cross projects?
```

These become important in enterprise GCP design.

---

# 93. Shared VPC Concept

Large organizations may centralize networking while allowing multiple service projects.

The important architecture idea:

```text
central network governance

+

decentralized workload projects
```

This can fit well with centralized platform engineering.

---

# 94. Governance Boundary

Central platform team may control:

```text
network

approved services

IAM patterns

golden templates
```

ML teams control:

```text
model logic

feature logic

evaluation
```

This keeps ownership clear.

---

# 95. Disaster Recovery for MLOps Metadata

Back up or reproduce:

```text
pipeline definitions

model metadata

artifact references

deployment state
```

Git can reconstruct some configuration.

GCS can preserve artifacts.

Managed service metadata still needs a DR strategy appropriate to business requirements.

---

# 96. Artifact Durability

Production model artifact should never exist only on:

```text
one notebook

one VM

one Kubernetes node
```

It belongs in durable managed storage with appropriate retention/versioning.

Obvious principle.

Frequently violated in immature environments.

---

# 97. Pipeline DR

If the orchestration control plane is temporarily unavailable:

```text
production inference should continue
```

New training may pause.

Again:

control plane vs serving plane.

This principle should now be automatic for you.

---

# 98. GKE Control Plane Failure vs Inference

If Kubernetes API temporarily has issues, already running workloads may continue depending on the failure mode.

Design inference so each request does not depend on:

```text
deployment controller

model registry

CI server
```

at runtime.

Data path should stay minimal.

---

# 99. Model Runtime Dependency Principle

Runtime request path ideally:

```text
Client
  |
  v
Gateway
  |
  v
Feature / Retrieval Dependency
  |
  v
Inference Runtime
```

Not:

```text
Client
 -> Git
 -> Pipeline Server
 -> Registry
 -> Deployment Controller
 -> Model
```

Keep control-plane systems out of synchronous request paths.

---

# 100. Choosing Vertex vs GKE — Interview Framework

Use these dimensions:

```text
1. Workload standardization

2. Runtime customization

3. GPU scheduling needs

4. Operational team size

5. Portability

6. Integration with GCP services

7. Cost

8. Security/governance

9. Developer experience

10. Scale
```

Then make a recommendation.

---

# 101. Example Decision

Requirement:

```text
XGBoost fraud model

1000 QPS

standard online serving

fully GCP-native

small platform team
```

Likely direction:

```text
managed Vertex AI endpoint
```

Why build Kubernetes complexity?

---

# 102. Another Decision

Requirement:

```text
70B open-source LLM

8-GPU tensor parallelism

custom continuous batching

special routing

strict token SLOs
```

Likely direction:

```text
GKE
+
specialized LLM runtime
```

such as vLLM or another appropriate runtime.

---

# 103. Another Decision

Requirement:

```text
100 ML teams

most use standard managed training

5 teams need specialized GPU serving
```

Good architecture:

```text
managed-by-default

custom GKE escape hatch
```

This is often better than building everything yourself.

---

# 104. Managed-by-Default Philosophy

A strong enterprise principle:

```text
Use managed capabilities
when they satisfy requirements.

Build custom infrastructure
only where requirements demand it.
```

This minimizes undifferentiated engineering work.

Senior architects understand the cost of ownership.

---

# 105. But Avoid Vendor Blindness

Managed services introduce:

```text
platform coupling

pricing model

feature constraints
```

If portability is a strategic requirement, architecture may favor more open interfaces.

Trade-offs, not ideology.

---

# 106. Migration Strategy

Suppose company currently has:

```text
notebooks

manual scripts

GCS

BigQuery
```

Do not migrate immediately into 20 new services.

Possible path:

```text
Step 1:
version code

Step 2:
containerize training

Step 3:
managed training

Step 4:
pipeline orchestration

Step 5:
registry

Step 6:
controlled deployment
```

Incremental platform adoption reduces risk.

---

# 107. Migration From Self-Hosted MLflow

Suppose teams already use MLflow heavily.

You may:

```text
keep MLflow
```

while moving training execution into Vertex.

Later decide whether registry/tracking migration creates enough benefit.

Platform migration should solve actual pain.

Do not migrate merely to simplify diagrams.

---

# 108. Migration From Kubeflow

If operations burden is high:

```text
Kubeflow Pipelines
-> Vertex AI Pipelines
```

may reduce maintenance.

But check:

```text
custom components

Kubernetes assumptions

identity

metadata

portability
```

before migrating.

---

# 109. Migration to Hybrid Model

Some teams may remain on GKE while standard training moves into managed Vertex.

This avoids:

```text
big-bang platform migration
```

Hybrid architecture can be transitional or permanent.

---

# 110. Senior Incident Scenario — Training Job Suddenly Costs 4x More

Investigate:

```text
GPU type changed?

worker count changed?

dataset larger?

job runtime increased?

cross-region data read?

checkpoint frequency?

data loader slower?
```

Managed service invoice is a symptom.

You still need system-level diagnosis.

---

# 111. Senior Incident Scenario — Endpoint Latency Increased

Check:

```text
traffic change

new model version

machine type

autoscaling

cold replicas

feature dependency

request size
```

Do not immediately blame Vertex.

Managed platform still sits inside a larger system.

---

# 112. Senior Incident Scenario — BigQuery Training Query Cost Explodes

Possible causes:

```text
partition filter removed

join cardinality exploded

backfill running

table scan widened
```

MLOps engineers need enough data-engineering knowledge to diagnose this.

---

# 113. Senior Incident Scenario — GKE LLM Pods Take 15 Minutes to Start

Investigate:

```text
node provisioning

image pull

model artifact download

cross-region storage

GPU initialization

model load
```

Break startup into stages.

Measure each separately.

---

# 114. Senior Incident Scenario — Region Failure

Questions:

```text
Is model deployed elsewhere?

Are artifacts replicated?

Are features available?

How does traffic fail over?

Is spare GPU capacity available?
```

A DR plan that assumes GPUs magically appear in another region is weak.

---

# 115. Architect Scenario — 100-Team Google Cloud ML Platform

Requirements:

```text
100 teams

batch + online ML

LLMs

regulated workloads

central governance

self-service
```

Possible layers:

```text
Developer layer:
Git / notebooks / portal

Data layer:
BigQuery / GCS / streaming

Training:
Vertex AI managed training

Workflow:
Vertex AI Pipelines

Registry:
Vertex AI Model Registry

Standard serving:
managed endpoints

Special serving:
GKE + KServe / vLLM / Triton

Governance:
IAM / policy / audit

Observability:
centralized monitoring
```

This is a strong architectural answer.

---

# 116. Platform API Above Google Services

Do not make every ML engineer learn every GCP service.

Internal API:

```text
TrainModel

DeployModel

CreateBatchPrediction
```

could map underneath to:

```text
Vertex AI

GKE

BigQuery
```

depending on workload.

The internal abstraction becomes the stable developer contract.

---

# 117. Why an Internal Platform Layer Still Matters

Without it:

Team A:

```text
uses Vertex directly
```

Team B:

```text
creates custom GKE deployments
```

Team C:

```text
runs scripts manually
```

Standards diverge.

A platform layer can enforce:

```text
naming

labels

IAM

monitoring

cost controls

deployment policy
```

---

# 118. Golden Path Example

Engineer specifies:

```text
model_type: classifier

traffic: online

latency_slo: 100ms

gpu: false
```

Platform may automatically choose:

```text
Vertex managed endpoint
```

Another:

```text
model_type: llm

size: 70B

tensor_parallel: 8
```

Platform chooses:

```text
GKE specialized serving
```

That is intent-based platform architecture.

---

# 119. System Design Question Framework

If interviewer says:

> Design MLOps on Google Cloud.

Do not immediately say:

> BigQuery, Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Vertex, GKE.

Start with:

```text
Scale?

Data type?

Training frequency?

Serving latency?

GPU needs?

Regions?

Compliance?

Team count?

Budget?
```

Then map requirements to services.

---

# 120. Example Interview Answer Structure

You can say:

> I would separate the platform into data, training, model lifecycle, serving, and governance planes. For structured analytical training data, BigQuery is a strong fit, with GCS for large artifacts and checkpoints. Managed Vertex training and pipelines reduce control-plane operations. I'd use the model registry for governed model versions. Standard models could use managed endpoints, while specialized LLM or custom GPU serving could run on GKE with vLLM, Triton, or KServe. IAM, networking, observability, and cost attribution would be standardized across both execution paths.

That already sounds much more senior than:

> We'll use Vertex AI.

---

# 121. Common Anti-Patterns

## Anti-Pattern 1

Using Vertex AI because "Google interview means Google services."

## Anti-Pattern 2

Using GKE for every small model.

## Anti-Pattern 3

Using managed endpoints for workloads requiring deep custom runtime control without evaluating constraints.

## Anti-Pattern 4

Putting control-plane dependencies in prediction request paths.

## Anti-Pattern 5

Broad admin service accounts for all ML jobs.

## Anti-Pattern 6

Cross-region training against massive datasets without considering network cost.

## Anti-Pattern 7

Assuming cloud GPU capacity is unlimited.

## Anti-Pattern 8

No model or artifact replication strategy.

## Anti-Pattern 9

Notebook-based direct production deployment.

## Anti-Pattern 10

No internal platform abstraction across managed and custom ML systems.

---

```text
                                      v
                               Model Registry
                                      |
                 +--------------------+--------------------+
                 |                                         |
                 v                                         v
        Managed Vertex Endpoint                          GKE
                                                   KServe / vLLM /
                                                   Triton / Ray
                 |                                         |
                 +--------------------+--------------------+
                                      |
                                      v
                                Observability
                                      |
                                      v
                              IAM / Cost / Policy
```

And remember the architect rule:

```text
Managed by default

Custom where justified
```

---

# 124. What You Must Remember From Chapter 13

1. **Vertex AI is a managed ML platform, not simply one model-serving service.**

2. **BigQuery commonly serves analytical and training-data workloads; GCS commonly stores large ML artifacts.**

3. **Pub/Sub and Dataflow are useful building blocks for event-driven and streaming ML data pipelines.**

4. **Vertex AI Custom Training provides managed execution for training code without forcing you to operate Kubernetes directly.**

5. **Vertex AI Pipelines automate reproducible ML workflows.**

6. **Model Registry manages model lifecycle and provenance; it should not sit inside every inference request.**

7. **Managed endpoints are attractive for standardized workloads; GKE is valuable when runtime, GPU scheduling, or serving behavior needs deeper customization.**

8. **Vertex AI and GKE are complementary, not mutually exclusive.**

9. **LLM workloads with vLLM, Triton, Ray, or specialized multi-GPU scheduling may justify custom GKE execution.**

10. **IAM, networking, artifact provenance, observability, and cost governance remain platform responsibilities even when infrastructure is managed.**

11. **Multi-region ML requires deliberate planning for model artifacts, features, traffic, data residency, and GPU capacity.**

12. **Managed services reduce operational burden but do not eliminate architecture decisions.**

13. **A mature internal ML platform can abstract both Vertex AI and GKE behind one self-service developer experience.**

14. **For Google-style interviews, start with requirements and system boundaries, then map those responsibilities to Google Cloud services.**
