# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 17 — GPU Infrastructure and Distributed ML Systems: CUDA, HBM, NVLink, RDMA, NCCL, Distributed Training, Parallelism, Scheduling, MIG, and Accelerator Clusters

---

# 1. Why an MLOps Architect Must Understand GPUs

At small scale, you can think:

```text
Model
  |
  v
GPU
```

At architect scale, this is nowhere near enough.

A large ML workload may depend on:

```text
Model
  |
  v
Framework
  |
  v
CUDA Runtime
  |
  v
GPU Driver
  |
  v
GPU
  |
  +---- HBM
  |
  +---- PCIe
  |
  +---- NVLink
  |
  +---- NVSwitch
  |
  +---- NIC / RDMA
  |
  v
Other GPUs
```

Across a cluster:

```text
GPU Server
    |
    v
High-Speed Network
    |
    v
GPU Server
    |
    v
Storage
```

Performance depends on the whole path.

---

# 2. Accelerator Infrastructure Is Distributed Systems

Large ML infrastructure combines:

```text
distributed systems

high-performance computing

networking

storage

scheduling

hardware

ML frameworks
```

Therefore:

> A senior MLOps architect cannot treat the GPU as a black box.

You do not need to design GPU silicon.

You do need to understand:

```text
where data moves

where memory lives

where synchronization occurs

where bottlenecks appear
```

---

# 3. CPU vs GPU Mental Model

A CPU is optimized primarily for:

```text
general-purpose computation

complex control flow

low-latency tasks

few powerful cores
```

A GPU is designed for:

```text
massive parallel computation

large numbers of similar operations

high memory bandwidth

matrix workloads
```

Machine learning contains huge amounts of matrix computation.

That is why GPUs dominate modern deep learning.

---

# 4. Simplified CPU Model

Conceptually:

```text
CPU

Core
Core
Core
Core
Core
Core
Core
Core
```

Each core is relatively powerful.

Good for:

```text
application logic

orchestration

data processing

serial tasks
```

---

# 5. Simplified GPU Model

Conceptually:

```text
GPU

Thousands of smaller execution units
working on parallel operations
```

Good for:

```text
matrix multiplication

vector operations

deep-learning kernels
```

---

# 6. GPU Is Not Automatically Faster

Suppose workload is:

```text
tiny Python function
```

Sending it to the GPU may add:

```text
data transfer

kernel launch

synchronization
```

overhead.

GPU acceleration works best when there is enough parallel computation to amortize overhead.

---

# 7. GPU Architecture Mental Model

A simplified accelerator:

```text
                 GPU
                  |
      +-----------+-----------+
      |                       |
      v                       v
 Compute Units              HBM
      |
      +---- Tensor Operations
      |
      +---- Vector Operations
      |
      +---- Scheduling
```

Real GPUs are much more complex.

For MLOps architecture, focus on:

```text
compute

memory

bandwidth

interconnect

power

topology
```

---

# 8. Streaming Multiprocessor

NVIDIA terminology commonly includes:

**SM — Streaming Multiprocessor**

A GPU contains many SMs.

Conceptually:

```text
GPU
 |
 +---- SM
 |
 +---- SM
 |
 +---- SM
 |
 +---- ...
```

SMs execute groups of threads.

---

# 9. CUDA Core

CUDA cores perform general numeric operations.

Conceptually:

```text
floating-point arithmetic

integer arithmetic
```

But modern AI performance increasingly depends on specialized tensor hardware.

---

# 10. Tensor Cores

Tensor Cores accelerate matrix operations heavily used by neural networks.

Example:

```text
A × B = C
```

where A and B are large matrices.

These operations dominate:

```text
transformers

CNNs

LLMs
```

---

# 11. Why Precision Matters

Possible formats:

```text
FP32

TF32

FP16

BF16

FP8

INT8

INT4
```

Lower precision may provide:

```text
higher throughput

lower memory usage

lower communication volume
```

but potentially affects:

```text
numerical stability

model quality
```

---

# 12. FP32

FP32:

```text
32-bit floating point
```

Historically common for training.

Benefits:

```text
precision

numerical range
```

Cost:

```text
more memory

more bandwidth

less accelerator throughput
```

than lower-precision formats.

---

# 13. FP16

FP16:

```text
16-bit floating point
```

Reduces memory approximately relative to FP32.

Can increase tensor throughput.

But FP16 has a smaller numerical range.

This can create:

```text
underflow

overflow
```

during training.

---

# 14. BF16

BF16:

```text
bfloat16
```

uses 16 bits but has a larger exponent range than FP16.

It is widely useful for modern deep-learning training.

Architect takeaway:

```text
precision affects

memory

performance

network traffic

training stability
```

---

# 15. Mixed Precision

Training may combine:

```text
FP32

+

FP16/BF16
```

Different operations use different precision.

Goal:

```text
preserve training stability

while increasing throughput
```

---

# 16. FP8

Modern accelerators may support FP8 operations.

Potential benefits:

```text
lower memory

higher throughput

lower communication volume
```

But:

```text
software support

model compatibility

numerical behavior
```

must be validated.

Architect principle:

> Hardware capability is useful only when the software stack and workload can exploit it.

---

# 17. GPU Memory

The accelerator has dedicated high-speed memory.

For data-center accelerators this is often:

```text
HBM
```

High Bandwidth Memory.

GPU memory stores things such as:

```text
model parameters

optimizer state

activations

gradients

KV cache

temporary tensors
```

---

# 18. Why GPU Memory Is Critical

A model may require:

```text
120 GB
```

of memory.

GPU has:

```text
80 GB
```

Now the problem is not compute.

The problem is:

```text
model does not fit
```

This drives many distributed strategies.

---

# 19. Model Weight Memory

Simplified:

```text
parameter_count
×
bytes_per_parameter
```

Example:

```text
70 billion parameters

× 2 bytes

≈ 140 GB
```

for approximately 16-bit model weights.

That alone exceeds many individual GPUs.

---

# 20. Training Memory Is Much Larger

Training needs more than weights.

Potential memory consumers:

```text
weights

gradients

optimizer states

activations

temporary buffers
```

For Adam-like optimization, optimizer state can consume substantial additional memory.

Therefore:

```text
70B model
```

may require far more than:

```text
140 GB
```

during full training.

---

# 21. Activation Memory

During forward pass:

```text
Layer 1
 |
 v
Layer 2
 |
 v
Layer 3
```

intermediate activations may need to be retained for backpropagation.

Large:

```text
batch size

sequence length

model depth
```

increase activation memory.

---

# 22. Gradient Memory

Training calculates gradients for trainable parameters.

If:

```text
70B parameters
```

are trainable, gradients themselves represent enormous memory.

This is one reason parameter-efficient tuning can drastically reduce training resource requirements.

---

# 23. Optimizer State

Adam-style optimizers may keep additional states per parameter.

Conceptually:

```text
parameter

gradient

moment estimate

variance estimate
```

This can make optimizer state one of the largest training-memory consumers.

---

# 24. Memory Determines Architecture

If workload fits:

```text
one GPU
```

architecture is simple.

If not, options include:

```text
model sharding

tensor parallelism

pipeline parallelism

ZeRO/FSDP

CPU offload

quantization
```

Model size directly changes infrastructure architecture.

---

# 25. HBM Bandwidth

HBM provides extremely high memory bandwidth.

Why does bandwidth matter?

Compute units constantly need:

```text
weights

activations

KV cache
```

If compute waits for memory:

```text
GPU cores idle
```

even though theoretical FLOPS are huge.

---

# 26. Compute-Bound vs Memory-Bound

Compute-bound:

```text
GPU arithmetic units
are the limiting factor
```

Memory-bound:

```text
memory bandwidth
is the limiting factor
```

Architects should not assume all ML workloads are compute-bound.

---

# 27. Arithmetic Intensity

Simplified idea:

```text
amount of computation
---------------------
amount of data moved
```

Higher arithmetic intensity can make better use of compute.

Low arithmetic intensity often becomes bandwidth limited.

---

# 28. GPU Utilization Can Mislead

Dashboard:

```text
GPU utilization = 95%
```

does not automatically mean:

```text
excellent performance
```

Maybe GPU spends time:

```text
stalling on memory

waiting for communication

running inefficient kernels
```

You need deeper telemetry.

---

# 29. GPU Memory Utilization

Another metric:

```text
HBM used = 78 GB / 80 GB
```

This tells capacity pressure.

But:

```text
memory allocated
```

does not mean:

```text
memory actively useful
```

Framework allocators can reserve large memory pools.

---

# 30. Memory Fragmentation

Suppose:

```text
10 GB free total
```

but free blocks are fragmented.

A request for:

```text
8 GB contiguous allocation
```

may still fail.

This can produce:

```text
CUDA out of memory
```

despite apparently available memory.

---

# 31. CUDA

CUDA is NVIDIA's parallel-computing platform and programming ecosystem.

Applications commonly interact through:

```text
PyTorch

TensorFlow

JAX
```

which use CUDA libraries underneath.

---

# 32. CUDA Software Stack

Simplified:

```text
PyTorch
   |
   v
CUDA Libraries
   |
   v
CUDA Runtime
   |
   v
NVIDIA Driver
   |
   v
GPU
```

Compatibility between these layers matters enormously.

---

# 33. Driver Compatibility

Example failure:

```text
container expects CUDA capability X

host driver too old
```

Result:

```text
application fails
```

This is why GPU platforms must manage:

```text
driver versions

CUDA versions

framework versions
```

carefully.

---

# 34. CUDA Toolkit

May include:

```text
compiler

libraries

development tools

runtime components
```

For platform teams, users often should not manually manage every CUDA component.

Standard runtime images help.

---

# 35. cuDNN

cuDNN provides optimized primitives for deep neural networks.

Frameworks use such libraries to accelerate operations.

Architect lesson:

```text
model performance
depends heavily on optimized libraries
```

not only hardware.

---

# 36. cuBLAS

BLAS libraries accelerate linear algebra.

Matrix multiplication is central to deep learning.

Optimized GEMM performance can strongly affect training and inference throughput.

---

# 37. Kernel

A GPU kernel is a function executed on the accelerator.

Model execution becomes many kernels.

Potential overhead:

```text
kernel launches

synchronization

memory movement
```

Optimization frameworks attempt to reduce these costs.

---

# 38. Kernel Fusion

Instead of:

```text
Operation A
-> memory
Operation B
-> memory
Operation C
```

fuse operations:

```text
A + B + C
```

inside fewer kernels.

Benefits may include:

```text
less memory traffic

less launch overhead
```

---

# 39. Compiled Graphs

Modern frameworks may compile model graphs to optimize:

```text
kernel fusion

memory planning

execution ordering
```

This can improve performance but adds:

```text
compilation time

compatibility complexity
```

---

# 40. CPU-GPU Data Transfer

Data often originates in host memory.

```text
CPU RAM
   |
 PCIe
   |
   v
GPU HBM
```

Moving data costs time.

If training loop repeatedly waits for CPU transfers, GPU sits idle.

---

# 41. PCIe

PCI Express connects devices such as:

```text
GPU

NIC

CPU
```

PCIe bandwidth is much lower than local HBM bandwidth.

Therefore:

```text
host-device transfer
```

can become a bottleneck.

---

# 42. Pinned Memory

Pinned host memory can improve CPU-to-GPU transfer efficiency.

Data pipelines may use:

```text
pinned buffers

prefetching

multiple workers
```

to keep GPUs fed.

---

# 43. GPU Starvation

GPU waits because:

```text
data loader slow

storage slow

CPU preprocessing slow

network slow
```

Dashboard may show:

```text
GPU utilization oscillates
```

Example:

```text
100%
20%
100%
15%
```

The GPU itself may be perfectly healthy.

---

# 44. Data Pipeline Matters

Training architecture:

```text
Object Storage
      |
      v
Data Loader
      |
      v
CPU Preprocessing
      |
      v
GPU
```

If storage delivers:

```text
500 MB/s
```

but GPU consumes:

```text
5 GB/s
```

compute is starved.

---

# 45. Local Dataset Cache

Large training clusters may cache datasets on:

```text
local NVMe
```

rather than repeatedly reading remote storage.

Benefits:

```text
higher throughput

lower network load

lower object-store request load
```

---

# 46. Dataset Sharding

Instead of one enormous file:

```text
dataset.tar = 20 TB
```

use many shards.

Benefits:

```text
parallel reading

distributed workers

better retry behavior
```

But too many tiny files can also become inefficient.

---

# 47. Small-File Problem

Millions of tiny objects can create:

```text
metadata overhead

request overhead

poor throughput
```

Storage format matters to ML performance.

GPU optimization begins before the GPU.

---

# 48. Multi-GPU Server

A server may contain:

```text
GPU 0
GPU 1
GPU 2
GPU 3
GPU 4
GPU 5
GPU 6
GPU 7
```

But not all GPU-to-GPU paths are equal.

Topology matters.

---

# 49. GPU Topology

Two GPUs may communicate through:

```text
NVLink
```

Another pair may need:

```text
PCIe
```

or even:

```text
CPU / NUMA path
```

Performance can differ dramatically.

---

# 50. NVLink

NVLink provides high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU connectivity.

Conceptually:

```text
GPU A
  ||
NVLink
  ||
GPU B
```

Useful for workloads requiring frequent communication.

---

# 51. Why NVLink Matters

Distributed model execution may exchange:

```text
activations

gradients

tensor shards
```

very frequently.

If communication is slow:

```text
GPUs wait
```

and expensive compute resources become underutilized.

---

# 52. NVSwitch

NVSwitch allows high-bandwidth connectivity among multiple GPUs in a server or accelerator system.

Conceptually:

```text
       NVSwitch
      /   |   \
     /    |    \
   GPU   GPU   GPU
```

This provides more uniform high-speed communication than relying solely on direct links.

---

# 53. Topology Within a Node

Architecture may resemble:

```text
CPU Socket A
  |
  +---- GPU 0
  +---- GPU 1
  +---- GPU 2
  +---- GPU 3

CPU Socket B
  |
  +---- GPU 4
  +---- GPU 5
  +---- GPU 6
  +---- GPU 7
```

NUMA placement can affect:

```text
CPU preprocessing

NIC access

GPU transfer
```

---

# 54. NUMA

NUMA means:

**Non-Uniform Memory Access**

In multi-socket servers, CPU memory access latency depends on where memory physically lives.

Poor placement can create unnecessary cross-socket traffic.

---

# 55. NUMA-Aware Placement

Example:

```text
GPU 0
```

is closest to:

```text
CPU Socket 0
NIC 0
```

If process uses:

```text
CPU Socket 1
NIC 1
```

traffic may cross internal interconnects unnecessarily.

High-performance systems often pin workloads according to topology.

---

# 56. Beyond One Node

Once training spans multiple servers:

```text
Node A
GPUs

Node B
GPUs
```

communication must cross the network.

Network now becomes part of the training system.

---

# 57. Ethernet vs High-Performance Fabric

Traditional Ethernet may work for some distributed workloads.

Large-scale training often benefits from:

```text
very high bandwidth

very low latency

RDMA

low congestion
```

High-performance networking becomes essential.

---

# 58. RDMA

RDMA:

**Remote Direct Memory Access**

Allows data movement between systems with reduced CPU involvement.

Conceptually:

```text
Memory Node A
      |
      | RDMA
      v
Memory Node B
```

avoiding some traditional network stack overhead.

---

# 59. Why RDMA Matters

Distributed training communicates enormous amounts of data.

Traditional networking path:

```text
GPU
 |
CPU
 |
Kernel
 |
Network Stack
 |
NIC
```

adds overhead.

RDMA can reduce CPU and software involvement.

---

# 60. GPUDirect RDMA

Conceptually:

```text
GPU Memory
    |
    v
NIC
    |
 Network
    |
    v
NIC
    |
    v
GPU Memory
```

This can avoid unnecessary staging through CPU memory.

Critical for high-performance distributed training.

---

# 61. InfiniBand

InfiniBand is a high-performance networking technology widely used in HPC and AI clusters.

Benefits include:

```text
high bandwidth

low latency

RDMA

strong congestion-control capabilities
```

---

# 62. RoCE

RoCE:

**RDMA over Converged Ethernet**

Provides RDMA capabilities over Ethernet networks.

Potential advantage:

```text
Ethernet ecosystem
```

But requires careful network engineering.

---

# 63. RoCE Is Not "Normal Ethernet"

For good RDMA performance, network design may require attention to:

```text
loss

congestion

buffering

ECN

PFC

routing
```

Misconfigured networks can destroy distributed training performance.

---

# 64. Network Bandwidth

Suppose each GPU generates:

```text
large gradient tensors
```

that need synchronization every training step.

If network bandwidth cannot keep up:

```text
communication time
>
compute time
```

scaling stops being effective.

---

# 65. Network Latency

Some collective operations require frequent synchronization.

Even small per-operation latency can accumulate across:

```text
thousands of communication operations
```

Low latency matters in addition to raw bandwidth.

---

# 66. Oversubscription

Imagine:

```text
100 GPU nodes
```

share insufficient uplink bandwidth.

The theoretical NIC rate might be high.

But aggregate fabric cannot support all nodes simultaneously.

This is network oversubscription.

---

# 67. Non-Blocking Fabric

Ideal AI fabric may attempt to provide:

```text
high bisection bandwidth
```

so many nodes can communicate simultaneously without severe contention.

This becomes expensive at large scale.

---

# 68. Fat-Tree / Clos Concepts

Large data-center fabrics often use multi-stage topologies.

Conceptually:

```text
        Spine
       /     \
      /       \
   Leaf       Leaf
   /  \       /  \
Node Node   Node Node
```

High-performance GPU clusters often require careful network topology design.

---

# 69. Network Topology Influences Scheduling

Job requiring:

```text
256 GPUs
```

should ideally be placed on nodes with:

```text
high-quality network locality
```

rather than randomly across the data center.

This is topology-aware scheduling at cluster scale.

---

# 70. NCCL

NCCL:

**NVIDIA Collective Communications Library**

It provides communication primitives optimized for NVIDIA GPUs.

Common operations:

```text
AllReduce

AllGather

ReduceScatter

Broadcast
```

---

# 71. Collective Communication

Distributed training often needs groups of workers to communicate collectively.

Instead of:

```text
Worker A sends independently
to every worker
```

optimized collective algorithms coordinate communication efficiently.

---

# 72. AllReduce

Imagine gradients:

```text
GPU 1 -> G1
GPU 2 -> G2
GPU 3 -> G3
GPU 4 -> G4
```

AllReduce computes:

```text
G = G1 + G2 + G3 + G4
```

and makes the result available to all participating GPUs.

Critical for data-parallel training.

---

# 73. Why AllReduce Is Expensive

Suppose model has:

```text
billions of parameters
```

Each step generates huge gradients.

Every step may require large-scale synchronization.

The network can become a major portion of training time.

---

# 74. Ring AllReduce Mental Model

Simplified ring:

```text
GPU1 -> GPU2 -> GPU3 -> GPU4
 ^                       |
 |_______________________|
```

Data is divided and circulated.

This can use bandwidth efficiently.

Actual NCCL algorithms may vary based on topology and workload.

---

# 75. Tree-Based Collectives

Another pattern uses tree communication.

```text
        GPU1
       /    \
    GPU2    GPU3
             |
            GPU4
```

Different algorithms trade:

```text
latency

bandwidth utilization
```

Libraries may choose algorithms dynamically.

---

# 76. NCCL Topology Discovery

NCCL tries to understand:

```text
NVLink

PCIe

NIC

GPU relationships
```

to construct efficient communication paths.

Bad hardware topology can still limit performance.

---

# 77. NCCL Failure

Distributed job may hang because:

```text
one worker dies

one NIC loses connectivity

collective call waits
```

Troubleshooting distributed communication is significantly harder than debugging single-GPU workloads.

---

# 78. Distributed Training Mental Model

Suppose model training takes:

```text
100 days
```

on one GPU.

If perfectly parallelizable:

```text
100 GPUs
```

might theoretically make it:

```text
1 day
```

But scaling is never perfectly linear.

---

# 79. Scaling Efficiency

Suppose:

```text
1 GPU = 100 samples/sec

8 GPUs = 700 samples/sec
```

Scaling efficiency:

```text
700
------
8 × 100

= 87.5%
```

Some capacity is lost to overhead.

---

# 80. Why Scaling Efficiency Falls

Reasons:

```text
communication

synchronization

stragglers

data loading

network contention

framework overhead
```

At large scale, communication can dominate.

---

# 81. Strong Scaling

Strong scaling asks:

> If total problem size stays constant and we add more GPUs, how much faster does it complete?

Example:

```text
same dataset

8 GPUs -> 10 hours

64 GPUs -> ?
```

Eventually scaling gains diminish.

---

# 82. Weak Scaling

Weak scaling asks:

> If we increase workload proportionally with resources, can throughput remain efficient?

Example:

```text
1 GPU
batch = 32

8 GPUs
batch = 256
```

Useful when training can tolerate larger global batches.

---

# 83. Global Batch Size

With data parallelism:

```text
8 GPUs
×
batch 32 each
=
global batch 256
```

Increasing GPU count often increases global batch size.

But model convergence may change.

---

# 84. Distributed Systems Can Change ML Behavior

Infrastructure decision:

```text
increase from 64 GPUs to 1024 GPUs
```

may require changing:

```text
batch size

learning rate

optimizer

training schedule
```

Therefore infrastructure scaling and ML science are connected.

---

# 85. Data Parallelism

Each GPU holds:

```text
full model
```

but processes different training samples.

```text
GPU 1
Model
Batch A

GPU 2
Model
Batch B

GPU 3
Model
Batch C
```

Then gradients are synchronized.

---

# 86. Data Parallel Training

Flow:

```text
Copy Model to Every GPU
          |
          v
Different Mini-Batches
          |
          v
Forward / Backward
          |
          v
Gradient Synchronization
          |
          v
Update Model
```

This is one of the most common distributed-training patterns.

---

# 87. Data Parallel Limitation

Every GPU must store:

```text
entire model
```

If model does not fit on one GPU:

```text
basic data parallelism cannot solve it
```

Need model-parallel techniques or state sharding.

---

# 88. Distributed Data Parallel

Frameworks such as PyTorch provide distributed data parallel mechanisms.

Each process commonly manages one GPU.

Gradients synchronize between processes.

Architecture:

```text
Process 0 -> GPU 0

Process 1 -> GPU 1

Process 2 -> GPU 2
```

---

# 89. Model Parallelism

Instead of putting full model on each GPU:

```text
Model
 |
 +---- Part A -> GPU 1
 |
 +---- Part B -> GPU 2
```

This allows models larger than a single GPU.

There are multiple forms.

---

# 90. Tensor Parallelism

Individual tensor operations are split across GPUs.

Example:

```text
Large Matrix
    |
 +--+--+
 |     |
 v     v
GPU1  GPU2
```

Both GPUs cooperate on the same layer.

---

# 91. Tensor Parallel Communication

Because GPUs jointly execute the same layers, they communicate frequently.

Therefore tensor parallelism benefits strongly from:

```text
NVLink

NVSwitch

fast local interconnect
```

It is usually preferable to keep tensor-parallel groups close together.

---

# 92. Tensor Parallel Placement

Bad:

```text
GPU 1
Region A

GPU 2
Region B
```

Impossible from practical latency perspective.

Even separate distant nodes may be inefficient.

Tensor-parallel ranks need excellent network locality.

---

# 93. Pipeline Parallelism

Split layers into stages.

```text
Layers 1-10
GPU 1

Layers 11-20
GPU 2

Layers 21-30
GPU 3
```

Data flows through stages.

---

# 94. Pipeline Bubble

If only one microbatch:

```text
GPU1 working

GPU2 waiting

GPU3 waiting
```

Then:

```text
GPU1 idle

GPU2 working

GPU3 waiting
```

Poor utilization.

Use multiple microbatches to pipeline execution.

---

# 95. Pipeline Microbatching

Concept:

```text
Time ->

GPU1: A B C D
GPU2:   A B C D
GPU3:     A B C D
```

This reduces idle periods.

Still, pipeline imbalance creates inefficiency.

---

# 96. Pipeline Stage Balance

If:

```text
Stage 1 = 50 ms

Stage 2 = 500 ms

Stage 3 = 60 ms
```

Stage 2 becomes bottleneck.

Stages should ideally have roughly balanced computational load.

---

# 97. Expert Parallelism

Mixture-of-Experts models contain many expert subnetworks.

Only some experts may activate for each token.

Experts can be distributed across GPUs.

```text
Token
 |
 v
Router
 |
 +---- Expert 1
 +---- Expert 7
```

This creates communication-heavy routing patterns.

---

# 98. MoE Communication

Tokens may need to move to GPUs hosting selected experts.

This often involves:

```text
All-to-All communication
```

Network design becomes particularly important.

---

# 99. Sequence Parallelism

Some transformer computations can be distributed across sequence dimensions.

This can reduce memory duplication in certain architectures.

Senior architects should understand that modern large-model training combines several parallelism dimensions.

---

# 100. Hybrid Parallelism

Large training job may combine:

```text
Data Parallelism

×

Tensor Parallelism

×

Pipeline Parallelism

×

Expert Parallelism
```

Example:

```text
2048 GPUs

Data parallel = 32
Tensor parallel = 8
Pipeline parallel = 8

32 × 8 × 8
=
2048 GPUs
```

---

# 101. Parallelism Topology Mapping

You should not randomly assign ranks.

Example:

```text
Tensor-parallel ranks
-> same NVSwitch domain

Pipeline stages
-> nearby nodes

Data-parallel replicas
-> can span broader fabric
```

Mapping logical parallelism to physical topology is a major optimization.

---

# 102. Device Mesh

Modern distributed frameworks may represent devices as a multi-dimensional mesh.

Example:

```text
DP × TP

4 × 8
```

Each dimension corresponds to a communication strategy.

This abstraction helps coordinate complex parallelism.

---

# 103. ZeRO

ZeRO reduces memory redundancy in distributed training.

Instead of every GPU storing every state, states are partitioned.

Conceptually:

```text
Optimizer States
Gradients
Parameters
```

can be sharded across workers depending on configuration.

---

# 104. ZeRO Stage Mental Model

Simplified:

```text
Stage 1
shard optimizer state

Stage 2
shard optimizer + gradients

Stage 3
shard optimizer + gradients + parameters
```

Higher sharding reduces memory duplication but increases communication complexity.

---

# 105. FSDP

Fully Sharded Data Parallel distributes model state across workers.

Conceptually:

```text
GPU 1
owns shard A

GPU 2
owns shard B

GPU 3
owns shard C
```

Relevant parameter shards are gathered when needed.

This allows much larger models to train.

---

# 106. Sharding Trade-Off

More sharding:

```text
less memory per GPU
```

but often:

```text
more communication

more complexity
```

Again:

```text
memory
vs
network
```

is a fundamental distributed-training trade-off.

---

# 107. Activation Checkpointing

Also called gradient checkpointing in many contexts.

Instead of storing every activation:

```text
discard some activations
```

and recompute them during backward pass.

Trade:

```text
less memory

more computation
```

---

# 108. Activation Checkpointing Trade-Off

Without checkpointing:

```text
memory high

compute lower
```

With checkpointing:

```text
memory lower

compute higher
```

Useful when GPU memory is the limiting resource.

---

# 109. CPU Offload

Some states can move to:

```text
CPU RAM
```

to reduce GPU-memory pressure.

But transfers through PCIe can slow training.

Useful when:

```text
capacity is more important than maximum throughput
```

---

# 110. NVMe Offload

Extreme memory-saving approaches may offload to:

```text
local SSD / NVMe
```

Capacity increases dramatically.

Performance can decrease substantially.

This demonstrates hierarchy:

```text
GPU HBM
fastest / smallest

CPU RAM
slower / larger

NVMe
slower / much larger
```

---

# 111. Memory Hierarchy

Keep this picture:

```text
Registers / Cache
       |
       v
GPU HBM
       |
       v
CPU RAM
       |
       v
Local NVMe
       |
       v
Network Storage
```

Moving farther down hierarchy generally increases:

```text
latency
```

and reduces effective bandwidth.

---

# 112. Training Throughput

Common measure:

```text
samples / second
```

or for language models:

```text
tokens / second
```

Total training performance depends on:

```text
compute

communication

data input

software efficiency
```

---

# 113. Model FLOPs Utilization

Large-model teams may measure how effectively actual training uses theoretical accelerator FLOPS.

Low utilization may indicate:

```text
communication bottleneck

small kernels

pipeline bubbles

memory bottleneck

input starvation
```

Theoretical GPU performance alone means very little.

---

# 114. Straggler

One worker is slower:

```text
GPU 1 = 100 ms

GPU 2 = 100 ms

GPU 3 = 100 ms

GPU 4 = 160 ms
```

Synchronous training step waits for:

```text
GPU 4
```

Entire system proceeds at straggler speed.

---

# 115. Straggler Causes

Possible causes:

```text
bad GPU

thermal throttling

network congestion

CPU contention

storage slowdown

NUMA placement

background workload

hardware errors
```

Stragglers become serious at fleet scale.

---

# 116. Synchronous Training

Workers synchronize regularly.

Benefit:

```text
simpler model consistency
```

Problem:

```text
slowest worker affects everyone
```

Most large modern training remains highly synchronization-sensitive.

---

# 117. Asynchronous Training

Workers may update independently.

Potential benefits:

```text
less waiting
```

Challenges:

```text
stale gradients

different convergence behavior

complexity
```

Infrastructure and algorithm design are intertwined.

---

# 118. Distributed Job Launch

To launch 512 GPUs, system must coordinate:

```text
nodes

processes

rank IDs

environment

network addresses

framework configuration
```

Orchestrators handle this complexity.

---

# 119. Rank

In distributed training each process often has a rank.

Example:

```text
rank 0
rank 1
rank 2
...
rank 511
```

Rank identifies participants in the distributed group.

---

# 120. Local Rank

A machine with:

```text
8 GPUs
```

may run:

```text
local_rank 0 -> GPU 0
...
local_rank 7 -> GPU 7
```

Global rank identifies worker across entire job.

---

# 121. World Size

World size:

```text
number of participating processes
```

Example:

```text
64 nodes

× 8 GPUs

=
512 processes
```

World size:

```text
512
```

if using one process per GPU.

---

# 122. Rendezvous

Workers need a mechanism to discover one another and establish the distributed group.

This initialization process is often called:

```text
rendezvous
```

Failures during rendezvous can prevent the job from starting.

---

# 123. Gang Scheduling

Distributed job requests:

```text
64 GPUs
```

Starting only:

```text
40 GPUs
```

may be useless.

Gang scheduling means:

> Schedule the required group of resources together.

Either:

```text
all required workers start
```

or:

```text
job waits
```

---

# 124. Why Kubernetes Default Scheduling Can Be Insufficient

Kubernetes schedules pods individually.

A 64-pod GPU job can end up:

```text
40 pods running

24 pods pending
```

The running GPUs may sit idle.

Specialized batch scheduling or gang scheduling helps.

---

# 125. Queueing for Distributed Training

Instead:

```text
Job A
needs 64 GPUs

Job B
needs 8 GPUs
```

Scheduler considers:

```text
priority

fairness

resource fit

topology

queue time
```

before admitting jobs.

---

# 126. Head-of-Line Blocking

Queue:

```text
Job A requires 512 GPUs

Job B requires 8 GPUs

Job C requires 4 GPUs
```

Only:

```text
100 GPUs available
```

If Job A blocks everything behind it:

```text
B and C wait unnecessarily
```

Scheduler needs intelligent queue policies.

---

# 127. Backfilling

While waiting for enough resources for a large job, scheduler may run smaller jobs that can complete before the reservation.

This is common HPC scheduling logic.

Goal:

```text
improve utilization
```

without starving large jobs.

---

# 128. Fair-Share Scheduling

Teams receive weighted access.

Example:

```text
Research = 30%

Search = 40%

Ads = 30%
```

Unused capacity can often be borrowed.

Long-term scheduling tries to preserve fair entitlement.

---

# 129. Priority Scheduling

Critical workload:

```text
P0 model serving
```

should not wait behind:

```text
experimental training
```

Priority classes must reflect business criticality.

---

# 130. Preemption

Scheduler may terminate lower-priority workload.

```text
Low-Priority Job
     |
     X
     |
GPU released
     |
     v
Critical Job
```

Training must checkpoint to tolerate this.

---

# 131. GPU Reservation

Some capacity may be reserved for:

```text
production inference
```

even if idle.

This appears inefficient.

But reservation provides reliability.

---

# 132. Utilization vs Reliability

Fleet utilization:

```text
99%
```

sounds excellent.

But no capacity remains for:

```text
failures

traffic spikes

critical jobs
```

Maximum utilization is not automatically optimal.

---

# 133. GPU Fragmentation at Fleet Scale

Suppose:

```text
100 GPUs free
```

but spread across:

```text
100 separate nodes
```

Job requires:

```text
8 GPUs/node
×
8 nodes
```

It still may not fit.

Capacity planning must consider:

```text
shape
```

not just total GPU count.

---

# 134. Resource Shape

Examples:

```text
1 GPU

8 GPUs same node

64 GPUs contiguous fabric

512 GPUs high-bandwidth island
```

These are very different resources.

A scheduler needs topology-aware resource accounting.

---

# 135. Accelerator Island

Large clusters may group GPUs into tightly connected domains.

Example:

```text
High-Speed Fabric Island
  |
  +---- 128 GPUs
```

Large jobs should preferably fit inside one high-bandwidth domain.

Cross-island traffic may be slower.

---

# 136. Placement Fragmentation

Many small jobs can consume scattered GPUs and prevent a large distributed job from obtaining contiguous resources.

Potential strategies:

```text
bin packing

reservations

defragmentation

job draining

queue planning
```

---

# 137. Defragmentation

Scheduler may move or wait for small jobs to finish so contiguous resources become available.

For stateful GPU workloads, migration is difficult.

Training checkpoint/resume makes this more feasible.

---

# 138. MIG

MIG:

**Multi-Instance GPU**

Certain NVIDIA GPUs can be partitioned into hardware-isolated GPU instances.

Conceptually:

```text
Physical GPU
 |
 +---- MIG Instance A
 |
 +---- MIG Instance B
 |
 +---- MIG Instance C
```

---

# 139. Why MIG Exists

A large GPU may be wasteful for tiny inference models.

MIG lets multiple workloads share one accelerator with stronger isolation than simple software sharing.

Potential benefits:

```text
higher utilization

predictable resource partitioning

tenant isolation
```

---

# 140. MIG Trade-Off

Partitioning reduces flexibility.

Suppose GPU is divided:

```text
small
small
small
```

then large workload arrives.

You may need:

```text
reconfigure GPU
```

which can disrupt workloads.

---

# 141. MIG Fragmentation

Even if total memory appears available across slices:

```text
10 GB
+
10 GB
+
10 GB
```

a workload needing:

```text
20 GB
```

cannot necessarily combine those instances.

Resource shape matters again.

---

# 142. Time Slicing

Another sharing strategy:

```text
Workload A

Workload B

Workload C
```

take turns using one GPU.

Unlike MIG, they may share the same physical GPU more dynamically.

---

# 143. Time-Slicing Trade-Off

Benefits:

```text
higher apparent utilization

simple sharing
```

Risks:

```text
performance interference

less predictable latency

memory contention
```

Often more appropriate for:

```text
development

experimentation
```

than strict latency-sensitive production.

---

# 144. GPU Sharing Decision

Ask:

```text
Is workload latency-sensitive?

How much GPU memory?

How bursty?

Security requirements?

Performance isolation requirements?
```

Then choose:

```text
dedicated GPU

MIG

time slicing

shared inference runtime
```

---

# 145. Shared Inference Runtime

Instead of giving every model its own GPU:

```text
Model A -> GPU

Model B -> GPU

Model C -> GPU
```

runtime may colocate models.

```text
GPU
 |
 +---- Model A
 +---- Model B
 +---- Model C
```

This improves utilization for small models.

---

# 146. Model Colocation Risks

Potential problems:

```text
memory contention

latency interference

one model OOM affects others

unpredictable batching
```

Colocation requires careful capacity management.

---

# 147. GPU OOM

Out-of-memory can occur because:

```text
model too large

batch too large

sequence too long

memory leak

fragmentation

concurrency spike

KV cache full
```

Response depends on workload.

---

# 148. OOM During Training

Possible mitigations:

```text
smaller batch

gradient accumulation

activation checkpointing

FSDP

ZeRO

lower precision

CPU offload
```

Do not simply add GPUs without understanding memory behavior.

---

# 149. Gradient Accumulation

Instead of global batch 256 at once:

```text
process batch 32

accumulate gradients

repeat 8 times

update
```

This reduces per-step memory requirement.

Trade:

```text
more execution steps
```

---

# 150. OOM During LLM Serving

Potential mitigations:

```text
reduce max context

reduce concurrency

reduce max output

quantize model

smaller KV cache per request

admission control
```

This is serving reliability, not merely hardware failure.

---

# 151. GPU Health

GPUs can experience:

```text
ECC errors

thermal issues

driver faults

memory errors

NVLink failures

Xid errors

hardware degradation
```

Fleet management needs accelerator health monitoring.

---

# 152. ECC

ECC memory detects/corrects certain memory errors.

Persistent or increasing ECC issues may indicate degraded hardware.

The platform may:

```text
cordon node

drain workloads

replace hardware
```

---

# 153. GPU Xid Errors

NVIDIA driver reports certain GPU errors through Xid codes.

Some indicate:

```text
application issues
```

others may indicate:

```text
driver

hardware

PCIe
```

problems.

Fleet automation can classify and remediate known failure patterns.

---

# 154. DCGM

NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager provides GPU telemetry and management capabilities.

Useful metrics may include:

```text
GPU utilization

memory usage

temperature

power

ECC

NVLink
```

Platform observability should integrate accelerator-level metrics.

---

# 155. GPU Temperature

High temperature may cause:

```text
thermal throttling
```

GPU clock reduces.

Training slows.

One hot GPU can become:

```text
distributed straggler
```

affecting hundreds of other GPUs.

---

# 156. Power Limits

Modern GPU clusters consume enormous power.

Power architecture can limit:

```text
how many GPUs

where they are installed

maximum clock
```

Data-center power becomes part of ML capacity planning.

---

# 157. Cooling

Large accelerator systems generate substantial heat.

Cooling constraints influence:

```text
rack density

GPU placement

capacity expansion
```

At hyperscale, MLOps architecture eventually touches physical data-center infrastructure.

---

# 158. GPU Node Failure

During training:

```text
Node 37
   X
```

Potential outcomes:

```text
entire job fails

elastic recovery

restore checkpoint
```

depending on framework.

---

# 159. Checkpoint Strategy for Large Training

If training consumes:

```text
1024 GPUs
```

every hour may represent enormous cost.

Checkpoint frequency should consider:

```text
failure probability

checkpoint time

storage bandwidth

lost compute
```

---

# 160. Distributed Checkpoint

Checkpoint may itself be sharded.

```text
GPU 1 -> shard 1

GPU 2 -> shard 2

...

GPU 1024 -> shard 1024
```

Restoration needs coordinated metadata.

---

# 161. Checkpoint Bottleneck

If 1024 GPUs simultaneously write:

```text
10 GB each
```

checkpoint size:

```text
10 TB
```

Storage must absorb huge burst bandwidth.

Checkpoint architecture is a storage architecture problem.

---

# 162. Asynchronous Checkpointing

Possible approach:

```text
GPU state
  |
  v
local memory / local storage
  |
  v
background upload
  |
  v
durable storage
```

This can reduce training pauses.

But failure semantics become more complex.

---

# 163. Checkpoint Consistency

All shards should represent:

```text
same training step
```

Partial checkpoint can be unusable.

Need:

```text
manifest

completion marker

atomic publication semantics
```

---

# 164. Training Job Restart

After failure:

```text
allocate equivalent topology

download checkpoint

restore optimizer

restore RNG state

restore scheduler

resume
```

Full reproducibility may require more than weights.

---

# 165. Elastic Job Recovery

Elastic systems can potentially replace failed workers.

But changing:

```text
world size
```

mid-training may affect:

```text
batch size

optimizer behavior

data partitioning
```

Architects must coordinate with ML framework behavior.

---

# 166. GPU Fleet Observability

Monitor at multiple layers.

### Hardware

```text
temperature

power

ECC

GPU health
```

### Runtime

```text
memory

utilization

kernel activity
```

### Communication

```text
NVLink bandwidth

network throughput

NCCL latency
```

### Workload

```text
tokens/sec

samples/sec

step time
```

---

# 167. Step-Time Monitoring

Training step:

```text
Step 1 = 2.1 sec
Step 2 = 2.0 sec
Step 3 = 2.2 sec
...
Step 5000 = 4.8 sec
```

Something degraded.

Possible:

```text
network congestion

straggler GPU

storage slowdown
```

Application-level performance metrics reveal problems hardware metrics may miss.

---

# 168. Communication-to-Compute Ratio

Measure:

```text
compute time

vs

communication time
```

Example:

```text
compute = 300 ms

AllReduce = 500 ms
```

Adding faster GPUs may not help.

Need network or parallelism optimization.

---

# 169. Network Telemetry

Monitor:

```text
bandwidth

packet loss

retransmission

ECN

RDMA errors

congestion
```

Training failures often originate outside CUDA.

---

# 170. Storage Telemetry

Monitor:

```text
read throughput

write throughput

latency

request errors

metadata latency
```

Large training workloads may overload shared storage.

---

# 171. Storage Noisy Neighbor

Team A launches:

```text
1000 training workers
```

all reading one dataset.

Storage bandwidth saturates.

Team B's jobs slow down.

Multi-tenancy includes storage fairness.

---

# 172. Network Noisy Neighbor

One distributed training job performs enormous:

```text
All-to-All
```

traffic.

Other jobs sharing fabric see increased latency.

Cluster scheduling may need network-aware isolation.

---

# 173. Fabric Partitioning

Large accelerator clusters may isolate traffic using:

```text
separate fabrics

QoS

routing domains

job placement
```

to reduce interference.

---

# 174. Job Topology Reservation

For a 1024-GPU training run, scheduler may reserve:

```text
specific racks

specific network blocks

specific switches
```

not merely 1024 random accelerators.

---

# 175. GPU Cluster Architecture

Conceptually:

```text
                  TRAINING CONTROL
                         |
                         v
                    SCHEDULER
                         |
          +--------------+--------------+
          |              |              |
          v              v              v
       GPU RACK       GPU RACK       GPU RACK
          |              |              |
      GPU Nodes       GPU Nodes       GPU Nodes
          |              |              |
          +------- High-Speed Fabric ---+
                         |
                         v
                      STORAGE
```

---

# 176. Separate Management Network

Production accelerator clusters may separate:

```text
management traffic

storage traffic

training communication
```

because training fabric needs predictable performance.

---

# 177. Control Network vs Data Network

Control:

```text
SSH

Kubernetes API

monitoring
```

Data:

```text
NCCL

RDMA

dataset transfer
```

These may have radically different bandwidth and reliability requirements.

---

# 178. GPU Cluster Provisioning

Node provisioning involves:

```text
OS

GPU driver

NIC driver

CUDA compatibility

container runtime

GPU runtime

monitoring

RDMA configuration
```

Configuration drift across nodes can cause subtle failures.

---

# 179. Immutable GPU Node Images

Instead of manually modifying nodes:

```text
SSH

install package

change driver
```

use versioned machine images.

```text
gpu-node-image-v17
```

Benefits:

```text
reproducibility

rollback

fleet consistency
```

---

# 180. Driver Upgrade

Changing GPU driver across 2000 nodes is high risk.

Use:

```text
canary nodes

test workload

small pool rollout

progressive deployment
```

Do not upgrade the entire accelerator fleet simultaneously.

---

# 181. CUDA Compatibility Matrix

Platform may support:

```text
Runtime A
Driver X
CUDA Y
Framework Z
```

Users should know supported combinations.

This becomes a platform contract.

---

# 182. Kubernetes Device Plugin

Kubernetes typically requires mechanisms to expose GPUs as schedulable resources.

Conceptually:

```text
Node
 |
 v
GPU Discovery
 |
 v
Kubernetes
 |
 v
nvidia.com/gpu = 8
```

Then pods request accelerators.

---

# 183. GPU Resource Request

Example:

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```

This reserves GPU resources.

But basic resource counting does not understand all advanced topology requirements.

---

# 184. GPU Operator

GPU infrastructure may be managed through operator-style automation.

Capabilities can include deployment of:

```text
drivers

device plugins

telemetry

runtime configuration
```

Centralizing this reduces manual node configuration.

---

# 185. Node Labels

Example:

```text
gpu-type=H100

gpu-memory=80GB

fabric=rdma

zone=a
```

Scheduler uses labels to place workloads.

But hand-maintained labels become dangerous.

Automate hardware discovery.

---

# 186. Taints and Tolerations

GPU nodes may be reserved for workloads that explicitly request GPU capabilities.

This prevents:

```text
random CPU-only pods
```

from consuming expensive accelerator nodes.

---

# 187. GPU Node Pools

Examples:

```text
L4 inference pool

H100 training pool

H200 large-memory pool
```

Each pool may have different:

```text
autoscaling

priority

cost

tenancy
```

---

# 188. Cluster Autoscaler and GPUs

GPU node autoscaling is difficult because:

```text
nodes expensive

startup slow

cloud quota limited

capacity may be unavailable
```

Autoscaler cannot guarantee accelerator supply.

---

# 189. Provisioning Delay

A GPU node may take:

```text
minutes
```

to become ready.

Then workload may need:

```text
container pull

dataset mount

model download
```

Effective startup can be much longer.

---

# 190. Warm GPU Nodes

Maintain:

```text
ready but unused nodes
```

for critical workloads.

Cost increases.

Queue latency decreases.

This is an explicit SLO trade-off.

---

# 191. Capacity Reservations

For business-critical GPU workloads, reserve capacity from the infrastructure provider when possible.

Otherwise:

```text
autoscaler requests GPU
```

may return:

```text
insufficient capacity
```

during regional scarcity.

---

# 192. Multi-Region GPU Capacity

Architecture:

```text
Region A
H100

Region B
H100

Region C
L4 only
```

Not every region has equivalent hardware.

Failover design must understand capability differences.

---

# 193. Hardware Fallback

Primary model requires:

```text
H100
```

Fallback hardware might run:

```text
quantized model
```

on:

```text
L4
```

or CPU.

This requires pretested alternative artifacts/configurations.

---

# 194. GPU Cost

A training job cost can be approximated:

```text
GPU count
×
runtime
×
GPU-hour price
```

But total cost also includes:

```text
CPU

storage

network

idle queue allocation

checkpointing
```

---

# 195. Cost per Training Run

Track:

```text
experiment = exp-712

GPU-hours = 8,430

storage = ...

network = ...

total = ...
```

This allows teams to compare model improvements against cost.

---

# 196. Cost per Token

LLM serving may track:

```text
GPU cost
-----------
tokens generated
```

or:

```text
cost per million tokens
```

This is more meaningful than cost per request when request sizes vary dramatically.

---

# 197. GPU Efficiency

Possible efficiency metric:

```text
useful training time
--------------------
allocated GPU time
```

If GPUs are allocated but waiting for:

```text
data

other workers

checkpointing

queue setup
```

you are paying for idle accelerators.

---

# 198. Queue Efficiency

A job waiting in queue consumes no GPU cost but increases:

```text
developer latency
```

Platform optimizes both:

```text
resource utilization

user wait time
```

---

# 199. Scheduling Trade-Off

Maximum utilization:

```text
pack everything tightly
```

may cause:

```text
long queue times for large jobs
```

Maximum responsiveness:

```text
reserve lots of capacity
```

causes:

```text
idle expensive GPUs
```

Architecture balances both.

---

# 200. Capacity Forecasting

Forecast:

```text
training demand

inference demand

GPU generation

model growth

team growth
```

GPU supply often has long procurement or reservation lead times.

Capacity planning cannot be purely reactive.

---

# 201. Training Demand Is Burstier Than CPU Demand

A research team may suddenly request:

```text
512 GPUs
for 14 days
```

Traditional autoscaling models may not handle this predictably.

Large GPU platforms benefit from:

```text
reservations

quotas

planning

scheduling windows
```

---

# 202. Failure Probability at Scale

Suppose one node has a very low daily failure probability.

With:

```text
1000 nodes
```

some node failure becomes likely.

Therefore:

> Large training jobs should expect hardware faults.

Reliability architecture must assume failures.

---

# 203. Hardware Burn-In

New accelerators may undergo stress testing before entering production.

Purpose:

```text
detect early hardware defects
```

before expensive distributed jobs rely on them.

---

# 204. Node Health Score

Platform can combine:

```text
ECC history

temperature

Xid events

network errors

performance tests
```

into a health assessment.

Suspect nodes can be excluded from critical jobs.

---

# 205. Quarantine

If node repeatedly causes:

```text
NCCL failures
```

do not repeatedly reschedule jobs onto it.

```text
cordon

quarantine

diagnose
```

Automatic health remediation reduces recurring incidents.

---

# 206. Performance Qualification

Healthy does not only mean:

```text
GPU responds
```

A GPU may perform:

```text
30% slower
```

than peers.

Fleet qualification should benchmark:

```text
compute

memory

NVLink

network
```

---

# 207. Slow GPU as Hidden Failure

One degraded accelerator inside:

```text
1024-GPU synchronous job
```

can lower performance of all 1024.

Therefore performance degradation is a reliability problem.

---

# 208. Distributed Training Incident

Symptoms:

```text
training step time increased 2×

GPU utilization lower

no application errors
```

Investigation:

```text
Which rank is slow?

Which node?

GPU clock?

ECC?

network path?

storage?

NCCL?
```

---

# 209. Troubleshooting Hierarchy

Start with:

```text
Application
   |
   v
Framework
   |
   v
CUDA / NCCL
   |
   v
GPU
   |
   v
PCIe / NVLink
   |
   v
NIC / Fabric
   |
   v
Storage
```

Distributed ML incidents require cross-layer diagnosis.

---

# 210. NCCL Timeout Incident

Potential causes:

```text
dead process

packet loss

NIC issue

GPU failure

network congestion

incorrect routing

rank misconfiguration
```

The timeout is a symptom, not necessarily the root cause.

---

# 211. GPU OOM Incident

Ask:

```text
Did model change?

Batch size?

Sequence length?

Precision?

Concurrency?

Framework allocator?

Memory leak?

Traffic distribution?
```

Do not immediately blame GPU capacity.

---

# 212. Low GPU Utilization Incident

Possible causes:

```text
slow data loader

CPU bottleneck

storage bottleneck

small batch

synchronization wait

communication overhead

too-small workload
```

Hardware replacement may accomplish nothing.

---

# 213. High GPU Utilization + Low Throughput

Possible:

```text
inefficient kernels

memory-bound workload

bad precision

thermal throttling

excessive recomputation
```

"GPU busy" does not equal "GPU efficient."

---

# 214. Distributed Training SLO

For platform:

```text
95% of 64-GPU jobs
start within 15 min
```

Possible reliability SLO:

```text
99% of infrastructure-caused job failures
recover from checkpoint
```

Platform SLOs should capture user outcomes.

---

# 215. GPU Platform SLOs

Examples:

```text
GPU provisioning success

queue latency

node health

job completion

serving availability

checkpoint durability
```

Do not use only:

```text
cluster uptime
```

---

# 216. Architect Scenario — 1,000-GPU Training Cluster

Requirements:

```text
1000 H-class GPUs

large transformer training

jobs from 8 to 512 GPUs

multi-tenant

high utilization
```

Discuss:

```text
rack topology

NVLink domains

high-speed fabric

RDMA

scheduler

gang scheduling

fair share

checkpointing

storage bandwidth

hardware health

capacity reservations
```

---

# 217. High-Level Training Cluster

```text
                        USERS
                          |
                          v
                     JOB API
                          |
                          v
                       QUEUE
                          |
                          v
                  GLOBAL SCHEDULER
                          |
          +---------------+---------------+
          |               |               |
          v               v               v
       GPU POD         GPU POD         GPU POD
          |               |               |
      NVSwitch         NVSwitch         NVSwitch
          |               |               |
          +------- RDMA / IB FABRIC ------+
                          |
                          v
                 HIGH-PERFORMANCE STORAGE
```

Supporting:

```text
checkpoint store

artifact registry

metrics

logs

metadata
```

---

# 218. Architect Scenario — 10,000-GPU Fleet

At this scale you need:

```text
multiple clusters

multiple fabrics

fleet management

global scheduler

capacity planning

failure-domain isolation
```

Architecture:

```text
               Global ML Scheduler
                  /     |     \
                 v      v      v
            Cluster A Cluster B Cluster C
```

Placement considers:

```text
GPU type

job size

fabric locality

data location

priority

tenant quota
```

---

# 219. Architect Scenario — LLM Training

Model:

```text
hundreds of billions of parameters
```

Requirements may exceed:

```text
single GPU

single server

single rack
```

Need hybrid parallelism:

```text
TP

PP

DP

possibly EP
```

The architecture discussion should connect:

```text
logical parallelism
```

to:

```text
physical network topology
```

---

# 220. Architect Scenario — LLM Serving

Serving requirements:

```text
low TTFT

high tokens/sec

large model

variable context

high concurrency
```

Architecture:

```text
Gateway
   |
   v
Admission Control
   |
   v
Model Router
   |
   v
GPU Runtime
   |
   +---- tensor-parallel group
   |
   +---- KV cache
```

---

# 221. Serving Tensor Parallelism

Large model may run on:

```text
4 GPUs
```

as one replica.

Then:

```text
4 GPUs = one serving unit
```

Capacity planning must count:

```text
replicas
```

not simply GPUs.

---

# 222. Replica Arithmetic

Suppose model requires:

```text
4 GPUs / replica
```

Cluster:

```text
64 GPUs
```

Theoretical max:

```text
16 replicas
```

But reserve capacity and topology fragmentation may reduce usable replicas.

---

# 223. Serving Topology

Prefer all four GPUs of one tensor-parallel replica within a high-speed interconnect domain.

Bad placement across slow fabric increases:

```text
token latency
```

because communication occurs every layer.

---

# 224. LLM Prefill

Prefill processes input tokens.

Large prompts cause:

```text
heavy compute
```

and create KV-cache state.

Prefill may be highly compute intensive.

---

# 225. LLM Decode

Decode generates tokens sequentially.

Each step is relatively small but repeated many times.

Performance often depends heavily on:

```text
memory bandwidth

KV-cache access
```

---

# 226. Prefill vs Decode Resource Behavior

Prefill:

```text
more compute-heavy
```

Decode:

```text
often more memory-bandwidth-sensitive
```

This creates opportunities for specialized scheduling and serving architecture.

---

# 227. Disaggregated Prefill / Decode

Advanced LLM platforms may separate:

```text
Prefill Workers

Decode Workers
```

Potential advantage:

```text
optimize hardware independently
```

But adds:

```text
KV-cache transfer

network complexity

routing complexity
```

---

# 228. KV Cache Transfer

If prefill and decode run on different workers:

```text
KV cache
```

must move between them.

This can be huge.

Network bandwidth and transfer latency become critical.

---

# 229. Continuous Batching

LLM runtime can continuously add new requests to active batches.

```text
Request A
Request B
Request C
```

finish at different times.

Continuous batching improves accelerator utilization.

---

# 230. Static Batching Problem

Traditional fixed batch:

```text
A = 10 tokens

B = 1000 tokens
```

A may effectively wait for B depending on execution strategy.

LLM runtimes need dynamic scheduling.

---

# 231. KV Cache Pressure

Concurrent requests consume KV cache.

Capacity is constrained by:

```text
model architecture

context length

number of sequences

precision
```

Therefore HBM capacity directly affects serving concurrency.

---

# 232. Paged KV Cache

Some runtimes manage KV-cache memory in pages rather than requiring large contiguous allocations.

This reduces:

```text
fragmentation

wasted memory
```

and enables better scheduling.

---

# 233. Prefix Caching

Requests sharing a common prefix may reuse previously computed KV state.

Example:

```text
large system prompt
```

repeated across requests.

Potential benefits:

```text
lower prefill cost

lower latency
```

Cache correctness must include:

```text
model version

prompt version

tenant/security context
```

---

# 234. LLM GPU Scheduling

Scheduler may consider:

```text
requested model

context length

max output

priority

tenant quota

available KV cache
```

This is more sophisticated than:

```text
find GPU with free memory
```

---

# 235. Token-Aware Admission

Instead of:

```text
100 requests max
```

calculate estimated workload:

```text
input tokens

expected output tokens
```

Large request consumes more capacity than a tiny one.

---

# 236. Sequence-Length Limits

A few extreme prompts can destroy cluster concurrency.

Platform may enforce:

```text
max input tokens

max output tokens

max total sequence length
```

These are reliability controls.

---

# 237. Model Routing by Hardware

Small model:

```text
L4 pool
```

Large model:

```text
H100/H200-class pool
```

Specialized giant model:

```text
multi-GPU NVLink pool
```

Routing should match model characteristics.

---

# 238. Quantized Serving

Quantization may allow:

```text
larger model on fewer GPUs
```

Example:

```text
FP16 -> 4 GPUs

INT4 -> potentially fewer GPUs
```

depending on model/runtime.

Benchmark:

```text
quality

latency

throughput
```

before deciding.

---

# 239. Larger GPU vs More GPUs

Option A:

```text
one large-memory accelerator
```

Option B:

```text
several smaller accelerators
```

B adds:

```text
communication

coordination

failure points
```

Therefore larger-memory hardware can simplify serving architecture even if per-GPU cost is higher.

---

# 240. Architect Decision — GPU Generation

Never ask only:

```text
Which GPU is fastest?
```

Ask:

```text
model fits?

HBM capacity?

memory bandwidth?

tensor performance?

interconnect?

power?

availability?

cost?

software compatibility?
```

Hardware selection is workload-driven.

---

# 241. Performance per Dollar

Compare:

```text
tokens/sec
-----------
cost/hour
```

or:

```text
training samples/sec
--------------------
cost/hour
```

The fastest GPU may not provide the best economics.

---

# 242. Performance per Watt

At data-center scale:

```text
power
```

may constrain fleet size.

Metric:

```text
useful throughput
-----------------
watts
```

becomes relevant.

---

# 243. Cluster Architecture Must Follow Workload

Different workloads:

### Small inference

```text
shared GPUs

MIG

L4-class accelerators
```

### Large LLM inference

```text
large-memory GPUs

NVLink

tensor parallelism
```

### Distributed training

```text
multi-node

RDMA

high-speed fabric

checkpoint storage
```

One GPU architecture does not fit everything.

---

# 244. GPU Procurement Strategy

Architects may need to consider:

```text
cloud

reserved cloud

on-prem

colocation
```

Decision involves:

```text
capital

utilization

elasticity

supply

operations
```

---

# 245. Cloud GPU Advantages

```text
fast initial access

elasticity

managed infrastructure

multiple regions
```

Potential challenges:

```text
high ongoing cost

capacity scarcity

egress

instance availability
```

---

# 246. On-Prem GPU Advantages

```text
predictable capacity

potential long-term economics

network customization

data locality
```

Challenges:

```text
large capital cost

procurement time

hardware lifecycle

power/cooling

operations
```

---

# 247. Hybrid GPU Strategy

Example:

```text
baseline training
-> owned/reserved cluster

burst workloads
-> cloud
```

This can balance:

```text
cost

capacity flexibility
```

but creates portability and data-movement challenges.

---

# 248. Data Gravity

Moving:

```text
petabytes
```

between environments may make cloud bursting impractical.

Compute should often move toward data rather than data toward compute.

---

# 249. Checkpoint Portability

Hybrid strategy becomes easier if checkpoint formats are portable across:

```text
clusters

GPU generations

regions
```

Version dependencies carefully.

---

# 250. Hardware Lifecycle

Accelerators evolve quickly.

Platform must manage:

```text
old generation

current generation

new generation
```

simultaneously.

Avoid hardcoding one accelerator type into user workflows.

---

# 251. Accelerator Abstraction

User requests:

```yaml
accelerator:
  memory: ">=80GB"
  count: 8
  interconnect: high-bandwidth
```

Platform maps to available hardware.

This creates future flexibility.

---

# 252. Hardware Capability Labels

Possible capabilities:

```text
tensor-fp8

memory-80gb

nvlink

rdma

mig
```

Workloads request capabilities rather than specific SKU names where practical.

---

# 253. Hardware Migration

When newer GPU becomes available:

```text
benchmark

validate numerical behavior

validate runtime

canary workload

expand adoption
```

Do not assume identical model behavior.

---

# 254. Reproducibility Across Hardware

Floating-point behavior may vary with:

```text
hardware

kernel

library

precision
```

Exact bitwise reproducibility is often difficult.

Production requirements should define what reproducibility means.

---

# 255. Determinism Cost

Forcing deterministic algorithms may reduce:

```text
performance
```

or limit optimized kernels.

Research may prioritize reproducibility.

Production serving may prioritize throughput.

---

# 256. GPU Security

Accelerators process:

```text
sensitive model weights

user data

embeddings

prompts
```

Security considerations include:

```text
tenant isolation

device reuse

memory handling

driver security

container security
```

---

# 257. Multi-Tenant GPU Security

Sharing a physical GPU increases concern about:

```text
resource isolation

side channels

memory isolation

denial of service
```

High-risk tenants may require dedicated devices.

---

# 258. GPU Supply Chain

Node image includes:

```text
driver

CUDA

firmware

container runtime
```

Each is part of the software/hardware supply chain.

Patch management matters.

---

# 259. GPU Incident Response

If accelerator driver vulnerability appears:

```text
identify affected nodes

identify workloads

prepare new image

canary

drain

upgrade

validate
```

Fleet inventory is essential.

---

# 260. Architect Scenario — Cross-Tenant GPU Contention

Problem:

```text
Tenant A
large training jobs

Tenant B
production inference
```

share fleet.

Tenant A saturates capacity.

Design:

```text
reserved inference pool

training quota

priority scheduling

preemption

separate queue

capacity alert
```

---

# 261. Architect Scenario — Training Network Saturation

1024-GPU job causes other workloads to slow.

Investigate:

```text
fabric topology

oversubscription

job placement

AllReduce traffic

QoS

other competing jobs
```

Potential solution:

```text
fabric-aware placement

isolated network domain

capacity controls
```

---

# 262. Architect Scenario — GPU Cluster Has 30% Utilization

Do not immediately reduce fleet.

Investigate:

```text
queue waiting for large topology

fragmentation

data starvation

low-demand period

reserved capacity

scheduler inefficiency

broken nodes
```

Low utilization may hide scheduling problems.

---

# 263. Architect Scenario — Large Job Waits Two Days

Cluster:

```text
1000 GPUs

800 currently free
```

Job needs:

```text
512 GPUs
```

Why wait?

Possible:

```text
cannot find contiguous topology

free GPUs wrong type

fabric islands fragmented

quota unavailable

hardware unhealthy
```

Total free capacity alone is insufficient.

---

# 264. Architect Scenario — LLM Serving OOM

Traffic unchanged.

Possible changes:

```text
average context length increased

output length increased

new prompt template

new KV-cache configuration

model version larger
```

Request count alone can hide workload growth.

---

# 265. Architect Scenario — Training Slows 25%

No code change.

Investigate:

```text
network congestion

straggler node

storage performance

driver update

thermal throttling

neighbor workload
```

Performance regressions are cross-layer incidents.

---

# 266. Architect Scenario — Region Cannot Allocate GPUs

Production demand rises.

Architecture should already support some combination of:

```text
warm capacity

reserved capacity

secondary region

smaller fallback model

request prioritization

load shedding
```

Cloud capacity should never be assumed infinite.

---

# 267. Common Anti-Pattern — Treat GPU as CPU

Scheduling:

```text
any GPU
any node
```

ignores:

```text
memory size

topology

network

GPU type
```

This causes poor performance and fragmentation.

---

# 268. Anti-Pattern — One Huge Shared GPU Pool

Training, inference, notebooks, and experiments all compete without policy.

Result:

```text
noisy neighbors

unpredictable latency

capacity incidents
```

Use workload-aware segmentation.

---

# 269. Anti-Pattern — GPU Utilization Is the Only Metric

You miss:

```text
memory bandwidth

network wait

data starvation

step time

KV cache

stragglers
```

Monitor the workload, not only device busy percentage.

---

# 270. Anti-Pattern — Add More GPUs to Fix Everything

If bottleneck is:

```text
storage

network

CPU preprocessing
```

more GPUs may increase waste.

Measure before scaling.

---

# 271. Anti-Pattern — Random Distributed Placement

Tensor-parallel workers spread across bad network paths.

Performance collapses.

Topology must be a scheduling input.

---

# 272. Anti-Pattern — No Checkpointing

A three-day 512-GPU job fails at hour 70.

You restart at hour zero.

This converts hardware failure into enormous financial waste.

---

# 273. Anti-Pattern — Checkpoint to Local Disk Only

Node fails.

Checkpoint disappears.

Durability matters.

---

# 274. Anti-Pattern — Infinite Retry

Hardware node is permanently defective.

Scheduler retries job onto same node repeatedly.

Use:

```text
failure classification

node quarantine

retry budget
```

---

# 275. Anti-Pattern — Latest CUDA Everywhere

Newest version may not be compatible with:

```text
framework

library

model runtime
```

GPU platforms need tested compatibility matrices.

---

# 276. Anti-Pattern — Upgrade Entire Fleet Together

Driver bug affects every GPU.

Blast radius becomes global.

Upgrade progressively.

---

# 277. Anti-Pattern — Maximum Utilization

Running fleet at 100% eliminates:

```text
failure headroom

priority capacity

traffic elasticity
```

Efficiency must respect reliability.

---

# 278. Anti-Pattern — Ignore Data Pipeline

GPUs cost millions.

They wait for:

```text
slow object storage
```

Optimization must be end-to-end.

---

# 279. Anti-Pattern — Ignore Network

Buying faster GPUs on the same slow fabric can make distributed scaling worse economically.

Accelerator and network upgrades must be planned together.

---

# 280. Anti-Pattern — Model Fits, Therefore Architecture Is Fine

The model fits in HBM.

But:

```text
KV cache

batch

activations

runtime memory
```

do not.

Capacity modeling requires realistic workload memory.

```text
Production Inference Capacity
```

```text
production reservation wins
```

---

# 291. Failure Walkthrough — One GPU Dies

Expected:

```text
health signal

distributed job failure/recovery

node quarantined if needed

checkpoint restored

replacement allocated
```

Do not allow repeated workloads onto known-bad hardware.

---

# 292. Failure Walkthrough — One Rack Loses Network

Affected jobs may lose:

```text
dozens or hundreds of GPUs
```

Scheduler should understand rack as a failure domain.

Critical serving replicas should not all occupy that domain.

---

# 293. Failure Walkthrough — Checkpoint Store Slow

If every training job blocks synchronously:

```text
step time increases
```

Potential strategies:

```text
asynchronous checkpointing

local staging

rate limiting

checkpoint staggering
```

---

# 294. Failure Walkthrough — 500-GPU Job Causes Fabric Congestion

Mitigate:

```text
identify communication pattern

inspect network telemetry

isolate job

re-place future jobs

adjust fabric QoS or topology
```

Scheduler and network architecture must cooperate.

---

# 295. Failure Walkthrough — Production Inference Needs 100 More GPUs

Training currently occupies most capacity.

Potential:

```text
use reserved headroom

scale warm pool

preempt eligible training

route to secondary cluster

activate fallback models
```

This must be policy-driven.

---

# 296. Architect Memory Map

Keep this in your head:

```text
                           ML WORKLOAD
                               |
                               v
                           FRAMEWORK
                               |
                               v
                            CUDA
                               |
                               v
                             GPU
                     +---------+---------+
                     |                   |
                     v                   v
                   COMPUTE              HBM
                     |
                     v
                 INTERCONNECT
                     |
         +-----------+-----------+
         |                       |
         v                       v
      NVLINK                   PCIe
         |
         v
      NVSWITCH
         |
         v
        NIC
         |
         v
   RDMA / IB / RoCE
         |
         v
     OTHER NODES
```

Around it:

```text
Scheduler

Topology

Storage

Checkpointing

Health Monitoring

Quota

Priority

Cost
```

---

# 297. Parallelism Memory Map

```text
                         LARGE MODEL
                              |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
          |                   |                   |
          v                   v                   v
        DATA               TENSOR              PIPELINE
      PARALLEL            PARALLEL             PARALLEL
          |                   |                   |
 Different Data        Same Layer Split      Layers Split
          |
          +-------------------+-------------------+
                              |
                              v
                         HYBRID PARALLEL
```

And potentially:

```text
Expert Parallelism

Sequence Parallelism

FSDP / ZeRO
```

---

# 298. Performance Memory Map

When training is slow, ask:

```text
Is compute saturated?

Is HBM bandwidth saturated?

Is memory capacity limited?

Is PCIe limiting?

Is NVLink healthy?

Is network communication slow?

Is NCCL waiting?

Is storage slow?

Is CPU preprocessing slow?

Is there a straggler?
```

This sequence is far more useful than:

```text
GPU utilization looks low.
Add GPUs.
```

---

# 299. The Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone asks:

> We need 1,000 GPUs. Design the cluster.

Do not begin:

```text
Buy 125 eight-GPU servers.
```

Ask:

```text
What workloads?

What model sizes?

Training or serving?

What parallelism?

What GPU memory?

What network bandwidth?

What data throughput?

What failure model?

What queue-time target?

What utilization target?

What checkpoint strategy?

What growth forecast?
```

Only then design hardware.

---

# 300. What You Must Remember From Chapter 17

1. **GPU infrastructure is a distributed-systems problem involving compute, memory, networking, storage, scheduling, and software.**

2. **GPU theoretical FLOPS alone do not determine ML performance.**

3. **HBM capacity and bandwidth are often as important as raw compute.**

4. **Training memory includes parameters, gradients, optimizer state, activations, and temporary buffers.**

5. **Precision changes memory consumption, communication volume, throughput, and potentially numerical behavior.**

6. **CUDA, drivers, frameworks, and GPU hardware form a compatibility stack that must be managed as a platform contract.**

7. **CPU-to-GPU transfers can starve expensive accelerators if the input pipeline cannot keep up.**

8. **PCIe, NVLink, NVSwitch, NUMA, and NIC topology directly influence accelerator performance.**

9. **Once workloads span machines, the network becomes part of the ML runtime.**

10. **RDMA and GPUDirect reduce data-movement overhead for distributed GPU workloads.**

11. **InfiniBand and well-engineered RoCE fabrics are important for high-performance distributed training.**

12. **NCCL implements high-performance GPU collective communication such as AllReduce.**

13. **Data parallelism replicates the model while dividing data.**

14. **Tensor parallelism divides operations within model layers and therefore requires very fast communication.**

15. **Pipeline parallelism divides model layers into stages and introduces pipeline bubbles.**

16. **Expert parallelism can create communication-heavy All-to-All patterns.**

17. **Large-model training commonly combines multiple parallelism dimensions simultaneously.**

18. **Logical parallelism must be mapped intelligently onto physical GPU and network topology.**

19. **ZeRO and FSDP reduce memory duplication by sharding distributed training state.**

20. **Activation checkpointing trades additional compute for lower memory usage.**

21. **CPU or NVMe offload trades slower memory access for increased effective capacity.**

22. **Scaling to more GPUs is useful only while communication and synchronization overhead remain acceptable.**

23. **A synchronous distributed job moves at approximately the speed of its slowest important participant.**

24. **Stragglers can come from GPUs, CPUs, storage, thermals, NUMA placement, or networking.**

25. **Gang scheduling is critical when distributed jobs require many accelerators simultaneously.**

26. **Total GPU count is not the same as usable capacity; GPU type, topology, node shape, and fragmentation matter.**

27. **Fair share, quota, priority, preemption, reservations, and backfilling are central accelerator-scheduling concepts.**

28. **MIG provides hardware partitioning for some GPUs, while time slicing provides a more flexible but less isolated form of sharing.**

29. **Shared GPU strategies must reflect workload latency, memory, security, and isolation requirements.**

30. **GPU health monitoring should include memory errors, temperature, power, driver faults, interconnect errors, and performance degradation.**

31. **A slow GPU can be more damaging than a dead GPU because it may silently slow an entire synchronous training job.**

32. **Large training workloads should assume node and accelerator failures will occur.**

33. **Durable, consistent checkpointing converts expensive hardware failure from total restart into bounded lost work.**

34. **Distributed checkpoints can themselves become a storage-scale problem.**

35. **GPU observability must connect hardware metrics with workload metrics such as step time, samples/sec, and tokens/sec.**

36. **Low GPU utilization does not prove insufficient workload; the bottleneck may be CPU, network, storage, or scheduling.**

37. **High GPU utilization does not prove efficient execution.**

38. **LLM serving capacity depends heavily on context length, KV cache, batching, output length, and active sequence count.**

39. **Tensor-parallel LLM replicas should be placed within fast interconnect domains.**

40. **Continuous batching and intelligent KV-cache management are fundamental techniques for efficient LLM serving.**

41. **Token-aware admission control is more meaningful than request-count limits for LLM workloads.**

42. **GPU autoscaling cannot solve regional hardware scarcity, long provisioning delays, or unavailable accelerator types.**

43. **Critical workloads may require reserved or warm accelerator capacity.**

44. **Maximum accelerator utilization can conflict with reliability and queue-time objectives.**

45. **GPU clusters should usually segment workloads according to their network, latency, reliability, and sharing characteristics.**

46. **Infrastructure capacity planning must consider resource shapes, not merely total accelerator counts.**

47. **At large scale, topology-aware global scheduling becomes as important as individual node scheduling.**

48. **Accelerator generation should be selected using memory, bandwidth, interconnect, software compatibility, cost, availability, and workload needs—not brand-newness alone.**

49. **The fastest accelerator is not necessarily the most cost-efficient accelerator.**

50. **At architect level, always follow the full path: data → CPU → GPU memory → compute → GPU interconnect → network → storage → scheduler → workload behavior.**

---

Your mental model should now have moved from:


to:

```text
GPU CLUSTER

Compute
+

+
Topology
+
NVLink
+
RDMA Fabric
+

+
```
