# Chapter 20 — ML Governance, Model Risk, Responsible AI, Compliance, Auditability, Approval Workflows, Lineage, and Enterprise Model Lifecycle Management

---

# 1. Why Governance Becomes an Architecture Problem

At small scale:

```text
Data Scientist
   |
   v
Train Model
   |
   v
Deploy
```

At enterprise scale:

```text
Who approved it?

What data trained it?

Which version is running?

What risks were evaluated?

Who owns it?

When must it be revalidated?

What happens if regulations change?

Can we reproduce the decision?
```

These are no longer documentation questions.

They become:

```text
platform

metadata

workflow

security

observability

policy
```

requirements.

---

# 2. Governance Is Not Bureaucracy

Poor governance:

```text
PDF forms

manual spreadsheets

email approvals

months of waiting
```

Good governance:

```text
automated evidence

risk-based controls

policy as code

clear ownership

self-service workflows
```

The goal is not:

```text
stop ML development
```

The goal is:

```text
allow ML development
within known risk boundaries
```

---

# 3. Governance Mental Model

Think:

```text
MODEL
  |
  +---- Owner
  |
  +---- Purpose
  |
  +---- Data
  |
  +---- Code
  |
  +---- Evaluation
  |
  +---- Risk
  |
  +---- Approval
  |
  +---- Deployment
  |
  +---- Monitoring
  |
  +---- Retirement
```

Governance follows the complete lifecycle.

---

# 4. Model Inventory

An enterprise should know:

```text
What models exist?
```

Not merely:

```text
What models are currently deployed?
```

Inventory may include:

```text
experimental models

production models

embedded vendor models

LLMs

rules + ML hybrids

shadow models

retired models
```

---

# 5. Why Inventory Matters

Without inventory you cannot reliably answer:

```text
Which systems use customer data?

Which models make financial decisions?

Which models use third-party APIs?

Which models are based on a foundation model?

Which models are affected by a feature change?
```

Inventory is foundational governance metadata.

---

# 6. Model Registry vs Model Inventory

Registry:

```text
technical artifact management
```

Inventory:

```text
enterprise governance view
```

Registry may know:

```text
fraud-model:v27
artifact URI
metrics
```

Inventory may additionally know:

```text
business purpose

risk tier

owner

approver

legal basis

review date

deployment locations
```

---

# 7. Model Record

A governed model record may contain:

```yaml
model_id: fraud-risk
version: 27

owner:
  team: risk-ml

purpose:
  predict_transaction_fraud

risk_tier:
  high

training_dataset:
  fraud-dataset-v91

approval_status:
  approved

next_review:
  2027-02-01
```

This becomes machine-readable governance state.

---

# 8. Model Ownership

Every production model should have:

```text
technical owner

business owner
```

Potentially also:

```text
risk owner

data owner
```

depending on organization.

---

# 9. Technical Owner

Responsible for:

```text
runtime

deployment

monitoring

technical remediation
```

Not necessarily responsible for whether the model should exist.

---

# 10. Business Owner

Responsible for:

```text
business purpose

decision policy

accepted business risk

expected value
```

A model without business ownership may continue operating after its purpose is obsolete.

---

# 11. Risk Owner

For high-impact use cases, risk responsibility may need explicit assignment.

Question:

```text
Who accepts residual risk?
```

This should never be ambiguous.

---

# 12. Model Purpose

Define:

```text
what the model is intended to do
```

Example:

```text
Estimate probability that
a card transaction is fraudulent
within the next decision cycle.
```

Not:

```text
AI fraud stuff
```

Precise purpose limits inappropriate reuse.

---

# 13. Intended Use

Document:

```text
supported use cases
```

Example:

```text
real-time fraud screening
for domestic card transactions
```

---

# 14. Out-of-Scope Use

Equally important:

```text
Do not use this model
for credit approval.
```

A model validated for one purpose may be unsafe for another.

---

# 15. Model Risk

Model risk is the possibility that a model causes harm or poor outcomes because of:

```text
incorrect assumptions

poor data

technical failure

misuse

bias

drift

implementation errors

insufficient oversight
```

---

# 16. Risk-Based Governance

Do not apply identical controls to:

```text
internal image-tagging experiment
```

and:

```text
credit decision model
```

Use risk tiers.

---

# 17. Example Risk Tiers

## Tier 1 — Low

```text
internal productivity

noncritical recommendation
```

## Tier 2 — Medium

```text
customer-facing ranking

business optimization
```

## Tier 3 — High

```text
financial decisions

safety-sensitive systems

regulated decisions
```

## Tier 4 — Critical

```text
systemic or high-impact automated decisioning
```

Exact categories depend on organization and regulation.

---

# 18. Risk Classification Inputs

Consider:

```text
impact on individuals

financial impact

safety impact

regulatory exposure

degree of automation

reversibility

data sensitivity

model complexity

third-party dependency
```

---

# 19. Automation Level

Risk differs between:

```text
model recommends
human decides
```

and:

```text
model decides automatically
```

Human involvement can reduce some risks, but only if human review is meaningful.

---

# 20. Decision Reversibility

Decision:

```text
which article to recommend
```

is relatively reversible.

Decision:

```text
deny critical financial service
```

may have major consequences.

Higher irreversibility generally requires stronger controls.

---

# 21. Exposure Scale

A minor model error affecting:

```text
10 internal users
```

is different from an error affecting:

```text
500 million users
```

Scale multiplies risk.

---

# 22. Risk Matrix

Example:

```text
Impact
  ^
  |
High |    Medium    High
     |
Low  |    Low       Medium
     +------------------------>
           Low       High
           Probability
```

Risk assessment considers both:

```text
impact
and
likelihood
```

---

# 23. Inherent vs Residual Risk

Inherent risk:

```text
risk before controls
```

Residual risk:

```text
risk after controls
```

Example:

```text
Inherent:
high

Controls:
human review
monitoring
fallback
approval

Residual:
medium
```

---

# 24. Governance Controls

Possible controls:

```text
data validation

bias testing

human approval

deployment restrictions

monitoring

audit logs

rollback

access control

periodic review
```

Controls should correspond to identified risks.

---

# 25. Control Evidence

It is not enough to say:

```text
we tested fairness
```

Evidence should answer:

```text
when?

using which dataset?

which metrics?

which version?

who reviewed it?

what result?
```

---

# 26. Evidence as Data

Prefer machine-readable evidence:

```yaml
evaluation:
  dataset: validation-v18
  code_commit: abc123
  model_version: 27
  metrics:
    recall: 0.94
  timestamp: ...
```

rather than only:

```text
screenshot in email
```

---

# 27. Evidence Graph

Think:

```text
Model Version
   |
   +---- Training Data
   |
   +---- Code Commit
   |
   +---- Evaluation
   |
   +---- Security Scan
   |
   +---- Approval
   |
   +---- Deployment
```

This graph supports auditability.

---

# 28. Approval Workflow

Typical high-risk flow:

```text
Train
  |
  v
Evaluate
  |
  v
Validate
  |
  v
Risk Review
  |
  v
Approval
  |
  v
Production
```

The platform should enforce this state machine.

---

# 29. Approval Is Not a Boolean

Different approvals may exist:

```text
technical approval

business approval

risk approval

security approval

privacy approval
```

depending on risk.

---

# 30. Approval State

Example:

```text
Technical: Approved

Security: Approved

Risk: Pending

Business: Approved
```

Production deployment remains blocked.

---

# 31. Separation of Duties

For high-risk systems:

```text
developer
```

should not necessarily be:

```text
sole approver
```

Independent review helps reduce conflicts and unnoticed errors.

---

# 32. Four-Eyes Principle

Certain actions require:

```text
two independent people
```

Example:

```text
production promotion
```

for critical model.

This can be encoded in workflow.

---

# 33. Approval Expiration

Approval from:

```text
3 years ago
```

may not remain valid after:

```text
major model changes

new data

regulatory changes
```

Approvals may need expiry or revalidation conditions.

---

# 34. Revalidation Trigger

Potential triggers:

```text
major model version

feature change

training-data change

new market

new population

quality degradation

regulatory change
```

Not every minor deployment requires full reapproval.

---

# 35. Material Change

Governance should define:

> What constitutes a material change?

Examples:

```text
architecture changed

training population changed

decision threshold changed significantly

foundation model provider changed

purpose expanded
```

Material changes trigger stronger review.

---

# 36. Non-Material Change

Potentially:

```text
infrastructure patch

logging update

nonfunctional scaling change
```

may not require full model validation.

But technical changes still require normal software release controls.

---

# 37. Change Classification

Automate:

```text
change submitted
       |
       v
classify change
       |
       +---- minor
       |
       +---- material
       |
       +---- critical
```

Workflow depends on classification.

---

# 38. Policy as Code

Example:

```text
if risk_tier == HIGH
and independent_validation != PASSED:
    deny_production_deployment
```

This turns governance into enforceable architecture.

---

# 39. Why Policy as Code Matters

Documents drift.

People forget.

Automated policy provides:

```text
consistency

repeatability

auditability

speed
```

---

# 40. Policy Decision Point

Architecture:

```text
Deployment Request
       |
       v
Policy Engine
       |
       +---- model metadata
       |
       +---- approval state
       |
       +---- risk tier
       |
       v
Allow / Deny
```

---

# 41. Policy Enforcement Point

Where policy is applied.

Examples:

```text
model registry promotion

deployment API

CI/CD pipeline

feature-store access

runtime gateway
```

High-risk controls should not depend only on documentation.

---

# 42. Defense in Depth

Do not rely on only:

```text
UI button disabled
```

Someone may use API directly.

Enforce policy at:

```text
authoritative backend
```

---

# 43. Model Lifecycle State Machine

Example:

```text
Draft
  |
  v
Development
  |
  v
Validation
  |
  v
Approved
  |
  v
Production
  |
  v
Deprecated
  |
  v
Retired
```

Transitions should be governed.

---

# 44. Invalid Transition

Example:

```text
Draft
  |
  X
  |
Production
```

should be impossible for high-risk models.

---

# 45. Model Promotion

Promotion should change:

```text
governance state
```

not rebuild weights.

Example:

```text
candidate
->
approved
->
production
```

Same immutable artifact.

---

# 46. Immutable Evidence

After approval:

```text
evaluation evidence
```

should not silently change.

If new evidence is generated:

```text
create new version
```

Preserve historical auditability.

---

# 47. Audit Trail

Record events:

```text
model created

evaluation completed

risk tier changed

approval granted

production deployment

traffic changed

model retired
```

with:

```text
who

when

what

previous state

new state
```

---

# 48. Audit Log Requirements

High-quality audit logs are:

```text
immutable

time-stamped

identity-linked

searchable

retained appropriately
```

---

# 49. Operational Logs vs Audit Logs

Operational:

```text
debug runtime
```

Audit:

```text
prove governance actions
```

Audit logging usually requires stronger integrity and retention.

---

# 50. Auditability

Auditor asks:

> Why was model v27 allowed into production?

System should answer through evidence.

```text
v27
 |
 +---- approved evaluation
 |
 +---- approved risk review
 |
 +---- security scan
 |
 +---- owner
 |
 +---- deployment event
```

Not:

```text
ask Bob, he remembers
```

---

# 51. Reproducibility

Governance often requires ability to reconstruct:

```text
what model existed

what data trained it

what code generated it

what evaluation justified it
```

This ties governance directly to MLOps lineage.

---

# 52. Full Model Lineage

```text
Source Data
    |
    v
Dataset Snapshot
    |
    v
Feature Version
    |
    v
Training Job
    |
    v
Model Artifact
    |
    v
Evaluation
    |
    v
Approval
    |
    v
Deployment
    |
    v
Predictions
```

---

# 53. Decision Lineage

For a specific decision:

```text
prediction_id
   |
   +---- input version
   |
   +---- feature values
   |
   +---- model version
   |
   +---- threshold
   |
   +---- policy/rules
   |
   +---- timestamp
```

This may be essential for regulated use cases.

---

# 54. Decision Reproduction

A historical prediction may not be exactly reproducible if:

```text
external dependencies changed

nondeterminism existed

features were mutable
```

Therefore architecture must decide what evidence to preserve.

---

# 55. Prediction Snapshot

For highly governed decisions, preserve enough information to explain:

```text
which inputs

which model

which configuration

which output
```

subject to privacy and retention rules.

---

# 56. Data Minimization Conflict

Auditability says:

```text
retain evidence
```

Privacy says:

```text
retain as little as necessary
```

Governance architecture must balance both.

---

# 57. Privacy by Design

Ask before collecting:

```text
Do we need this field?
```

Avoid:

```text
collect everything
just in case
```

Data minimization reduces:

```text
security risk

privacy risk

storage cost
```

---

# 58. Purpose Limitation

Data collected for one purpose should not automatically be reused for:

```text
unrelated ML training
```

without appropriate legal and policy basis.

Platform metadata can track allowed purposes.

---

# 59. Data Classification

Example:

```text
Public

Internal

Confidential

Restricted
```

Data classification influences:

```text
access

encryption

retention

region

training eligibility
```

---

# 60. Sensitive Feature Governance

Feature registry may mark:

```text
PII

financial

biometric

protected attribute
```

Policies can restrict model use.

---

# 61. Protected Attributes

Some attributes may require special handling.

Even if excluded directly, correlated proxies may still produce unfair outcomes.

Fairness is not solved by:

```text
remove one column
```

---

# 62. Fairness

Fairness asks whether system outcomes are appropriately equitable across relevant groups.

There is no single universal fairness metric.

Different contexts require different definitions.

---

# 63. Group Fairness

Compare outcomes across groups.

Example:

```text
approval rate group A

vs

approval rate group B
```

Differences may warrant investigation.

But equal approval rates are not automatically the correct fairness objective.

---

# 64. Equal Opportunity

One concept:

```text
true positive rates
```

should be comparable across groups.

Relevant when access to positive outcome is important.

---

# 65. Equalized Odds

Conceptually compares both:

```text
true positive rates

false positive rates
```

across groups.

Different fairness definitions can conflict.

---

# 66. Demographic Parity

Outcome rates are similar across groups.

This may or may not be appropriate depending on underlying context and policy.

Architect lesson:

> Fairness metric selection is a domain, legal, and policy decision—not merely a technical choice.

---

# 67. Individual Fairness

Concept:

```text
similar individuals
should receive similar outcomes
```

Defining:

```text
similar
```

is itself difficult.

---

# 68. Fairness Evaluation Dataset

Fairness metrics depend on:

```text
representative evaluation data
```

If subgroup has only:

```text
12 examples
```

metric may be unreliable.

---

# 69. Intersectional Evaluation

A model may perform acceptably for:

```text
Group A

Group B
```

independently but poorly for:

```text
A ∩ B
```

Intersectional slices can reveal hidden failures.

---

# 70. Slice Cardinality Challenge

Checking every combination creates:

```text
millions of slices
```

Use:

```text
risk-informed predefined slices

statistical safeguards

offline analysis
```

---

# 71. Fairness Monitoring in Production

Offline fairness evaluation is not enough.

Population may change.

Track appropriate outcome metrics over time.

But preserve privacy.

---

# 72. Sensitive Attribute Monitoring

To evaluate fairness, you may need sensitive attributes.

Yet collecting them can itself be restricted.

This is a governance challenge requiring:

```text
privacy

legal

risk
```

coordination.

---

# 73. Explainability

Explainability asks:

```text
Why did the model produce this output?
```

But explanations have several meanings.

---

# 74. Global Explanation

Understand overall model behavior.

Examples:

```text
important features

general relationships

decision patterns
```

---

# 75. Local Explanation

Explain one prediction:

```text
Why was transaction X
given risk score 0.91?
```

---

# 76. Explanation vs Causality

Feature importance does not automatically prove:

```text
causal relationship
```

An explanation method may show association within model behavior.

Do not overclaim.

---

# 77. Explanation Stability

If tiny input change creates completely different explanation:

```text
trust may decrease
```

Explanation systems themselves require validation.

---

# 78. Explainability as Product Requirement

Some applications need:

```text
human-readable reason codes
```

If so, model architecture may need to support that from the beginning.

Do not add explainability after deployment as an afterthought.

---

# 79. Reason Codes

Example:

```text
Decision:
manual review

Reasons:
- unusually high transaction amount
- new device
- abnormal geographic pattern
```

Reason-code design should correspond to actual decision logic.

---

# 80. Human Oversight

Human oversight can take several forms:

```text
human-in-the-loop

human-on-the-loop

human-in-command
```

---

# 81. Human-in-the-Loop

Model proposes.

Human approves each decision.

```text
Model
  |
  v
Human
  |
  v
Action
```

---

# 82. Human-on-the-Loop

System acts automatically.

Human monitors and can intervene.

Useful for:

```text
large-scale automation
```

where review of every event is impossible.

---

# 83. Human-in-Command

Humans retain authority over:

```text
whether

where

how
```

system operates.

This is broader governance.

---

# 84. Meaningful Human Review

A person clicking:

```text
Approve
```

on 5,000 decisions/hour without adequate context is not meaningful oversight.

Human review needs:

```text
time

information

authority

training
```

---

# 85. Automation Bias

Humans may over-trust model recommendations.

Design UI to avoid making:

```text
AI says yes
```

appear automatically authoritative.

---

# 86. Escalation

Model should know when:

```text
confidence low

input unusual

policy ambiguous
```

and escalate.

Example:

```text
Auto Approve

Manual Review

Auto Reject
```

with defined thresholds.

---

# 87. Abstention

Sometimes best model action is:

```text
I cannot decide reliably.
```

Architectures can support abstention.

This is often better than forced low-confidence automation.

---

# 88. Confidence Is Not Certainty

A probability score:

```text
0.99
```

does not guarantee correctness.

Calibration and out-of-distribution behavior matter.

---

# 89. Out-of-Distribution Input

Model receives input unlike training data.

Potential response:

```text
fallback

manual review

low-confidence state
```

rather than silently trusting prediction.

---

# 90. Model Card

A model card is structured documentation describing a model.

Typical fields:

```text
purpose

owner

training data

evaluation

limitations

risk

intended use

monitoring
```

---

# 91. Model Card Should Be Generated

Do not rely entirely on manual writing.

Platform can populate:

```text
model version

dataset

metrics

runtime

owners

deployment locations
```

automatically.

Humans add:

```text
purpose

limitations

risk interpretation
```

---

# 92. Living Model Card

Model card should update when:

```text
new evaluation

new deployment

new review

new monitoring status
```

It should not be a static forgotten PDF.

---

# 93. Data Sheet

Datasets may also need documentation.

Include:

```text
source

collection method

population

limitations

sensitive fields

retention

license

quality
```

Model governance depends on data governance.

---

# 94. Dataset Approval

High-risk training datasets may require:

```text
privacy review

legal review

quality review
```

before training eligibility.

---

# 95. Dataset Eligibility Policy

Example:

```text
if classification == RESTRICTED
and model_project not approved:
    deny_training_access
```

Again:

```text
policy as code
```

---

# 96. Data Provenance

Need to know:

```text
where data came from
```

Especially for:

```text
third-party data

web data

licensed datasets

foundation-model training
```

---

# 97. Licensing

A technically accessible dataset is not automatically legally usable.

Metadata may include:

```text
license

allowed usage

redistribution restrictions

expiry
```

---

# 98. Model Artifact Provenance

Similarly:

```text
foundation model

embedding model

reranker
```

may come from third party.

Track:

```text
vendor

version

license

terms

security assessment
```

---

# 99. Third-Party Model Risk

Using external model introduces:

```text
vendor dependency

availability risk

data-sharing risk

model changes

policy changes

pricing changes
```

Governance must include vendor risk.

---

# 100. SaaS Model Governance

If sending data to external API:

```text
What data leaves organization?

Where is it processed?

Is it retained?

Is it used for training?

Which region?

What contract governs it?
```

Architecture needs controls.

---

# 101. Data Egress Policy

LLM gateway can enforce:

```text
which applications
can send which data
to which providers
```

Example:

```text
Restricted Data
  X
External Public LLM
```

---

# 102. LLM Gateway as Governance Layer

Architecture:

```text
Applications
    |
    v
Enterprise LLM Gateway
    |
    +---- Auth
    |
    +---- Policy
    |
    +---- Redaction
    |
    +---- Provider Routing
    |
    +---- Logging
    |
    v
Model Providers
```

This centralizes controls.

---

# 103. Foundation Model Registry

Track approved foundation models:

```text
provider

model name

version

risk assessment

approved use cases

regions

cost

retirement date
```

Applications reference approved entries.

---

# 104. Foundation Model Version Changes

A provider may change:

```text
behavior

safety

pricing

latency
```

even when API name remains stable.

Pin versions when possible and evaluate changes.

---

# 105. LLM Governance Stack

A governed generative application includes:

```text
Foundation Model

Prompt

Retrieval

Tools

Guardrails

Business Policy
```

Governance cannot focus only on base model.

---

# 106. Prompt Governance

Prompt can materially change system behavior.

Track:

```text
prompt_id

version

owner

approval

deployment
```

---

# 107. Prompt as Production Artifact

Changing:

```text
"You may approve refunds"
```

to:

```text
"Automatically approve refunds"
```

could be more significant than a model update.

Prompts need version control.

---

# 108. Prompt Approval

High-risk agent prompts may require:

```text
review

testing

security evaluation
```

before production.

---

# 109. Prompt Injection Risk

Prompt governance must also account for:

```text
untrusted user input

retrieved content

tool output
```

These can inject instructions.

---

# 110. System Prompt Confidentiality

Do not treat:

```text
system prompt secrecy
```

as a security boundary.

Authorization must exist outside model instructions.

---

# 111. RAG Governance

RAG introduces:

```text
documents

chunks

embeddings

indexes

retrievers

rerankers
```

Each has governance implications.

---

# 112. Knowledge Source Approval

Only approved sources may be indexed.

Example:

```text
internal HR assistant
```

should not accidentally retrieve:

```text
executive confidential data
```

---

# 113. Document ACL Propagation

If user cannot access source document:

```text
user should not receive
retrieved chunk
```

Vector search must preserve authorization semantics.

---

# 114. Index Is Derived Sensitive Data

Embedding or vector index may encode information from sensitive source content.

Treat it as:

```text
governed data asset
```

not harmless cache.

---

# 115. Index Lineage

Track:

```text
source corpus version

chunking version

embedding model

index build

retriever config
```

Bad RAG response may originate in any of them.

---

# 116. RAG Freshness

Governance may require:

```text
documents updated within X hours
```

for policies or procedures.

Stale index can produce incorrect operational guidance.

---

# 117. Citation Requirement

Certain applications may require:

```text
every factual answer
must cite approved evidence
```

This can be enforced through application policy and evaluation.

---

# 118. RAG Deletion

Source document deleted.

Need to ensure:

```text
chunks removed

embeddings removed

indexes updated

caches invalidated
```

Derived data lifecycle matters.

---

# 119. Agent Governance

Agents can:

```text
read

reason

call tools

modify systems
```

Their risk is much higher than passive chat.

---

# 120. Read vs Write Tools

Classify tools:

```text
READ

WRITE

HIGH-IMPACT WRITE
```

Examples:

```text
search database = read

create calendar event = write

transfer money = high-impact write
```

Controls should differ.

---

# 121. Least-Privilege Agent Tools

Agent should receive:

```text
minimum permissions
```

needed for task.

Avoid:

```text
agent has admin credentials
for every system
```

---

# 122. Tool Authorization

Architecture:

```text
Agent proposes tool call
        |
        v
Authorization Layer
        |
        +---- Allow
        |
        +---- Deny
        |
        +---- Human Approval
```

Never rely solely on model deciding whether action is allowed.

---

# 123. Human Confirmation

High-impact action:

```text
delete customer account
```

may require explicit human confirmation.

This is a policy control.

---

# 124. Agent Action Audit

Record:

```text
agent version

model version

user

tool

action

authorization

result
```

This supports investigation.

---

# 125. Agent Loop Limits

An agent can enter:

```text
tool call

retry

tool call

retry
```

forever.

Governance controls:

```text
max steps

time budget

cost budget

tool budget
```

---

# 126. Financial Action Limit

Example:

```text
Agent can refund <= ₹5,000 automatically.

Above that:
human approval.
```

Business policy belongs outside the model.

---

# 127. Agent Scope

Define explicitly:

```text
what agent may do

what agent must never do
```

This is analogous to model intended use.

---

# 128. Agent Kill Switch

High-risk agent platform needs:

```text
global disable

tool-specific disable

tenant disable
```

for incident response.

---

# 129. Emergency Disable

If harmful behavior discovered:

```text
disable agent execution
```

without waiting for complete application redeployment.

Architecture should support rapid containment.

---

# 130. Model Kill Switch

Similarly:

```text
model version v27
```

can be blocked globally.

Serving platform stops new traffic to it.

---

# 131. Feature Kill Switch

Bad feature:

```text
feature-v8
```

may affect 50 models.

Platform can:

```text
disable feature

fallback

route models
```

This requires dependency metadata.

---

# 132. Governance Incident Response

Governance incident might involve:

```text
unauthorized data

biased outcome

unapproved model

audit gap

misbehaving agent
```

Incident process differs from ordinary latency outage.

---

# 133. Containment

Immediate actions:

```text
stop model

disable tool

freeze deployment

block dataset

revoke credentials
```

Goal:

```text
prevent further impact
```

---

# 134. Impact Assessment

Determine:

```text
which users?

which decisions?

which time window?

which model version?

which data?
```

Decision lineage is essential.

---

# 135. Remediation

Could include:

```text
reprocess decisions

notify affected stakeholders

retrain model

correct data

change policy
```

Governance incidents often extend beyond technical rollback.

---

# 136. Model Retirement

Models should not run forever.

Reasons:

```text
obsolete business purpose

better replacement

expired approval

unsupported runtime

poor performance

regulatory change
```

---

# 137. Deprecation

Before retirement:

```text
mark deprecated
```

Notify dependent teams.

Block new integrations.

Allow migration window.

---

# 138. Consumer Discovery

Before deleting model endpoint:

```text
who uses it?
```

Need:

```text
traffic telemetry

service dependency metadata
```

---

# 139. Retirement Workflow

```text
Deprecated
    |
    v
Consumers Migrated
    |
    v
Traffic = 0
    |
    v
Archive Evidence
    |
    v
Delete Runtime
    |
    v
Retired
```

---

# 140. Artifact Retention

Retiring serving does not necessarily mean deleting:

```text
model artifact

evaluation

approval

audit evidence
```

Retention depends on policy.

---

# 141. Model Expiration

For some models:

```text
approval_valid_until
```

may be required.

After date:

```text
revalidation required
```

Platform can warn before expiry.

---

# 142. Review Schedule

Possible:

```text
low risk -> annual

high risk -> quarterly

critical -> continuous + formal review
```

Exact policy varies.

---

# 143. Continuous Monitoring vs Periodic Validation

Continuous:

```text
drift

quality

fairness

SLO
```

Periodic:

```text
formal governance review
```

Both can coexist.

---

# 144. Continuous Compliance

Instead of annual scramble:

```text
collect evidence continuously
```

Example:

```text
approved artifact

scan results

deployment logs

monitoring history

access logs
```

already available.

---

# 145. Compliance Evidence Pipeline

```text
Platform Events
      |
      v
Evidence Collector
      |
      v
Evidence Store
      |
      v
Audit Report
```

This reduces manual effort.

---

# 146. Evidence Store

Should provide:

```text
immutability

searchability

retention

access controls

timestamps
```

Potentially separate from normal operational databases.

---

# 147. Control Mapping

One automated control may satisfy multiple requirements.

Example:

```text
immutable deployment audit log
```

supports:

```text
security

governance

change management

audit
```

Architects should reuse controls.

---

# 148. Control Effectiveness

A control exists:

```text
production approval required
```

But users bypass it through:

```text
direct Kubernetes access
```

Control exists on paper but is ineffective.

Architecture must test effectiveness.

---

# 149. Preventive Controls

Stop bad action.

Examples:

```text
deny unapproved deployment

deny unauthorized data access
```

---

# 150. Detective Controls

Detect bad state.

Examples:

```text
alert on unregistered production endpoint

detect expired model approval
```

---

# 151. Corrective Controls

Recover after issue.

Examples:

```text
rollback model

remove bad dataset

revoke access
```

Mature governance uses all three.

---

# 152. Governance Control Hierarchy

Prefer:

```text
automated preventive control
```

when safe and feasible.

Then:

```text
automated detective control
```

Then manual process when necessary.

---

# 153. Exception Workflow

Sometimes business needs exception.

Do not bypass controls informally.

Use:

```text
exception request

reason

scope

approver

expiration
```

---

# 154. Exception Expiration

Every temporary exception should have:

```text
expiry date
```

Otherwise temporary becomes permanent.

---

# 155. Exception Monitoring

Dashboard:

```text
active exceptions

expired exceptions

high-risk exceptions
```

Governance should track technical debt.

---

# 156. Policy Versioning

Policies evolve.

Decision:

```text
deployment approved
```

should be attributable to:

```text
policy version
```

used at that time.

---

# 157. Historical Policy Reconstruction

Auditor asks:

> Why was deployment allowed six months ago?

Need:

```text
policy-v12
```

not only today's:

```text
policy-v18
```

---

# 158. Governance API

Potential capabilities:

```text
register_model()

classify_risk()

submit_evaluation()

request_approval()

approve_model()

retire_model()
```

Governance should expose APIs, not only manual portals.

---

# 159. Governance Control Plane

Architecture:

```text
             MODEL GOVERNANCE PLATFORM
                       |
       +---------------+---------------+
       |               |               |
       v               v               v
    INVENTORY         POLICY         WORKFLOW
       |               |               |
       +---------------+---------------+
                       |
                       v
                 EVIDENCE GRAPH
                       |
       +---------------+---------------+
       |                               |
       v                               v
   MODEL REGISTRY                 AUDIT STORE
```

---

# 160. Integration With ML Platform

```text
Training
   |
   v
Registry
   |
   v
Governance
   |
   v
Approval
   |
   v
Deployment
```

Governance should be part of the golden path.

---

# 161. Deployment Enforcement

Production deployment API queries:

```text
model governance status
```

If:

```text
APPROVED
```

continue.

If:

```text
PENDING
```

deny.

---

# 162. Runtime Enforcement

In highly controlled environments, runtime gateway may verify:

```text
model still approved

model not expired

model not revoked
```

before routing.

Be careful not to make control-plane availability a hard serving dependency.

---

# 163. Cached Governance State

Serving data plane can cache:

```text
last-known-good approval state
```

so governance control-plane outage does not stop valid inference.

Revocations require carefully designed propagation.

---

# 164. Revocation

If model becomes unsafe:

```text
REVOKED
```

must propagate rapidly.

Possible:

```text
push event

gateway blocklist

deployment controller
```

---

# 165. Revocation vs Availability

Tension:

```text
serve during control-plane outage
```

versus:

```text
immediately stop revoked model
```

Design may use:

```text
signed policy snapshots

short TTL

regional replicas
```

to balance both.

---

# 166. Signed Governance Metadata

Approval state may be digitally signed.

Serving components verify:

```text
artifact identity

approval metadata

signature
```

This can strengthen integrity.

---

# 167. Artifact Signing

Model artifact can be signed after trusted build/approval.

Deployment verifies signature.

This helps ensure:

```text
approved artifact
=
deployed artifact
```

---

# 168. Provenance Attestation

Attestation may record:

```text
how artifact was built

from which source

which pipeline

which dependencies
```

This connects software supply-chain security with ML governance.

---

# 169. Model Integrity

Hash:

```text
SHA256(model artifact)
```

is recorded.

Production verifies:

```text
hash matches registry record
```

Prevents silent artifact modification.

---

# 170. Governance and CI/CD

Pipeline:

```text
Commit
  |
  v
Test
  |
  v
Train
  |
  v
Evaluate
  |
  v
Register
  |
  v
Governance Gate
  |
  v
Deploy
```

This is continuous governed delivery.

---

# 171. Evaluation Gate

Example policy:

```text
recall >= 0.90

precision >= 0.85

latency <= 100ms
```

If candidate fails:

```text
cannot promote
```

But thresholds should be versioned by use case.

---

# 172. Relative Evaluation Gate

Sometimes candidate must beat champion.

Example:

```text
candidate quality
>=
champion quality - tolerance
```

and:

```text
cost increase <= limit
```

---

# 173. Multi-Objective Governance

Production decision may consider:

```text
quality

latency

cost

fairness

security
```

A model superior in one dimension may be unacceptable overall.

---

# 174. Governance Scorecard

Example:

```text
Quality         PASS

Latency         PASS

Fairness        PASS

Security        PASS

Cost            WARN

Documentation   PASS
```

Promotion policy uses the full scorecard.

---

# 175. Hard Gate vs Soft Gate

Hard:

```text
security vulnerability
-> block
```

Soft:

```text
cost 5% above target
-> warning
```

Different controls have different enforcement strength.

---

# 176. Risk Acceptance

Sometimes residual risk remains.

Authorized business/risk owner explicitly accepts:

```text
risk description

scope

duration

mitigation
```

This should be auditable.

---

# 177. Risk Acceptance Is Not Permanent

Set:

```text
expiration

review date
```

otherwise unresolved risk becomes invisible.

---

# 178. Model Validation

Validation should challenge:

```text
model methodology

data

assumptions

performance

limitations
```

For high-risk models, validation may be independent from development.

---

# 179. Development vs Validation

Development team:

```text
builds model
```

Validation team:

```text
tests whether evidence supports use
```

This separation is common in model-risk frameworks.

---

# 180. Validation Dataset Independence

If possible, validation should avoid simply repeating the developer's exact evaluation assumptions.

Independent validation may use:

```text
separate test sets

stress tests

alternative metrics
```

---

# 181. Stress Testing

Test model under unusual conditions:

```text
economic shock

extreme transaction volume

missing features

distribution shift

rare segments
```

Goal:

```text
understand failure boundaries
```

---

# 182. Scenario Analysis

Ask:

```text
What happens if
critical feature drifts 30%?
```

or:

```text
What happens if
new customer segment becomes 50% of traffic?
```

This informs contingency plans.

---

# 183. Sensitivity Analysis

Change inputs and observe outputs.

Useful for understanding:

```text
stability

dependencies

unexpected sensitivity
```

---

# 184. Robustness Testing

Evaluate against:

```text
noise

missing data

outliers

input perturbations
```

Critical models should not fail unpredictably.

---

# 185. Adversarial Testing

Depending on use case:

```text
fraud evasion

prompt injection

malformed input

abuse attempts
```

should be included.

---

# 186. Red Teaming

For high-risk generative systems:

```text
structured adversarial evaluation
```

tests:

```text
safety boundaries

security

harmful behavior

tool misuse
```

Findings become governance evidence.

---

# 187. Red-Team Findings

Track:

```text
finding ID

severity

affected version

mitigation

verification

status
```

Do not leave findings only in presentation decks.

---

# 188. Risk Register

A governance platform may maintain:

```text
identified risk

severity

owner

mitigation

status

review date
```

linked to model versions.

---

# 189. Known Limitation

Example:

```text
Model has lower recall
for merchants with <30 days history.
```

Record explicitly.

Operational controls can compensate:

```text
manual review
```

---

# 190. Limitation-Aware Routing

If input falls into known weak region:

```text
route to fallback

manual review

alternative model
```

Governance can influence runtime architecture.

---

# 191. Fairness Mitigation

Potential strategies:

```text
better data

reweighting

threshold policies

human review

remove problematic features
```

No universal solution.

Evaluate resulting business and fairness trade-offs.

---

# 192. Performance-Fairness Trade-Off

A change may:

```text
slightly reduce aggregate accuracy
```

while:

```text
significantly improve subgroup outcomes
```

Governance decision is multi-objective.

---

# 193. Explainability-Fidelity Trade-Off

Simple explanation may be easy to understand but less faithful.

High-fidelity explanation may be complex.

Choose based on audience:

```text
customer

operator

risk reviewer

data scientist
```

---

# 194. Governance UX

Poor:

```text
50-page form
```

Good:

```text
metadata auto-filled

only missing human judgment requested
```

Automate evidence gathering.

---

# 195. Developer Experience Matters

If governance process takes:

```text
8 weeks
```

for low-risk model, teams may bypass it.

Risk-based automation improves both:

```text
compliance
and
adoption
```

---

# 196. Governance Golden Path

For standard low-risk model:

```text
Train
 |
Evaluate
 |
Automated Risk Classification
 |
Automated Checks
 |
Self-Service Approval
 |
Deploy
```

High risk:

```text
additional human review
```

---

# 197. Progressive Governance

Controls increase with risk.

```text
Low Risk
  |
  +---- automated
  |
Medium
  |
  +---- automated + owner approval
  |
High
  |
  +---- independent review
  |
Critical
  |
  +---- formal governance board
```

---

# 198. Governance Bottleneck Metric

Measure:

```text
time waiting for approval
```

If 90% of lifecycle is queue time:

```text
workflow needs improvement
```

Governance platform itself needs product metrics.

---

# 199. Governance Platform SLO

Example:

```text
95% of low-risk model reviews
complete within 1 business day
```

High-risk reviews may have different targets.

---

# 200. Approval Queue Observability

Monitor:

```text
pending reviews

age

reviewer workload

rejection reasons
```

This exposes organizational bottlenecks.

---

# 201. Governance Metrics

Possible:

```text
% production models registered

% models with owners

% expired approvals

% with current monitoring

time to approval

open critical risks
```

---

# 202. Governance Coverage

Target:

```text
100% production models
have inventory record
```

Shadow or manually deployed models violate control.

---

# 203. Rogue Model Detection

Compare:

```text
production endpoints
```

against:

```text
approved model inventory
```

If endpoint exists without governance record:

```text
alert
```

This is detective control.

---

# 204. Runtime Discovery

Periodically scan:

```text
Kubernetes

cloud endpoints

serverless

API gateways
```

to discover unknown ML workloads.

Inventory should reflect reality.

---

# 205. Shadow AI

Employees may use unapproved external AI tools.

Risks:

```text
data leakage

unreviewed models

compliance gaps
```

Governance strategy includes safe approved alternatives.

---

# 206. Governance Should Enable Safe Adoption

Only saying:

```text
No AI allowed
```

often pushes usage underground.

Better:

```text
approved tools

approved data classes

approved use cases
```

with clear boundaries.

---

# 207. Model Risk Monitoring

Risk profile can change after deployment.

Example:

```text
traffic volume increases 100×
```

Impact increases.

Risk classification may need re-evaluation.

---

# 208. Scope Expansion

Model originally:

```text
internal recommendation
```

later used:

```text
customer-facing automated decision
```

Same model.

Completely different risk.

Use-case metadata matters.

---

# 209. New Geography

Deployment expands to:

```text
new country
```

Potentially new:

```text
laws

populations

languages

data rules
```

Governance must re-evaluate.

---

# 210. New Population

Model trained on:

```text
adults
```

later applied to:

```text
children
```

This is material scope change.

---

# 211. Monitoring Threshold Governance

Model quality threshold:

```text
recall < 80%
```

may trigger shutdown.

Changing threshold to:

```text
recall < 50%
```

is itself a governed change.

---

# 212. Kill Criteria

Define before incident:

```text
When must model automatically
or manually stop serving?
```

Examples:

```text
critical quality drop

security breach

expired approval

invalid data source
```

---

# 213. Graceful Degradation Under Governance

Instead of complete outage:

```text
high-risk model disabled
```

system may use:

```text
manual workflow

rules engine

older approved model
```

Pre-approved fallbacks matter.

---

# 214. Fallback Governance

Fallback artifact also requires:

```text
approval

monitoring

validity
```

A fallback nobody tested for two years is not safe.

---

# 215. Last-Known-Good

Maintain:

```text
current production

last-known-good approved model
```

Rollback should be operationally simple.

---

# 216. Governance During Incident

Emergency rollback may bypass normal approval delays.

But:

```text
emergency process
```

should itself be predefined and audited.

---

# 217. Break-Glass Access

Emergency operator may receive temporary elevated permissions.

Requirements:

```text
strong authentication

reason

audit

automatic expiration
```

---

# 218. Break-Glass Is Not Normal Workflow

If teams use emergency access every week:

```text
governance design is broken
```

Investigate why normal path is inadequate.

---

# 219. Regulatory Mapping

Policies may map model use cases to relevant regulatory obligations.

Architecture should not hardcode one jurisdiction's logic into every service.

Central governance metadata helps.

---

# 220. Regulation Changes

When policy changes:

```text
identify affected models
```

using metadata such as:

```text
geography

use case

data classes

risk tier
```

This is another reason inventory matters.

---

# 221. Impact Query

Example:

```text
Find all production models
used for automated customer decisions
in Region X
using sensitive financial data.
```

A mature governance graph can answer quickly.

---

# 222. Enterprise Policy Taxonomy

Policies can be grouped:

```text
Security

Privacy

Model Risk

Responsible AI

Data Governance

Operational Reliability

Vendor Risk
```

One model may be subject to several.

---

# 223. Policy Conflict

Security policy:

```text
retain logs 1 year
```

Privacy policy:

```text
delete sensitive data after 30 days
```

Architecture may resolve by:

```text
retain metadata
while removing raw sensitive payload
```

Policy conflicts require deliberate design.

---

# 224. Evidence Minimization

Store:

```text
proof of evaluation
```

without necessarily retaining:

```text
every raw user input
```

Cryptographic hashes, summaries, and immutable metadata may sometimes provide sufficient evidence.

---

# 225. Audit Query Performance

An auditor may need:

```text
2 years of deployment history
```

Audit architecture should support efficient search.

Do not keep critical evidence only in cold unindexed logs without retrieval plan.

---

# 226. Long-Term Schema Evolution

Governance records may need retention for years.

Metadata schema will change.

Need:

```text
backward compatibility

migration strategy

versioned schemas
```

---

# 227. Evidence Immutability vs Correction

Suppose governance record contains mistake.

Do not silently overwrite history.

Use:

```text
correction event
```

preserving original record and correction reason.

---

# 228. Event-Sourced Audit

Architecture:

```text
ModelRegistered

RiskClassified

ApprovalGranted

DeploymentCreated

ApprovalRevoked
```

Current governance state can be derived from immutable event history.

---

# 229. Current State + Audit Log

Practical design often combines:

```text
current-state database
```

for fast queries

and:

```text
append-only audit log
```

for history.

---

# 230. Governance Metadata Consistency

If model registry says:

```text
version 18
```

but governance inventory says:

```text
version 17 production
```

which is authoritative?

Define source-of-truth relationships.

---

# 231. Resource Identity

Use stable IDs:

```text
model_id

version_id

deployment_id

dataset_id

approval_id
```

Avoid joining systems only by mutable names.

---

# 232. Global Unique Identity

For large enterprise:

```text
same model name
```

may exist in several teams.

Resource identity should include proper namespace.

---

# 233. Governance Multi-Tenancy

Shared governance platform serves:

```text
thousands of teams
```

Need:

```text
tenant isolation

delegated administration

global policy

local policy
```

---

# 234. Global vs Local Policy

Global:

```text
all production models need owner
```

Business-unit policy:

```text
finance models need independent validator
```

Project policy:

```text
this application requires human approval
```

Policy composition must be predictable.

---

# 235. Policy Precedence

If global policy says:

```text
deny external model
```

local project cannot simply:

```text
allow external model
```

Define precedence rules.

---

# 236. Policy Conflict Detection

System should identify:

```text
two policies produce incompatible requirements
```

before deployment time where possible.

---

# 237. Policy Testing

Policy code deserves:

```text
unit tests

integration tests

simulation
```

Bad policy deployment can block every production model.

---

# 238. Policy Canary

Roll out new policy to:

```text
small subset

simulation mode
```

before enforcing globally.

Observe:

```text
how many deployments would be denied?
```

---

# 239. Dry-Run Policy

New policy reports:

```text
would deny 312 models
```

without enforcement.

Teams can remediate before activation.

---

# 240. Governance Control-Plane Reliability

If governance platform is down:

```text
should existing models stop?
```

Usually:

```text
no
```

for many use cases.

New governed actions may pause.

---

# 241. Existing Serving vs New Change

Governance outage:

```text
existing approved inference
continues
```

but:

```text
new production deployment
blocked
```

This mirrors control-plane/data-plane separation.

---

# 242. Governance DR

Protect:

```text
inventory

approval state

audit trail

policy versions

evidence
```

Some may be irreplaceable governance records.

---

# 243. Governance RPO/RTO

Potential:

```text
approval database
RPO near zero

model inventory
RTO 4 hours
```

Different governance components have different criticality.

---

# 244. Audit Data Durability

Audit evidence may require:

```text
very high durability
```

because losing it can create regulatory exposure even if serving still works.

---

# 245. Regional Governance

Global enterprise may have:

```text
global standards

regional regulation

local approval authority
```

Architecture needs hierarchy.

---

# 246. Data Residency for Governance

Audit records themselves may contain sensitive data.

Governance data may also have residency constraints.

---

# 247. Cross-Region Policy Distribution

Global policy:

```text
v27
```

needs propagation to regional enforcement points.

Track:

```text
policy version by region
```

to detect drift.

---

# 248. Governance Configuration Drift

Desired:

```text
all regions policy-v27
```

Actual:

```text
US v27

EU v27

India v24
```

This is a governance incident.

---

# 249. Signed Policy Bundles

Regions can receive:

```text
versioned signed policy bundle
```

and verify authenticity.

Useful for distributed enforcement.

---

# 250. Model Risk Dashboard

Fleet view:

```text
Critical Models: 22

High Risk: 181

Expired Approval: 4

Monitoring Breach: 11

Open Critical Findings: 2
```

Executives and platform teams need different views.

---

# 251. Governance Dashboard for Model Team

Show:

```text
approval state

missing evidence

next review

open findings

monitoring status
```

Make compliance actionable.

---

# 252. Governance Notifications

Notify before:

```text
approval expires

dataset license expires

model runtime retires

review deadline
```

Prevent last-minute emergencies.

---

# 253. Automated Evidence Collection

Pull:

```text
training metrics

security scans

model evaluation

deployment history

monitoring results
```

from existing systems.

Humans should not manually upload screenshots when machine evidence exists.

---

# 254. Manual Evidence

Some evidence requires human judgment:

```text
business rationale

ethical analysis

known limitations
```

Platform should distinguish:

```text
automatically generated

human-authored
```

---

# 255. Attestation

Reviewer may attest:

```text
I reviewed evaluation
and accept this model
for defined purpose.
```

Store:

```text
identity

timestamp

scope

version
```

---

# 256. Approval Scope

Approval may be valid for:

```text
model v18

country India

product A

traffic <= 20%
```

Not necessarily globally.

Scope needs structured representation.

---

# 257. Conditional Approval

Example:

```text
Approved provided:
manual review rate >= 5%
```

Platform can continuously verify condition.

---

# 258. Continuous Policy Monitoring

After deployment, evaluate:

```text
approval still valid?

traffic within scope?

monitoring active?

quality within limits?
```

Governance is not finished at deployment.

---

# 259. Runtime Policy Violation

Model approved for:

```text
Region A
```

traffic appears from:

```text
Region B
```

Policy monitor alerts or blocks depending on risk.

---

# 260. Model Usage Governance

Track:

```text
who calls model

for what application

which environment
```

Model endpoint should not become uncontrolled shared service.

---

# 261. Consumer Registration

Applications register dependency:

```text
application X
uses
model Y
```

Benefits:

```text
impact analysis

retirement planning

risk propagation
```

---

# 262. Transitive Risk

Application uses:

```text
Model A
```

which uses:

```text
Feature B
```

which uses:

```text
Third-party dataset C
```

A license issue in C can affect entire chain.

Governance graph should support transitive queries.

---

# 263. Foundation Model Dependency Graph

```text
Customer Agent
   |
   +---- Prompt v9
   |
   +---- RAG Index v12
   |
   +---- Foundation Model F
   |
   +---- Tools
```

Changing F may affect many applications.

---

# 264. Provider Outage Governance

If external LLM unavailable:

```text
fallback to another provider?
```

Only if fallback is:

```text
approved

tested

data-compatible
```

Operational DR must respect governance.

---

# 265. Model Substitution Risk

Fallback from:

```text
Model A
```

to:

```text
Model B
```

can change:

```text
quality

safety

privacy

pricing

behavior
```

Fallback is a governed deployment choice.

---

# 266. Vendor Model Update

Vendor silently updates model.

Monitoring detects:

```text
prediction behavior changed
```

Need vendor version controls or strong shadow evaluation where possible.

---

# 267. Third-Party Model Exit Strategy

Architect should ask:

```text
If provider becomes unavailable
or unacceptable,
how do we migrate?
```

Avoid irreversible dependency.

---

# 268. Governance for Embedding Models

Changing embedding model may invalidate:

```text
vector index
```

Governance metadata should tie:

```text
index version
```

to:

```text
embedding model version
```

---

# 269. Governance for Rerankers

Reranker can materially change retrieved context.

Treat as production model artifact.

Evaluate and version it.

---

# 270. Governance for Guardrails

Safety classifier or guardrail itself is:

```text
a model/system
```

It needs:

```text
version

evaluation

monitoring
```

Do not assume guardrail is infallible.

---

# 271. Recursive Governance

Model governance platform may use ML.

Example:

```text
LLM automatically summarizes risk evidence
```

That supporting model also needs appropriate governance.

---

# 272. Automated Evaluation Judges

LLM-as-judge can accelerate evaluation.

But judge has:

```text
bias

variance

prompt sensitivity

model dependency
```

For high-risk decisions, do not blindly trust one automated judge.

---

# 273. Human Benchmarking of Judges

Validate automated evaluator against:

```text
human-labeled benchmark
```

Measure agreement and known limitations.

---

# 274. Evaluation Versioning

Store:

```text
judge model

judge prompt

evaluation dataset

metric code
```

so evaluation results are reproducible.

---

# 275. Continuous Red Teaming

For high-risk generative applications:

```text
periodic adversarial tests
```

against production versions can detect regressions.

---

# 276. Governance and Monitoring Integration

Monitoring finds:

```text
quality threshold breached
```

Governance workflow can automatically:

```text
open review

restrict traffic

mark model degraded
```

---

# 277. Automated Governance Response

Example:

```text
High-Risk Model
Recall < 70%
for 3 consecutive windows
       |
       v
Set status = DEGRADED
       |
       v
Page owner
       |
       v
Freeze new traffic increase
```

Automation should be carefully tested.

---

# 278. Automatic Shutdown

For some critical safety conditions:

```text
immediate shutdown
```

may be justified.

For others, false positives may be worse.

Risk analysis determines automation.

---

# 279. Governance State vs Runtime State

Governance:

```text
APPROVED
```

Runtime:

```text
HEALTHY
```

These are separate.

A model can be:

```text
approved but unhealthy
```

or:

```text
technically healthy but unapproved
```

Both dimensions matter.

---

# 280. Model State Matrix

```text
                Runtime
             Healthy   Unhealthy

Approved       Serve     Mitigate

Unapproved     Block     Block
```

Simplified, but useful mental model.

---

# 281. Governance Anti-Pattern — Spreadsheet Inventory

Spreadsheet contains:

```text
model names
```

but is outdated.

Production reality differs.

Inventory should integrate automatically with platform state.

---

# 282. Anti-Pattern — Governance After Deployment

Team deploys first.

Then asks:

```text
Can someone approve this?
```

Governance should be in release path.

---

# 283. Anti-Pattern — Same Controls for Everything

Makes low-risk development painfully slow.

Use risk-based controls.

---

# 284. Anti-Pattern — Manual Evidence Collection

Engineers spend days copying metrics into documents.

Automate evidence from source systems.

---

# 285. Anti-Pattern — Approval Without Version

Reviewer approves:

```text
fraud model
```

but which version?

Approval must bind to immutable artifact/version.

---

# 286. Anti-Pattern — Approval Without Scope

Approved for:

```text
internal pilot
```

later used globally.

Scope expansion should trigger review.

---

# 287. Anti-Pattern — Human Review as Magic

Human approval is useless if reviewers lack:

```text
context

time

authority
```

Design meaningful oversight.

---

# 288. Anti-Pattern — Fairness Is One Metric

No universal fairness score exists.

Choose appropriate metrics based on domain and policy.

---

# 289. Anti-Pattern — Explainability Equals Causality

Feature contribution is not proof of causal reason.

Do not misrepresent explanation outputs.

---

# 290. Anti-Pattern — Remove Protected Attribute and Declare Fairness

Proxy variables may retain correlated information.

Evaluate outcomes empirically.

---

# 291. Anti-Pattern — LLM Governance Only at Model Level

Production behavior also depends on:

```text
prompt

RAG

tools

guardrails

application logic
```

Govern complete system.

---

# 292. Anti-Pattern — Agent Has Broad Credentials

One prompt-injection incident becomes:

```text
enterprise compromise
```

Use least privilege and external authorization.

---

# 293. Anti-Pattern — Prompt as Untracked String

Prompt changed manually in UI.

Behavior changes.

No one knows when.

Version prompts.

---

# 294. Anti-Pattern — RAG Index Has No ACLs

Search retrieves documents user should not access.

Authorization must propagate to retrieval.

---

# 295. Anti-Pattern — Fallback Is Ungoverned

Primary model fails.

System automatically routes to old unapproved model.

DR cannot ignore governance.

---

# 296. Anti-Pattern — Retire Runtime but Delete Evidence

Later audit asks about historical decision.

Evidence is gone.

Serving lifecycle and evidence lifecycle are separate.

---

# 297. Anti-Pattern — Permanent Exception

Temporary bypass:

```text
expires never
```

becomes hidden policy failure.

All exceptions need ownership and expiry.

---

# 298. Anti-Pattern — Governance Control Plane Is Serving Dependency

Governance database goes down.

Every prediction fails.

Cache approved state and separate planes where appropriate.

---

# 299. Anti-Pattern — No Revocation Path

Unsafe model discovered.

Only way to stop it:

```text
manually edit 40 deployments
```

Build centralized revocation mechanisms.

---

6. Why document out-of-scope use?

7. What is model risk?

9. Inherent vs residual risk?

10. Why does decision reversibility affect risk?

---

## Risk Classification

11. How would you classify model risk?

12. What factors determine risk tier?

13. Why does degree of automation matter?

14. Why does user impact scale matter?

15. How does sensitive data affect model risk?

16. What constitutes a material model change?

17. When should model revalidation occur?

---

## Approval

19. Why should approval bind to immutable model version?

20. What is separation of duties?

21. What is the four-eyes principle?

22. When should approvals expire?

23. How would you handle emergency deployment?

24. What is conditional approval?

25. What evidence should an approver review?

---

## Policy as Code

26. What is policy as code?

27. Policy decision point vs enforcement point?

28. Where should ML governance policies be enforced?

29. How do you prevent API bypass of UI controls?

30. How should policy versions be managed?

31. How do you safely deploy a new policy?

32. What is dry-run policy evaluation?

---

## Lineage / Audit

33. What is model lineage?

34. What is decision lineage?

35. Why are stable resource IDs important?

36. What should an audit log contain?

37. Operational logs vs audit logs?

38. Why should governance evidence be immutable?

39. How would you reproduce a historical production decision?

40. What is provenance attestation?

41. Why sign model artifacts?

---

## Responsible AI

42. What is fairness?

43. Why is there no universal fairness metric?

44. What is demographic parity?

45. What is equal opportunity?

46. What is equalized odds?

47. What is individual fairness?

48. Why are intersectional slices important?

49. What makes fairness monitoring difficult?

50. What is explainability?

51. Global vs local explanations?

52. Why is explainability not causality?

53. What is meaningful human oversight?

54. Human-in-the-loop vs human-on-the-loop?

55. What is automation bias?

56. Why is model abstention useful?

---

## Privacy

57. What is data minimization?

58. What is purpose limitation?

59. How should sensitive features be governed?

60. Why can auditability conflict with privacy?

61. How would you retain evidence without retaining unnecessary raw user data?

62. How does data residency affect governance?

63. How should deletion propagate into derived ML assets?

---

## Model Cards / Documentation

64. What is a model card?

65. What should a model card contain?

66. Why should model cards be partially generated automatically?

67. What is a data sheet?

68. Why document model limitations?

69. How would you keep documentation synchronized with production state?

---

## Third-Party Models

70. What additional risks exist when using external models?

71. How do you govern SaaS LLM providers?

72. What data-egress controls are needed?

73. Why pin model versions when possible?

74. What is a foundation-model registry?

75. How would you handle vendor model changes?

76. What is a third-party model exit strategy?

---

## LLM / RAG

77. Why is prompt a governed production artifact?

78. What should prompt metadata include?

79. What is RAG governance?

80. Why must document ACLs propagate to vector search?

81. Why should embedding indexes be treated as sensitive derived data?

82. How do you govern embedding model changes?

83. How do you govern rerankers?

84. How should document deletion propagate through RAG?

85. Why are citations alone not enough to guarantee groundedness?

---

## Agents

86. Why are agents higher risk than passive chatbots?

87. How should agent tools be classified?

88. What is external tool authorization?

89. Why should agents use least privilege?

93. Why should agents have step and cost limits?

94. How would you govern a refund agent?

## Lifecycle

95. When should a model be retired?

# 314. Governance Failure Walkthrough — Policy Engine Down

Existing approved serving:

```text
continues
```

```text
temporarily blocked
```

```text
cached signed policy state
```

where appropriate.

# 315. Failure Walkthrough — Audit Store Down

```text
may buffer
```


if audit evidence is mandatory.

```text
backups
```

# 317. Failure Walkthrough — Unapproved Endpoint Detected

Detective control finds:

```text
production endpoint
not in inventory
```

```text
register incident
```

# 318. Failure Walkthrough — Prompt Change Causes Harmful Behavior

```text
prompt-v19
```

deployed at:

```text
14:02
```

```text

```

Then update governance evidence and investigate approval failure.

---

# 319. Failure Walkthrough — RAG Leaks Confidential Document

Investigate:

```text
document ACL

index metadata

retrieval filter

cache

user identity
```

Contain:

```text

remove document chunks

fix authorization
```

# 320. Failure Walkthrough — Agent Executes Unauthorized Action

```text

which credentials?

which authorization decision?

which model/prompt?

```

# 330. Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> We need AI governance.

Do not answer:

```text
Let's create an approval form.
```

Ask:

```text
What decisions do these models make?

Which are high impact?

Which data classes do they use?

What evidence must exist?

Who owns risk?

Which controls can be automated?

Where must policy be enforced?

How do we know what is running?

How do we revoke it?

How do we reconstruct a historical decision?

How do we prevent governance
from becoming a delivery bottleneck?
```

That is enterprise ML governance architecture.

# 331. What You Must Remember From Chapter 20

1. **ML governance is the system of ownership, evidence, policy, approval, monitoring, and lifecycle controls around ML systems.**

2. **Governance is an architecture concern when controls must operate consistently across thousands of models and teams.**

3. **A model registry manages artifacts; a model inventory provides the enterprise governance view.**

4. **Every production model should have clear technical and business ownership.**

5. **Models must have explicitly documented intended and prohibited use cases.**

6. **Risk-based governance prevents low-risk experimentation from receiving the same controls as high-impact automated decisioning.**

7. **Model risk depends on impact, automation, scale, reversibility, data sensitivity, and context.**

8. **Inherent risk describes risk before controls; residual risk describes what remains afterward.**

9. **Governance evidence should be machine-readable and directly linked to immutable model versions wherever possible.**

10. **Approvals should bind to specific artifacts, purposes, environments, and scopes rather than vague model names.**

11. **High-risk workflows may require separation of duties and independent validation.**

12. **Material changes should trigger appropriate revalidation rather than treating every change identically.**

13. **Policy as code converts governance requirements into consistent, automated enforcement.**

14. **Policies must be enforced at authoritative backend boundaries, not only in UI workflows.**

15. **Model lifecycle should be implemented as explicit governed states and transitions.**

16. **Audit trails must record who changed what, when, and why.**

17. **Decision lineage connects individual production outcomes to model, feature, threshold, policy, and input context.**

18. **Reproducibility and auditability depend on immutable datasets, artifacts, configuration, and evidence.**

19. **Privacy and governance can conflict; evidence should be retained without unnecessarily retaining sensitive raw data.**

20. **Data minimization and purpose limitation should influence training and serving architecture.**

21. **Fairness is context-dependent and cannot be reduced to one universal metric.**

22. **Removing a protected attribute does not automatically eliminate unfairness or proxy effects.**

23. **Explainability is not the same as causality, and explanation methods themselves require validation.**

24. **Human oversight is meaningful only when reviewers have information, time, authority, and the ability to disagree with the model.**

25. **Abstention and escalation can be safer than forcing a model to make low-confidence decisions.**

26. **Model cards and dataset documentation should combine automatically generated evidence with human interpretation.**

27. **Third-party models introduce vendor, privacy, availability, versioning, and policy risk.**

28. **Enterprise LLM gateways can centralize identity, data controls, provider policy, routing, and auditing.**

29. **Foundation models should be inventoried and approved like other significant production dependencies.**

30. **Prompt versions are production artifacts because prompt changes can materially change application behavior.**

31. **RAG governance must cover source documents, ACLs, chunking, embeddings, indexes, retrieval, freshness, and deletion.**

32. **Vector indexes derived from sensitive documents must themselves be treated as governed data assets.**

33. **Agents are higher risk because they can act on systems rather than merely generate text.**

34. **Agent tool permissions must use least privilege and external authorization rather than trusting model instructions.**

35. **High-impact agent actions should support human confirmation, hard limits, and rapid kill switches.**

36. **Model and agent revocation must be first-class runtime capabilities.**

37. **Fallback models and providers must be governed and tested before they are needed.**

38. **Retiring a runtime does not necessarily mean deleting its audit and evidence history.**

39. **Model approvals and risk acceptances should expire or be revalidated when appropriate.**

40. **Continuous compliance collects evidence throughout the lifecycle rather than assembling it manually before audits.**

41. **Preventive, detective, and corrective controls are all necessary in mature governance programs.**

42. **Temporary governance exceptions should have ownership, scope, justification, and automatic expiration.**

43. **Policy versions themselves need testing, auditability, staged rollout, and rollback.**

44. **Governance control-plane failures should not unnecessarily terminate already approved production inference.**

45. **Existing serving, new deployments, and revocations may require different behavior during governance outages.**

46. **Governance data such as approvals, risk records, audit evidence, and policy versions requires its own DR strategy.**

47. **Enterprise model governance requires integration between model registry, data catalog, observability, security, CI/CD, and identity systems.**

48. **Governance should be built into the platform golden path so the safest path is also the easiest path.**

49. **The success of governance should be measured not only by compliance but by coverage, risk reduction, time to approval, and user adoption.**

50. **At architect level, governance means designing a system where every important ML decision has an owner, evidence, policy context, lifecycle, monitoring strategy, and reliable path to containment or retirement.**
