## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 22 — Cost Engineering and FinOps for ML: GPU Economics, Unit Economics, Capacity Efficiency, Cloud Cost Architecture, Showback, Chargeback, Training Optimization, and LLM Cost Control

---

# 1. Why Cost Is an Architecture Property

An ML platform can be:

```text
reliable

secure

scalable

accurate
```

and still fail because:

```text
it costs too much to operate
```

For senior architects:

> Cost is not something Finance analyzes after deployment.

It must influence architecture before deployment.

---

# 2. ML Cost Is Different From Ordinary Application Cost

Traditional service cost may be dominated by:

```text
CPU

memory

database

network
```

ML adds expensive dimensions:

```text
GPU / TPU accelerators

training experiments

large checkpoints

petabyte-scale datasets

vector databases

embedding generation

LLM tokens

high-bandwidth networking
```

---

# 3. FinOps

FinOps combines:

```text
engineering

finance

operations

business
```

to understand and optimize cloud economics.

For MLOps:

```text
ML FinOps
=
Cloud FinOps
+
Accelerator Economics
+
Model Economics
+
Experiment Economics
```

---

# 4. Cost Visibility Comes First

You cannot optimize:

```text
what you cannot attribute
```

Start by knowing:

```text
which team?

which model?

which training run?

which endpoint?

which tenant?

which project?
```

generated the cost.

---

# 5. Total Cost of Ownership

Do not calculate only:

```text
GPU cost
```

Real TCO may include:

```text
accelerators

CPU hosts

RAM

storage

network

managed services

observability

licenses

engineering operations
```

---

# 6. Direct vs Indirect Cost

Direct:

```text
GPU-hours for training
```

Indirect:

```text
shared scheduler

logging system

artifact registry

platform engineering
```

Both matter for business economics.

---

# 7. Fixed vs Variable Cost

Fixed-like:

```text
reserved GPU fleet

baseline platform

licenses
```

Variable:

```text
token volume

training hours

network egress

on-demand compute
```

Understanding which costs scale with usage is essential.

---

# 8. Unit Economics

Instead of asking:

```text
How much does the ML platform cost?
```

ask:

```text
What does one useful unit cost?
```

Examples:

```text
cost per prediction

cost per 1,000 predictions

cost per million tokens

cost per training run

cost per successful experiment

cost per customer interaction
```

---

# 9. Why Unit Economics Matters

Suppose monthly inference cost:

```text
₹50 million
```

That number alone tells little.

If serving:

```text
50 billion predictions
```

unit economics may be excellent.

If serving:

```text
5 million predictions
```

it may be terrible.

---

# 10. Basic Cost Equation

Conceptually:

```text
Total Cost
=
Compute
+
Storage
+
Network
+
Managed Services
+
Operational Overhead
```

Each component requires separate optimization.

---

# 11. GPU-Hour

A common training cost unit:

```text
1 GPU
used for
1 hour
=
1 GPU-hour
```

Example:

```text
64 GPUs
×
10 hours
=
640 GPU-hours
```

---

# 12. Training Run Cost

Simplified:

```text
Training Cost
=
GPU Count
× Runtime
× Cost per GPU-hour
```

Plus:

```text
storage

CPU

network

orchestration
```

---

# 13. GPU-Hours Can Mislead

Suppose:

```text
Run A
100 GPUs
× 10 hr
=
1000 GPU-hours
```

Run B:

```text
200 GPUs
× 4 hr
=
800 GPU-hours
```

Run B uses more GPUs but costs less accelerator time.

Scale-out can sometimes reduce total cost.

---

# 14. Faster Is Sometimes Cheaper

If expensive GPU is:

```text
2× hourly price
```

but executes workload:

```text
4× faster
```

then total cost may decrease.

Always compare:

```text
cost per completed workload
```

not hourly rate alone.

---

# 15. Performance per Dollar

Useful metric:

```text
Useful Throughput
-----------------
Cost
```

Examples:

```text
tokens/sec per dollar

samples/sec per dollar
```

---

# 16. Time-to-Result Has Economic Value

A model experiment completing:

```text
today
```

instead of:

```text
next week
```

may have value beyond compute cost.

Optimization can target:

```text
cost

latency to insight
```

simultaneously.

---

# 17. Cost vs Opportunity Cost

Saving:

```text
20% GPU cost
```

while increasing researcher wait time:

```text
5×
```

might be a poor business trade.

Architecture decisions should include human productivity.

---

# 18. Cost of Queue Time

Queue time does not directly consume GPU.

But it can delay:

```text
experiments

launches

incident fixes

retraining
```

Therefore platform economics includes:

```text
developer time
```

---

# 19. Cost of Failed Experiments

Run:

```text
256 GPUs
for 24 hours
```

then fails because:

```text
bad dataset
```

All compute was wasted.

Preventing bad runs through early validation can provide enormous savings.

---

# 20. Cost Avoidance

Cost optimization is not only:

```text
cheaper hardware
```

It includes avoiding unnecessary work.

Examples:

```text
fail fast

reuse features

reuse embeddings

cache datasets

stop bad experiments
```

---

# 21. Training Cost Decomposition

Training cost may include:

```text
data preparation

dataset scan

GPU training

checkpointing

evaluation

hyperparameter search
```

Do not optimize only main training loop.

---

# 22. Experiment Cost

An experiment can trigger:

```text
data query

feature generation

training

evaluation

artifact storage
```

A mature platform attaches cost to experiment ID.

---

# 23. Cost per Successful Experiment

Suppose:

```text
100 experiments

10 produce meaningful results

total cost = ₹1M
```

Then:

```text
cost per useful result
≈ ₹100k
```

This can expose excessive trial-and-error.

---

# 24. Hyperparameter Search Cost

If:

```text
100 trials
```

each cost:

```text
₹10k
```

search costs:

```text
₹1M
```

Need to ask whether all trials deserve equal resources.

---

# 25. Early Stopping

If trial clearly performs poorly:

```text
stop it early
```

instead of running to completion.

This can dramatically reduce HPO cost.

---

# 26. Successive Halving Mental Model

Give many candidates small budgets.

```text
100 candidates
      |
      v
20 promising
      |
      v
5 promising
      |
      v
1 winner
```

Spend more only on promising trials.

---

# 27. Cheap Proxy Evaluation

Before full expensive training:

```text
smaller dataset

fewer epochs

smaller model
```

may reject obviously bad configurations.

Be careful that the proxy remains predictive of final performance.

---

# 28. Progressive Experiment Scaling

Start:

```text
1 GPU
```

then:

```text
8 GPUs
```

then:

```text
256 GPUs
```

only after evidence supports scaling.

This prevents wasting giant clusters on broken code.

---

# 29. Preflight Validation

Before GPU allocation:

```text
schema valid?

dataset exists?

code imports?

container starts?

checkpoint valid?

permissions work?
```

Run inexpensive checks first.

---

# 30. GPU Cost of Idle Time

Suppose 512 GPUs allocated.

Training waits:

```text
20 minutes
```

for dataset download.

Wasted:

```text
512 × 1/3 hour
≈ 171 GPU-hours
```

Every startup inefficiency multiplies at scale.

---

# 31. Pre-Stage Before Allocation

Better:

```text
container image

dataset cache

checkpoint
```

prepared before expensive GPU reservation.

Allocate accelerator only when workload can start.

---

# 32. Resource Acquisition Ordering

Bad:

```text
Acquire GPUs

then download 20 TB dataset
```

Better:

```text
prepare data
validate runtime
then acquire GPUs
```

where architecture permits.

---

# 33. GPU Utilization vs Cost Efficiency

GPU utilization:

```text
90%
```

may still be economically poor if:

```text
workload could run on cheaper GPU
```

or:

```text
model is oversized
```

Utilization is not the same as cost efficiency.

---

# 34. Allocated vs Useful GPU Time

Track:

```text
allocated GPU-hours
```

and:

```text
productive GPU-hours
```

Difference is waste.

---

# 35. Useful Compute Ratio

Conceptually:

```text
Useful Compute Time
-------------------
Allocated Accelerator Time
```

Waste sources:

```text
data waiting

job startup

checkpointing

stragglers

failures
```

---

# 36. GPU Occupancy Is Not Business Value

A GPU running at 100% for:

```text
unnecessary experiment
```

is still waste.

FinOps asks:

```text
Was the computation valuable?
```

not merely busy.

---

# 37. Right-Sizing

Workload asks:

```text
8 GPUs
```

but needs:

```text
2
```

Then 75% capacity is unnecessary.

Right-sizing aligns requested resources with workload needs.

---

# 38. Over-Requesting Memory

Pod asks:

```text
256 GB CPU RAM
```

uses:

```text
20 GB
```

This can prevent efficient bin packing.

Cost appears as idle capacity.

---

# 39. Over-Requesting GPUs

Notebook reserves:

```text
1 large GPU
```

while running only light preprocessing.

Use CPU for CPU work.

---

# 40. GPU Type Right-Sizing

Do not use premium training GPU for:

```text
tiny embedding model
```

if a cheaper accelerator satisfies:

```text
latency

memory

throughput
```

requirements.

---

# 41. Hardware Profiles

Platform can expose:

```text
small-inference

standard-training

large-memory-training

high-bandwidth-distributed
```

rather than requiring users to understand every SKU.

---

# 42. Cost-Aware Placement

Scheduler considers:

```text
cost

availability

data locality

hardware fit

priority
```

not just:

```text
first cluster with capacity
```

---

# 43. Cheapest Is Not Always Cheapest

Region A GPU:

```text
lower hourly price
```

but dataset in Region B.

Cross-region transfer may erase savings.

Architecture should calculate:

```text
compute + data movement
```

together.

---

# 44. Data Gravity Economics

Moving:

```text
1 PB
```

for one training run may cost more than moving compute to the dataset.

Therefore:

```text
schedule compute near data
```

when practical.

---

# 45. Network Egress

Cloud architectures often charge for certain data transfers.

Potential expensive paths:

```text
cross-region

internet egress

cross-cloud
```

Track ML data movement explicitly.

---

# 46. Training Egress Trap

Dataset in:

```text
Cloud A
```

GPU capacity in:

```text
Cloud B
```

Daily transfer:

```text
100 TB
```

may make multi-cloud training economically unattractive.

---

# 47. Multi-Cloud Economics

Benefits:

```text
capacity access

vendor diversification

specialized services
```

Costs:

```text
data transfer

duplicate platforms

operational complexity

discount fragmentation
```

Multi-cloud is not automatically cost optimization.

---

# 48. Reserved Capacity

Commit to capacity in exchange for:

```text
price predictability

supply predictability
```

Best for:

```text
steady baseline demand
```

---

# 49. On-Demand Capacity

Useful for:

```text
bursty demand

unknown workloads

temporary experiments
```

but often more expensive per hour.

---

# 50. Spot / Preemptible Compute

Provider may reclaim machine.

Usually cheaper.

Ideal for workloads that are:

```text
restartable

checkpointable

fault tolerant
```

---

# 51. Spot Economics

Suppose:

```text
spot = 40% cost of on-demand
```

but job restarts often.

True cost:

```text
discounted compute
+
lost work
+
recovery overhead
```

Still may be attractive if checkpointing is good.

---

# 52. Checkpoint Economics

More frequent checkpoints:

```text
less lost compute
```

but:

```text
more storage I/O

more training interruption
```

There is an economic optimum.

---

# 53. Expected Lost Work

Conceptually:

```text
Expected Loss
≈
Failure Frequency
×
Average Work Lost per Failure
×
GPU Cost
```

Checkpoint interval affects average lost work.

---

# 54. Checkpoint Frequency Trade-Off

Every:

```text
5 minutes
```

may waste I/O.

Every:

```text
12 hours
```

may waste enormous compute after failure.

Choose based on:

```text
job size

failure probability

checkpoint duration

GPU cost
```

---

# 55. Capacity Commit Mix

Mature platform may use:

```text
reserved baseline

+

on-demand burst

+

spot batch workloads
```

rather than one purchase model.

---

# 56. Base vs Burst Capacity

Example:

```text
70% predictable demand
-> reserved

20% burst
-> on-demand

10% opportunistic
-> spot
```

Exact ratios depend on business.

---

# 57. Capacity Utilization

Reserved capacity is only economical if used sufficiently.

Unused reservation:

```text
still costs money
```

Track:

```text
committed capacity utilization
```

---

# 58. Reservation Waste

Team reserves:

```text
100 GPUs
```

average usage:

```text
20
```

80% idle.

Better:

```text
shared capacity pool
```

if isolation permits.

---

# 59. Shared GPU Pool Economics

Benefits:

```text
higher utilization

bursty demand aggregation

less stranded capacity
```

Challenges:

```text
queueing

isolation

fairness
```

---

# 60. Statistical Multiplexing

Team A peaks Monday.

Team B peaks Wednesday.

Shared fleet may need:

```text
less total capacity
```

than separate dedicated fleets.

This is a major economic benefit of platforms.

---

# 61. Dedicated Fleet Cost

Dedicated hardware may be justified for:

```text
strict security

predictable latency

guaranteed supply
```

Cost optimization must respect constraints.

---

# 62. Cost vs Isolation

Shared:

```text
cheaper
```

Dedicated:

```text
stronger isolation
```

Architects must quantify the premium for isolation.

---

# 63. Cost of Reliability

High availability often requires:

```text
replicas

multi-zone

warm standby

headroom
```

All increase cost.

Reliability is not free.

---

# 64. Reliability Premium

Example:

```text
1 replica
cost = X

3 replicas across zones
cost ≈ 3X
```

before efficiency gains.

Business must understand the cost of stronger SLOs.

---

# 65. SLO Cost Curve

Increasing from:

```text
99%
```

to:

```text
99.9%
```

may be relatively affordable.

Increasing to:

```text
99.999%
```

may require dramatically more redundancy.

Reliability cost is nonlinear.

---

# 66. Headroom Economics

Operating cluster at:

```text
100% utilization
```

maximizes apparent efficiency.

But provides:

```text
zero failure capacity

zero burst capacity
```

Some idle capacity is intentional insurance.

---

# 67. Cost of Headroom

If fleet:

```text
1000 GPUs
```

and maintain:

```text
15% headroom
```

150 GPUs may appear unused.

But they buy:

```text
failure tolerance

traffic elasticity

priority response
```

---

# 68. Warm Capacity

Warm nodes cost money while idle.

Benefit:

```text
lower startup latency
```

Therefore use where queue/startup SLO has economic value.

---

# 69. Cold Capacity

Scale from zero.

Cheaper while idle.

But:

```text
provisioning delay

model load delay
```

may hurt interactive workloads.

---

# 70. Training vs Inference Economics

Training is often:

```text
batch

interruptible

scheduled
```

Inference is often:

```text
latency-sensitive

always available

traffic-driven
```

Optimization strategies differ.

---

# 71. Training Can Chase Cheap Capacity

Some training jobs can wait for:

```text
spot availability

cheaper region

off-peak capacity
```

Serving usually has less flexibility.

---

# 72. Deadline-Aware Scheduling

Job requirement:

```text
finish by tomorrow 08:00
```

Scheduler can choose:

```text
cheapest capacity
```

that still meets deadline.

This is better than immediate scheduling for all batch work.

---

# 73. Cost-Aware Queueing

Low-priority experiment:

```text
wait for cheaper capacity
```

Critical retraining:

```text
use expensive capacity now
```

Priority maps business value to cost.

---

# 74. Carbon / Energy-Aware Scheduling

Some organizations may also optimize:

```text
energy use

carbon intensity
```

when workload deadlines permit.

This adds another scheduling dimension.

---

# 75. Inference Unit Cost

Useful metric:

```text
Serving Cost
------------
Predictions
```

Example:

```text
₹ per million predictions
```

---

# 76. Inference Cost Components

```text
GPU/CPU runtime

idle replicas

model loading

feature lookup

network

logging

caches
```

Model runtime is only part of the bill.

---

# 77. Idle Replica Cost

Endpoint receives:

```text
10 requests/hour
```

but has:

```text
4 large GPUs
```

always running.

Unit cost becomes enormous.

---

# 78. Scale-to-Zero

For infrequent workloads:

```text
zero replicas when idle
```

may save substantial cost.

Trade-off:

```text
cold-start latency
```

---

# 79. Cold-Start Cost

Cold start can include:

```text
node provisioning

container pull

model download

GPU initialization

warmup
```

Large models may take substantial time.

---

# 80. Scale-to-Zero Decision

Good for:

```text
offline inference

internal low-frequency models
```

Poor for:

```text
latency-critical real-time API
```

unless warm-start architecture exists.

---

# 81. Minimum Replica Count

Set based on:

```text
availability requirement

traffic baseline

startup duration
```

Not arbitrary default.

---

# 82. Autoscaling Economics

Too slow:

```text
SLO violations
```

Too aggressive:

```text
unused replicas
```

Autoscaling is both reliability and FinOps control.

---

# 83. Reactive Autoscaling

Scale after:

```text
traffic rises
```

Simple.

But slow GPU startup can lag demand.

---

# 84. Predictive Scaling

Use known pattern:

```text
traffic peaks daily at 18:00
```

pre-scale before the peak.

This may reduce headroom needs.

---

# 85. Queue-Based Scaling

For inference:

```text
queue length

queue age
```

can reflect actual pressure better than CPU utilization.

---

# 86. Token-Based LLM Autoscaling

LLM demand varies with:

```text
input tokens

output tokens

active sequences
```

Requests/sec alone is weak.

Scale using workload units closer to:

```text
tokens
```

---

# 87. Cost per Token

Conceptually:

```text
Total Serving Cost
------------------
Total Tokens
```

Often express as:

```text
cost per million tokens
```

---

# 88. Input vs Output Token Economics

Input tokens consume:

```text
prefill compute

context memory
```

Output tokens consume:

```text
repeated decode computation
```

The economic profile differs.

---

# 89. Long Context Is Expensive

Increasing context from:

```text
4k
```

to:

```text
100k tokens
```

can increase:

```text
prefill compute

KV-cache memory

latency
```

dramatically.

Long context should have a business reason.

---

# 90. Prompt Bloat

System prompt grows from:

```text
1,000 tokens
```

to:

```text
8,000 tokens
```

and is repeated for every request.

Monthly cost can multiply silently.

Prompt length is a FinOps metric.

---

# 91. Prompt Compression

Remove:

```text
duplicate instructions

unused examples

verbose boilerplate
```

while preserving quality.

This can reduce:

```text
cost

TTFT

memory pressure
```

---

# 92. Context Selection

Do not insert:

```text
entire knowledge base
```

into every prompt.

Retrieve only relevant context.

RAG is partly a cost architecture.

---

# 93. RAG Context Cost

Retrieve:

```text
50 chunks
```

when only:

```text
5
```

are useful.

You pay for:

```text
embedding/retrieval

reranking

input tokens

KV cache
```

---

# 94. Retrieval Top-K Economics

Higher K may improve recall but increases:

```text
context size

latency

token cost
```

Tune based on measured quality.

---

# 95. Reranker Economics

Reranker adds:

```text
compute

latency
```

but may reduce context size and improve quality.

Total system cost may decrease if fewer irrelevant tokens reach expensive LLM.

---

# 96. Embedding Cost

RAG requires embeddings for:

```text
documents

queries
```

Costs include:

```text
embedding model inference

indexing compute

storage
```

---

# 97. Embedding Reuse

Document unchanged?

Do not recompute embedding.

Use:

```text
content hash
```

to identify reusable outputs.

---

# 98. Incremental Indexing

Instead of rebuilding:

```text
1 billion document index
```

daily:

```text
update only changed documents
```

when architecture permits.

---

# 99. Vector Storage Cost

Vector database stores:

```text
embedding vectors

metadata

indexes

replicas
```

Larger embedding dimensions increase storage.

---

# 100. Embedding Dimension Economics

Suppose:

```text
768 dimensions
```

versus:

```text
3072 dimensions
```

Higher dimension increases:

```text
memory

storage

network
```

and potentially retrieval cost.

Evaluate whether quality gain justifies it.

---

# 101. Vector Replication Cost

Three replicas improve availability.

But storage and memory may roughly multiply.

Again:

```text
reliability has a price
```

---

# 102. Retrieval Cache

Frequently repeated queries may reuse:

```text
retrieval results
```

if freshness and security allow.

Cache keys must include:

```text
tenant

ACL context

index version
```

to avoid leaks.

---

# 103. LLM Response Cache

For deterministic or reusable requests:

```text
cache full response
```

can eliminate model cost.

But check:

```text
personalization

freshness

security

nondeterminism
```

---

# 104. Semantic Cache

Requests with similar meaning may share results.

Potential savings:

```text
LLM calls avoided
```

But incorrect semantic matches can harm quality.

---

# 105. Cache Economics

A cache costs:

```text
storage

memory

operations
```

Use when:

```text
saved downstream compute
>
cache cost
```

---

# 106. Cache Hit Rate

If cache costs ₹X and avoids only:

```text
0.1%
```

of calls, it may not be worthwhile.

Measure:

```text
hit rate

cost avoided
```

---

# 107. Model Routing

Not every request needs the largest model.

Architecture:

```text
Request
   |
   v
Router
   |
   +---- Small Model
   |
   +---- Medium Model
   |
   +---- Large Model
```

---

# 108. Complexity-Based Routing

Simple requests:

```text
small cheap model
```

Complex requests:

```text
large capable model
```

This can reduce average cost significantly.

---

# 109. Cascaded Models

Flow:

```text
Small Model
   |
   +---- confident -> answer
   |
   +---- uncertain -> Large Model
```

Large model handles only difficult requests.

---

# 110. Cascade Economics

Suppose:

```text
80% requests solved by small model
```

Only:

```text
20%
```

use expensive model.

Total cost can drop dramatically.

But route quality must be monitored.

---

# 111. Router Error Cost

Wrong routing:

```text
hard request -> cheap weak model
```

harms quality.

Too conservative routing:

```text
everything -> giant model
```

removes savings.

Routing itself needs evaluation.

---

# 112. Quality per Dollar

Useful objective:

```text
Quality Score
-------------
Cost
```

Architecture should seek Pareto-efficient points.

---

# 113. Pareto Frontier

A model is dominated if another option is:

```text
cheaper
AND
better quality
```

Useful model choices live near frontier between:

```text
quality

latency

cost
```

---

# 114. Model Size Economics

Larger model often increases:

```text
memory

compute

latency

cost
```

but may improve quality.

Architects should ask:

```text
How much quality do we gain
per additional dollar?
```

---

# 115. Distillation

Train smaller model to imitate larger teacher.

Potential result:

```text
similar task quality

much lower serving cost
```

Useful for narrow high-volume tasks.

---

# 116. Quantization

Reducing weight precision can reduce:

```text
memory footprint

memory bandwidth

hardware requirement
```

and improve throughput.

Must validate:

```text
quality
```

---

# 117. Quantization Economics

If model moves from:

```text
4 GPUs
```

to:

```text
2 GPUs
```

per replica with acceptable quality, serving cost can change dramatically.

---

# 118. Batching

Process multiple requests together.

Benefits:

```text
higher GPU efficiency

higher throughput
```

Trade:

```text
queue wait latency
```

---

# 119. Batch Size Economics

Larger batch:

```text
better throughput
```

up to limits.

But can increase:

```text
latency

memory
```

Optimize against SLO.

---

# 120. Dynamic Batching

Wait briefly to combine requests.

Example:

```text
batch window = few milliseconds
```

Can improve utilization while maintaining latency target.

---

# 121. Continuous Batching

For LLMs, requests join and leave active execution continuously.

This improves:

```text
GPU utilization

tokens/sec
```

and lowers unit cost.

---

# 122. KV Cache Economics

KV cache consumes HBM per active sequence.

If memory fills:

```text
fewer concurrent users
```

Cost per token rises.

Efficient KV management improves economics.

---

# 123. Paged KV Cache

Reduces fragmentation and can increase concurrency.

Higher concurrency:

```text
more useful work
per GPU
```

---

# 124. Prefix Cache Economics

Repeated long system prompt:

```text
shared prefix
```

can sometimes reuse cached computation.

This reduces repeated prefill work.

---

# 125. Speculative Decoding

A smaller model may propose tokens while a larger model verifies them.

Goal:

```text
increase decode throughput
```

Architecture complexity increases.

Economic value depends on actual hardware/runtime results.

---

# 126. Disaggregated Serving Economics

Separate:

```text
prefill

decode
```

onto specialized pools.

Potential:

```text
better hardware utilization
```

but introduces:

```text
network

KV transfer

operational complexity
```

Only worthwhile at sufficient scale.

---

# 127. Multi-Model Serving

Instead of one dedicated GPU per small model:

```text
many small models
share serving runtime
```

improves utilization.

---

# 128. Model Colocation

Potential savings:

```text
less idle GPU capacity
```

Risks:

```text
noisy neighbors

memory pressure

latency variance
```

---

# 129. Idle Model Eviction

Unload rarely used model from GPU.

Load when needed.

This improves capacity but causes:

```text
cold-start latency
```

---

# 130. Model Cache

Keep most frequently used models resident.

Evict cold models.

This becomes:

```text
cache management
```

for accelerators.

---

# 131. Cost of Model Loading

Repeatedly downloading:

```text
20 GB model
```

causes:

```text
storage I/O

network

startup delay
```

Local caches can reduce this.

---

# 132. Artifact Cache Economics

Node-local model cache consumes disk.

Benefit:

```text
reduced startup time

reduced registry bandwidth
```

Evaluate cache hit rate.

---

# 133. Feature Platform Cost

Features consume:

```text
batch compute

streaming compute

online storage

offline storage

network
```

A feature reused by many models may be economical.

---

# 134. Duplicate Features Waste

Ten teams compute same:

```text
customer_30d_spend
```

independently.

Cost multiplies.

Feature reuse is FinOps.

---

# 135. Materialize vs Compute On Demand

Materialize:

```text
pay once

store result
```

Compute on demand:

```text
pay every query
```

Choose based on:

```text
reuse frequency

storage cost

freshness
```

---

# 136. Feature TTL

Do not retain every feature forever.

Set retention based on:

```text
training needs

audit needs

recomputation cost
```

---

# 137. Streaming Cost

Always-running stream processors incur baseline cost.

Ask whether a feature really needs:

```text
sub-second freshness
```

or:

```text
hourly batch
```

would suffice.

---

# 138. Freshness Has a Price

Approximate pattern:

```text
daily batch
<
hourly microbatch
<
real-time streaming
```

in complexity and often cost.

Use the slowest freshness tier satisfying business requirements.

---

# 139. Over-Engineering Freshness

Feature used for monthly churn model does not need:

```text
10 ms updates
```

Avoid realtime architecture without realtime value.

---

# 140. Data Storage Economics

Major dimensions:

```text
volume

replication

retention

access frequency

file layout
```

---

# 141. Hot vs Cold Storage

Hot:

```text
fast
expensive
```

Cold:

```text
slow
cheap
```

Move old datasets down tiers when possible.

---

# 142. Lifecycle Policy

Example:

```text
0-30 days -> hot

31-365 days -> standard object

>365 days -> archive
```

based on actual usage.

---

# 143. Training Dataset Retention

Do not keep:

```text
every temporary experiment dataset
forever
```

But preserve:

```text
production dataset lineage
```

as governance requires.

---

# 144. Intermediate Data Cleanup

ETL often creates:

```text
temporary joins

staging tables

shuffle outputs
```

Use TTLs.

Storage creep is often invisible.

---

# 145. Small-File Cost

Millions of tiny objects increase:

```text
metadata operations

API calls

query overhead
```

Compaction can lower operational and compute cost.

---

# 146. Compression Economics

Compression saves:

```text
storage

network
```

at cost of:

```text
CPU
```

Choose formats/codecs based on workload.

---

# 147. Columnar Storage Savings

Read only:

```text
10 of 500 columns
```

rather than entire dataset.

Less I/O means:

```text
lower query cost

faster training preparation
```

---

# 148. Partition Pruning Savings

If query needs:

```text
one day
```

do not scan:

```text
five years
```

Physical data design is financial engineering.

---

# 149. Data Query Cost Visibility

Attribute large scans to:

```text
query

pipeline

team

experiment
```

so repeated expensive patterns become visible.

---

# 150. Observability Cost

Metrics, logs, traces, prediction logs can become substantial.

Major drivers:

```text
volume

cardinality

retention

indexing
```

---

# 151. Log Cost

Logging:

```text
1 KB/request
×
1M RPS
```

creates massive daily data volume.

Use:

```text
sampling

aggregation

retention tiers
```

---

# 152. Trace Cost

100% tracing may be unnecessary.

Use:

```text
sample normal

retain errors

retain slow traces
```

to preserve diagnostic value.

---

# 153. Metrics Cardinality Cost

One label:

```text
request_id
```

can explode time-series count.

Observability governance is also cost governance.

---

# 154. Prediction Logging Cost

Raw inputs and predictions for every request may be huge.

Possible:

```text
sample

aggregate

retain metadata

tier old records
```

while preserving monitoring needs.

---

# 155. Cost of Compliance

Security and governance may require:

```text
long retention

replication

audit logging
```

These costs should be planned explicitly rather than treated as accidental overhead.

---

# 156. Cost Attribution

Every resource should ideally map to:

```text
team

application

environment

model

cost center
```

---

# 157. Resource Tags / Labels

Examples:

```text
team=risk

model=fraud-v31

environment=prod

project=payments
```

Use standardized metadata.

---

# 158. Missing Cost Tags

Untagged GPU:

```text
₹500k/month
```

cannot be assigned.

Create:

```text
unknown/unallocated cost
```

dashboard and drive it down.

---

# 159. Showback

Show teams:

```text
what they consumed
```

without directly billing their budget.

Useful for:

```text
awareness

behavior change
```

---

# 160. Chargeback

Actually allocate cost to:

```text
team

business unit

project
```

This creates stronger economic incentives.

---

# 161. Showback Before Chargeback

If attribution is inaccurate:

```text
chargeback creates distrust
```

Start with showback until data quality is strong.

---

# 162. Shared Cost Allocation

Shared platform costs:

```text
control plane

monitoring

registry
```

must be allocated somehow.

Options:

```text
equal share

usage-based

revenue-based

central platform budget
```

No single universal method.

---

# 163. Direct Allocation

Training GPU cost can often be mapped directly to:

```text
job ID
```

This is easy.

---

# 164. Indirect Allocation

Shared Kafka or observability cluster needs allocation formula.

Examples:

```text
events processed

storage consumed

request volume
```

---

# 165. Cost Allocation Should Be Explainable

Team should understand:

```text
why did we receive this cost?
```

Opaque allocation destroys trust.

---

# 166. Cost Dashboard

Useful hierarchy:

```text
Company
  |
  v
Business Unit
  |
  v
Team
  |
  v
Project
  |
  v
Model / Job
```

---

# 167. Cost Dashboard Questions

Answer:

```text
What costs the most?

What changed?

Which team grew?

Which workloads are inefficient?

What is idle?

What can be optimized?
```

---

# 168. Cost Trend

Display:

```text
daily

weekly

monthly
```

and compare with:

```text
usage growth
```

Cost increase is not necessarily bad if business volume increased.

---

# 169. Normalized Cost

If traffic doubled and cost rose 50%:

```text
unit cost improved
```

Therefore always pair:

```text
absolute cost

unit cost
```

---

# 170. Cost per Prediction Trend

Example:

```text
January: ₹0.010

February: ₹0.008

March: ₹0.006
```

Even if total spend rises, efficiency improves.

---

# 171. Cost per Token Trend

Track by:

```text
model

tenant

application

prompt version
```

This can expose prompt bloat or inefficient routing.

---

# 172. Cost per Training Step

Useful during optimization:

```text
cost / step
```

or:

```text
cost / billion training tokens
```

---

# 173. Cost per Quality Point

Example:

```text
Model A:
91% quality
₹1M/month

Model B:
92%
₹4M/month
```

Additional:

```text
1 percentage point
costs ₹3M/month
```

Business can decide if justified.

---

# 174. Budget

A budget defines expected spending.

Example:

```text
Team A
monthly ML budget
= ₹2M
```

---

# 175. Budget Is Not Quota

Budget:

```text
financial target
```

Quota:

```text
resource limit
```

They can interact but are not identical.

---

# 176. Soft Budget Alert

At:

```text
80%
```

notify team.

At:

```text
100%
```

escalate.

Do not automatically terminate production because a budget threshold was crossed unless policy explicitly requires it.

---

# 177. Hard Spend Limit

Useful for:

```text
experimental sandbox

student project

noncritical agent
```

where uncontrolled spend is unacceptable.

---

# 178. LLM User Budget

Per user/tenant:

```text
max tokens/day

max cost/day
```

prevents abuse.

---

# 179. Experiment Budget

Training request:

```text
estimated cost = ₹400k
```

Team budget remaining:

```text
₹100k
```

Platform can:

```text
warn

require approval

block
```

according to policy.

---

# 180. Pre-Run Cost Estimate

Before submission calculate:

```text
requested GPU count

estimated duration

storage

expected cost
```

This improves decision-making.

---

# 181. Prediction Uncertainty

Runtime estimate may be inaccurate.

Cost estimate should provide:

```text
range
```

rather than false precision.

Example:

```text
expected ₹100k-₹150k
```

---

# 182. Cost Approval Threshold

Large run:

```text
estimated > ₹1M
```

may require manager approval.

Small run:

```text
self-service
```

Risk-based financial governance.

---

# 183. Cost Anomaly Detection

Alert when:

```text
daily cost increases 5×
```

without corresponding usage growth.

Possible causes:

```text
runaway jobs

logging storm

autoscaling bug

agent loop
```

---

# 184. Cost Spike Context

Anomaly alert should show:

```text
which service

which resource

which deployment

which team

what changed
```

Cost observability benefits from deployment markers.

---

# 185. Runaway Training Job

Training stopped improving 12 hours ago.

Still running.

Could implement:

```text
max runtime

no-progress detection

budget limit
```

---

# 186. Zombie Resources

Examples:

```text
notebook forgotten

GPU VM with no workload

old endpoint

unused disk

orphaned snapshot
```

Automated cleanup saves money.

---

# 187. TTL Resources

Nonproduction resources can default to:

```text
expire after 24 hours
```

unless extended.

This is a strong FinOps control.

---

# 188. Idle Resource Detection

Measure:

```text
allocated

vs

used
```

for:

```text
GPUs

CPU

storage

endpoints
```

# 189. Idle Notebook Shutdown

Interactive environments commonly waste capacity.

Auto-stop after:

```text
defined inactivity period
```

# 190. Idle Endpoint Detection

Model endpoint:

```text
0 requests in 30 days
```

Candidate for:

```text
scale-to-zero

retirement
```

Large dataset not read for:

```text
12 months
```

may be moved to cheaper storage.

Need governance before deletion.

# 192. Cost Optimization Lifecycle

```text
Measure
  |
  v
Attribute
  |
  v
Analyze
  |
  v
Optimize
  |
  v
Verify
```

Then repeat.

# 193. Optimization Without Measurement

Example:

```text
switch to smaller GPU
```

but throughput collapses.

Total cost increases.

Always benchmark.

---

# 194. Benchmarking

Measure workload on representative hardware.

Capture:

```text
throughput

latency

memory

cost
```

not synthetic hardware specs alone.

---

# 195. Benchmark Reproducibility

Record:

```text
model version

runtime

batch size

sequence length

precision

hardware
```

Otherwise comparisons are meaningless.

---

# 196. Cost Regression Testing

Candidate runtime:

```text
quality same

latency same

cost +40%
```

CI/CD should be able to flag this.

---

# 197. Performance Budget

Release may require:

```text
p99 <= 100 ms

cost <= ₹X / 1M predictions
```

Cost becomes a release criterion.

---

# 198. LLM Cost Regression

Prompt v17:

```text
2,000 avg input tokens
```

Prompt v18:

```text
8,000
```

Quality unchanged.

Block or warn before full rollout.

# 199. Model Cost Contract

Model deployment metadata can specify:

```yaml
economics:
  max_cost_per_1m_predictions: ...
  target_gpu_utilization: ...
  max_idle_ratio: ...
```

Platform tracks compliance.

# 200. Efficiency SLO

Example:

```text
95% of production GPU-hours
must execute useful model work
```

Cost SLOs need careful design but can guide platform teams.

---

# 201. Cost Ownership

Every expensive system needs an owner accountable for:

```text
technical behavior

economic behavior
```

Platform should make cost visible to that owner.

---

# 202. FinOps Team vs Platform Team

FinOps provides:

```text
financial governance

reporting

commit strategy
```

Platform team provides:

```text
technical controls

resource attribution

optimization mechanisms
```

They should collaborate.

---

# 203. Central vs Team Optimization

Central platform optimizes:

```text
fleet commitments

shared clusters

pricing agreements
```

Individual teams optimize:

```text
model size

batch size

prompt length

training frequency
```

# 204. Cost Guardrails

Platform can enforce defaults:

```text
idle shutdown

max GPU count

runtime limit

approved hardware

budget alert
```

while allowing exceptions.

# 205. Cost-Aware Golden Path

A standard deployment gets:

```text
autoscaling

right-sized profile

cost attribution

budget tracking

idle detection

unit-cost dashboard
```

automatically.

# 206. Financial Blast Radius

# 207. Agent Financial Blast Radius

Agent can recursively call expensive model.

Without limits:

Controls:

```text
steps

tokens

time

dollars
```

```text
5000 GPUs
```

for:

Platform should require:

```text
cost estimate

approval
```

# 210. Queue Priority by Business Value

```text
>

launch-critical training

normal experiments

>
```

Expensive resources should follow business importance.

# 211. Cost-Aware Preemption

```text
critical high-value workload
```

# 215. Procurement Risk

and become less competitive quickly.

```text
memory

cost efficiency
```

# 217. Migration Economics

```text
users
```

```text
low-growth
```

rather than one exact estimate.

```text
weekly

holiday
```

# 226. Cost Allocation Across Regions

```text
hardware

energy

service pricing

network
```

# 227. Cheapest Region Fallacy

Do not route sensitive European data across world to save:

```text
5%
```

if latency or regulatory requirements prohibit it.

Cost is constrained optimization.

# 228. Optimization Objective

Architectural objective might be:

```text
minimize cost
subject to:

quality >= Q

p99 latency <= L

availability >= A

security policy satisfied
```

This is the correct mental model.

# 229. Constrained Optimization

Never optimize:

```text
cost alone
```

because system also needs:

```text
quality

reliability

security

developer velocity
```

# 230. Cost / Reliability / Quality Triangle

```text
          QUALITY
            /\
           /  \
          /    \
         /      \
        /        \
     COST ------ RELIABILITY
```

Architecture continuously balances all three.

# 231. Cost Anti-Pattern — Cheapest GPU

Selecting based only on:

```text
hourly price
```

ignores:

```text
throughput

memory

job duration
```

---

# 232. Anti-Pattern — 100% Fleet Utilization

Looks efficient.

Creates:

```text
huge queues

no reliability headroom
```

Cost efficiency must include operational outcomes.

---

# 233. Anti-Pattern — Dedicated GPU per Model

Thousands of low-traffic models each get one GPU.

Result:

```text
massive idle capacity
```

Use multi-model serving or scale-to-zero where appropriate.

---

# 234. Anti-Pattern — Always Use Biggest Model

Simple classification requests go to giant LLM.

Use routing/cascades.

---

# 235. Anti-Pattern — No Token Limits

One request sends:

```text
200k-token context
```

and generates massive output.

Define budgets.

---

# 236. Anti-Pattern — Full Reindex Every Day

Only 1% documents change.

Yet all embeddings recomputed.

Use incremental updates.

---

# 237. Anti-Pattern — Recompute Shared Features

Hundreds of teams independently calculate same feature.

Platform reuse saves compute.

---

# 238. Anti-Pattern — Keep Everything Hot

Five-year-old training data remains on expensive low-latency storage.

Use lifecycle tiers.

---

# 239. Anti-Pattern — Log Everything Forever

Observability bill becomes comparable to serving bill.

Design retention intentionally.

---

# 240. Anti-Pattern — Chargeback Before Accurate Attribution

Teams distrust bills and fight the platform.

Fix attribution first.

---

# 241. Anti-Pattern — Budget as Kill Switch for Production

Monthly budget exhausted.

Critical fraud API automatically shuts down.

Financial policy must distinguish:

```text
critical production

experimental workloads
```

---

# 242. Anti-Pattern — Ignore Engineering Cost

Build complex optimization saving:

```text
₹100k/year
```

while consuming:

```text
₹5M/year engineering effort
```

Optimization itself has ROI.

---

# 243. Anti-Pattern — Optimization Without Benchmark

Switch configuration based on intuition.

Unit cost worsens.

Always verify experimentally.

# 279. Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> Our GPU bill is too high.

Do not answer:

```text
Use cheaper GPUs.
```

Ask:

```text
Which workloads drive spend?

What is unit cost?

How much accelerator time is useful?

Are workloads right-sized?

What is queue behavior?

Which hardware gives best cost-per-result?

Are experiments failing late?

Can workloads use spot?

Is data waiting after GPU allocation?

Is model size justified?

Can requests be routed to smaller models?

Are prompts oversized?

Are shared features being recomputed?

What costs are fixed vs variable?

How much reliability headroom is intentional?
```

This is architect-level cost engineering.

---

# 280. What You Must Remember From Chapter 22

1. **Cost is an architecture property, not merely a Finance report.**

2. **ML TCO includes accelerators, CPUs, storage, networking, data systems, observability, and platform operations.**

3. **Unit economics are more useful than raw spend when evaluating efficiency.**

4. **Training cost should be measured per run, experiment, useful result, and business outcome where possible.**

5. **A more expensive accelerator can be cheaper overall if it completes the workload sufficiently faster.**

6. **GPU-hour price alone is not a valid hardware-selection metric.**

7. **Developer queue time and time-to-result have real economic value even when GPUs are not running.**

8. **Failed experiments can be one of the largest sources of ML infrastructure waste.**

9. **Cheap preflight validation should occur before expensive accelerator allocation.**

10. **At large scale, a few minutes of idle GPU time can represent hundreds of GPU-hours.**

11. **Right-sizing applies to GPU count, GPU type, CPU, memory, storage, and topology.**

12. **GPU utilization does not prove business or economic efficiency.**

13. **Cost-aware scheduling should consider hardware fit, price, data locality, priority, and workload deadlines.**

14. **Data movement can erase apparent savings from cheaper compute in another region or cloud.**

15. **Reserved capacity is most useful for predictable baseline demand; on-demand and spot can handle different kinds of burst.**

16. **Spot/preemptible compute is most attractive for checkpointable and restartable workloads.**

17. **Checkpoint frequency has an economic optimum between I/O overhead and lost compute after failure.**

18. **Shared accelerator pools gain economic efficiency through statistical multiplexing of independent demand.**

19. **Dedicated resources may be economically justified when security, isolation, or reliability requires them.**

20. **High availability, warm capacity, multi-region design, and headroom all have explicit reliability premiums.**

21. **Operating infrastructure at 100% utilization can be economically harmful if it creates queueing and reliability failures.**

22. **Training and inference have different economic profiles and therefore need different capacity strategies.**

23. **Batch workloads can often use deadline-aware scheduling and cheaper capacity.**

24. **Inference unit cost should be tracked as cost per useful serving unit rather than total monthly spend alone.**

25. **Scale-to-zero can reduce idle cost but trades against cold-start latency.**

26. **Autoscaling is both a reliability mechanism and a financial-control system.**

27. **LLM capacity should be modeled using tokens, context length, active sequences, and output generation—not request counts alone.**

28. **Long prompts and large contexts increase prefill compute, KV-cache pressure, latency, and cost.**

29. **Prompt length should be monitored as a production economic metric.**

30. **RAG cost includes embedding, indexing, retrieval, reranking, context tokens, and model inference.**

31. **Embedding and indexing should be incremental whenever possible rather than recomputing unchanged content.**

32. **Caches should be evaluated by cost avoided, not merely hit rate.**

33. **Model routing and cascades can dramatically reduce LLM cost by reserving expensive models for difficult requests.**

34. **Quality-per-dollar is often a better architectural objective than maximum benchmark quality.**

35. **Distillation and quantization can materially reduce serving cost when quality remains acceptable.**

36. **Batching improves accelerator economics by increasing useful work per device, but excessive batching can violate latency SLOs.**

37. **Efficient KV-cache management directly influences LLM concurrency and cost per token.**

38. **Multi-model serving can eliminate large amounts of stranded accelerator capacity for low-volume models.**

39. **Feature reuse and shared transformations are financial optimizations as well as platform abstractions.**

40. **Real-time data freshness should only be purchased when the business actually needs real-time behavior.**

41. **Storage lifecycle policies, compression, partitioning, column pruning, and compaction can materially reduce ML data costs.**

42. **Observability itself needs FinOps controls because logging, tracing, and high-cardinality metrics can become extremely expensive.**

43. **Every significant ML cost should be attributable to a team, model, project, or business owner.**

44. **Showback builds awareness; chargeback creates direct budget accountability.**

45. **Chargeback should not be introduced before attribution data is trusted.**

46. **Absolute cost should always be interpreted together with normalized unit cost and business growth.**

47. **Budgets and quotas are different: one is financial governance, the other resource enforcement.**

48. **Large training jobs benefit from cost estimates and approval thresholds before execution.**

49. **Cost anomaly detection should correlate spending changes with deployments, prompts, models, and workload behavior.**

50. **Zombie resources, idle notebooks, inactive endpoints, and forgotten datasets are common sources of silent waste.**

51. **TTL and automatic cleanup are among the highest-leverage nonproduction FinOps controls.**

52. **Benchmark every optimization on representative workloads instead of assuming cheaper resources mean cheaper outcomes.**

53. **Cost regression can be tested during releases just like latency or quality regression.**

54. **Cloud cost forecasting should be driver-based using traffic, tokens, experiments, and business growth.**

55. **Commitment planning balances the premium of insufficient reservations against the waste of overcommitting.**

56. **Cost optimization is a constrained optimization problem: quality, reliability, security, latency, and developer productivity remain requirements.**

57. **The cheapest architecture is not the one with the smallest cloud bill if it destroys product quality or engineering velocity.**

58. **Cost guardrails should be embedded into the ML platform golden path through right-sizing, budgets, limits, cost attribution, and idle cleanup.**

59. **For autonomous agents and large training systems, explicitly limit financial blast radius.**

60. **At architect level, FinOps means connecting technical resource decisions to measurable business value and continuously improving the amount of useful ML outcome produced per dollar.**


Chapter 23 is where all previous chapters stop being separate concepts and become **one complete Senior / Staff / Principal-level ML platform architecture**.

# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 23 — Enterprise ML Platform System Design: Building a Google-Scale End-to-End MLOps Architecture From First Principles

---

# 1. Why This Chapter Is Different

Until now, we studied individual architectural domains:

```text
Data

Training

GPU Infrastructure

Model Serving

Reliability

Platform Engineering

Observability

Governance

Security

FinOps
```

Real architect interviews do not ask:

```text
Explain Kafka.

Explain Kubernetes.

Explain feature stores.
```

They ask:

> Design the entire ML platform.

You must connect everything.

---

# 2. The Architect's Real Job

A senior architect does not optimize one component.

They balance:

```text
Developer Velocity

ML Quality

Reliability

Security

Governance

Cost

Scalability

Operational Complexity
```

The final architecture is a compromise between all of them.

---

# 3. The System We Will Design

Assume a global company with:

```text
10,000 ML engineers

2,000 ML teams

100,000 registered models

10,000 production model deployments

50,000 training jobs/day

10,000+ GPUs

5 geographic regions

100 PB+ ML data

classical ML

deep learning

LLMs

RAG

agents
```

The platform must support both:

```text
research experimentation
```

and:

```text
highly regulated production ML
```

---

# 4. Core Platform Requirements

Users should be able to:

```text
discover data

develop experiments

submit training

track experiments

build datasets

manage features

register models

evaluate models

promote models

deploy models

monitor models

roll back models
```

without manually assembling infrastructure.

---

# 5. Non-Functional Requirements

Target:

```text
high availability

tenant isolation

global operation

auditability

reproducibility

cost attribution

policy enforcement

horizontal scalability
```

---

# 6. Architect Interview Rule

Before drawing architecture, clarify:

```text
Users?

Scale?

Workload types?

Latency requirements?

Availability requirements?

Data size?

Security requirements?

Regulatory constraints?

Cost sensitivity?
```

Do not begin with Kubernetes.

---

# 7. Functional Requirements

Example:

```text
FR1 Submit training jobs

FR2 Track experiments

FR3 Register model versions

FR4 Deploy models

FR5 Build online/offline features

FR6 Support batch and online inference

FR7 Support LLM/RAG workloads

FR8 Support governance approvals
```

---

# 8. Non-Functional Requirements

Example:

```text
NFR1 Control plane 99.95%

NFR2 Online inference 99.99%

NFR3 p99 inference < 100 ms for selected models

NFR4 Tenant isolation

NFR5 Multi-region operation

NFR6 RPO/RTO targets

NFR7 Reproducible training

NFR8 Cost attribution
```

---

# 9. Workload Classes

Never treat all ML compute the same.

Separate:

```text
interactive notebooks

batch preprocessing

CPU training

single-GPU training

distributed GPU training

batch inference

online CPU inference

online GPU inference

LLM serving

embedding generation
```

Each has different scheduling and reliability requirements.

---

# 10. Research vs Production

Research favors:

```text
flexibility

fast experimentation

custom packages
```

Production favors:

```text
immutability

security

reproducibility

governance

reliability
```

This should influence platform architecture.

---

# 11. The Fundamental Layer Model

Think:

```text
USER EXPERIENCE
      |
      v
PLATFORM CONTROL PLANE
      |
      v
COMPUTE / DATA PLANE
      |
      v
CLOUD / INFRASTRUCTURE
```

This pattern will appear everywhere.

---

# 12. High-Level Architecture

```text
                         USERS
                           |
                           v
                    ML PLATFORM API
                           |
        +------------------+------------------+
        |                  |                  |
        v                  v                  v
    TRAINING            MODELS            FEATURES
    CONTROL             CONTROL           CONTROL
        |                  |                  |
        +------------------+------------------+
                           |
                           v
                  PLATFORM CONTROL PLANE
                           |
       +-------------------+-------------------+
       |                   |                   |
       v                   v                   v
   DATA PLANE         COMPUTE PLANE       SERVING PLANE
       |                   |                   |
       v                   v                   v
   LAKEHOUSE          CPU/GPU FLEETS       INFERENCE
```

Around everything:

```text
Identity

Policy

Observability

Governance

Cost
```

---

# 13. Control Plane

The control plane manages:

```text
intent

metadata

policy

placement

lifecycle
```

It should not perform the heavy ML work itself.

---

# 14. Data Plane

The data plane executes:

```text
training

data processing

feature computation

model inference
```

at scale.

---

# 15. Why Separate the Planes?

Suppose control plane database fails.

Existing production inference should ideally:

```text
continue serving
```

This prevents:

```text
metadata outage
=
global inference outage
```

---

# 16. Desired State

User declares:

```yaml
kind: ModelDeployment

model: fraud-v31

replicas:
  min: 5
  max: 100

region:
  - india
  - europe
```

Platform tries to make reality match this desired state.

---

# 17. Reconciliation Loop

```text
Desired State
     |
     v
Controller
     |
     v
Observe Actual State
     |
     v
Difference?
     |
     +---- yes -> reconcile
```

This is a powerful distributed-systems pattern.

---

# 18. Why Controllers Are Useful

Transient failure:

```text
pod creation fails
```

Controller retries until:

```text
desired state reached
```

Users do not manually repair every partial failure.

---

# 19. Platform API

The API should expose ML concepts.

Examples:

```text
TrainingJob

Dataset

Feature

ModelVersion

ModelDeployment

Evaluation

Endpoint
```

Not raw cloud resources.

---

# 20. Bad Platform API

```text
CreatePod()

CreateLoadBalancer()

CreatePersistentVolume()
```

This exposes infrastructure rather than ML intent.

---

# 21. Better Platform API

```text
train(model_spec)

deploy(model_version)

create_feature(feature_spec)
```

Platform handles infrastructure.

---

# 22. API Stability

Infrastructure can change:

```text
Kubernetes version

cloud provider

GPU generation
```

while platform API remains stable.

This protects users from infrastructure churn.

---

# 23. API Versioning

Use:

```text
v1

v1beta2

v2
```

with migration policies.

Do not break thousands of teams overnight.

---

# 24. Long-Running Operations

Training requests may take hours.

API should return:

```text
operation_id
```

not hold HTTP request open.

---

# 25. Async API Pattern

```text
POST /training-jobs
      |
      v
202 Accepted
operation_id=123
```

Then:

```text
GET /operations/123
```

---

# 26. Idempotency

If client retries:

```text
submit training
```

network timeout should not create:

```text
10 duplicate 256-GPU jobs
```

Use idempotency keys.

---

# 27. Platform Metadata Database

Needs to store:

```text
resource specifications

ownership

state

operations

policies

references
```

Use durable transactional storage.

---

# 28. Metadata Is Not Artifact Storage

Do not put:

```text
500 GB model
```

inside control-plane relational database.

Store:

```text
metadata -> DB

artifact -> object storage
```

---

# 29. Object Storage

Used for:

```text
datasets

models

checkpoints

logs

evaluation artifacts
```

Ideal because of:

```text
scale

durability

cost
```

---

# 30. Resource Identity

Every resource should have immutable ID:

```text
training_job_id

model_version_id

dataset_version_id

deployment_id
```

Names can be mutable.

IDs should not.

---

# 31. Event-Driven Control Plane

When training succeeds:

```text
TrainingCompleted
```

event can trigger:

```text
model registration

evaluation

lineage update

notification
```

without synchronously coupling every service.

---

# 32. Event Bus

Control-plane events:

```text
ModelRegistered

DeploymentCreated

DeploymentHealthy

EvaluationCompleted

PolicyDenied
```

Support loose coupling.

---

# 33. Eventual Consistency

Not every service sees update instantly.

Example:

```text
registry updated
```

then:

```text
search index updated 2 sec later
```

This is often acceptable.

---

# 34. Strong Consistency Where Required

Approval transition:

```text
PENDING -> APPROVED
```

may need transactional consistency.

Different workflows require different consistency guarantees.

---

# 35. Training Architecture

```text
User
 |
 v
Training API
 |
 v
Admission
 |
 v
Global Queue
 |
 v
Scheduler
 |
 v
Cluster Agent
 |
 v
Training Job
```

---

# 36. Admission Control

Before scheduling:

```text
identity valid?

quota available?

dataset authorized?

hardware allowed?

budget available?

policy satisfied?
```

Reject impossible jobs early.

---

# 37. Global Queue

Separate submission from execution.

Benefits:

```text
burst absorption

fairness

priority

backpressure
```

---

# 38. Job Priority

Example:

```text
P0 production incident

P1 launch-critical training

P2 routine production

P3 research

P4 opportunistic
```

Priority should reflect business criticality.

---

# 39. Fair Share

If Team A submits:

```text
5000 jobs
```

it should not consume all GPUs.

Scheduler tracks fair-share entitlement.

---

# 40. Entitlement vs Physical Capacity

Team may be entitled to:

```text
10% fleet
```

but can temporarily borrow unused capacity.

This improves utilization.

---

# 41. Preemption

When high-priority job arrives:

```text
preempt lower-priority checkpointable job
```

if needed.

Preemption policy must consider lost work.

---

# 42. Gang Scheduling

Distributed job needs:

```text
64 GPUs
```

simultaneously.

Scheduling 63 GPUs is useless.

Reserve the complete gang.

---

# 43. Topology-Aware Scheduling

For tensor-parallel workload:

```text
8 GPUs
```

prefer same:

```text
NVSwitch domain
```

rather than random GPUs across network.

---

# 44. Global Scheduler

Chooses:

```text
region

cluster

hardware pool

capacity class
```

based on:

```text
data locality

cost

availability

policy

deadline

priority
```

---

# 45. Local Scheduler

Within selected cluster decides:

```text
node

GPU

topology
```

This separation scales better.

---

# 46. Cluster Agent

Instead of global control plane directly managing every cluster:

```text
Global Control
       |
       v
Cluster Agent
       |
       v
Local Kubernetes
```

Agent reduces cross-region control coupling.

---

# 47. Pull-Based Agent

Cluster agent can:

```text
pull desired work
```

from global control plane.

Benefits:

```text
firewall simplicity

regional isolation

less inbound connectivity
```

---

# 48. GPU Fleet Segmentation

Separate pools:

```text
LLM Training

General Training

Production Inference

Research

Spot
```

because their SLOs differ.

---

# 49. Protected Inference Capacity

Production serving should not be starved by:

```text
research training burst
```

Reserve critical capacity.

---

# 50. Borrowing Idle Capacity

If inference reserve is idle:

```text
research may borrow
```

but must be preemptible when production demand rises.

---

# 51. Hardware Abstraction

Users request:

```text
accelerator_profile: large-memory-training
```

not:

```text
specific GPU SKU forever
```

Platform maps profile to available hardware.

---

# 52. Hardware Capability Metadata

Track:

```text
HBM

compute capability

interconnect

precision support

region

cost
```

Scheduler uses capabilities.

---

# 53. Training Environment

Job container includes:

```text
framework

code

dependencies
```

Platform adds:

```text
identity

data mounts

telemetry

scheduler metadata
```

---

# 54. Research Containers

Allow flexibility.

Production candidates should ideally originate from:

```text
approved versioned runtime
```

or trusted build process.

---

# 55. Dataset Inputs

TrainingJob references:

```text
dataset_version_id
```

not mutable:

```text
latest/
```

This is essential for reproducibility.

---

# 56. Data Architecture

```text
Operational Sources
        |
        v
      CDC
        |
        v
     Event Bus
       / \
      /   \
     v     v
Streaming  Lakehouse
    |          |
    v          v
Online     Historical
Features    Features
```

---

# 57. Batch Data

Object storage + lakehouse supports:

```text
large historical scans

backfills

training datasets
```

---

# 58. Streaming Data

Event bus supports:

```text
real-time features

fraud signals

recommendations

monitoring
```

---

# 59. Schema Contracts

Every major data product has:

```text
schema

semantics

owner

freshness

quality
```

Breaking changes should be caught before consumers fail.

---

# 60. Data Quality Gates

Before expensive training:

```text
schema

volume

freshness

null rate

distribution
```

validated.

---

# 61. Training Dataset Builder

```text
Entities
   +
Prediction Times
   |
   v
Point-In-Time Feature Join
   |
   v
Labels
   |
   v
Dataset Snapshot
```

Produces immutable training dataset version.

---

# 62. Point-in-Time Correctness

Historical features must be:

```text
available at prediction time
```

not present-day values.

Otherwise evaluation leaks future information.

---

# 63. Dataset Manifest

Contains:

```text
snapshot ID

schema

file references

row count

time range

checksums
```

Training references the manifest.

---

# 64. Dataset Locality

Large training jobs should be scheduled near:

```text
dataset storage
```

to avoid:

```text
network bottleneck

egress cost
```

---

# 65. Dataset Cache

```text
Object Storage
     |
     v
Regional Cache
     |
     v
Node NVMe
     |
     v
Training Worker
```

High-reuse datasets benefit from caching.

---

# 66. Feature Platform

Feature lifecycle:

```text
Data Source
    |
    v
Transformation
    |
    +---- Offline Store
    |
    +---- Online Store
```

---

# 67. Offline Store

Optimized for:

```text
historical joins

training

batch scoring
```

---

# 68. Online Store

Optimized for:

```text
low latency

high QPS

current feature values
```

---

# 69. Feature Registry

Contains:

```text
name

version

type

owner

source

freshness

transformation

default semantics
```

---

# 70. Feature Reuse

Platform should make trusted features discoverable.

This reduces:

```text
duplicate computation

training-serving skew
```

---

# 71. Feature Materialization

Batch/stream processors write feature values to:

```text
offline

online
```

stores using canonical feature definitions.

---

# 72. Freshness SLO

Example:

```text
fraud_transaction_count_10m
freshness < 30 sec
```

Monitoring enforces this.

---

# 73. Model Training Flow

```text
Dataset
   |
   v
Training Job
   |
   v
Checkpoint
   |
   v
Final Model
   |
   v
Evaluation
```

---

# 74. Experiment Tracking

Capture:

```text
parameters

metrics

code version

dataset version

runtime

hardware

artifacts
```

---

# 75. Experiment Identity

Every run should have:

```text
experiment_id

run_id
```

linking metadata.

---

# 76. Reproducibility

A run should reference:

```text
code commit

container digest

dataset snapshot

feature version

training config

random seed where relevant
```

---

# 77. Checkpoint Architecture

Large distributed training writes:

```text
sharded checkpoint
```

to durable storage.

Use:

```text
async checkpointing

parallel writes

manifest
```

where appropriate.

---

# 78. Checkpoint Reliability

Need to detect:

```text
partial checkpoint

corrupt shard

missing metadata
```

before treating checkpoint as valid.

---

# 79. Experiment Promotion

Research run:

```text
Run #812
```

produces candidate model.

Candidate does not automatically become production.

---

# 80. Model Registry

Registry stores:

```text
model metadata

artifact reference

version

metrics

lineage

stage
```

---

# 81. Immutable Model Versions

```text
fraud:v31
```

must never silently change contents.

New model:

```text
fraud:v32
```

---

# 82. Model Packaging

Package may include:

```text
weights

preprocessing

signature

schema

runtime requirements
```

Do not assume weights alone are sufficient.

---

# 83. Evaluation Platform

Evaluate:

```text
quality

robustness

latency

cost

fairness

safety
```

depending on risk.

---

# 84. Evaluation Dataset

Reference immutable:

```text
evaluation_dataset_version
```

so candidate comparisons are reproducible.

---

# 85. Champion-Challenger

Candidate compared with production champion.

Potential gate:

```text
quality not worse

latency acceptable

cost acceptable
```

---

# 86. Governance Flow

```text
Model Candidate
      |
      v
Risk Classification
      |
      v
Required Evidence
      |
      v
Approvals
      |
      v
Production Eligible
```

---

# 87. Risk-Based Controls

Low-risk recommendation model:

```text
mostly automated
```

High-risk financial model:

```text
independent validation
+
human approvals
```

---

# 88. Policy as Code

Deployment rule:

```text
if environment == production
and model.approved != true:
    deny
```

Security/governance become enforceable.

---

# 89. Deployment Control Plane

```text
User
 |
 v
Deployment API
 |
 v
Policy
 |
 v
Placement
 |
 v
Regional Serving Control
 |
 v
Inference Runtime
```

---

# 90. ModelDeployment Resource

Example:

```yaml
model: fraud:v31

traffic:
  canary: 5%

autoscaling:
  min: 10
  max: 200

slo:
  p99_ms: 50
```

---

# 91. Serving Plane Separation

Serving plane should not require synchronous calls to:

```text
model registry

governance DB

central metadata DB
```

for every request.

Cache required configuration locally.

---

# 92. Model Loading

Regional control plane resolves:

```text
model digest

artifact location

runtime

configuration
```

then data plane loads immutable artifact.

---

# 93. Artifact Cache

Use:

```text
regional model cache

node-local cache
```

for large weights.

Reduces load times and registry bandwidth.

---

# 94. Serving Architecture

```text
Client
  |
  v
Global Gateway
  |
  v
Regional Gateway
  |
  v
Model Router
  |
  v
Inference Replica
```

---

# 95. Global Routing

Choose region based on:

```text
latency

health

residency

capacity
```

---

# 96. Regional Routing

Select:

```text
model version

replica

hardware pool
```

---

# 97. Online Feature Fetch

```text
Request
  |
  +---- Feature Store
  |
  +---- Model Runtime
```

Feature latency belongs in end-to-end budget.

---

# 98. Feature Fetch Parallelism

Independent feature groups can sometimes be fetched in parallel.

Avoid unnecessary sequential dependency chains.

---

# 99. Serving Deadlines

Request has:

```text
overall deadline
```

Downstream calls receive smaller sub-deadlines.

Prevent one dependency from consuming entire request budget.

---

# 100. Fallback Model

If primary model fails:

```text
fallback model

cached result

rules

manual workflow
```

depending on business.

---

# 101. Last-Known-Good

Keep a known healthy model version ready.

Rollback should be:

```text
fast

automated

tested
```

---

# 102. Canary Deployment

```text
95% -> v31

5% -> v32
```

Compare:

```text
latency

errors

quality signals

business metrics
```

---

# 103. Shadow Deployment

Candidate gets mirrored requests but does not affect user.

Useful for:

```text
performance

prediction disagreement

capacity testing
```

---

# 104. Traffic Controller

Supports:

```text
canary

blue/green

A/B

shadow

rollback
```

Traffic configuration itself is versioned.

---

# 105. Autoscaling

Classical models:

```text
RPS

latency

queue
```

LLMs:

```text
tokens/sec

active sequences

KV cache

queue age
```

---

# 106. Admission Control for Serving

If overloaded:

```text
reject low-priority requests

queue within limits

route to cheaper fallback
```

Do not allow infinite queues.

---

# 107. Backpressure

If downstream capacity is saturated:

```text
stop accepting unlimited work
```

Otherwise latency becomes unbounded.

---

# 108. Multi-Model Serving

Thousands of low-traffic models should not each get:

```text
dedicated accelerator
```

Use:

```text
model cache

shared runtimes

dynamic loading
```

where appropriate.

---

# 109. High-Criticality Models

Critical models may receive:

```text
dedicated replicas

reserved capacity

stronger isolation
```

Cost increases, reliability improves.

---

# 110. LLM Platform

```text
Application
   |
   v
LLM Gateway
   |
   v
Model Router
   |
   +---- Small Model
   |
   +---- Large Model
   |
   +---- External Provider
```

# 111. LLM Gateway Responsibilities

```text
authentication

rate limiting

token budgets

provider policy

data classification

routing

observability

cost tracking
```

---

# 112. LLM Serving Fleet

Separate pools by:

```text
model family

memory requirement

quantization

latency tier
```

---

# 113. Continuous Batching

LLM runtime dynamically groups active requests.

Improves:

```text
throughput

GPU economics
```

---

# 114. KV Cache

Must monitor:

```text
utilization

capacity
```

because it often limits concurrency.

---

# 115. Long Context

Context length influences:

```text
TTFT

HBM

throughput

cost
```

Admission control may cap context by tenant.

```text
Documents
   |
   v
Ingestion
   |
   v
Chunking
   |
   v
Embedding
   |
   v

   |
   v
Retrieval
   |
   v
Reranking
   |
   v
LLM
```

---

# 117. RAG Governance

Preserve:

```text
document ACL

source

version

classification
```

through entire retrieval path.

---

# 118. RAG Multi-Tenancy

Possible:

```text
shared index + ACL filtering

tenant namespaces

dedicated index
```

# 119. RAG Freshness

Document updates must propagate to:

```text
indexes

caches
```

with measurable SLO.

# 120. Agent Platform

```text
User
 |
 v
Agent Runtime
 |
 v
Planner / Model
 |
 v
Tool Gateway
 |
 v
Enterprise Systems
```

---

# 121. Tool Gateway

Never let agent directly receive:

```text
database admin password
```

Tool gateway handles:

```text
authorization

validation

audit

limits
```

---

# 122. Agent Authorization Context

Decision considers:

```text
user identity

agent identity

tool

resource

requested action
```

---

# 123. High-Impact Actions

For:

```text
refund money

delete records

change access

send external messages
```

may require:

```text
human confirmation
```

---

# 124. Agent Sandboxing

Generated code executes in:

```text
ephemeral

restricted

low-privilege
```

environment.

---

# 125. Agent Financial Limits

Define:

```text
max steps

max tokens

max cost

max tool calls
```

per request.

---

# 126. Identity Architecture

Human:

```text
Enterprise Identity Provider
```

Workload:

```text
Workload Identity Federation
```

Avoid long-lived static secrets.

---

# 127. Workload Identity Flow

```text
Pod
 |
 v
Service Identity
 |
 v
Short-Lived Token
 |
 v
Cloud Service
```

---

# 128. Least Privilege

Training job gets:

```text
read dataset X

```

not:

```text

```

# 129. Secret Management

Use managed secret system.

Applications reference:

```text

```

# 130. Network Architecture

Separate:


to reduce blast radius.

# 131. Egress Control

Research workloads should not freely exfiltrate:

```text
sensitive data
```
