---

# 132. Kubernetes Security

Use:

```text
RBAC

admission policy

network policy

non-root containers

signed images

restricted privileges
```

---

# 133. Tenant Isolation

Isolation dimensions:

```text
identity

network

compute

storage

metadata

observability

GPU
```

Namespaces alone are insufficient.

---

# 134. Security Cell

High-level:

```text
Region
 |
 +---- Cell 1
 |
 +---- Cell 2
 |
 +---- Cell 3
```

Each cell limits:

```text
tenants

credentials

failure blast radius
```

---

# 135. Cell Architecture

Why?

A broken:

```text
runtime

policy

network

tenant
```

affects only one cell.

This improves both security and reliability.

---

# 136. Artifact Supply Chain

```text
Source
 |
 v
Build
 |
 v
Scan
 |
 v
Sign
 |
 v
Registry
 |
 v
Verify
 |
 v
Run
```

Applies to:

```text
containers

models
```

---

# 137. SBOM

Track dependencies for runtimes.

When vulnerability appears, query:

```text
which deployed models use affected library?
```

---

# 138. Model Integrity

Model artifact identified by:

```text
cryptographic digest
```

and optionally signature.

Deployment validates identity.

---

# 139. Observability Architecture

```text
Applications
   |
   +---- Metrics
   |
   +---- Logs
   |
   +---- Traces
   |
   v
Regional Collectors
   |
   v
Observability Backends
```

---

# 140. ML Observability

Add:

```text
feature freshness

data quality

prediction drift

model quality

labels

cost
```

---

# 141. Prediction Telemetry

Record enough metadata to attribute predictions to:

```text
model version

feature version

deployment

prompt version

retriever version
```

as appropriate.

---

# 142. Quality Feedback

```text
Prediction
    |
    v
Prediction Store
    |
    v
Ground Truth
    |
    v
Quality Computation
```

Labels may arrive much later.

---

# 143. Change Correlation

Record events:

```text
model deployed

feature changed

prompt changed

runtime upgraded
```

alongside operational metrics.

---

# 144. Alerting

Page on:

```text
user-impacting symptoms

fast SLO burn

critical data failure
```

Do not page on every metric anomaly.

---

# 145. Platform SLOs

Separate SLOs for:

```text
control plane

training submission

model deployment

online inference

feature freshness
```

---

# 146. Example Control-Plane SLO

```text
99.95% API availability
```

Could tolerate more downtime than production inference.

---

# 147. Example Serving SLO

```text
99.99% successful predictions

p99 < 100 ms
```

for critical model tier.

---

# 148. Error Budgets

Use remaining error budget to guide:

```text
release velocity

risk tolerance
```

---

# 149. Reliability Dependency Graph

```text
Inference
 |
 +---- Gateway
 |
 +---- Feature Store
 |
 +---- Model Runtime
```

End-to-end availability cannot exceed weakest mandatory dependencies without fallback.

---

# 150. Timeout Architecture

Every network call gets:

```text
bounded timeout
```

No infinite waits.

---

# 151. Retry Policy

Retry only:

```text
transient errors
```

with:

```text
backoff

jitter

retry budget
```

Avoid retry storms.

---

# 152. Circuit Breakers

If dependency is failing:

```text
stop sending unlimited requests
```

and fail fast/fallback.

---

# 153. Bulkheads

Separate resource pools so:

```text
failure in one workload
```

does not consume all capacity.

---

# 154. Graceful Degradation

Examples:

```text
fallback model

cached feature

static recommendation

manual review
```

depending on semantics.

---

# 155. Regional Failure

If Region A unavailable:

```text
Global Router
   |
   v
Region B
```

if residency and capacity allow.

---

# 156. Zone Failure

Each critical region should survive:

```text
single-zone loss
```

if required by SLO.

---

# 157. Capacity Under Failure

Normal capacity:

```text
1000 replicas
```

If one zone fails, remaining zones must absorb traffic.

Capacity planning must include failure mode.

---

# 158. Control-Plane Regionality

Options:

```text
global control plane

regional control planes

hybrid global + regional
```

At large scale hybrid is often useful.

---

# 159. Global Control Responsibilities

Potential:

```text
global catalog

policy

quota

model metadata

placement
```

---

# 160. Regional Control Responsibilities

Potential:

```text
local deployment

local cluster health

regional routing

regional cache
```

---

# 161. Global Outage Behavior

If global metadata unavailable:

```text
existing regional inference continues
```

but:

```text
new global placement may pause
```

---

# 162. Regional Autonomy

Each region should retain enough cached desired state to operate temporarily during global disconnection.

This increases resilience.

---

# 163. Disaster Recovery

Define:

```text
RTO

RPO
```

for:

```text
metadata DB

model registry

artifact store

governance evidence

feature state
```

---

# 164. Rebuildable vs Irreplaceable

Rebuildable:

```text
derived features

indexes

caches
```

Irreplaceable/critical:

```text
source data

audit evidence

certain metadata
```

Backup strategy differs.

---

# 165. Governance Architecture

```text
Model Inventory
      |
      +---- Ownership
      |
      +---- Risk
      |
      +---- Evaluation
      |
      +---- Approval
      |
      +---- Monitoring
```

---

# 166. Deployment Governance Gate

Production deployment asks:

```text
Is artifact approved
for this environment,
region,
purpose?
```

---

# 167. Governance Control-Plane Failure

Existing approved inference normally continues using:

```text
cached approval state
```

New deployments may block.

---

# 168. Rapid Revocation

Unsafe model:

```text
status = REVOKED
```

propagates to:

```text
deployment controllers

routers

regional caches
```

---

# 169. Model Inventory

Every production model must be discoverable.

Rogue endpoints should trigger alerts.

---

# 170. Data Governance

Track:

```text
dataset owner

classification

retention

allowed purpose

lineage
```

---

# 171. Privacy

Minimize sensitive data.

Do not automatically expose raw production data to notebooks.

Use:

```text
masked

sampled

approved secure environments
```

---

# 172. FinOps Architecture

```text
Resource Usage
      |
      v
Cost Attribution
      |
      v
Cost Warehouse
      |
      v
Showback / Chargeback
```

---

# 173. Cost Dimensions

Attribute to:

```text
team

project

model

training job

endpoint

tenant
```

---

# 174. Training Cost Guardrails

Before huge job:

```text
estimate cost

check quota

check budget

validate data

validate code
```

---

# 175. Serving Unit Economics

Track:

```text
cost per million predictions
```

or:

```text
cost per successful task
```

---

# 176. LLM Unit Economics

Track:

```text
input tokens

output tokens

model

cache use

cost

task success
```

---

# 177. Cost-Aware Scheduling

Choose:

```text
reserved

on-demand

spot
```

based on:

```text
priority

deadline

checkpointability
```

---

# 178. Cost-Aware Model Routing

Simple requests may use:

```text
small model
```

Complex:

```text
large model
```

Optimize:

```text
quality per dollar
```

---

# 179. Developer Experience

A platform that is technically perfect but painful will be bypassed.

Measure:

```text
time to first training job

time to deploy

failure rate

support tickets
```

---

# 180. CLI

Example:

```text
ml train config.yaml

ml deploy fraud:v31
```

CLI should wrap stable platform APIs.

---

# 181. SDK

Useful for notebooks and automation.

Example:

```python
platform.train(...)
```

But API remains source of truth.

---

# 182. UI

Useful for:

```text
discovery

visualization

approvals

operations
```

Do not make UI the only interface.

---

# 183. Templates

Provide project scaffolds:

```text
training template

serving template

feature template

RAG template
```

This creates paved roads.

---

# 184. Golden Paths

Standard workload gets:

```text
security

observability

cost tags

governance

reliability defaults
```

automatically.

---

# 185. Escape Hatches

Advanced teams may need custom behavior.

Allow controlled overrides.

Otherwise teams bypass platform entirely.

---

# 186. Platform Product Metrics

Measure:

```text
adoption

time to production

training success rate

deployment success rate

support load

developer satisfaction
```

---

# 187. Platform Adoption

If only:

```text
20% teams
```

use platform:

```text
architecture may be technically good
but organizationally unsuccessful
```

---

# 188. Build vs Buy

For each capability ask:

```text
strategic differentiator?

commodity capability?

integration cost?

operational burden?
```

Do not build everything.

---

# 189. Managed Services

Pros:

```text
faster delivery

less operations
```

Cons:

```text
cost

lock-in

limits
```

---

# 190. Open Source

Pros:

```text
control

ecosystem

portability
```

Cons:

```text
integration

operations

upgrades
```

---

# 191. Custom Platform

Build custom only where organization has unique scale/workflows or differentiation.

Avoid reinventing commodity databases.

---

# 192. Thin Platform

Mostly exposes underlying tools.

Pros:

```text
flexibility
```

Cons:

```text
complex UX

inconsistent practices
```

---

# 193. Thick Platform

Provides strong abstractions.

Pros:

```text
simplicity

governance

consistency
```

Cons:

```text
can constrain advanced teams
```

Balanced design is usually best.

---

# 194. Anti-Pattern — Tool Collection

```text
Kubernetes
+
MLflow
+
Airflow
+
Kafka
```

is not automatically an ML platform.

A platform needs:

```text
integrated workflows

stable APIs

ownership

SLOs

self-service
```

---

# 195. Anti-Pattern — Expose Raw Kubernetes

Forcing every data scientist to know:

```text
Deployments

Services

PVCs

RBAC
```

is poor platform abstraction.

---

# 196. Anti-Pattern — Hide Everything

Platform so rigid that advanced teams cannot express legitimate workloads.

Provide escape hatches.

---

# 197. Anti-Pattern — One Giant Cluster

One cluster for:

```text
research

training

production

regulated workloads
```

creates:

```text
blast radius

security problems

scheduling contention
```

---

# 198. Anti-Pattern — One Global Database on Every Request

Central metadata DB becomes synchronous dependency for worldwide serving.

Cache/configure locally.

---

# 199. Anti-Pattern — Registry in Request Path

Prediction should not query registry before every inference.

Resolve artifact during deployment.

---

# 200. Anti-Pattern — Unlimited Tenant Access

One team can consume:

```text
all GPU capacity
```

Use:

```text
quota

fair share

priority
```

---

# 201. Anti-Pattern — Manual Production Promotion

Production deployment via:

```text
Slack message

SSH

kubectl
```

does not scale.

Use governed APIs.

---

# 202. Anti-Pattern — No Resource Ownership

Every:

```text
model

feature

dataset

pipeline
```

needs owner.

---

# 203. Anti-Pattern — No Cost Ownership

Platform pays all costs centrally.

Teams have no visibility.

Waste increases.

---

# 204. Anti-Pattern — Monitoring Only Infrastructure

CPU healthy.

Model quality destroyed.

ML monitoring must include:

```text
data

features

quality

business
```

---

# 205. Anti-Pattern — One SLO for Everything

Training UI and fraud inference do not need same availability.

Use service tiers.

---

# 206. Service Tiers

Example:

```text
Tier 0 Critical

Tier 1 Production

Tier 2 Internal

Tier 3 Research
```

Each gets different:

```text
SLO

DR

security

cost
```

---

# 207. Tier 0

Example:

```text
payment fraud scoring
```

Might require:

```text
multi-zone

reserved capacity

fast rollback

24x7 paging
```

---

# 208. Tier 3

Research notebook may tolerate:

```text
hours of downtime
```

Do not pay Tier-0 reliability cost.

---

# 209. Capacity Estimation

Architect interview expects rough math.

Suppose:

```text
1B predictions/day
```

Average QPS:

```text
1,000,000,000 / 86,400
≈ 11,574 QPS
```

Peak may be:

```text
5× average
≈ 58k QPS
```

---

# 210. Replica Estimate

If one replica supports:

```text
200 QPS
```

then peak:

```text
58k / 200
≈ 290 replicas
```

Add:

```text
headroom

zone-failure capacity
```

---

# 211. Storage Estimate

100k model versions.

Average artifact:

```text
10 GB
```

Raw:

```text
~1 PB
```

before replicas/caches/checkpoints.

Architects should estimate orders of magnitude.

---

# 212. Training Queue Estimate

50k jobs/day:

```text
~0.58 jobs/sec average submission
```

But burst may be much higher.

Control plane must handle:

```text
request spikes
```

even though execution lasts hours.

---

# 213. Metadata Scale

Suppose every job creates:

```text
100 metadata events
```

50k/day gives:

```text
5M events/day
```

Not huge compared with data plane.

Control plane can often use conventional databases if carefully designed.

---

# 214. Important Architect Principle

Do not over-engineer control-plane scale just because data scale is enormous.

A 100 PB data platform may still have:

```text
millions
```

rather than trillions of metadata records.

Separate data-plane and metadata-plane sizing.

---

# 215. Multi-Region Model

Example:

```text
Global API
   |
   +---- US Region
   |
   +---- EU Region
   |
   +---- India Region
   |
   +---- APAC Region
   |
   +---- DR Region
```

---

# 216. Global Catalog

Stores logical resources.

Regional systems cache relevant state.

---

# 217. Regional Data Residency

Models trained on certain datasets may be restricted to:

```text
specific regions
```

Placement engine enforces this.

---

# 218. Multi-Region Feature Stores

Some features:

```text
globally replicated
```

Others:

```text
region-local
```

Consistency model depends on business.

---

# 219. Global Model Deployment

Logical deployment:

```text
fraud:v31
```

may have regional instances:

```text
India deployment

Europe deployment

US deployment
```

under one global resource.

---

# 220. Regional Version Skew

During rollout:

```text
US = v31

EU = v31

India = v30
```

Platform should expose this explicitly.

---

# 221. Global Failure Isolation

Region outage should not cause:

```text
global control storm
```

Regional controllers handle local recovery first.

---

# 222. Fleet Upgrades

Never upgrade:

```text
all clusters

all drivers

all runtimes
```

simultaneously.

Use:

```text
canary cell

small fleet

progressive rollout
```

---

# 223. Configuration Drift

Desired:

```text
runtime-v9
```

Actual:

```text
some clusters v7
```

Fleet manager continuously detects drift.

---

# 224. Platform Upgrade Strategy

Version:

```text
API

controllers

agents

runtime images

drivers
```

independently where possible.

---

# 225. Backward Compatibility

New global control plane must continue working with:

```text
older regional agents
```

during rolling upgrades.

---

# 226. Control-Plane Scaling

Partition workload by:

```text
tenant

region

resource type
```

if necessary.

Avoid one controller processing all global resources serially.

---

# 227. Queue Partitioning

High-volume events can be partitioned by:

```text
resource ID

tenant

region
```

to enable parallel processing while preserving local ordering.

---

# 228. Leader Election

Controllers may have multiple replicas.

One leader handles certain reconciliation domains.

Or resources can be sharded.

---

# 229. Hot Tenant

One large team may create disproportionate control-plane load.

Rate-limit and isolate noisy tenants.

---

# 230. API Rate Limits

Apply:

```text
per user

per tenant

per endpoint
```

to protect control plane.

---

# 231. Partial Failure

Deployment creates:

```text
model config

service

autoscaler
```

then fails.

Controller needs:

```text
retry

reconciliation

garbage collection
```

---

# 232. Finalizers / Cleanup

When deleting logical resource:

```text
cleanup child resources
```

before marking deletion complete.

Avoid orphaned infrastructure.

---

# 233. Orphan Detection

Periodic sweep detects:

```text
GPU endpoint
with no owning deployment record
```

Clean or quarantine.

---

# 234. Resource TTL

Temporary:

```text
notebooks

experiments

preview endpoints
```

should expire automatically.

---

# 235. Model Lifecycle

```text
Development
    |
    v
Candidate
    |
    v
Approved
    |
    v
Production
    |
    v
Deprecated
    |
    v
Retired
```

---

# 236. Resource Deletion Semantics

Deleting deployment should not automatically delete:

```text
model evidence

training lineage
```

Serving lifecycle differs from audit lifecycle.

---

# 237. Platform Disaster Recovery

Protect:

```text
metadata DB

artifact registry

governance store

audit logs

configuration
```

Test recovery.

---

# 238. Backup Is Not DR

A backup is only useful if:

```text
restore works
```

Perform game days.

---

# 239. Recovery Storm

After regional outage:

```text
10,000 models
```

all try to reload simultaneously.

Can overload:

```text
artifact storage

network

GPU nodes
```

Throttle recovery.

---

# 240. Priority Recovery

Restore:

```text
Tier 0 first

Tier 1 next

research last
```

Do not recover everything equally.

---

# 241. Model Cache During DR

Regional artifact caches can reduce load on central registry during mass recovery.

---

# 242. Dependency Failure Matrix

For each dependency document:

```text
Failure

User Impact

Fallback

Retry?

Alert?

RTO?
```

This makes reliability explicit.

---

# 243. Example — Registry Down

Existing inference:

```text
continues
```

New model loads:

```text
may fail unless cached
```

Training:

```text
can complete locally
```

Registration may queue.

---

# 244. Example — Feature Store Down

Critical model may:

```text
fallback
```

or:

```text
fail closed
```

based on semantics.

---

# 245. Example — Global Scheduler Down

Existing training:

```text
continues
```

New placements:

```text
pause
```

Regional serving unaffected.

---

# 246. Example — Observability Backend Down

ML serving:

```text
continues
```

Telemetry may buffer/drop based on policy.

---

# 247. Example — Governance DB Down

Existing approved serving:

```text
continues
```

New high-risk production changes:

```text
blocked
```

---

# 248. Example — Cost Pipeline Down

Workloads usually:

```text
continue
```

but cost enforcement may temporarily use cached quota/budget.

---

# 249. Platform Team Structure

Possible teams:

```text
ML Developer Platform

Training Infrastructure

Serving Infrastructure

Data/Feature Platform

GPU Infrastructure

ML Reliability

Security/Governance
```

Avoid excessive fragmentation.

---

# 250. Platform Ownership Boundaries

Each capability needs clear owner and API contract.

Avoid:

```text
everyone owns the platform
```

which means nobody does.

---

# 251. Build Sequence

Do not build 100 capabilities on day one.

Start with highest-friction workflows.

Example:

```text
1 Training

2 Registry

3 Deployment

4 Observability

5 Feature platform

6 Governance
```

depending on organization.

---

# 252. Platform Roadmap

Phase 1:

```text
standard training/deployment
```

Phase 2:

```text
self-service + observability
```

Phase 3:

```text
multi-tenancy + GPU scheduling
```

Phase 4:

```text
governance + multi-region + LLM
```

---

# 253. Premature Platformization

If company has:

```text
3 ML engineers
```

do not build Google-scale control plane.

Architecture should match organizational scale.

---

# 254. Platform Threshold

Platform investment becomes valuable when teams repeatedly solve:

```text
same infrastructure problems
```

independently.

---

# 255. Architect Interview Framework

When asked:

> Design a global ML platform.

Use:

```text
1 Requirements

2 Scale estimates

3 API / user workflows

4 High-level architecture

5 Data architecture

6 Training architecture

7 Serving architecture

8 Reliability

9 Security

10 Governance

11 Observability

12 Cost

13 Failure scenarios

14 Trade-offs
```

---

# 256. Step 1 — Requirements

Ask:

```text
classical ML or LLM?

batch or online?

latency target?

training scale?

multi-region?

regulated?

multi-tenant?
```

---

# 257. Step 2 — Estimate Scale

Do approximate:

```text
QPS

GPU-hours

storage

model count

job count
```

Do not need exact numbers.

Demonstrate quantitative thinking.

---

# 258. Step 3 — Identify Critical Path

For inference:

```text
Client
-> Gateway
-> Features
-> Model
-> Response
```

Optimize reliability and latency here.

---

# 259. Step 4 — Separate Planes

Explain:

```text
control plane
!=
data plane
```

This is a strong senior-level signal.

---

# 260. Step 5 — Explain State

For every component ask:

```text
Where is durable state?

What is source of truth?

What can be rebuilt?
```

---

# 261. Step 6 — Discuss Scaling Dimension

Training scheduler scales by:

```text
jobs

clusters

GPU resources
```

Serving scales by:

```text
traffic

models

regions
```

Metadata scales differently.

---

# 262. Step 7 — Discuss Consistency

Explain where you need:

```text
strong consistency
```

versus:

```text
eventual consistency
```

---

# 263. Step 8 — Discuss Failure

Pick components and say:

```text
what if this dies?
```

Strong architects proactively discuss failure modes.

---

# 264. Step 9 — Discuss Security

Mention:

```text
workload identity

least privilege

artifact signing

tenant isolation

network controls
```

---

# 265. Step 10 — Discuss Cost

Mention:

```text
shared GPU pool

right-sizing

cost-aware scheduling

showback

unit economics
```

---

# 266. Step 11 — Discuss Trade-Offs

Never present architecture as perfect.

Say:

```text
This improves X
but costs Y.
```

That is architect behavior.

---

# 267. Trade-Off Example — Shared Cluster

Pros:

```text
utilization

operations
```

Cons:

```text
blast radius

noisy neighbors
```

---

# 268. Trade-Off Example — Dedicated Clusters

Pros:

```text
isolation

predictability
```

Cons:

```text
cost

fragmentation
```

---

# 269. Trade-Off Example — Global Control Plane

Pros:

```text
consistent governance

simple global view
```

Cons:

```text
global dependency

latency
```

Hybrid regional architecture can reduce risk.

---

# 270. Trade-Off Example — Strong Consistency

Pros:

```text
simple correctness
```

Cons:

```text
latency

availability under partitions
```

Use only where required.

---

# 271. Trade-Off Example — Preloading Models

Pros:

```text
low latency
```

Cons:

```text
idle GPU cost
```

Dynamic loading improves economics but increases cold starts.

---

# 272. Trade-Off Example — Real-Time Features

Pros:

```text
freshness
```

Cons:

```text
complexity

cost
```

Do not stream everything.

---

# 273. Full Enterprise Architecture

```text
                              DEVELOPERS
                                  |
                                  v
                         +------------------+
                         |  ML PLATFORM API |
                         +------------------+
                                  |
      +---------------------------+---------------------------+
      |                           |                           |
      v                           v                           v
 TRAINING CTRL                MODEL CTRL                 FEATURE CTRL
      |                           |                           |
      +---------------------------+---------------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
                       GLOBAL CONTROL PLANE
                                  |
          +-----------------------+-----------------------+
          |                       |                       |
          v                       v                       v
      METADATA                 POLICY                 CATALOG
          |                       |                       |
          +-----------------------+-----------------------+
                                  |
                                  v
                        GLOBAL PLACEMENT
                                  |
        +-------------------------+-------------------------+
        |                         |                         |
        v                         v                         v
     REGION A                  REGION B                  REGION C
        |                         |                         |
        v                         v                         v
  REGIONAL CONTROL         REGIONAL CONTROL         REGIONAL CONTROL
        |                         |                         |
   +----+----+               +----+----+               +----+----+
   |         |               |         |               |         |

   |         |               |         |               |         |
```

Shared data systems:

```text

```

# 274. Request Path Architecture

```text
Client
  |
  v
Global Load Balancer
  |
  v
Regional Gateway
  |
  v
Admission / Auth
  |
  v
Model Router
  |
  +---- Feature Fetch
  |
  v
Inference Runtime
  |
  v
Response
```

Keep path minimal.

---

# 275. Keep Control Services Off the Request Path

Do not synchronously call:

```text
registry

catalog

governance

billing
```

for every prediction.

Use deployment-time resolution and cached configuration.

---

# 276. Training Path Architecture

```text
Developer
   |
   v
Training API
   |
   v
Admission
   |
   v
Queue
   |
   v
Global Scheduler
```

# 283. Failure Walkthrough — Global Control Plane Down

Expected:

```text
existing inference continues

existing training continues

regional controllers keep operating

new global submissions may queue
```

This demonstrates plane separation.

---

# 284. Failure Walkthrough — Region Lost

Global router:

```text
stops traffic to region
```

Critical workloads fail over where:

```text
capacity

residency

policy
```

allow.

---

# 285. Failure Walkthrough — GPU Fleet Saturated

Scheduler:

```text
protects production inference

queues research

uses burst capacity

preempts low-priority jobs
```

---

# 286. Failure Walkthrough — Registry Outage

Existing loaded models:

```text
serve
```

New deployment:

```text
uses regional cache
or waits
```

---

# 287. Failure Walkthrough — Bad Feature Release

Telemetry detects:

```text
distribution shift

quality drop
```

Feature lineage identifies dependent models.

Rollback feature version.

---

# 288. Failure Walkthrough — Malicious Model Artifact

Deployment verifies:

```text
digest

signature

approval
```

and refuses unknown artifact.

---

# 289. Failure Walkthrough — LLM Provider Outage

Router can:

```text
use internal model

alternate approved provider

degrade capability
```

depending on governance.

---

# 290. Failure Walkthrough — Runaway Agent

Budget controller detects:

```text
excessive tokens/tool calls
```

terminates execution.

Financial and operational blast radius stays bounded.

---

# 291. Failure Walkthrough — Observability Cardinality Explosion

Tenant adds:

```text
request_id
```

to metric label.

Telemetry gateway enforces cardinality policy and protects shared backend.

---

# 292. Failure Walkthrough — Training Data Poisoning

Data-quality/security signals flag source anomalies.

Release pipeline:

```text
blocks model promotion
```

until validated.

---

# 293. Failure Walkthrough — Governance Revocation

Critical flaw found.

Model marked:

```text
REVOKED
```

Regional controllers stop traffic and activate approved fallback.

```text
[ ] Workload classes identified

[ ] Scale estimated

[ ] Data architecture defined

[ ] Training architecture defined

[ ] Feature architecture defined

[ ] Registry defined

[ ] Serving path minimized

[ ] Deployment strategy defined

[ ] Multi-region behavior defined
```

# 300. Google-Style Interview Questions

## Architecture

1. Design a platform for 10,000 ML engineers.

2. How would you separate control and data planes?

3. What should the ML platform API expose?

4. How would you scale control-plane metadata?

5. What is the source of truth for desired state?

6. How would reconciliation work?

7. How do regional agents communicate with the global plane?

8. How do you avoid control-plane outages affecting inference?

---

## Training

9. Design a global distributed training platform.

10. How do you schedule 1,000-GPU jobs?

11. How do you handle gang scheduling?

12. How do you implement fair-share GPU scheduling?

13. How would preemption work?

14. How do you prevent training from starving inference?

15. How do you schedule based on GPU topology?

16. How do you handle spot interruptions?

17. How do you design checkpoint storage?

18. How do you recover from failed distributed jobs?

---

## Data

19. Design ML data architecture for 100 PB.

20. How do you combine streaming and batch features?

21. How do you guarantee point-in-time correctness?

22. How do you version datasets?

23. How do you avoid training-serving skew?

24. How do you execute petabyte-scale backfills safely?

25. How does dataset locality affect scheduler decisions?

---

## Serving

26. Design a global model-serving platform.

27. How do you serve 10,000 models?

28. How do you handle low-traffic GPU models?

29. How do you design model caching?

30. How do you implement canary releases?

31. How do you implement fallback models?

32. How do you autoscale GPU inference?

33. What if the model registry goes down?

34. How do you maintain 99.99% availability?

---

## LLM

35. Design a multi-tenant LLM platform.

36. How do you route between small and large models?

37. How do you control token cost?

38. How do you autoscale using token demand?

39. How do you manage KV cache pressure?

40. Design enterprise RAG.

41. Design secure agent tool execution.

42. How do you support multiple LLM providers safely?

---

## Reliability

43. What happens when a region fails?

44. How much capacity should remain after zone failure?

45. How do you prevent retry storms?

46. How do you recover thousands of models after outage?

47. What are your SLOs?

48. How do error budgets influence releases?

49. Which dependencies belong on the critical path?

---

## Security

50. Design workload identity.

51. How do you isolate tenants?

52. How do you secure model artifacts?

53. How do you secure training jobs running arbitrary Python?

54. How do you secure RAG ACLs?

55. How do you prevent agents from exceeding user permissions?

56. What happens if one GPU node is compromised?

57. Why are namespaces insufficient for strict isolation?

---

## Governance

58. How do models become production eligible?

59. How do you enforce model approvals?

60. How do you revoke a model globally?

61. How do you track lineage from prediction to model/data?

62. How do you support high-risk vs low-risk workflows?

63. How do governance systems behave during outages?

---

## Observability

64. What does an ML serving dashboard contain?

65. How do you monitor feature freshness?

66. How do you detect training-serving skew?

67. How do you connect predictions to delayed labels?

68. How do you monitor LLM systems?

69. How do you prevent observability cardinality explosions?

---

## Cost

70. How do you attribute GPU cost?

71. How do you calculate cost per prediction?

72. How do you maximize GPU fleet efficiency?

73. How do you choose reserved vs spot capacity?

74. How do you prevent forgotten notebooks wasting GPUs?

75. How do you optimize LLM cost?

76. Why isn't 100% GPU utilization always optimal?

---

For a 45-minute interview:

```text
0-5 min
Requirements

5-10 min
Scale estimates

10-20 min
High-level architecture

20-30 min
Deep dive

30-38 min
Reliability + security

38-43 min
Scaling + cost

43-45 min
Trade-offs / summary
```

If interviewer asks:

```text
training-heavy company
```

```text
scheduler
```

If online ML:

```text

SLO
```

If GenAI:

```text

RAG

agent security
```

# 303. What Senior Candidates Do Differently

Junior:

```text
names tools
```

Senior:

```text
defines interfaces

failure domains

trade-offs
```

Architect:

```text
connects organization,
economics,
security,
reliability,
and long-term evolution
```

---

# 304. Tool-Agnostic Thinking

Instead of:

```text
Use Kafka
```

say:

```text
We need a durable partitioned event log
with replay and consumer scaling.
Kafka is one implementation option.
```

This demonstrates architecture rather than product memorization.

---

# 305. When to Name Technologies

After explaining requirement.

Example:

```text
Need scalable columnar lake storage
with snapshots and schema evolution.

Options include:
Iceberg-like / Delta-like table formats.
```

Reason first.

Tool second.

---

# 306. Capacity Math Signal

Even rough calculations strongly improve system-design answers.

Example:

```text
1B requests/day
≈ 12k average QPS

Assume 5× peak
≈ 60k QPS
```

Then size replicas.

---

# 307. Failure Thinking Signal

For every box ask:

```text
What happens if this box disappears?
```

This habit separates architects from diagram drawers.

---

# 308. Cost Thinking Signal

For every expensive component ask:

```text
What is the unit cost?

What is idle?

What can be shared?

What can use cheaper capacity?
```

---

# 309. Security Thinking Signal

For every trust boundary ask:

```text
Who is calling?

What identity?

What permission?

What if compromised?
```

---

# 310. Data Correctness Signal

For ML always ask:

```text
Which dataset version?

Which feature version?

Point-in-time correct?

What if data is stale?
```

---

# 311. Operational Thinking Signal

Ask:

```text
How will on-call debug this at 3 AM?
```

If architecture cannot answer, observability design is incomplete.

---

# 312. Platform Thinking Signal

Ask:

```text
How will 2,000 teams use this
without opening tickets?
```

This leads to:

```text
APIs

self-service

golden paths

templates
```

---

# 313. Evolution Thinking Signal

Ask:

```text
How do we migrate GPU generations?

How do we upgrade runtimes?

How do we version APIs?

How do we deprecate old models?
```

Architectures must survive change.

# 316. What You Must Remember From Chapter 23

1. **An enterprise ML platform is a distributed system serving both human developers and machine workloads.**

2. **The first step in ML platform design is defining users, workload classes, scale, and business constraints—not selecting tools.**

3. **Research, training, data processing, and production inference have different reliability and security requirements and should not be treated as one workload class.**

4. **Control-plane/data-plane separation is one of the most important architecture patterns in large ML systems.**

5. **The control plane manages intent, policy, metadata, placement, and lifecycle; the data plane performs expensive ML work.**

6. **Existing inference should normally survive temporary failures of central registries, metadata systems, governance services, and global schedulers.**

7. **Declarative APIs and reconciliation loops make large platforms resilient to partial failures.**

8. **Platform APIs should expose ML concepts rather than forcing users to manage raw infrastructure objects.**

9. **Long-running operations should be asynchronous and idempotent.**

10. **Metadata and large ML artifacts belong in different storage systems.**

11. **Global event-driven control planes reduce synchronous coupling between platform capabilities.**

12. **GPU scheduling requires global placement, local topology awareness, gang scheduling, quota, priority, fair share, and preemption.**

13. **Production inference capacity must be protected from opportunistic research demand.**

14. **Shared accelerator pools improve economics through statistical multiplexing but require isolation and fair scheduling.**

15. **Hardware profiles make applications portable across accelerator generations.**

16. **Training must reference immutable dataset and runtime versions to remain reproducible.**

17. **Point-in-time correctness is essential when historical features are used for supervised learning.**

18. **Feature platforms must align offline history with online serving semantics to prevent training-serving skew.**

19. **Experiment tracking should connect code, data, configuration, hardware, metrics, and artifacts.**

20. **Production model artifacts should be immutable, versioned, evaluated, governed, and cryptographically identifiable.**

21. **Model deployment is a lifecycle operation, not merely starting a container.**

22. **Canary, shadow, blue/green, and rollback mechanisms should be first-class serving-platform capabilities.**

23. **The production inference critical path should contain as few synchronous dependencies as possible.**

24. **Timeouts, deadlines, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads, and graceful degradation must be designed explicitly.**

25. **LLM serving requires token-aware admission, KV-cache management, batching, routing, and cost controls beyond ordinary request-based autoscaling.**

26. **RAG platforms must preserve source ACLs, lineage, versioning, and data freshness through the entire retrieval lifecycle.**

27. **Agent platforms require deterministic external authorization around every high-impact tool action.**

28. **Human and workload identities should be short-lived, scoped, and governed through least privilege.**

29. **Security isolation must span identity, compute, storage, network, metadata, telemetry, and GPUs.**

30. **Cell architectures limit both security blast radius and reliability blast radius.**

31. **Containers and model artifacts should move through trusted build, signing, registration, and verification pipelines.**

32. **ML observability combines traditional service telemetry with data, features, predictions, labels, quality, and cost.**

33. **Production quality cannot be understood without connecting predictions to later ground-truth outcomes where labels exist.**

34. **Model, feature, prompt, retriever, runtime, and configuration changes should all appear as observable deployment events.**

35. **Not every service requires the same SLO; reliability should be tiered by business criticality.**

36. **Capacity planning must consider failure capacity, not only normal traffic.**

37. **Regional systems should retain enough autonomy to continue important work when global control systems become unavailable.**

38. **Disaster recovery planning starts by distinguishing irreplaceable state from rebuildable derived state.**

39. **Model governance should be integrated into the deployment path rather than implemented as paperwork outside the platform.**

40. **Rapid global revocation of unsafe models must be a first-class capability.**

41. **FinOps requires workload-level attribution, unit economics, budget controls, cost-aware scheduling, and shared-fleet efficiency.**

42. **The goal is not maximum hardware utilization; the goal is the best useful business outcome for the required reliability, quality, and cost.**

43. **A successful ML platform is a product and must optimize developer experience, adoption, and time to production.**

44. **Golden paths should automatically provide security, observability, governance, cost attribution, and reliability defaults.**

45. **Escape hatches are necessary because advanced workloads will eventually exceed standard abstractions.**

46. **A collection of open-source tools is not automatically a platform; platform value comes from integrated workflows and stable interfaces.**

47. **Architects must reason quantitatively about QPS, storage, GPU-hours, capacity, and cost even when estimates are rough.**

48. **Strong system-design answers describe not only the happy path but also control-plane failure, regional outage, capacity exhaustion, corrupt data, and bad deployments.**

49. **The best architecture decisions explicitly state trade-offs rather than pretending every design choice has only benefits.**

50. **At senior architect level, the ML platform is best understood as one integrated socio-technical system connecting developers, data, compute, models, runtime, policy, economics, and operations.**
