# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 26 — Linux, Networking, Kubernetes, and Cloud Infrastructure Deep Dive for MLOps Architects

---

# 1. Why Infrastructure Depth Matters

Many ML incidents look like:

```text
Model is healthy.

Code is correct.

Deployment succeeded.

But requests are timing out.
```

The actual problem may be:

```text
DNS

TCP

memory pressure

cgroups

ephemeral storage

node networking

load balancer

NAT

kube-proxy/CNI

GPU driver

cloud quota
```

A senior MLOps architect must understand the layers below the application.

---

# 2. The Infrastructure Stack

Think:

```text
Application
    |
    v
ML Runtime
    |
    v
Container
    |
    v
Kubernetes
    |
    v
Linux
    |
    v
Network / Storage
    |
    v
Cloud Infrastructure
    |
    v
Physical Hardware
```

Failures can originate at any layer.

---

# 3. The Senior Debugging Principle

When a production service fails, do not ask only:

```text
What is wrong with the code?
```

Ask:

```text
Which layer violated an assumption?
```

---

# 4. Linux Is the Ground Truth

Containers do not replace Linux.

Kubernetes does not replace Linux.

Your workloads still rely on:

```text
processes

memory

filesystem

sockets

CPU scheduling

kernel behavior
```

Understanding Linux explains many container and Kubernetes behaviors.

---

# 5. Linux Process

A process is a running program with:

```text
PID

address space

threads

file descriptors

environment

credentials
```

---

# 6. Parent and Child Processes

Processes form a hierarchy.

```text
init/systemd
   |
   +---- container runtime
   |
   +---- kubelet
```

Inside containers, your process may become PID 1 in its namespace.

---

# 7. Process ID

Each process has a PID.

Example:

```text
PID 3921
```

But container PID namespace may show:

```text
PID 1
```

for the same workload from inside the container.

---

# 8. Threads

A process may have multiple threads sharing:

```text
address space

open files

heap
```

while each thread has:

```text
stack

execution state
```

---

# 9. Context Switching

CPU switches between runnable threads/processes.

Excessive context switching can indicate:

```text
too many threads

lock contention

oversubscription
```

---

# 10. CPU Scheduling

Linux scheduler decides which runnable process gets CPU time.

A container requesting:

```text
4 CPUs
```

does not mean it gets four permanently dedicated physical cores unless explicitly configured.

---

# 11. CPU Time vs Wall Time

CPU time:

```text
actual processor execution
```

Wall time:

```text
elapsed real-world time
```

A task can take 10 seconds wall time but only 1 second CPU if it spends most time waiting.

---

# 12. Load Average

Linux load average roughly represents runnable or uninterruptible tasks over time.

High load can result from:

```text
CPU saturation

I/O wait
```

not merely CPU usage.

---

# 13. User vs System CPU

User CPU:

```text
application execution
```

System CPU:

```text
kernel work
```

High system CPU may indicate:

```text
network processing

filesystem overhead

syscalls
```

---

# 14. Steal Time

In virtualized environments, CPU steal indicates time when VM wanted CPU but hypervisor ran something else.

High steal can mean:

```text
host contention
```

This may explain performance instability.

---

# 15. Nice Priority

Linux scheduler supports relative priority using nice values.

But for containers, resource governance is normally handled through cgroups and orchestration.

---

# 16. Signals

Common:

```text
SIGTERM

SIGKILL

SIGINT

SIGHUP
```

---

# 17. SIGTERM

Polite shutdown request.

Application can:

```text
stop accepting traffic

flush state

close connections

exit
```

---

# 18. SIGKILL

Immediate termination.

Cannot be caught.

Use only when process fails to stop gracefully.

---

# 19. Zombie Process

A child process exited, but parent has not collected exit status.

Zombie consumes little memory but occupies PID table entry.

Large numbers can indicate bad process management.

---

# 20. PID 1 Behavior

PID 1 has special signal/reaping responsibilities.

Poor container entrypoints can cause:

```text
signals not propagated

zombie children
```

---

# 21. File Descriptor

Linux represents many resources as file descriptors:

```text
files

TCP sockets

pipes

devices
```

---

# 22. File Descriptor Exhaustion

Service may fail with:

```text
too many open files
```

Causes:

```text
socket leak

file leak

too-low ulimit
```

---

# 23. Socket Is a File Descriptor

Every network connection consumes one.

A service with hundreds of thousands of connections needs sufficient FD limits.

---

# 24. Process Limits

Common limits include:

```text
open files

process count

locked memory
```

Poor limits can become invisible bottlenecks.

---

# 25. Virtual Memory

Each process sees a virtual address space.

Kernel maps virtual memory to:

```text
physical RAM

shared pages

memory-mapped files

swap
```

---

# 26. Why Virtual Memory Matters

A process showing:

```text
100 GB virtual size
```

does not necessarily consume:

```text
100 GB physical RAM
```

Understand resident memory.

---

# 27. RSS

Resident Set Size:

```text
memory pages currently resident in RAM
```

Often more relevant than virtual size.

---

# 28. Heap

Dynamic allocations commonly live on heap.

Examples:

```text
Python objects

model buffers

dataframes
```

---

# 29. Stack

Each thread has a stack.

Used for:

```text
function calls

local variables

execution frames
```

---

# 30. Memory-Mapped Files

Applications can map files into address space.

Useful for:

```text
large model weights

datasets

shared libraries
```

without explicitly reading everything first.

---

# 31. Page

Linux memory operates in pages.

Memory management, page cache, and faults operate at page granularity.

---

# 32. Page Fault

When process accesses page not currently mapped/resident.

Minor fault:

```text
page available without disk I/O
```

Major fault:

```text
requires storage access
```

Large major-fault rates can hurt latency.

---

# 33. Page Cache

Linux uses unused RAM to cache filesystem data.

This explains why:

```text
free RAM is low
```

does not automatically mean memory shortage.

Cached pages can often be reclaimed.

---

# 34. Page Cache and ML

Repeatedly loading:

```text
same dataset

same model artifact
```

may become much faster after first read because of page cache.

---

# 35. Warm vs Cold Read

Cold:

```text
storage -> RAM
```

Warm:

```text
page cache -> application
```

Benchmarking must distinguish them.

---

# 36. Swap

Swap moves memory pages to slower storage.

For latency-sensitive inference, heavy swapping is usually disastrous.

---

# 37. Container Memory and Swap

Container behavior depends on cgroup and host configuration.

Do not assume swap behavior is identical across environments.

---

# 38. Out-of-Memory Condition

When system/container cannot satisfy memory needs, kernel may trigger OOM handling.

---

# 39. OOM Killer

Linux may kill selected process to recover memory.

Kubernetes may report:

```text
OOMKilled
```

---

# 40. Memory Limit

Container memory limit creates a cgroup boundary.

If workload exceeds limit:

```text
container may be killed
```

even if node still has memory.

---

# 41. Node-Level OOM

If whole node is under severe memory pressure:

```text
multiple workloads
```

may be affected.

This is a larger failure domain.

---

# 42. Memory Leak

Application continuously retains objects no longer needed.

Symptoms:

```text
RSS climbs over hours/days
```

Eventually:

```text
OOM
```

---

# 43. Cache vs Memory Leak

A cache growing forever looks like a leak operationally.

Every cache needs:

```text
capacity

TTL

eviction policy
```

---

# 44. Fragmentation

Free memory may exist but not in ideal layout for allocation.

Relevant especially to:

```text
GPU HBM

native allocators
```

---

# 45. Huge Pages

Large memory pages reduce page table overhead for some workloads.

Can benefit:

```text
databases

high-performance computing
```

but require deliberate configuration.

---

# 46. NUMA

Large servers have multiple NUMA nodes.

Memory access to local NUMA node is faster than remote node.

---

# 47. NUMA and GPUs

GPU may be physically nearer certain CPUs/NICs.

Bad placement can cause:

```text
cross-socket traffic

reduced PCIe bandwidth
```

---

# 48. NUMA-Aware ML Scheduling

For high-performance training:

```text
GPU

CPU

NIC
```

topology should align where possible.

---

# 49. cgroups

Control groups enforce/measure resource usage.

They underpin container resource limits.

---

# 50. cgroup Resource Domains

Examples:

```text
CPU

memory

I/O

process count
```

---

# 51. CPU Request vs CPU Limit

Kubernetes request affects:

```text
scheduling
```

CPU limit affects:

```text
runtime throttling
```

These are different.

---

# 52. CPU Throttling

A container can be throttled when it consumes its CPU quota.

Symptoms:

```text
CPU metric not obviously saturated

latency rises

throttled time increases
```

---

# 53. Why CPU Limits Can Hurt Latency

A bursty service may briefly need more CPU.

Strict low limit prevents burst.

p99 can suffer.

---

# 54. Memory Is Different From CPU

CPU can be throttled.

Memory cannot be "slowly throttled" in the same way.

Exceed memory limit:

```text
risk OOM
```

---

# 55. Namespaces

Linux namespaces create isolation views for:

```text
PID

network

mounts

users

hostname
```

Containers heavily rely on them.

---

# 56. PID Namespace

Process inside container sees isolated process tree.

---

# 57. Network Namespace

Container gets its own:

```text
interfaces

routes

ports
```

---

# 58. Mount Namespace

Controls filesystem mount visibility.

---

# 59. User Namespace

Can map container users to different host users.

Useful for reducing privilege.

---

# 60. Container Is Not a VM

A container:

```text
shares host kernel
```

A VM:

```text
runs its own guest kernel
```

Containers are lighter but have different isolation properties.

---

# 61. Syscall Boundary

Container process still calls host kernel.

Kernel vulnerabilities matter.

---

# 62. Container Escape Risk

A vulnerability or excessive privilege can allow workload to affect host.

Controls include:

```text
non-root

seccomp

restricted capabilities

sandbox runtimes
```

---

# 63. Filesystem Layers

Container images commonly use layered filesystems.

Writing large temporary data into writable layer may be inefficient.

---

# 64. Ephemeral Storage

Pods often use node-local ephemeral storage for:

```text
logs

temporary files

container writable layer
```

---

# 65. Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion

A workload writing:

```text
huge checkpoints
```

to local container filesystem can fill node disk.

Other pods may fail.

---

# 66. Persistent Storage vs Ephemeral Storage

Ephemeral:

```text
lifetime tied to pod/node
```

Persistent:

```text
managed beyond pod lifecycle
```

Choose intentionally.

---

# 67. Linux I/O

Storage latency depends on:

```text
device

filesystem

queue depth

access pattern

page cache
```

---

# 68. Sequential vs Random I/O

Sequential reads generally exploit storage bandwidth efficiently.

Random small reads stress latency/IOPS.

ML data layout strongly affects this.

---

# 69. IOPS

Input/output operations per second.

Important for:

```text
many small files

metadata-heavy workloads
```

---

# 70. Throughput

Bytes per second.

Important for:

```text
large dataset scans

model loading

checkpoints
```

---

# 71. Storage Latency

Important for:

```text
small synchronous lookups

metadata

databases
```

Different systems optimize different dimensions.

---

# 72. Disk Queue

If storage receives more operations than it can complete:

```text
queue grows

latency increases
```

---

# 73. Small File Problem

Millions of tiny files cause:

```text
metadata overhead

open/close overhead

poor throughput
```

This matters at both data and filesystem level.

---

# 74. Inodes

Each filesystem object consumes metadata/inode resources.

You can run out of inodes before bytes.

---

# 75. Linux Networking Foundation

Before Kubernetes networking, understand:

```text
IP

TCP

UDP

DNS

routing

NAT

TLS

HTTP
```

---

# 76. IP Address

Identifies network interface/end point at network layer.

Examples:

```text
10.0.1.15

2001:db8::...
```

---

# 77. Private IP

Private address ranges are not globally internet-routable.

Common cloud VPCs heavily use private IPs.

---

# 78. Subnet

Logical IP range.

Example:

```text
10.20.0.0/24
```

contains 256 addresses in raw IPv4 address space.

Some cloud providers reserve some addresses.

---

# 79. CIDR

Notation:

```text
10.0.0.0/16
```

Prefix length determines network size.

Architects should be comfortable with basic subnetting.

---

# 80. Routing

Routing determines:

```text
where packets go next
```

based on destination.

---

# 81. Routing Table

Example:

```text
10.1.0.0/16 -> local

0.0.0.0/0 -> NAT gateway
```

---

# 82. Default Route

```text
0.0.0.0/0
```

matches destinations not covered by more specific route.

---

# 83. Longest Prefix Match

Routing chooses most specific matching route.

This is fundamental to understanding network behavior.

---

# 84. TCP

TCP provides:

```text
reliable ordered byte stream
```

on top of IP.

---

# 85. TCP Connection

Typically established using three-way handshake:

```text
SYN

SYN-ACK

ACK
```

---

# 86. TCP Connection Setup Cost

Creating new connection costs:

```text
network round trips

kernel state
```

At scale, reuse matters.

---

# 87. Connection Pooling

Reuse existing TCP/TLS connections.

Benefits:

```text
lower latency

less handshake overhead

fewer sockets churn
```

---

# 88. Keepalive

Long-lived connection can stay open and be reused.

Need to coordinate:

```text
client timeout

server timeout

load balancer timeout
```

---

# 89. Half-Open/Stale Connections

Network devices may silently drop idle connection state.

Client thinks connection exists.

Next request fails.

Connection pool must handle stale connections.

---

# 90. TCP Retransmission

If packet appears lost:

```text
TCP retransmits
```

Packet loss can create dramatic tail latency.

---

# 91. Packet Loss

Even small loss on high-throughput flows can materially hurt performance.

Important for:

```text
distributed training fabrics
```

---

# 92. TCP Congestion Control

TCP adapts sending rate based on inferred network congestion.

Network tuning matters in high-bandwidth workloads.

---

# 93. Latency

Network latency includes:

```text
propagation

routing

queueing

serialization

processing
```

Cross-region physical distance cannot be optimized away.

---

# 94. Bandwidth-Delay Product

High-bandwidth long-distance links need enough in-flight data to fully use capacity.

Useful for understanding cross-region transfers.

---

# 95. UDP

Connectionless datagram protocol.

No built-in reliable ordered delivery.

Used by protocols such as:

```text
DNS in many cases

QUIC underlying transport
```

---

# 96. DNS

Maps names to records.

Example:

```text
feature-store.internal
->
10.20.3.18
```

---

# 97. DNS Query Path

Conceptually:

```text
Application
    |
    v
Resolver
    |
    v
DNS Service
    |
    v
Authoritative Records
```

---

# 98. DNS Caching

Resolvers cache responses according to TTL.

This improves performance but means changes may not propagate instantly.

---

# 99. DNS TTL Trade-Off

Low TTL:

```text
fast changes

more DNS load
```

High TTL:

```text
efficient caching

slow failover/change propagation
```

---

# 100. DNS Failure Symptoms

Possible:

```text
name not found

temporary resolution failure

intermittent connection errors
```

Debug DNS separately from TCP.

---

# 101. DNS in Kubernetes

Services get internal DNS names.

Example concept:

```text
model-server.ml.svc.cluster.local
```

---

# 102. DNS Search Domains

Kubernetes may expand short names using search domains.

This can generate multiple DNS queries.

---

# 103. DNS Scaling Problem

Thousands of pods making excessive lookups can overwhelm cluster DNS.

Caching helps.

---

# 104. Connection Storm

A rollout causes:

```text
10,000 pods
```

to open DB connections simultaneously.

Database or proxy collapses.

Rate limit startup and size pools carefully.

---

# 105. TLS

TLS provides:

```text
encryption

integrity

server authentication
```

and optionally client authentication.

---

# 106. TLS Handshake

Establishes:

```text
cryptographic parameters

peer identity

session keys
```

before application data.

---

# 107. TLS Certificate

Binds identity to public key via trusted certificate authority chain.

---

# 108. Certificate Expiry

A common production incident:

```text
everything worked yesterday

TLS fails today
```

Monitor certificate expiry proactively.

---

# 109. Hostname Verification

Certificate must match expected hostname.

Otherwise:

```text
TLS validation fails
```

---

# 110. Mutual TLS

Both client and server authenticate with certificates.

Common in service-to-service security.

---

# 111. mTLS Trade-Off

Benefits:

```text
strong workload identity

encrypted transport
```

Costs:

```text
certificate lifecycle

operational complexity
```

---

# 112. HTTP

Application protocol commonly running over TCP/TLS.

---

# 113. HTTP/1.1

Supports persistent connections.

But concurrent request behavior has limitations compared with modern protocols.

---

# 114. HTTP/2

Supports multiplexing many logical streams over one connection.

Often used by:

```text
gRPC
```

---

# 115. gRPC

RPC framework generally built on HTTP/2 and protobuf-like schemas.

Useful for:

```text
service-to-service APIs

streaming

strong contracts
```

---

# 116. REST vs gRPC

REST:

```text
human-friendly

broad compatibility
```

gRPC:

```text
strong schemas

efficient binary transport

streaming
```

Choice depends on clients and system needs.

---

# 117. HTTP Timeout Layers

Potential:

```text
client timeout

gateway timeout

load balancer timeout

server timeout

downstream timeout
```

Misalignment causes mysterious failures.

---

# 118. Timeout Budget

If client timeout:

```text
1 second
```

server should not spend:

```text
5 seconds
```

continuing useless work.

---

# 119. Proxy

A proxy forwards traffic on behalf of client/server.

---

# 120. Reverse Proxy

Sits in front of backend servers.

Handles:

```text
routing

TLS

load balancing

rate limiting
```

---

# 121. Load Balancer

Distributes traffic across backend instances.

---

# 122. Layer 4 vs Layer 7 Load Balancing

L4:

```text
TCP/UDP-level
```

L7:

```text
HTTP-aware
```

L7 can route by:

```text
host

path

headers
```

---

# 123. Health Checks

Load balancer needs to know whether backend should receive traffic.

Health check should represent:

```text
serving readiness
```

not merely process existence.

---

# 124. Sticky Sessions

Traffic from same client may be kept on same backend.

Useful sometimes, but can:

```text
create imbalance

complicate failover
```

Stateless services usually avoid requiring stickiness.

---

# 125. NAT

Network Address Translation changes source/destination addressing.

Common for private hosts accessing internet.

---

# 126. NAT Gateway

Private workloads may route outbound traffic through shared NAT.

Potential bottlenecks:

```text
connection count

port exhaustion

throughput

cost
```

---

# 127. SNAT Port Exhaustion

Thousands of outbound connections through limited source addresses can exhaust ephemeral port space.

Symptoms:

```text
intermittent connection failures
```

---

# 128. Egress Architecture

High-volume ML APIs calling external LLM providers may generate enormous outbound traffic.

Consider:

```text
NAT capacity

egress cost

connection reuse
```

---

# 129. Firewall

Controls allowed network flows.

Cloud versions include:

```text
security groups

network ACLs

firewall policies
```

depending on provider.

---

# 130. Stateful Firewall

Tracks connections.

Return traffic may be automatically allowed.

---

# 131. Stateless ACL

Each direction may require explicit rules.

Understand semantics of chosen network control.

---

# 132. VPC

Virtual Private Cloud provides isolated network boundary in cloud.

Includes:

```text
subnets

routes

firewalls

private services

gateways
```

---

# 133. Public vs Private Subnet

Conceptually:

```text
public subnet
has direct route to internet gateway

private subnet
does not
```

Exact provider semantics vary.

---

# 134. Internet Gateway

Provides internet connectivity for eligible public resources.

---

# 135. NAT Gateway

Allows outbound access from private networks without direct inbound exposure.

---

# 136. Private Service Endpoint

Access managed cloud service without traversing public internet.

Useful for:

```text
object storage

managed databases

secret managers
```

---

# 137. VPC Peering

Connects separate VPCs.

Potential issue:

```text
non-transitive routing
```

in many architectures.

---

# 138. Transit Hub

Central routing construct can connect many networks more systematically.

Useful at enterprise scale.

---

# 139. CIDR Planning

Poor IP planning causes painful future expansion.

Need capacity for:

```text
pods

nodes

services

future regions

peered networks
```

---

# 140. Overlapping CIDRs

Two networks both use:

```text
10.0.0.0/16
```

Connecting them becomes difficult.

Plan globally.

---

# 141. Kubernetes Node

A machine running workloads.

Key components include:

```text
kubelet

container runtime

networking

storage plugins
```

---

# 142. Kubernetes Control Plane

Main components conceptually:

```text
API Server

Scheduler

Controller Manager

etcd
```

---

# 143. API Server

Central API interface.

All desired state changes flow through it.

---

# 144. etcd

Distributed key-value store used for Kubernetes cluster state.

It is critical.

---

# 145. etcd Characteristics

Needs:

```text
low latency

durability

quorum
```

Slow storage or network can affect whole control plane.

---

# 146. etcd Is Not Application Database

Do not use Kubernetes API/etcd as arbitrary high-volume ML metadata warehouse.

Store workload-specific metadata elsewhere.

---

# 147. Kubernetes Scheduler

Watches unscheduled pods and selects nodes.

Considers:

```text
resource requests

affinity

taints

topology

plugins
```

---

# 148. Scheduler Filtering

First removes nodes that cannot run pod.

Reasons:

```text
insufficient memory

wrong GPU

taint not tolerated

affinity mismatch
```

---

# 149. Scheduler Scoring

Then ranks feasible nodes.

May prefer:

```text
balanced utilization

affinity

topology
```

---

# 150. Default Scheduler Limitation for Large ML Jobs

It schedules pods individually.

Distributed training may need:

```text
gang semantics

topology coordination

queue fairness
```

beyond default behavior.

---

# 151. kubelet

Agent on each node.

Responsibilities include:

```text
ensure pods running

manage containers

run probes

report status
```

---

# 152. Container Runtime

Actually creates/manages containers.

Kubernetes delegates through runtime interfaces.

---

# 153. Pod Lifecycle

Conceptually:

```text
Pending

Running

Succeeded

Failed
```

with detailed container states inside.

---

# 154. Pod Pending

Means not fully scheduled/running yet.

Investigate scheduler events.

---

# 155. Pod Running Does Not Mean Ready

Container can be alive while readiness probe fails.

Service may correctly exclude it from traffic.

---

# 156. Pod Termination

Typical flow:

```text
mark terminating

remove from service endpoints

send SIGTERM

wait grace period

SIGKILL if necessary
```

Exact timing matters during rollouts.

---

# 157. Termination Grace Period

Must be long enough for:

```text
in-flight inference

checkpoint flush

consumer shutdown
```

but not absurdly long.

---

# 158. preStop Hook

Can perform work before termination.

Use carefully; it consumes termination grace period.

---

# 159. Deployment Rolling Update

New replicas are gradually introduced while old ones are removed.

Key controls:

```text
maxSurge

maxUnavailable
```

---

# 160. Bad Model Rollout

If readiness only checks:

```text
HTTP process alive
```

but not model load/health:

```text
broken pods may receive traffic
```

Readiness must reflect real serving state.

---

# 161. ReplicaSet

Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage desired pod replicas.

---

# 162. StatefulSet

Provides ordered/stable pod identities and persistent volume associations.

Useful for selected stateful systems.

---

# 163. DaemonSet

Runs a pod on every/selected node.

Common for:

```text
logging agents

monitoring agents

GPU device plugins
```

---

# 164. Job

Runs batch workload to completion.

---

# 165. CronJob

Creates Jobs on schedule.

---

# 166. Service

Stable virtual endpoint over dynamic pods.

---

# 167. Service Selector

Selects pods using labels.

Wrong labels can produce:

```text
Service with zero endpoints
```

while pods look healthy.

---

# 168. Endpoint / EndpointSlice

Represents actual backend endpoints behind Service.

Critical debugging object.

---

# 169. ClusterIP

Internal virtual service address.

---

# 170. NodePort

Exposes service on node ports.

Often underlying mechanism for some external load balancer integrations.

---

# 171. LoadBalancer Service

Requests cloud/provider integration for external/internal load balancer.

---

# 172. Ingress

HTTP routing abstraction traditionally used for external web traffic.

---

# 173. Gateway API Concept

More expressive newer-style traffic routing abstraction.

Supports structured roles and richer routing.

Architecturally useful for platform traffic management.

---

# 174. Service Discovery

Pods discover services via:

```text
DNS

service virtual IP
```

---

# 175. kube-proxy Concept

Historically programs network forwarding rules for Services.

Modern CNIs may implement service routing differently.

Do not over-assume specific data path.

---

# 176. CNI

Container Network Interface plugins provide pod networking.

Responsibilities may include:

```text
IP allocation

routing

network policy

service acceleration
```

depending on implementation.

---

# 177. Pod IP

Each pod generally receives network identity/IP.

Exact routing model depends on CNI.

---

# 178. Overlay Network

Encapsulates pod traffic across nodes.

Pros:

```text
flexible addressing
```

Cons:

```text
encapsulation overhead

MTU complexity
```

---

# 179. Native Routing

Pod addresses may be routed directly in underlying network.

Can reduce encapsulation overhead but needs infrastructure support.

---

# 180. MTU

Maximum Transmission Unit.

If packet larger than supported path:

```text
fragmentation

drop

path MTU issues
```

may occur.

---

# 181. MTU and Overlay

Encapsulation adds headers.

Therefore pod network MTU often must be smaller than physical network MTU.

Misconfiguration causes strange large-packet failures.

---

# 182. Network Policy

Restricts pod communication.

Example:

```text
Inference
-> Feature Store
allowed

Inference
-> Training DB
denied
```

---

# 183. Default-Deny

Security posture:

```text
deny unless explicitly allowed
```

stronger than:

```text
everything can talk to everything
```

---

# 184. Network Policy Debugging

If traffic fails:

```text
source policy?

destination policy?

namespace selector?

pod selector?

port?
```

---

# 185. CSI

Container Storage Interface plugins integrate persistent storage systems.

---

# 186. PersistentVolume

Represents storage resource.

---

# 187. PersistentVolumeClaim

Workload requests storage.

---

# 188. StorageClass

Defines provisioning characteristics.

Examples:

```text
fast SSD

general purpose

shared filesystem
```

---

# 189. Volume Access Mode

Different storage may support:

```text
single-node write

multi-node read/write
```

Choose according to workload.

---

# 190. Stateful ML Workload

Examples:

```text
notebooks

local caches

checkpoint staging
```

may need persistent volumes.

But many scalable services should keep durable state outside individual pods.

---

# 191. Node-Local NVMe

Very fast temporary storage.

Useful for:

```text
dataset cache

model cache

shuffle
```

but may disappear with node.

---

# 192. Local Cache Principle

Anything on local ephemeral disk should be:

```text
rebuildable
```

unless extra durability mechanism exists.

---

# 193. GPU Scheduling in Kubernetes

GPU exposed as extended resource via device plugins or operators.

Pod requests discrete units.

---

# 194. Device Plugin

Advertises available accelerator devices to kubelet/scheduler.

---

# 195. GPU Node Labels

Useful labels:

```text
gpu_family

gpu_memory

interconnect

driver_version
```

support capability-aware placement.

---

# 196. GPU Taints

Prevent ordinary workloads from consuming expensive GPU nodes.

---

# 197. GPU Daemon Components

Often include:

```text
device plugin

monitoring agent

driver management
```

depending on platform design.

---

# 198. GPU Driver Lives Near Host

GPU driver interacts deeply with host kernel/hardware.

Driver rollout is infrastructure lifecycle work.

---

# 199. CUDA Compatibility

Application stack must align with:

```text
driver

CUDA runtime

framework
```

Compatibility matrices matter operationally.

---

# 200. GPU Node Upgrade

Safe approach:

```text
cordon

drain

upgrade/canary

health validation

return to pool
```

---

# 201. Cordon

Marks node unschedulable for new pods.

Existing pods may continue.

---

# 202. Drain

Evicts workloads safely where possible to prepare node maintenance.

Must consider:

```text
PDB

DaemonSets

local storage
```

---

# 203. GPU Health

Monitor:

```text
ECC

Xid

temperature

power

link health
```

Bad GPU may be slower rather than completely dead.

---

# 204. Kubernetes Autoscaling Layers

Could include:

```text
HPA

VPA

cluster/node autoscaler

custom workload autoscaling
```

---

# 205. HPA

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts replica count based on metrics.

---

# 206. CPU-Based HPA

Works well for some CPU services.

For GPU/LLM workloads, CPU may be poor signal.

---

# 207. Custom Metrics

Better signals may include:

```text
queue age

RPS

GPU utilization

tokens/sec

active sequences
```

---

# 208. VPA

Vertical Pod Autoscaler recommends or adjusts resource requests.

Useful for right-sizing selected workloads.

---

# 209. VPA Trade-Off

Changing resources may require pod restart.

Not ideal for every latency-critical workload.

---

# 210. Cluster Autoscaler

Adds/removes nodes according to unschedulable demand and node utilization.

---

# 211. GPU Autoscaling Challenge

GPU nodes may take:

```text
minutes
```

to provision and initialize.

Reactive scaling may be too slow for sudden inference spikes.

---

# 212. Warm Pools

Maintain prepared spare nodes.

Trade:

```text
faster scale-up

higher idle cost
```

---

# 213. Node Provisioning Path

Conceptually:

```text
cloud VM allocation

boot

network attach

disk attach

driver/runtime setup

kubelet register

health checks

ready
```

Each stage can fail.

---

# 214. Autoscaler Feedback Loop

Poorly tuned scaling can oscillate:

```text
scale up

traffic drops

scale down

traffic rises

scale up again
```

Use stabilization windows/hysteresis.

---

# 215. Bin Packing

Scheduler tries to place workloads efficiently.

Over-requested resources reduce packing efficiency.

---

# 216. Fragmentation

Cluster has free resources but not in required shapes.

Example:

```text
8 free GPUs
```

but:

```text
1 GPU on each of 8 nodes
```

while job needs:

```text
8 GPUs same node
```

Unschedulable.

---

# 217. Topology Fragmentation

Even more important for:

```text
NVLink/NVSwitch domains

rack locality

RDMA fabric
```

---

# 218. PriorityClass

Kubernetes can represent workload priorities.

But enterprise ML scheduling often needs higher-level fairness and quota above this.

---

# 219. Preemption

Higher-priority pod can displace lower-priority workloads.

But ML preemption should consider:

```text
checkpointability

lost GPU work

business importance
```

---

# 220. PodDisruptionBudget

Protects against too many voluntary evictions.

Does not prevent:

```text
node crash

hardware failure
```

---

# 221. Node Affinity

Restrict/prefer specific nodes.

Example:

```text
GPU family = H100-class
```

---

# 222. Pod Anti-Affinity

Keep replicas apart to reduce correlated failure.

---

# 223. Topology Spread Constraints

Express desired spread across:

```text
zones

nodes

regions/cells
```

within cluster context.

---

# 224. Cloud Object Storage

Designed for:

```text
massive scale

durability

object semantics
```

Ideal for:

```text
datasets

models

checkpoints
```

---

# 225. Object Storage Is Not POSIX Filesystem

Operations differ.

Common semantics:

```text
GET object

PUT object

LIST prefix
```

Do not design assuming local filesystem behavior.

---

# 226. Object Immutability

Versioned immutable objects work well for:

```text
models

dataset manifests

checkpoints
```

---

# 227. Multipart Upload

Large objects can be uploaded in parallel chunks.

Useful for huge model/checkpoint artifacts.

---

# 228. Partial Upload

Failed multipart upload may leave temporary parts/resources.

Lifecycle cleanup matters.

---

# 229. Storage Consistency

Modern object stores often provide strong behavior for many basic operations, but architects should confirm exact semantics of chosen provider/service.

Do not build correctness on vague assumptions.

---

# 230. Managed Database

Cloud-managed databases reduce operational burden.

Still need to plan:

```text
connections

HA

backups

capacity

indexes

failover
```

---

# 231. Multi-AZ Database

Replicated across zones for higher availability.

But:

```text
replication
```

does not automatically equal:

```text
backup
```

---

# 232. Backup

Protects against:

```text
logical corruption

accidental deletion

historical recovery
```

---

# 233. Replica

Protects availability/read scale.

Can replicate corruption too.

---

# 234. Read Replica

Offload read traffic.

But replication lag means it may return stale state.

---

# 235. Connection Proxy

Can pool/multiplex DB connections.

Useful with:

```text
serverless

many pods
```

but adds another dependency.

---

# 236. Managed Cache

Low-latency key-value systems useful for:

```text
online features

sessions

metadata caches
```

Need eviction and durability semantics.

---

# 237. Cache Failure

If cache is optional:

```text
fallback to source
```

But during total cache outage:

```text
source may receive massive surge
```

Protect source.

---

# 238. Cache Stampede

Popular key expires.

Thousands of requests recompute simultaneously.

Use:

```text
single-flight

staggered TTL

refresh ahead
```

---

# 239. Cloud Load Balancer

Managed external/internal load balancing reduces operations.

Still consider:

```text
health check behavior

connection timeout

regional scope

TLS

capacity limits
```

---

# 240. Cloud Quotas

Providers enforce quotas for:

```text
VMs

GPUs

IP addresses

load balancers

storage operations
```

Capacity planning must include quotas.

---

# 241. Quota Incident

Autoscaler requests:

```text
100 more GPU VMs
```

cloud responds:

```text
quota exceeded
```

System cannot scale despite architectural capacity assumptions.

Monitor quota headroom.

---

# 242. API Rate Limits

Cloud control-plane APIs may rate-limit provisioning operations.

Mass recovery can hit these limits.

---

# 243. Thundering Herd During Recovery

After outage:

```text
thousands of pods

hundreds of nodes

many model loads
```

start simultaneously.

This can overwhelm:

```text
cloud APIs

DNS

object storage

registry

database
```

Use staged recovery.

---

# 244. Multi-Region Infrastructure

Each region may contain:

```text
regional Kubernetes cells

regional data stores

artifact caches

serving gateways
```

with global coordination above.

---

# 245. Region as Failure Domain

Treat region loss as possible.

Do not assume:

```text
multi-zone
=
multi-region
```

---

# 246. Cross-Region Latency

Physical distance adds unavoidable latency.

For latency-sensitive inference:

```text
serve near user/data
```

where possible.

---

# 247. Cross-Region Egress

Large data transfers may create:

```text
high cost

long transfer time
```

Train near data when possible.

---

# 248. Active-Active

Multiple regions simultaneously serve production traffic.

Pros:

```text
fast failover

capacity already warm
```

Cons:

```text
cost

state consistency complexity
```

---

# 249. Active-Passive

Primary serves.

Secondary is standby.

Pros:

```text
simpler state model

lower operating cost
```

Cons:

```text
slower recovery

cold capacity risk
```

---

# 250. DNS-Based Failover

Can change DNS records to redirect traffic.

But TTL/caching means failover is not instantaneous.

---

# 251. Anycast / Global Load Balancing

Global networking can route users to healthy nearby regions.

Useful for low-latency global services.

---

# 252. Data Residency

Routing cannot ignore legal/business boundaries.

A failed region does not automatically mean:

```text
send data anywhere
```

---

# 253. Multi-Region Metadata

Global metadata may need:

```text
global source of truth

regional replicas/caches
```

depending on consistency requirements.

---

# 254. Split-Brain Risk

If disconnected regions both accept conflicting writes:

```text
how are conflicts resolved?
```

Architect must define ownership or reconciliation.

---

# 255. Single-Writer by Resource

One strategy:

```text
resource has one authoritative region
```

Other regions read/replicate.

Simpler conflict semantics.

---

# 256. Home-Region Pattern

Tenant/resource gets:

```text
home region
```

for authoritative writes.

Serving can still be globally distributed.

---

# 257. Cloud IAM

Identity controls access to resources.

Avoid embedding broad static access keys.

Use:

```text
federated identities

workload identity

short-lived tokens
```

---

# 258. Cloud Resource Hierarchy

Enterprise clouds often organize:

```text
organization

folders/accounts/projects

resources
```

Isolation boundaries should align with risk and ownership.

---

# 259. Account/Project Isolation

Separate:

```text
production

development

regulated workloads
```

to reduce blast radius.

---

# 260. Shared Network vs Shared Account

Central networking can coexist with separated workload accounts/projects.

Architecture should separate:

```text
network connectivity
```

from:

```text
administrative ownership
```

---

# 261. Infrastructure as Code

Cloud networks, clusters, IAM, and storage should be declarative.

Benefits:

```text
review

reproducibility

audit

drift detection
```

---

# 262. Immutable Infrastructure

Rather than manually patching servers indefinitely:

```text
build new image

replace nodes
```

where possible.

This improves reproducibility.

---

# 263. Golden Node Image

GPU node image can standardize:

```text
OS

drivers

runtime components

security configuration
```

---

# 264. Image Versioning

Nodes should report:

```text
image_version
```

so fleet drift is visible.

---

# 265. Canary Infrastructure Upgrade

Upgrade:

```text
1 small cell
```

before:

```text
entire fleet
```

Measure:

```text
job failures

latency

GPU performance
```

---

# 266. Configuration Drift

Desired:

```text
driver vX
```

actual:

```text
some nodes vY
```

Fleet management should detect divergence automatically.

---

# 267. Linux Debugging Workflow

Start:

```text
1. Is process alive?

2. Is CPU/memory normal?

3. Is disk healthy?

4. Is network reachable?

5. Are dependencies available?
```

---

# 268. Process Troubleshooting

Check:

```text
PID

exit code

restart count

signals

open files

threads
```

---

# 269. CPU Troubleshooting

Ask:

```text
CPU saturated?

one core saturated?

throttled?

I/O wait?

context switching?
```

---

# 270. Memory Troubleshooting

Ask:

```text
RSS growing?

cgroup limit?

node pressure?

cache?

swap?

OOM history?
```

---

# 271. Disk Troubleshooting

Ask:

```text
space?

inodes?

I/O latency?

throughput?

queue depth?
```

---

# 272. Network Troubleshooting

Layered approach:

```text
DNS

route

TCP

TLS

HTTP

application
```

---

# 273. DNS Test

Question:

```text
Does name resolve
to expected address?
```

Do not test only application.

---

# 274. TCP Test

Question:

```text
Can I establish connection
to IP:port?
```

---

# 275. TLS Test

Question:

```text
Does certificate validate?

correct hostname?

valid dates?

trusted CA?
```

---

# 276. HTTP Test

Question:

```text
What status?

What headers?

Which backend?
```

---

# 277. Kubernetes Debugging Workflow

```text
Deployment
   |
   v
ReplicaSet
   |
   v
Pod
   |
   v
Container
   |
   v
Service
   |
   v
Endpoint
   |
   v
Network
```

Walk downward.

---

# 278. Pod Pending Workflow

Check:

```text
events

resource requests

GPU availability

affinity

taints

PVC binding
```

---

# 279. Pod Crash Workflow

Check:

```text
container exit code

previous logs

OOM status

missing config

permissions
```

---

# 280. Pod Ready=False Workflow

Check:

```text
readiness probe result

model loading

dependency state

application logs
```

---

# 281. Service Unreachable Workflow

Check:

```text
DNS

Service object

selector

EndpointSlice

pod readiness

network policy

container port
```

---

# 282. Intermittent Connection Failure

Consider:

```text
NAT exhaustion

load balancer idle timeout

DNS changes

pod churn

packet loss
```

---

# 283. High p99, Good Average

Look for:

```text
queueing

retransmissions

cold starts

GC pauses

slow downstream replicas

stragglers
```

Tail behavior matters.

---

# 284. Connection Pool Incident

Symptoms:

```text
requests wait

DB healthy

application CPU low
```

Pool may be exhausted.

Monitor:

```text
active

idle

waiting
```

---

# 285. DNS Storm

Thousands of short-lived requests repeatedly resolve same service.

Mitigate:

```text
connection reuse

DNS caching

node-local caching
```

where appropriate.

---

# 286. Node Disk Full Incident

Causes may include:

```text
container logs

unused images

temporary model files

dataset cache
```

Node enters pressure and evicts pods.

---

# 287. Image Garbage Collection

Container runtimes should remove unused images when needed.

Large ML images can consume significant disk.

---

# 288. Model Cache vs Node Disk

Model cache improves cold start but can fill node disk.

Need:

```text
size limit

LRU

watermarks
```

---

# 289. GPU Node Unhealthy Incident

Symptoms:

```text
jobs hang

one rank slow

Xid errors
```

Response:

```text
quarantine node

reschedule workload

diagnose hardware/driver
```

---

# 290. Distributed Training Network Incident

Step time doubles.

Check:

```text
collective time

NIC errors

packet loss

RDMA state

topology placement

oversubscription
```

---

# 291. Storage Bottleneck Incident

GPU utilization low.

Storage saturated.

Architecture fix may be:

```text
dataset sharding

prefetch

local NVMe cache

larger files

better throughput tier
```

---

# 292. Cloud Quota Incident

Pods remain pending even though autoscaler wants nodes.

Cloud event says:

```text
quota exceeded
```

This is not Kubernetes scheduler failure.

---

# 293. Load Balancer Health Check Incident

Pods healthy internally.

LB marks all backends unhealthy because:

```text
wrong port/path

firewall

health response
```

Understand entire network path.

---

# 294. NAT Saturation Incident

Thousands of inference workers call external API.

Symptoms:

```text
random outbound connection timeouts

internal traffic healthy
```

Check NAT capacity and connection reuse.

---

# 295. MTU Incident

Small requests succeed.

Large payloads fail/hang.

Potential:

```text
path MTU problem
```

especially with overlays/VPNs.

---

# 296. Certificate Expiry Incident

Service-to-service traffic suddenly fails simultaneously.

Always inspect:

```text
certificate validity window
```

---

# 297. Kubernetes API Server Overload

Too many controllers/watchers or excessive object churn can overload API server.

Symptoms:

```text
slow kubectl

controller retries

delayed scheduling
```

---

# 298. Watch Instead of Poll

Controllers should often use:

```text
watch/informer patterns
```

instead of repeatedly listing all objects.

Reduces API pressure.

---

# 299. Controller Resync Storm

Thousands of objects reconciled simultaneously.

Can overwhelm APIs/downstream systems.

Use:

```text
work queues

rate limits

jitter
```

---

# 300. Architecture Anti-Pattern — Kubernetes Everywhere

Not every component needs Kubernetes.

Managed database/object storage may be simpler and more reliable.

---

# 301. Anti-Pattern — One Huge Cluster for Everything

Creates:

```text
massive blast radius

resource contention

security complexity
```

Use workload/cell segmentation.

---

# 302. Anti-Pattern — CPU Limit Everywhere by Habit

Can produce unnecessary throttling.

Use deliberate policies based on workload.

---

# 303. Anti-Pattern — No Resource Requests

Scheduler lacks accurate placement information.

Cluster becomes unstable under contention.

---

# 304. Anti-Pattern — Requests Equal Limits for Every Workload

Sometimes appropriate.

Sometimes wastes burst capability.

Understand trade-off rather than applying universal rule.

---

# 305. Anti-Pattern — Liveness Depends on Database

Database outage triggers restart of every application pod.

Makes outage worse.

---

# 306. Anti-Pattern — Readiness Checks Only Process

Model server receives traffic before model is loaded.

Readiness must represent serving capability.

---

# 307. Anti-Pattern — Unlimited Node-Local Cache

Eventually fills disk and destabilizes node.

---

# 308. Anti-Pattern — Cross-Region Data by Default

Creates:

```text
latency

egress cost

residency problems
```

---

# 309. Anti-Pattern — Public Endpoints for Internal ML Services

Unnecessary exposure increases attack surface.

Prefer private connectivity.

---

# 310. Anti-Pattern — Static Cloud Keys

Long-lived keys spread across notebooks and CI.

Use workload federation.

---

# 311. Anti-Pattern — No Cloud Quota Monitoring

Autoscaling plan exists on paper but cannot allocate resources during incident.

---

# 312. Anti-Pattern — No Connection Limits

Every pod opens large connection pools.

Database reaches connection ceiling.

---

# 313. Anti-Pattern — New Connection Per Request

Causes:

```text
TCP handshake overhead

TLS handshake overhead

port churn
```

Use pooling.

---

# 314. Anti-Pattern — Ignore DNS

Service failures often blamed on application while DNS is overloaded/misconfigured.

---

# 315. Anti-Pattern — Treat Packet Loss as Only Network Team Problem

Distributed training performance depends directly on network health.

Platform team needs relevant telemetry.

---

# 316. Anti-Pattern — Multi-Zone Equals DR

Zone redundancy protects zone failures.

Region DR is separate.

---

# 317. Anti-Pattern — Backup Equals High Availability

Backups support recovery.

They do not keep service continuously available.

---

# 318. Anti-Pattern — Replica Equals Backup

Replication can propagate deletion/corruption.

Backups preserve historical state.

---

# 319. Anti-Pattern — Build Global Active-Active Without Conflict Model

Multiple writers require explicit consistency semantics.

---

# 320. Anti-Pattern — Scale by Restarting

Restarting pods may temporarily hide leaks/connection bugs.

Find root cause.

---

# 321. Infrastructure Capacity Checklist

For each workload ask:

```text
CPU?

RAM?

disk?

IOPS?

network bandwidth?

connections?

GPU?

HBM?

GPU topology?
```

---

# 322. Network Capacity Checklist

Ask:

```text
peak RPS?

payload size?

connections?

cross-zone?

cross-region?

egress?

NAT?

TLS?
```

---

# 323. Kubernetes Readiness Checklist

```text
[ ] requests defined

[ ] limits intentional

[ ] readiness accurate

[ ] liveness safe

[ ] startup probe if needed

[ ] graceful shutdown

[ ] topology spread

[ ] PDB if critical

[ ] service account scoped

[ ] network policy

[ ] ephemeral storage bounded
```

---

```text
[ ] correct driver

[ ] runtime compatibility

[ ] GPU health monitoring

[ ] topology labels

[ ] taints

[ ] local storage capacity

[ ] NIC/RDMA health

[ ] power/thermal health

[ ] node image version
```

---

# 325. Cloud Infrastructure Checklist

```text
[ ] CIDR plan

[ ] subnet capacity

[ ] route design

[ ] private endpoints

[ ] egress architecture

[ ] NAT capacity

[ ] cloud quotas

[ ] IAM boundaries

[ ] multi-AZ state

[ ] backups

[ ] region DR
```

---

# 326. Architect Scenario — Global Model Serving

Requirements:

```text
3 regions

100k RPS peak

p99 < 100 ms

GPU inference
```

Infrastructure design:

```text
Global Load Balancer
        |
   +----+----+
   |         |
   v         v
Region A   Region B
   |         |
Regional   Regional
Gateway    Gateway
   |         |
GPU Cells GPU Cells
```

Each region has:

```text
multi-zone capacity

artifact cache

private feature store

local observability
```

---

# 327. Scenario — Regional Failure

Global router stops sending traffic to failed region.

Remaining regions must already have:

```text
capacity

model artifacts

required data

policy eligibility
```

Failover is not just DNS.

---

# 328. Scenario — 1,000-GPU Training Job

Need:

```text
large contiguous allocation

high-speed fabric

storage throughput

checkpoint path

topology-aware placement
```

Infrastructure:

```text
Training Controller
      |
      v
Gang Scheduler
      |
      v
GPU Cell
      |
      +---- RDMA Fabric
      |
      +---- Checkpoint Storage
```

---

# 329. Scenario — Shared Notebook Platform

Need:

```text
interactive pods

per-user identity

idle shutdown

restricted egress

persistent workspace
```

Architecture should separate notebooks from production serving.

---

# 330. Scenario — External LLM API Gateway

Outbound path:

```text
Application
    |
    v
AI Gateway
    |
    v
Egress Proxy/NAT
    |
    v
External Provider
```

Monitor:

```text
connection reuse

NAT ports

TLS

provider latency

egress cost
```

---

# 331. Scenario — Object Storage Outage

Existing models already loaded:

```text
continue serving
```

New model loads/checkpoints:

```text
affected
```

Regional cache reduces dependency.

---

# 332. Scenario — Database Failover

Control plane experiences brief write disruption.

Clients should:

```text
retry boundedly

use idempotency
```

Existing data-plane workloads continue.

---

# 333. Scenario — Node Group Upgrade

Process:

```text
canary node

validate

cordon/drain batch

upgrade

monitor

continue
```

Do not replace entire GPU fleet at once.

---

# 334. Scenario — DNS Failure

If cluster DNS unhealthy:

```text
service names fail

IP connectivity may still work
```

This distinction narrows diagnosis immediately.

---

# 335. Scenario — Network Policy Misconfiguration

Deployment healthy.

Service endpoints exist.

TCP timeout occurs only between specific namespaces.

Inspect network policies.

---

# 336. Scenario — CPU Throttling

Pod shows:

```text
CPU usage = 1 core
```

limit:

```text
1 core
```

request bursts require 2 cores.

p99 grows.

Monitor throttling metrics before scaling replicas blindly.

---

# 337. Scenario — Memory Pressure

Node hosts:

```text
multiple model servers
```

all near limits.

Page cache drops.

Disk reads increase.

Model p99 increases before OOM occurs.

Infrastructure issues can appear as latency first.

---

# 338. Scenario — Storage Cache Benefit

First model load:

```text
60 sec
```

second:

```text
8 sec
```

because artifact now in local/page cache.

Benchmark cold and warm separately.

---

# 339. Scenario — Connection Pool Misconfiguration

100 pods.

Each has pool:

```text
100 DB connections
```

Potential:

```text
10,000 connections
```

DB supports:

```text
2,000
```

System fails during rollout.

---

# 340. Scenario — Recovery Storm

After region outage, 5,000 serving replicas restart.

Each downloads 20 GB model.

Requested:

```text
100 TB
```

of simultaneous model transfer.

Need:

```text
regional cache

rate limiting

priority recovery
```

---

# 341. Scenario — NodeLocal DNS Cache

Large cluster overwhelms central DNS.

Adding node-local caching can reduce repeated upstream queries.

But still fix:

```text
bad client lookup patterns
```

when appropriate.

---

# 342. Scenario — Private Registry Unreachable

Pods show:

```text
ImagePullBackOff
```

Investigate:

```text
DNS

private endpoint

registry auth

route

firewall
```

---

# 343. Scenario — GPU Driver Regression

After driver rollout:

```text
training throughput -25%
```

Application unchanged.

This is why infrastructure changes need performance canaries.

---

# 344. Scenario — NIC Failure

One node has degraded network.

Distributed job's entire step time follows slowest rank.

Quarantine slow node.

---

# 350. Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> Kubernetes is slow.

Do not accept the statement.

Ask:

```text
API server?

scheduler?

pod startup?

image pull?

node provisioning?

DNS?

service networking?

application latency?
```

"Kubernetes is slow" is not a diagnosis.

---

# 351. Another Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> The network is down.

Ask:

```text
DNS resolution fails?

route missing?

TCP timeout?

TLS error?

HTTP 503?

packet loss?

one region or all?
```

Turn vague symptoms into layers.

---

# 352. Another Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> We need more GPUs.

Ask:

```text
GPU actually compute-bound?

data starvation?

network-bound?

memory-bound?

poor batching?

topology issue?

queueing issue?
```

More hardware is not automatically the answer.

---

# 353. Another Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> Scale the pods.

Ask:

```text
Which bottleneck?

Can downstream scale?

Do we have DB connections?

Can load balancer handle it?

Will cloud quota allow nodes?
```

Scaling one layer can overload another.

---

# 354. The End-to-End Principle

A production ML request is only as healthy as the chain:

```text
Client

Gateway

DNS

Network

Pod

Feature Store

Model Runtime

GPU

Storage
```

One slow link dominates user experience.

---

# 355. Infrastructure Design Principle — Bound the Blast Radius

Separate:

```text
research

production

regulated workloads

critical serving
```

where necessary.

Infrastructure boundaries are architectural safety mechanisms.

---

# 356. Infrastructure Design Principle — Prefer Rebuildable Nodes

Nodes should be replaceable.

Persist durable state externally.

This simplifies:

```text
upgrade

recovery

security response
```

---

# 357. Infrastructure Design Principle — Keep State Intentional

Ask:

```text
If this node disappears,
what data is lost?
```

If answer surprises you, architecture is wrong.

---

# 358. Infrastructure Design Principle — Keep Critical Paths Short

Every proxy, DNS lookup, service hop, and synchronous dependency adds:

```text
latency

failure probability
```

Use only what provides real value.

---

# 359. Infrastructure Design Principle — Measure the Kernel-Level Reality

High-level metrics can hide:

```text
CPU throttling

packet loss

disk pressure

FD exhaustion

page faults
```

Infrastructure observability needs lower-level telemetry.

---

# 360. Infrastructure Design Principle — Design for Recovery, Not Only Normal Operation

Capacity during:

```text
zone loss

node replacement

mass model reload

cluster upgrade
```

can be more important than normal-state capacity.

---

# 361. What You Must Remember From Chapter 26

1. **Every ML platform ultimately runs on operating-system, network, storage, and hardware primitives.**

2. **Containers and Kubernetes abstract Linux; they do not eliminate the need to understand Linux.**

3. **Processes, threads, signals, file descriptors, virtual memory, and cgroups explain many production failures.**

4. **RSS is different from virtual memory size and is often more useful when diagnosing real memory pressure.**

5. **Linux page cache can dramatically affect model and dataset load performance, so cold and warm benchmarks must be distinguished.**

6. **Heavy swapping is generally disastrous for latency-sensitive inference workloads.**

7. **OOM conditions can happen at either container/cgroup or node level and have different blast radii.**

8. **Every cache must be bounded; otherwise a cache can become an operational memory leak.**

9. **NUMA placement matters for high-performance GPU, CPU, and NIC communication.**

10. **cgroups are foundational to container CPU, memory, and I/O governance.**

11. **CPU requests affect placement while CPU limits can throttle runtime behavior.**

12. **Memory limits are fundamentally harsher than CPU limits because memory cannot simply be throttled when exhausted.**

13. **Linux namespaces provide container isolation views for processes, networking, mounts, and users.**

14. **Containers share the host kernel and therefore do not provide the exact same isolation model as virtual machines.**

15. **File-descriptor exhaustion can break both filesystem and networking behavior because sockets are file descriptors.**

16. **Ephemeral storage must be explicitly bounded because model caches, logs, and temporary datasets can fill a node.**

17. **Storage must be reasoned about in terms of latency, throughput, IOPS, access pattern, and durability.**

18. **The small-file problem creates overhead at filesystem, object-store, and distributed data-processing layers.**

19. **Network debugging should proceed through DNS → routing → TCP → TLS → application protocol.**

20. **TCP connection establishment and TLS handshakes have real latency and resource cost, making connection reuse important.**

21. **Packet loss can cause severe tail-latency and distributed-training performance degradation even when average network health looks acceptable.**

22. **DNS caching improves performance but makes failover and endpoint changes non-instantaneous.**

23. **TLS certificate lifecycle is production infrastructure, and certificate expiry can become a full service outage.**

24. **mTLS strengthens workload authentication but introduces certificate-management and operational complexity.**

25. **HTTP/2 and gRPC can improve service-to-service efficiency through multiplexing and typed interfaces.**

26. **Timeouts must be aligned across clients, proxies, load balancers, servers, and downstream services.**

27. **NAT can become a scaling bottleneck for high-volume outbound ML and LLM traffic.**

28. **CIDR and subnet planning are long-term architectural concerns because overlapping or undersized networks are difficult to fix later.**

29. **Private service connectivity reduces unnecessary public exposure and often improves security posture.**

30. **Kubernetes control-plane health depends critically on API server and etcd behavior.**

31. **etcd should store Kubernetes cluster state, not become a general-purpose ML metadata warehouse.**

32. **Kubernetes scheduler places individual pods, while large distributed ML often needs additional gang, queue, quota, and topology scheduling.**

33. **kubelet manages pod lifecycle on each node and is central to probe execution and container management.**

34. **A Pod can be Running while still not Ready to serve production traffic.**

35. **Graceful termination must be designed because Kubernetes routinely drains, upgrades, and replaces workloads.**

36. **Service selectors and EndpointSlices are critical when debugging Kubernetes service connectivity.**

37. **CNI determines pod-networking behavior, and networking details differ significantly across implementations.**

38. **Overlay networks introduce encapsulation and MTU considerations that can produce strange packet-size-dependent failures.**

39. **NetworkPolicy should be used as a real isolation layer rather than assuming namespaces isolate traffic automatically.**

40. **Persistent and ephemeral storage have different lifecycle semantics and must not be confused.**

41. **Node-local NVMe is excellent for caches and temporary data only when data is safely rebuildable.**

42. **GPU scheduling requires device discovery, hardware metadata, driver management, node policies, and topology awareness.**

43. **GPU driver and CUDA/runtime upgrades should be canaried because infrastructure changes can silently reduce model performance.**

44. **Horizontal autoscaling must use workload-appropriate signals; CPU is often insufficient for GPU and LLM services.**

45. **GPU nodes provision slowly, making warm capacity and predictive scaling relevant for latency-sensitive workloads.**

46. **Resource fragmentation means total free capacity can look sufficient while required workload shapes remain unschedulable.**

47. **Topology fragmentation is particularly important for multi-GPU and distributed training jobs.**

48. **Object storage is ideal for large immutable ML artifacts but should not be treated exactly like a POSIX filesystem.**

49. **Backups, replicas, and high availability solve different problems and should never be treated as synonyms.**

50. **A cache outage can create a secondary outage by flooding the underlying source with traffic.**

51. **Cloud quotas and control-plane API limits are real scaling constraints and must be monitored before incidents occur.**

52. **Mass recovery can create a thundering herd across cloud APIs, DNS, artifact stores, networks, and databases.**

53. **Multi-zone availability is not equivalent to multi-region disaster recovery.**

54. **Cross-region latency and data-transfer cost make regional locality important for both inference and training.**

55. **Active-active improves recovery speed but increases cost and state-consistency complexity.**

56. **Any multi-writer multi-region design needs explicit conflict and ownership semantics.**

57. **Cloud workload identity and short-lived credentials are preferable to distributing static access keys across workloads.**

58. **Separate cloud projects/accounts can provide strong administrative and blast-radius isolation for production and regulated workloads.**

59. **Immutable infrastructure and versioned node images make large fleets easier to reproduce and recover.**

60. **Infrastructure upgrades should use canaries, progressive rollout, health validation, and rollback—not fleet-wide changes.**

61. **When debugging Linux, inspect CPU, memory, disk, network, and process state systematically rather than restarting blindly.**

62. **When debugging Kubernetes, follow the chain from Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod → Container → Service → Endpoint → Network.**

63. **A pending pod can be caused by resources, GPU shape, taints, affinity, storage, or external cloud capacity.**

64. **An unreachable Service can be caused by selectors, readiness, endpoints, network policy, DNS, or application port configuration.**

65. **High p99 latency with healthy averages often indicates queueing, packet loss, stragglers, cold starts, or slow downstream replicas.**

66. **Connection-pool sizing must be considered across the entire replica fleet, not per process in isolation.**

67. **Model caches and image caches improve startup but require bounded node-disk management.**

68. **One degraded NIC or GPU can slow an entire synchronous distributed training job because all ranks wait for the slowest participant.**

69. **Storage bottlenecks commonly appear as low GPU utilization rather than obvious storage errors.**

70. **Autoscaling cannot solve cloud quota shortages, network bottlenecks, or downstream database limits.**

71. **"Kubernetes is slow" and "the network is down" are symptoms, not diagnoses; architects decompose them into measurable layers.**

72. **Infrastructure capacity planning must cover normal operation, failures, upgrades, and recovery storms.**

73. **Nodes should be as disposable as possible, while durable state remains in replicated external systems.**

74. **Every local piece of data should have an explicit answer to whether it is cache, temporary state, or durable state.**

75. **Critical request paths should minimize unnecessary proxies, remote calls, and synchronous infrastructure dependencies.**

76. **At senior architect level, infrastructure expertise means understanding how application-level symptoms map down to kernel, network, scheduler, storage, and cloud behaviors.**

---
