# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 27 — Data Structures, Algorithms, and Distributed Systems Interview Mastery for Senior MLOps Engineers

---

# 1. Why Algorithms Matter for an MLOps Architect

You are not preparing to become a competitive programmer.

You are preparing to build systems containing:

```text
queues

caches

schedulers

dependency graphs

resource allocators

rate limiters

shards

replicas

stream processors
```

All of them depend on data structures and algorithms.

---

# 2. The Interview Transition

A system-design interview may begin:

> Design a distributed ML training platform.

Then suddenly become:

> Implement the scheduler's ready queue.

Or:

> How would you detect cycles in the pipeline DAG?

Or:

> Implement an LRU model cache.

You must be comfortable moving:

```text
Architecture
    |
    v
Algorithm
    |
    v
Data Structure
    |
    v
Production Implementation
```

---

# 3. What You Actually Need to Master

For senior MLOps roles, prioritize:

```text
Arrays / Lists

Hash Maps

Sets

Stacks

Queues

Deques

Heaps

Linked Lists

Trees

Graphs

Tries

Union-Find

Binary Search

Intervals

Sliding Windows

Topological Sort

Shortest Paths

LRU Caches

Consistent Hashing

Bloom Filters
```

Then connect them to distributed systems.

---

# 4. Complexity Is Engineering Economics

Big-O tells you how work grows.

Suppose an operation costs:

```text
O(n²)
```

At:

```text
n = 100
```

maybe acceptable.

At:

```text
n = 10,000,000
```

probably disastrous.

---

# 5. Common Complexities

```text
O(1)
constant

O(log n)
logarithmic

O(n)
linear

O(n log n)
sorting-class

O(n²)
quadratic

O(2^n)
exponential
```

---

# 6. Complexity Is Not the Entire Story

Two algorithms both:

```text
O(n)
```

may differ hugely due to:

```text
memory locality

constant factors

network calls

disk access

serialization
```

Distributed systems require more than asymptotic analysis.

---

# 7. Ask Three Complexity Questions

For every solution:

```text
Time complexity?

Space complexity?

External I/O complexity?
```

In MLOps, the third is often the most expensive.

---

# 8. Example

Algorithm A:

```text
O(n)
```

but performs:

```text
n remote database calls
```

Algorithm B:

```text
O(n)
```

with:

```text
one batch query
```

Algorithm B may be orders of magnitude faster.

---

# 9. Arrays / Python Lists

Arrays provide efficient:

```text
index access
```

Conceptually:

```text
O(1)
```

for index lookup.

---

# 10. Array Strengths

Good for:

```text
ordered data

sequential iteration

binary search

compact storage
```

---

# 11. Array Weaknesses

Insertion near beginning may require shifting many elements:

```text
O(n)
```

---

# 12. MLOps Use Cases for Arrays

Examples:

```text
time-series samples

latency buckets

sorted model versions

training metrics

token sequences
```

---

# 13. Hash Map

A hash map stores:

```text
key -> value
```

Examples:

```text
job_id -> job state

model_id -> metadata

tenant_id -> quota
```

---

# 14. Average Hash Lookup

Usually:

```text
O(1)
```

average lookup/insertion.

This makes hash maps one of the most important structures in platform engineering.

---

# 15. Hash Collision

Different keys may map to same internal bucket.

Implementations handle collisions internally.

Worst-case complexity can degrade, though modern runtimes mitigate many attacks.

---

# 16. Hashability

A dictionary key must have stable hash semantics.

In Python, common immutable keys:

```text
string

integer

tuple of hashable values
```

---

# 17. Composite Keys

Useful:

```python
key = (tenant_id, model_id, version)
```

for cache/index lookup.

---

# 18. MLOps Hash-Map Example

Scheduler may maintain:

```text
running_jobs[job_id]

tenant_usage[tenant_id]

node_capacity[node_id]
```

Fast lookups are essential.

---

# 19. Set

A set stores unique values.

Operations:

```text
insert

contains

remove
```

average:

```text
O(1)
```

---

# 20. Sets in MLOps

Useful for:

```text
completed dependencies

visited graph nodes

active model IDs

deduplicated event IDs
```

---

# 21. Deduplication

Given event IDs:

```text
A B B C A
```

set gives:

```text
A B C
```

For billions of events, however, an in-memory set may become too large.

That leads to probabilistic structures later.

---

# 22. Stack

Last-In-First-Out:

```text
push

pop
```

Example:

```text
A
B
C <- top
```

C leaves first.

---

# 23. Stack Use Cases

```text
DFS

expression evaluation

undo

dependency traversal
```

---

# 24. Queue

First-In-First-Out:

```text
enqueue

dequeue
```

Used everywhere in distributed systems.

---

# 25. MLOps Queue Use Cases

```text
training jobs

deployment operations

feature processing

retry queues

task execution
```

---

# 26. Queue Is an Architectural Primitive

A queue gives:

```text
decoupling

burst buffering

backpressure point

ordering opportunities
```

It is much more than a programming data structure.

---

# 27. Deque

Double-ended queue.

Supports efficient:

```text
append left

append right

pop left

pop right
```

Typically:

```text
O(1)
```

---

# 28. Deque Use Cases

```text
sliding windows

BFS

work stealing

rate limiters
```

---

# 29. Heap

Heap efficiently retrieves:

```text
minimum
```

or:

```text
maximum
```

depending on implementation.

---

# 30. Heap Complexity

Insertion:

```text
O(log n)
```

Pop min/max:

```text
O(log n)
```

Peek:

```text
O(1)
```

---

# 31. Why Heaps Matter to Schedulers

Imagine 1 million queued jobs.

You repeatedly need:

```text
highest priority job
```

Sorting all jobs repeatedly is wasteful.

A priority heap is a natural structure.

---

# 32. Priority Queue

Conceptually:

```text
(priority, job)
```

Highest/lowest priority returned efficiently.

---

# 33. Multi-Criteria Priority

Scheduler priority may include:

```text
business priority

submission time

fair-share score

deadline
```

Heap key might conceptually be:

```text
(priority, fairness_score, submit_time)
```

---

# 34. Stable Ordering

If two jobs have same priority, define tie-breaker.

Example:

```text
earlier submission wins
```

Without deterministic tie-breaking, behavior becomes unpredictable.

---

# 35. Top-K Problem

Need top 100 largest GPU consumers among 1 million teams.

Full sort:

```text
O(n log n)
```

Fixed-size heap:

```text
O(n log k)
```

when:

```text
k << n
```

---

# 36. Linked List

Nodes contain:

```text
value

next
```

or:

```text
previous

next
```

for doubly linked list.

---

# 37. Linked-List Strength

If you already know the node:

```text
remove in O(1)
```

with a doubly linked list.

---

# 38. Linked-List Weakness

Random access is:

```text
O(n)
```

No direct indexing.

---

# 39. Why Linked Lists Matter

Classic LRU cache uses:

```text
Hash Map
+
Doubly Linked List
```

---

# 40. LRU Cache

LRU means:

```text
Least Recently Used
```

When cache is full, evict item that has not been accessed for longest time.

---

# 41. LRU Requirements

Want:

```text
get(key) -> O(1)

put(key) -> O(1)
```

---

# 42. LRU Architecture

```text
Hash Map
    |
    v
key -> linked-list node

Linked List:
Most Recent <----> Least Recent
```

---

# 43. LRU Get

When key accessed:

```text
find node via hash map

move node to front
```

Both:

```text
O(1)
```

---

# 44. LRU Put

If key exists:

```text
update

move to front
```

If full:

```text
remove tail

delete from map

insert new front
```

---

# 45. ML Model Cache

Suppose GPU memory capacity:

```text
80 GB
```

Models:

```text
A = 20 GB

B = 30 GB

C = 50 GB
```

A model cache needs capacity measured in:

```text
bytes
```

not merely number of entries.

---

# 46. Weighted LRU

Each object has size.

To load model C:

```text
evict multiple least-recently-used models
until enough HBM is free
```

This is a practical extension of interview LRU.

---

# 47. Single-Flight Loading

Two requests simultaneously miss model A.

Bad:

```text
Request 1 -> load A

Request 2 -> load A

Request 3 -> load A
```

Good:

```text
one load

others await same future
```

This prevents load storms.

---

# 48. Trees

Hierarchical structure.

Examples:

```text
filesystem

organization hierarchy

configuration tree
```

---

# 49. Binary Tree

Each node has at most two children.

---

# 50. Binary Search Tree

Maintains:

```text
left < node < right
```

Conceptually enabling logarithmic operations when balanced.

---

# 51. Balanced Trees

Examples conceptually:

```text
AVL

Red-Black Tree
```

Height remains:

```text
O(log n)
```

---

# 52. Tree Use in Systems

Balanced ordered structures can support:

```text
sorted indexes

range queries

scheduler ordering
```

Databases often use tree families such as B-trees.

---

# 53. B-Tree Concept

Optimized for storage systems by keeping many keys per node.

Reduces disk page accesses.

Common in databases.

---

# 54. B+ Tree Concept

Data typically resides in leaves.

Leaves are linked for efficient range scans.

Excellent for:

```text
ordered indexes

range queries
```

---

# 55. Why Database Indexes Use B-Trees

Disk/storage access is expensive.

Wide tree branching means:

```text
few page reads
```

to find a value among millions/billions of records.

---

# 56. Trie

Prefix tree.

Useful for:

```text
prefix lookup

autocomplete

routing
```

---

# 57. Trie Example

Keys:

```text
model

monitor

money
```

share prefix:

```text
mo
```

---

# 58. Trie Use in Platform Systems

Possible:

```text
resource path lookup

API route matching

prefix policies

configuration search
```

---

# 59. Graph

Many MLOps problems are graphs.

Examples:

```text
pipeline dependencies

dataset lineage

model lineage

service dependencies

network topology
```

---

# 60. Graph Terminology

```text
vertex/node

edge

directed

undirected

weighted

cyclic

acyclic
```

---

# 61. Directed Graph

Edge:

```text
A -> B
```

does not imply:

```text
B -> A
```

Pipeline dependency graphs are directed.

---

# 62. DAG

Directed Acyclic Graph.

Most workflow systems model pipelines as DAGs.

---

# 63. Graph Representation

Two common choices:

```text
adjacency list

adjacency matrix
```

---

# 64. Adjacency List

Store:

```text
node -> neighbors
```

Efficient for sparse graphs.

Typical pipeline DAGs are sparse.

---

# 65. Adjacency Matrix

N × N matrix.

Memory:

```text
O(V²)
```

Useful mainly for dense graphs or certain algorithms.

---

# 66. BFS

Breadth-First Search.

Explores:

```text
level by level
```

using queue.

---

# 67. BFS Complexity

```text
O(V + E)
```

with adjacency lists.

---

# 68. BFS Use Cases

```text
shortest path in unweighted graph

dependency distance

service-hop analysis
```

---

# 69. DFS

Depth-First Search.

Uses:

```text
stack

or recursion
```

---

# 70. DFS Complexity

Also:

```text
O(V + E)
```

---

# 71. DFS Use Cases

```text
cycle detection

dependency traversal

connected components

topological sorting
```

---

# 72. Pipeline Cycle Detection

Invalid:

```text
Feature A -> Feature B
Feature B -> Feature C
Feature C -> Feature A
```

A DAG scheduler must reject this.

---

# 73. DFS Cycle Detection

Track states:

```text
UNVISITED

VISITING

VISITED
```

Encounter:

```text
VISITING
```

neighbor again => cycle.

---

# 74. Topological Sort

Produces valid dependency order.

Example:

```text
A -> B
A -> C
B -> D
C -> D
```

Possible order:

```text
A B C D
```

or:

```text
A C B D
```

---

# 75. Kahn's Algorithm

Topological sorting using indegree.

Steps:

```text
1. Calculate indegree.

2. Put indegree=0 nodes in queue.

3. Pop one.

4. Reduce neighbors' indegree.

5. Add newly-zero nodes.
```

---

# 76. Detecting Cycle With Kahn's Algorithm

If processed nodes:

```text
<
total nodes
```

then graph contains cycle.

---

# 77. DAG Executor

Execution uses:

```text
indegree

ready queue

worker pool
```

---

# 78. DAG Parallelism

Example:

```text
        A
       / \
      B   C
       \ /
        D
```

After A:

```text
B and C
```

can execute simultaneously.

---

# 79. Critical Path

Longest dependency path determines minimum possible completion time.

Even infinite workers cannot execute faster than critical path.

---

# 80. Critical-Path Example

```text
A=1m
B=10m
C=2m
D=1m
```

with:

```text
A -> B -> D
A -> C -> D
```

Critical path:

```text
A-B-D = 12m
```

---

# 81. Why Critical Path Matters

Pipeline optimization should focus on:

```text
critical-path stages
```

not merely the most expensive total stage.

---

# 82. Weighted Graph

Edges have costs.

Examples:

```text
latency

network cost

distance

risk
```

---

# 83. Dijkstra's Algorithm

Find shortest path when edge weights are non-negative.

Complexity with heap approximately:

```text
O((V + E) log V)
```

---

# 84. MLOps Dijkstra Use Case

Could conceptualize placement:

```text
compute cluster

network links

data locality cost
```

and search lowest-cost route/placement.

Real schedulers often use heuristics instead because objectives are multidimensional.

---

# 85. Bellman-Ford

Handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles.

Less common directly in MLOps interviews but useful graph knowledge.

---

# 86. Union-Find

Also called:

```text
Disjoint Set Union
```

Supports:

```text
find component

union components
```

very efficiently.

---

# 87. Union-Find Use Cases

```text
connectivity

cluster grouping

network components

deduplication groups
```

---

# 88. Path Compression

Speeds repeated `find()` calls by flattening parent hierarchy.

---

# 89. Union by Rank/Size

Attach smaller tree under larger tree.

Combined with path compression, operations are nearly constant amortized time.

---

# 90. Binary Search

Search sorted space by repeatedly halving.

Complexity:

```text
O(log n)
```

---

# 91. Standard Binary Search

```text
low

high

mid
```

Compare target to mid.

Discard half each iteration.

---

# 92. Binary Search on Answer

More powerful pattern:

> Find smallest resource value satisfying a monotonic condition.

---

# 93. Example — Minimum GPU Count

Suppose runtime decreases as GPUs increase.

Need minimum GPUs such that:

```text
training_time <= 8 hours
```

If feasibility is monotonic:

```text
binary search GPU count
```

---

# 94. Example — Autoscaling Capacity

Find minimum replicas satisfying:

```text
predicted p99 <= target
```

if capacity model is monotonic.

---

# 95. Intervals

Many scheduling problems involve:

```text
[start, end]
```

Examples:

```text
GPU reservations

maintenance windows

training slots
```

---

# 96. Interval Overlap

Two intervals overlap when:

```text
max(start1, start2)
<=
min(end1, end2)
```

depending on endpoint semantics.

---

# 97. Merge Intervals

Sort intervals by start:

```text
O(n log n)
```

Then merge overlapping ranges.

---

# 98. Scheduling Use Case

GPU reservations:

```text
09:00-10:00

09:30-11:00

13:00-14:00
```

merge first two:

```text
09:00-11:00
```

---

# 99. Meeting Rooms Pattern

Given jobs with intervals, calculate maximum concurrent jobs.

Useful mental model for:

```text
capacity planning

reservation overlap
```

---

# 100. Sweep Line Algorithm

Sort start/end events.

Maintain current active count.

Useful for:

```text
peak concurrency

resource usage

capacity windows
```

---

# 101. Sliding Window

Maintain information over recent subset of sequence.

Example:

```text
last 5 minutes
```

of requests.

---

# 102. Sliding-Window Use Cases

```text
rate limiting

rolling fraud features

latency statistics

traffic anomaly detection
```

---

# 103. Fixed-Size Sliding Window

For last N elements:

```text
add new

remove oldest
```

often using deque.

---

# 104. Time-Based Window

Remove entries older than:

```text
now - window_size
```

---

# 105. Sliding-Window Rate Limiter

Per user maintain request timestamps.

On each request:

```text
drop timestamps older than 60s

if count >= limit:
    reject
```

---

# 106. Exact Sliding Window Complexity

At scale, storing every timestamp may be expensive.

Alternatives:

```text
fixed windows

token bucket

approximate counters
```

---

# 107. Two Pointers

Often used for:

```text
sorted arrays

window problems

range constraints
```

---

# 108. Monotonic Queue

Deque maintaining monotonic values.

Can compute sliding-window maximum in:

```text
O(n)
```

---

# 109. Sliding Max Use Case

Monitor:

```text
maximum queue latency
over last 5 minutes
```

without scanning entire window each time.

---

# 110. Prefix Sum

Precompute cumulative values.

Then interval sum:

```text
O(1)
```

after:

```text
O(n)
```

preprocessing.

---

# 111. Prefix Sum Use Case

Given GPU usage per minute:

```text
usage[0..n]
```

answer many interval-cost queries efficiently.

---

# 112. Difference Array

Efficiently apply many range updates.

Example:

```text
reserve 8 GPUs
from minute 100 to 200
```

Apply boundaries then prefix-sum later.

---

# 113. Scheduling Capacity Planning

Many reservation intervals can be aggregated with:

```text
difference array

sweep line
```

to find future capacity demand.

---

# 114. Sorting

Sorting is often the simplest way to unlock a problem.

Examples:

```text
interval merging

deduplication

ranking

event processing
```

---

# 115. Stable Sort

Preserves original order among equal keys.

Useful when secondary ordering already encoded.

---

# 116. Custom Comparator / Key

Scheduler may sort by:

```text
priority

deadline

submit_time
```

---

# 117. Quickselect

Find kth-largest/smallest without full sorting.

Average:

```text
O(n)
```

Useful when only percentile/order statistic is needed.

---

# 118. Percentile Caveat

Exact p99 over huge distributed telemetry is expensive.

Production systems often use:

```text
histograms

quantile sketches
```

instead.

---

# 119. Reservoir Sampling

Sample K items uniformly from stream of unknown/huge size.

Memory:

```text
O(k)
```

---

# 120. Reservoir Sampling Use Case

You receive:

```text
billions of predictions
```

but want:

```text
10,000 representative examples
```

for debugging/evaluation.

---

# 121. Streaming Algorithms

Large-scale systems cannot retain everything.

Need summaries.

Examples:

```text
counts

sketches

samples

histograms
```

---

# 122. Count-Min Sketch

Approximate frequency estimation.

Useful when exact per-key counts are too expensive.

Allows:

```text
small memory
```

with bounded overestimation.

---

# 123. Heavy Hitters

Need to know:

```text
which tenants dominate traffic?
```

Approximate heavy-hitter algorithms may be enough.

---

# 124. HyperLogLog Concept

Approximate distinct count using very little memory.

Use:

```text
number of unique users

unique model IDs
```

when exact count unnecessary.

---

# 125. Approximation Is an Architecture Decision

Ask:

```text
Does business require exact answer?
```

If not, approximate algorithms can massively improve scale/cost.

---

# 126. Bloom Filter

Probabilistic membership test.

Properties:

```text
false positives possible

false negatives absent
```

for inserted items under normal operation.

---

# 127. Bloom Filter Flow

```text
Definitely not present?
-> no expensive lookup

Maybe present?
-> check real store
```

---

# 128. Bloom Filter MLOps Use Cases

```text
artifact existence checks

event dedup prefilter

cache lookup avoidance

dataset membership
```

---

# 129. Bloom Filter Trade-Off

Smaller bitset:

```text
more false positives
```

More bits/hash functions:

```text
lower false-positive rate
```

but more memory/work.

---

# 130. Count Bloom/Cuckoo Variants

Some variants support deletion or different performance properties.

Know conceptually; do not overfocus unless role requires it.

---

# 131. Consistent Hashing

Problem:

```text
100 cache nodes

add 1 node
```

Normal modulo hashing may remap most keys.

Consistent hashing reduces remapping.

---

# 132. Hash Ring

Nodes and keys mapped to conceptual ring.

Key assigned to next node clockwise.

---

# 133. Adding a Node

Only keys near new node's position move.

This helps elastic distributed caches.

---

# 134. Virtual Nodes

Each physical node gets many positions on ring.

Benefits:

```text
better balance

easier heterogeneous weighting
```

---

# 135. Consistent Hashing Use Cases

```text
model cache sharding

feature cache

distributed metadata cache

tenant placement
```

---

# 136. Rendezvous Hashing

Alternative consistent assignment.

For each key, compute score for nodes.

Pick highest.

Advantages:

```text
simple

good balance

minimal movement
```

Useful in distributed ownership.

---

# 137. Sharding

Partition data across multiple nodes.

Goal:

```text
scale storage

scale throughput
```

---

# 138. Shard Key

The most important sharding choice.

Examples:

```text
tenant_id

user_id

model_id
```

---

# 139. Good Shard Key

Should ideally:

```text
distribute load evenly

support common queries

avoid hot partitions
```

---

# 140. Hot Shard

If shard key:

```text
tenant_id
```

and one tenant handles:

```text
80% of traffic
```

one shard overloads.

---

# 141. Composite Sharding

Could use:

```text
tenant_id + hash(entity_id)
```

to distribute a huge tenant.

But cross-partition queries become harder.

---

# 142. Range Sharding

Example:

```text
A-F -> shard1

G-M -> shard2
```

Good for ordered/range queries.

Risk:

```text
uneven ranges
```

---

# 143. Hash Sharding

```text
hash(key) % N
```

usually distributes evenly.

But resizing from N to N+1 remaps many keys.

Consistent hashing helps.

---

# 144. Directory-Based Sharding

Maintain:

```text
key/range -> shard
```

mapping service.

Flexible but introduces metadata dependency.

---

# 145. Rebalancing

When node added/removed:

```text
move data
```

without overwhelming network/storage.

Rebalancing itself is production workload.

---

# 146. Replication

Maintain multiple copies.

Goals:

```text
availability

durability

read scalability
```

---

# 147. Leader-Follower Replication

One leader accepts writes.

Followers replicate.

---

# 148. Advantages

```text
simple conflict semantics

ordered writes
```

---

# 149. Disadvantages

```text
leader bottleneck

failover required
```

---

# 150. Replication Lag

Follower may be behind leader.

Read from follower may return stale data.

---

# 151. Read-After-Write Problem

User writes:

```text
model stage = approved
```

then reads follower immediately and sees:

```text
pending
```

Need consistency strategy.

---

# 152. Read-Your-Writes

Possible solutions:

```text
read from leader temporarily

session routing

version-aware reads
```

---

# 153. Multi-Leader Replication

Multiple locations accept writes.

Useful geographically.

But conflicts become fundamental.

---

# 154. Conflict Example

Region A:

```text
model status = approved
```

Region B:

```text
model status = revoked
```

What wins?

This is not a database implementation detail.

It is business semantics.

---

# 155. Leaderless Replication

Clients may write to/read from multiple replicas.

Often associated with quorum-based systems.

---

# 156. Quorum

Suppose:

```text
N = total replicas

W = writes required

R = reads required
```

Classic relationship:

```text
R + W > N
```

can provide overlap between read/write replica sets under assumptions.

---

# 157. Example

```text
N = 3

W = 2

R = 2
```

Any read quorum overlaps last successful write quorum.

---

# 158. Quorum Does Not Magically Solve Everything

Still need to handle:

```text
concurrent writes

repairs

clock/version semantics

failed replicas
```

---

# 159. CAP Theorem

Under network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee both:

```text
strong consistency

availability
```

for every operation.

Partition tolerance is assumed for distributed systems.

---

# 160. CAP Is Often Misused

Do not say:

```text
System is CP.
```

without explaining:

```text
which operations?

which partition scenario?

what does consistency mean?
```

---

# 161. ML Platform CAP Example

During cross-region partition:

```text
existing inference
```

may remain available using cached model.

But:

```text
global model approval mutation
```

may stop to preserve correctness.

Different operations choose differently.

---

# 162. PACELC Intuition

Even without partition, systems trade:

```text
latency

consistency
```

This is often more practically useful than simplistic CAP labels.

---

# 163. Strong Consistency

Reads observe most recent committed write according to chosen model.

Useful for:

```text
quota allocation

critical approvals

unique ownership
```

---

# 164. Eventual Consistency

Replicas converge if updates stop.

Useful for:

```text
search indexes

catalog views

telemetry aggregation
```

---

# 165. Causal Consistency

Preserves causally related ordering.

Stronger than eventual, weaker than total global ordering.

Useful conceptual model for distributed collaboration.

---

# 166. Linearizability

Operations appear to occur atomically in real-time order.

Powerful but costly across distant regions.

---

# 167. Serializability

Database transaction property:

```text
concurrent transactions behave
as if executed in some serial order
```

Different from linearizability.

---

# 168. Consensus

Distributed nodes agree on shared sequence/state despite failures.

Canonical algorithms include:

```text
Raft

Paxos-family
```

You generally need conceptual understanding, not full implementation.

---

# 169. Why Consensus Matters

Used for:

```text
leader election

replicated metadata

configuration state

distributed coordination
```

---

# 170. Consensus Cannot Eliminate Physics

Wide-area consensus pays:

```text
network latency
```

A global strongly consistent write may require cross-region round trips.

---

# 171. Raft Mental Model

Roles:

```text
Leader

Follower

Candidate
```

Leader receives writes and replicates log entries.

---

# 172. Raft Majority

Committed entry generally requires replication to majority.

With 5 members:

```text
majority = 3
```

---

# 173. Why Odd Replica Counts

Going from:

```text
3 -> 4
```

does not increase tolerated failures in a majority quorum.

3 tolerates 1 failure.

4 still requires 3 majority, tolerating 1.

5 tolerates 2.

---

# 174. Consensus Availability

With 3 nodes:

```text
2 must communicate
```

to make progress.

Network partition with 1 vs 2:

```text
2-node side continues
```

1-node side cannot commit.

---

# 175. Split Brain

Two independent leaders making conflicting writes.

Consensus protocols are designed to prevent valid concurrent leaders from committing conflicting histories.

---

# 176. Leader Election

A system chooses one coordinator.

Useful for:

```text
scheduler shard

controller

migration

singleton maintenance task
```

---

# 177. Lease

Leader ownership expires unless periodically renewed.

---

# 178. Lease Problem

Old leader pauses due to:

```text
GC

network delay
```

Lease expires.

New leader takes over.

Old leader resumes and still thinks it owns resource.

---

# 179. Fencing Token

Every lease gets monotonically increasing token:

```text
101

102

103
```

Storage accepts only newest token.

Old leader token:

```text
101
```

cannot mutate after newer:

```text
102
```

exists.

---

# 180. Distributed Lock

A lock across processes/machines.

Useful sometimes.

Dangerous if implementation ignores:

```text
lease expiry

network partitions

process pauses

fencing
```

---

# 181. Prefer Idempotency Over Locks When Possible

If operation can safely execute multiple times, you reduce coordination requirements.

This improves availability and simplicity.

---

# 182. Logical Clock

Physical clocks are imperfect.

Logical clocks order distributed events without relying entirely on wall time.

---

# 183. Lamport Clock

Each process maintains counter.

Rules conceptually:

```text
increment on local event

send counter with message

receiver = max(local, received) + 1
```

Provides causal-compatible ordering.

---

# 184. Lamport Clock Limitation

If:

```text
L(A) < L(B)
```

does not necessarily prove:

```text
A caused B
```

Only causal implication works one way.

---

# 185. Vector Clock

Each participant tracks vector of logical counters.

Can distinguish:

```text
causal ordering

concurrent events
```

more precisely.

---

# 186. Vector Clock Trade-Off

Metadata grows with number of participants.

Not practical for arbitrary huge systems without adaptation.

---

# 187. Hybrid Logical Clocks

Combine physical time with logical ordering.

Useful in modern distributed databases.

Know conceptually.

---

# 188. Clock Skew

Two servers:

```text
A = 10:00:03

B = 09:59:57
```

Ordering events by wall clock alone can be wrong.

---

# 189. Why Clock Skew Matters in ML

Examples:

```text
feature event ordering

lease expiry

prediction/label joins

audit timelines
```

---

# 190. Monotonic Time

For measuring elapsed duration use monotonic clock.

Wall time can jump.

---

# 191. Idempotency

One of the most important distributed-systems ideas.

Operation can execute repeatedly without changing intended final result after first success.

---

# 192. Idempotent Example

```text
SET replicas = 10
```

Repeated:

```text
still 10
```

---

# 193. Non-Idempotent Example

```text
ADD 10 replicas
```

Repeated twice:

```text
+20
```

---

# 194. Idempotency in Payments-Like Actions

For:

```text
create expensive training job

deploy model

bill inference
```

duplicates can be costly.

Use stable operation IDs.

---

# 195. Idempotency Storage

Persist:

```text
idempotency_key
+
operation result
```

under uniqueness constraint.

---

# 196. Exactly-Once Delivery

Often requested.

Hard across arbitrary distributed side effects.

Ask:

```text
exactly once where?
```

---

# 197. Better Mental Model

Frequently design:

```text
at-least-once delivery

+

idempotent processing

=

exactly-once business effect
```

within defined scope.

---

# 198. At-Most-Once

Message processed:

```text
zero or one times
```

May lose work.

---

# 199. At-Least-Once

Message processed:

```text
one or more times
```

No loss under assumptions, but duplicates possible.

---

# 200. Retry Is Duplicate Generation

Every retry creates possibility that previous attempt actually succeeded but response was lost.

Therefore:

```text
retries
```

and:

```text
idempotency
```

belong together.

---

# 201. Backoff

When dependency fails, retry increasingly slowly.

---

# 202. Exponential Backoff

Example:

```text
100 ms

200 ms

400 ms

800 ms
```

---

# 203. Jitter

Add randomness so clients do not retry synchronously.

---

# 204. Retry Budget

Bound total retry amplification.

If base traffic:

```text
100k RPS
```

and every request retries 5 times:

```text
500k extra RPS
```

during outage.

That can prevent recovery.

---

# 205. Timeout

Every remote operation needs bounded waiting.

Without timeout:

```text
threads/connections/requests accumulate
```

---

# 206. Deadline

End-to-end request has total allowed time.

Each downstream operation should respect remaining budget.

---

# 207. Cancellation

If upstream no longer cares about result:

```text
cancel downstream work
```

where possible.

Especially important for expensive inference or database scans.

---

# 208. Backpressure

System signals upstream to slow down because downstream cannot keep up.

---

# 209. Without Backpressure

```text
Producer: 10k/s

Consumer: 8k/s
```

Backlog:

```text
+2k/s forever
```

Eventually:

```text
memory/disk/latency failure
```

---

# 210. Bounded Queue

Queue capacity forces explicit overload behavior.

When full:

```text
block

reject

shed

spill
```

according to semantics.

---

# 211. Load Shedding

Reject lower-value work to protect system.

Example:

```text
research inference rejected
```

while:

```text
production fraud scoring preserved
```

---

# 212. Admission Control

Before accepting work, ask:

```text
Do we have capacity?
```

Better to reject early than accept work that will time out later.

---

# 213. Little's Law

```text
L = λW
```

Where:

```text
L = average number in system

λ = arrival rate

W = average time in system
```

---

# 214. Example

If:

```text
100 requests/sec
```

and average latency:

```text
0.2 sec
```

then average concurrency:

```text
20 requests
```

---

# 215. Little's Law for Training Queue

If:

```text
100 jobs/hour
```

and average time in system:

```text
5 hours
```

average jobs in system:

```text
500
```

This helps reason about queue depth and capacity.

---

# 216. Queueing Explodes Near Saturation

As utilization approaches:

```text
100%
```

waiting time often rises nonlinearly.

This is why:

```text
100% utilization
```

is not always desirable.

---

# 217. Producer-Consumer Problem

Classic concurrency problem.

Producer:

```text
creates tasks
```

Consumer:

```text
processes tasks
```

Need:

```text
queue

synchronization

backpressure
```

---

# 218. Work Stealing

Workers with empty queues may steal tasks from busy workers.

Improves load balancing for irregular workloads.

---

# 219. Work Stealing in Distributed Systems

Potential in:

```text
task schedulers

parallel pipeline execution
```

but locality constraints matter.

Stealing a task far from its data may be expensive.

---

# 220. Fair Queueing

One tenant should not monopolize worker pool.

Possible:

```text
per-tenant queue

round-robin

weighted fair queue
```

---

# 221. Weighted Fair Queue

Tenant A weight:

```text
2
```

Tenant B:

```text
1
```

Over time A gets roughly twice the service share under demand.

---

# 222. Starvation

Strict priority:

```text
P0 always before P3
```

can cause P3 jobs to never execute.

---

# 223. Aging

Increase effective priority as job waits.

Prevents indefinite starvation.

---

# 224. Scheduler Objective Is Multi-Dimensional

Real scheduler balances:

```text
priority

fairness

utilization

topology

cost

deadlines
```

No single heap ordering perfectly solves all of them.

---

# 225. Greedy Algorithms

At each step choose locally attractive option.

Often fast and useful.

May not find global optimum.

---

# 226. Greedy Scheduling Example

Assign next job to:

```text
first node with enough resources
```

Fast.

But may fragment GPUs.

---

# 227. Bin Packing

Given items and bins, fit items minimizing bins used.

GPU scheduling resembles multidimensional bin packing.

This problem is computationally difficult in general.

---

# 228. Why Schedulers Use Heuristics

Exact optimal packing at large scale may be too slow.

Schedulers use:

```text
first fit

best fit

scoring heuristics

limited search
```

---

# 229. First-Fit

Place workload on first suitable node.

Simple and fast.

Potential poor packing.

---

# 230. Best-Fit

Choose node leaving smallest remaining resource.

Can improve packing but may increase search complexity.

---

# 231. Multi-Dimensional Packing

A workload consumes:

```text
CPU

memory

GPU

network
```

A node may have enough GPU but insufficient CPU.

Resource shape matters.

---

# 232. Dominant Resource

For one workload:

```text
GPU usage = 90%

CPU usage = 20%

memory = 30%
```

GPU is dominant resource.

---

# 233. Dominant Resource Fairness

Fairness across users consuming different resource mixes.

Conceptually each user's dominant share is compared.

Useful for multi-resource cluster schedulers.

---

# 234. Deadline Scheduling

If jobs have deadlines:

```text
earliest deadline first
```

is one classic strategy under certain assumptions.

---

# 235. Shortest Job First

Can reduce average completion time.

But large jobs can starve.

Again, optimization target matters.

---

# 236. Shortest Remaining Processing Time

Preemptive version of shortest-job logic.

Excellent average latency theoretically but requires runtime estimates and may be unfair.

---

# 237. Runtime Prediction

ML scheduler may estimate:

```text
job duration
```

from history.

Prediction errors can distort scheduling.

Always design fallback when estimate inaccurate.

---

# 238. Dynamic Programming

Break problem into overlapping subproblems.

Often interview favorite.

Less directly common in everyday MLOps platform code, but foundational.

---

# 239. DP Recognition

Look for:

```text
optimal solution composed
from smaller optimal solutions
```

with repeated states.

---

# 240. Memoization

Top-down DP caching results.

---

# 241. Tabulation

Bottom-up DP.

---

# 242. Knapsack Analogy

GPU placement can resemble constrained optimization:

```text
choose jobs
to maximize value
within limited capacity
```

Real scheduling adds far more dimensions.

---

# 243. Why Not Solve Scheduler With Exact DP?

State space explodes.

At thousands of nodes/jobs, exact optimization may be too slow.

Use heuristics/approximation.

---

# 244. Greedy vs Optimal Trade-Off

In infrastructure:

```text
good solution in 10 ms
```

may be better than:

```text
optimal solution in 10 minutes
```

because system state changes continuously.

---

# 245. Randomization

Randomized algorithms can reduce pathological patterns.

Examples:

```text
randomized load balancing

sampling

jitter
```

---

# 246. Power of Two Choices

Choose two random servers.

Send request to less loaded one.

Surprisingly effective load balancing.

---

# 247. Why It Works

Much better than one random choice with very low overhead.

Useful conceptual strategy for large distributed pools.

---

# 248. Consistent Hashing vs Load-Aware Routing

Consistent hashing:

```text
stable placement
```

Load-aware:

```text
better current balance
```

Sometimes combine:

```text
small candidate set via hash

choose least loaded candidate
```

---

# 249. Locality-Aware Routing

For model cache:

```text
prefer node already holding model
```

to avoid expensive reload.

But do not overload that node.

---

# 250. Cache Affinity Trade-Off

Strong affinity:

```text
higher cache hit rate
```

but:

```text
possible hotspots
```

Dynamic routing balances locality and load.

---

# 251. Replication Factor

If model stored on:

```text
3 serving nodes
```

routing has multiple locality-compatible targets.

This can improve both availability and load balance.

---

# 252. Gossip Protocols

Nodes periodically exchange state with peers.

Used for:

```text
membership

failure detection

eventual state dissemination
```

---

# 253. Gossip Advantages

```text
decentralized

scalable

resilient
```

---

# 254. Gossip Disadvantages

```text
eventual convergence

duplicate messages

stale information
```

Not for operations requiring immediate strong agreement.

---

# 255. Failure Detection Is Imperfect

If node does not respond:

```text
dead?
```

Maybe:

```text
network delayed

process paused

packet loss
```

You cannot perfectly distinguish failure from delay in asynchronous distributed systems.

---

# 256. Heartbeats

Nodes periodically announce:

```text
I'm alive.
```

Missing heartbeat triggers suspicion.

---

# 257. Heartbeat Interval Trade-Off

Short:

```text
fast detection

more overhead

more false positives
```

Long:

```text
slow detection

less overhead
```

---

# 258. Phi-Accrual Style Thinking

Rather than binary timeout, estimate suspicion based on heartbeat arrival distribution.

Conceptually useful for adaptive failure detection.

---

# 259. Replicated State Machine

If multiple nodes execute same deterministic operations in same order:

```text
same state
```

This underpins many consensus systems.

---

# 260. Determinism Matters

If operation includes:

```text
random()
```

or:

```text
current_time()
```

without controlled input, replicas may diverge.

---

# 261. Event Sourcing

Store events:

```text
ModelCreated

ModelApproved

ModelDeployed

ModelRetired
```

Then derive current state.

---

# 262. Advantages

```text
auditability

history

replay
```

---

# 263. Disadvantages

```text
replay complexity

schema evolution

large logs

derived-state rebuilding
```

---

# 264. Snapshotting

Instead of replaying:

```text
10 billion events
```

save periodic state snapshot.

Then replay only newer events.

---

# 265. CQRS Concept

Separate:

```text
write model

read model
```

when their scaling/query requirements differ.

Do not use automatically; complexity must be justified.

---

# 266. Transactional Outbox

Database transaction writes:

```text
business state

outbox event
```

atomically.

Background publisher sends event.

---

# 267. Why Outbox Exists

Without it:

```text
DB write succeeds

event publish fails
```

downstream systems never learn state changed.

---

# 268. Outbox Duplicate Publication

Publisher may send same event more than once after retries.

Consumers should still be idempotent.

---

# 269. Saga

Coordinates multi-service workflow without one global ACID transaction.

---

# 270. Saga Example

Model deployment:

```text
reserve capacity

create endpoint

configure routing

register monitoring
```

If routing fails:

```text
delete endpoint

release capacity
```

as compensating actions.

---

# 271. Compensation Is Not Undo

Some actions cannot truly be reversed.

Example:

```text
email sent
```

You cannot unsend it.

Compensation might:

```text
send correction
```

---

# 272. Distributed Transaction Trade-Off

Strong coordination:

```text
simpler global correctness
```

but:

```text
lower availability

higher latency

more complexity
```

Prefer local transactions + idempotency when appropriate.

---

# 273. Two-Phase Commit Concept

Coordinator asks participants:

```text
prepare?
```

then:

```text
commit
```

Strong atomicity but coordinator/participant failures create complexity and blocking risks.

---

# 274. Why Microservice Systems Often Avoid Global 2PC

Operational complexity and coupling are high.

Use:

```text
outbox

sagas

idempotency
```

where business semantics permit.

---

# 275. Distributed Counter

Simple:

```text
one database row
```

can become hotspot.

---

# 276. Sharded Counter

Partition counter:

```text
counter_1

counter_2

...

counter_n
```

Writers update different shards.

Readers sum them.

---

# 277. Exactness Trade-Off

Reading every shard for every request may be expensive.

You may maintain asynchronous aggregate.

---

# 278. CRDT Concept

Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types allow replicas to independently update and later merge without conflicts under defined semantics.

---

# 279. G-Counter

Grow-only distributed counter.

Each replica increments its own component.

Merge uses component-wise max.

Total is sum.

---

# 280. CRDT Trade-Off

Excellent for certain mergeable data types.

Not suitable for arbitrary business constraints such as:

```text
global GPU allocation
must never exceed 1000
```

because this requires coordination.

---

# 281. Coordination-Avoidance Principle

If business invariant can tolerate independent operations:

```text
avoid coordination
```

If invariant requires global bound:

```text
coordinate
```

---

# 282. Example — Global Quota

Requirement:

```text
tenant can never have >100 GPUs
```

Two regions independently allocate 80 each.

Total:

```text
160
```

Violation.

Need:

```text
central coordination

regional quota partitioning

or escrow-like reservation
```

---

# 283. Quota Partitioning

Allocate:

```text
Region A: 60

Region B: 40
```

Regions can operate independently within local quota.

Global invariant remains bounded.

---

# 284. Escrow-Style Thinking

Distribute rights to perform constrained operation.

Useful for reducing coordination while preserving global limits.

---

# 285. Distributed Cache Consistency

Cache may contain stale data.

Question:

```text
Is stale acceptable?
```

---

# 286. Cache-Aside Pattern

Read:

```text
cache hit -> return

cache miss -> DB -> cache -> return
```

---

# 287. Cache Invalidation

On update:

```text
write DB

invalidate cache
```

But ordering/failure creates race conditions.

---

# 288. Write-Through

Write cache and backing store as part of path.

Simpler reads but write availability may depend on cache.

---

# 289. Write-Behind

Write cache first, persist asynchronously.

Higher write performance but durability/consistency risk.

---

# 290. Versioned Cache

Store object with version:

```text
model:v31
```

rather than overwriting:

```text
model:latest
```

Immutable versioning simplifies correctness.

---

# 291. Cache Stampede

Popular key expires.

Thousands of requests miss simultaneously.

---

# 292. Stampede Mitigation

```text
single-flight

jittered TTLs

refresh-ahead

stale-while-revalidate
```

---

# 293. Stale-While-Revalidate

Serve slightly stale cached value while one worker refreshes.

Works only if temporary staleness is safe.

---

# 294. Negative Caching

Cache:

```text
resource not found
```

briefly.

Prevents repeated expensive lookup for invalid IDs.

Need short TTL because resource may later appear.

---

# 295. Rate Limiting Algorithms

Important:

```text
fixed window

sliding window

token bucket

leaky bucket
```

---

# 296. Fixed Window

Example:

```text
100 requests
per minute
```

Counter resets on minute boundary.

---

# 297. Boundary Burst Problem

User sends:

```text
100 at 12:00:59

100 at 12:01:00
```

Effectively:

```text
200 requests in 1 second
```

yet within both windows.

---

# 298. Sliding Window

More accurate recent-period enforcement.

More storage/computation.

---

# 299. Token Bucket

Bucket capacity:

```text
B
```

Refill:

```text
R tokens/sec
```

Request consumes token.

Allows controlled bursts.

---

# 300. Token Bucket MLOps Use Case

LLM tenant:

```text
bucket measured in tokens
```

not requests.

Large prompt consumes more allowance.

---

# 301. Leaky Bucket

Requests enter bucket/queue and leave at steady rate.

Good for smoothing bursts.

---

# 302. Distributed Rate Limiter

With many gateway replicas, local counters are insufficient for strict global limit.

Options:

```text
central counter

partitioned ownership

approximate local limits

distributed store
```

---

# 303. Strict vs Approximate Rate Limits

Strict global limit requires more coordination.

Many systems accept slight temporary overshoot for better availability.

---

# 304. Circuit Breaker Algorithm

Track failures.

States:

```text
CLOSED

OPEN

HALF_OPEN
```

---

# 305. CLOSED

Requests flow normally.

Failures accumulate.

---

# 306. OPEN

Requests fail fast.

Dependency gets recovery time.

---

# 307. HALF_OPEN

Allow small number of probes.

If healthy:

```text
close
```

If still bad:

```text
open
```

---

# 308. Bulkhead

Partition resource pools.

Example:

```text
Tenant A thread pool

Tenant B thread pool
```

or:

```text
training DB pool

serving DB pool
```

One overload does not consume everything.

---

# 309. Load Balancing Algorithms

Examples:

```text
round robin

least connections

weighted round robin

power of two choices

consistent hash
```

---

# 310. Round Robin

Simple and stateless.

Works when backend capacity/request cost roughly equal.

---

# 311. Least Connections

Prefer backend with fewer active connections.

Better when request duration varies.

---

# 312. Weighted Round Robin

Larger servers get more requests.

Useful heterogeneous fleets.

---

# 313. Consistent Hash Routing

Useful when request needs locality:

```text
same model

same tenant

same cached context
```

---

# 314. Adaptive Load Balancing

Use observed:

```text
latency

queue

errors
```

to route away from degraded backends.

Be careful with unstable feedback loops.

---

# 315. Hedged Requests

If one request is unusually slow, send duplicate to another replica after delay.

Return first response.

---

# 316. Why Hedging Helps

Reduces tail latency when rare stragglers dominate p99.

---

# 317. Hedging Cost

Increases:

```text
load

compute

duplicate work
```

Use sparingly and only for idempotent operations.

---

# 318. Speculative Execution

Distributed batch systems may duplicate slow task on another worker.

Whichever finishes first wins.

Helps with stragglers.

---

# 319. Training Caveat

You usually cannot casually duplicate one synchronous distributed training rank.

Speculative execution is easier for independent batch tasks.

---

# 320. MapReduce Mental Model

Map:

```text
process partitions independently
```

Shuffle:

```text
group by key
```

Reduce:

```text
aggregate
```

Still foundational for distributed data processing.

---

# 321. Shuffle

Often the expensive part.

Requires:

```text
network

disk

serialization
```

---

# 322. Data Skew

One key receives huge share.

One reducer becomes bottleneck.

---

# 323. Salting

Split hot key into subkeys:

```text
merchant123#0

merchant123#1

...
```

aggregate partially, then merge.

---

# 324. Broadcast Join

If one table is small:

```text
send it to all workers
```

avoid massive shuffle of large table.

---

# 325. Hash Join

Partition both sides by join key.

Efficient when distributions manageable.

---

# 326. Sort-Merge Join

Sort by join key then merge.

Useful for large ordered datasets.

---

# 327. External Sorting

Dataset larger than memory.

Process:

```text
sort chunks

write runs to disk

merge runs
```

Important conceptual algorithm for big-data systems.

---

# 328. Partitioning for Parallelism

Break dataset into:

```text
N partitions
```

workers operate concurrently.

Need enough partitions for parallelism but not millions of tiny partitions.

---

# 329. Partition Count Trade-Off

Too few:

```text
poor parallelism
```

Too many:

```text
metadata overhead

small files

scheduling overhead
```

---

# 330. Sampling

Useful for:

```text
debugging

approximate statistics

evaluation

canaries
```

---

# 331. Stratified Sampling

Ensure important segments are represented.

For ML monitoring, random sample may miss:

```text
rare fraud

minority slice

high-value customer
```

---

# 332. Hash-Based Deterministic Sampling

Example:

```text
hash(prediction_id) % 100 < 1
```

gives stable ~1% sample.

Useful for consistent telemetry sampling.

---

# 333. Sampling Bias

Sampling strategy can distort model-quality conclusions.

Statistical correctness matters alongside algorithm efficiency.

---

# 334. Median vs Mean

Mean sensitive to outliers.

Median robust.

For latency:

```text
p50
```

is median.

But production users often care about:

```text
p95/p99
```

too.

---

# 335. Online Mean

Maintain:

```text
count

running sum
```

or numerically stable incremental formulas.

No need to retain all values.

---

# 336. Online Variance

Algorithms exist to calculate variance incrementally without storing whole stream.

Useful in streaming monitoring.

---

# 337. Quantile Estimation

Exact percentile requires storing/sorting substantial data.

Large telemetry systems use approximate sketches/histograms.

---

# 338. Histogram

Store counts in ranges:

```text
0-10 ms

10-50 ms

50-100 ms
...
```

Cheap aggregation across machines.

---

# 339. Histogram Bucket Design

Bad buckets can make p99 impossible to estimate accurately.

Choose according to expected latency distribution/SLOs.

---

# 340. Distributed Aggregation

Metrics from many replicas should merge associatively where possible.

This allows hierarchical aggregation:

```text
pod

node

region

global
```

---

# 341. Associative Operations

Examples:

```text
sum

min

max
```

easy to distribute.

Median is not directly mergeable from only local medians.

---

# 342. Commutativity

If operation order does not matter:

```text
a + b = b + a
```

distributed aggregation becomes easier.

---

# 343. Idempotent Merge

Set union is idempotent:

```text
A ∪ A = A
```

Useful property in distributed convergence.

---

# 344. Monoid Thinking

Associative operation + identity element.

Useful abstraction for distributed aggregation.

Example:

```text
(sum, 0)
```

This is more theoretical, but powerful when designing scalable reductions.

---

# 345. Interview Problem — LRU Cache

Expected:

```text
hash map
+
doubly linked list
```

Discuss:

```text
O(1) get

O(1) put
```

Then extend to:

```text
model size

concurrency

single-flight
```

for MLOps.

---

# 346. Interview Problem — Top-K GPU Consumers

Input:

```text
millions of usage records
```

Need:

```text
top 100 teams
```

Approach:

```text
aggregate by team
+
size-100 heap
```

---

# 347. Interview Problem — Pipeline Cycle Detection

Input:

```text
task dependencies
```

Need validate DAG.

Use:

```text
DFS colors

or Kahn's algorithm
```

Complexity:

```text
O(V + E)
```

---

# 348. Interview Problem — DAG Executor

Need execute tasks in parallel when dependencies satisfied.

Use:

```text
indegree map

ready queue

worker pool
```

---

# 349. Interview Problem — Rate Limiter

Start with:

```text
token bucket
```

Then interviewer may ask:

> Make it distributed.

Discuss:

```text
centralized counter

partition ownership

approximation

consistency trade-offs
```

---

# 350. Interview Problem — Model Cache

Requirements:

```text
100 GB capacity

models variable size

multiple concurrent requests

expensive load
```

Use:

```text
weighted LRU

per-model single-flight

eviction lock

reference/pin count
```

---

# 351. Pinning

Do not evict model while active request uses it.

Track:

```text
reference count
```

or leases.

---

# 352. Eviction Race

Thread A selects model for eviction.

Thread B starts request using same model.

Need synchronization/state transition.

---

# 353. Cache State Machine

Possible:

```text
LOADING

READY

EVICTING

FAILED
```

Concurrency becomes explicit.

---

# 354. Interview Problem — Scheduler

Requirements:

```text
priority

tenant fairness

GPU count

deadline
```

Do not jump directly to one heap.

Explain:

```text
priority queues per tenant

fair-share selection between tenants

topology placement after job choice
```

---

# 355. Hierarchical Scheduling

```text
Global:
which tenant/job?

Local:
which nodes/GPUs?
```

Separating these reduces algorithmic complexity.

---

# 356. Interview Problem — Sliding Window Metrics

Need maximum requests/sec over last 5 minutes.

Use:

```text
deque

or time buckets
```

depending on precision/volume.

---

# 357. High-Volume Variant

At 10M events/sec, storing every timestamp is impossible.

Use:

```text
per-second buckets

stream aggregation
```

---

# 358. Interview Problem — Deduplicate Events

Small scale:

```text
hash set
```

Large bounded window:

```text
set + TTL
```

Very large approximate:

```text
Bloom filter
```

Persistent exact:

```text
database uniqueness / idempotency table
```

---

# 359. The Correct Answer Changes With Scale

This is a senior-level insight.

Algorithm questions often intentionally evolve from:

```text
one process
```

to:

```text
distributed production system
```

---

# 360. Interview Problem — Find Available GPU Slot

Given reservation intervals, find earliest gap of length T.

Use:

```text
sort intervals

merge

scan gaps
```

---

# 361. Interview Problem — Peak GPU Demand

Given reservation intervals with GPU amounts.

Use:

```text
sweep line
```

Events:

```text
start -> +GPU

end -> -GPU
```

Track maximum.

---

# 362. Interview Problem — Dependency Impact

Given lineage graph:

> Which production models depend on dataset X?

Run graph traversal from dataset through downstream edges.

Use:

```text
BFS/DFS
```

---

# 363. Interview Problem — Shortest Failure Path

Given service dependency graph with edge latency.

Find lowest-latency fallback route.

Could use Dijkstra if modeled appropriately.

---

# 364. Interview Problem — Distributed Job Ownership

Need assign jobs to controller replicas.

Use:

```text
consistent/rendezvous hashing
```

so adding controller moves limited ownership.

---

# 365. Interview Problem — Unique User Count

Exact:

```text
set
```

Huge stream:

```text
HyperLogLog-like approximation
```

Explain trade-off.

---

# 366. Interview Problem — Frequent Feature IDs

Need top frequent features among billions of requests.

Options:

```text
exact distributed aggregation

Count-Min Sketch + candidate tracking
```

depending on memory/accuracy.

---

# 367. Interview Problem — Random Prediction Sample

Stream unknown length.

Need uniform 10k sample.

Use:

```text
reservoir sampling
```

---

# 368. Interview Problem — Distributed Counter

If approximate dashboard:

```text
local counters + periodic aggregation
```

If strict billing:

```text
durable event ledger
```

Requirements change architecture.

---

# 369. Interview Problem — Leader Election

Do not implement naive:

```text
if lock file absent:
    become leader
```

Discuss:

```text
quorum-backed coordinator

leases

fencing
```

---

# 370. Interview Problem — Global Quota

Need:

```text
max 100 GPUs globally
```

Options:

```text
strong centralized allocator

regional quota partitioning

escrow tokens
```

Discuss latency/availability trade-offs.

---

# 371. Interview Problem — Deployment Workflow

Steps across multiple services.

Need partial failure recovery.

Use:

```text
state machine

idempotent steps

saga/compensation

reconciliation
```

---

# 372. Interview Problem — Event Publication

Need database state and event to remain consistent.

Use:

```text
transactional outbox
```

---

# 373. Interview Problem — Slow Worker

One worker is 10× slower.

For independent batch tasks:

```text
speculative duplicate
```

may help.

For synchronized training:

```text
diagnose/remove straggler
```

different semantics.

---

# 374. Interview Problem — Hot Partition

Partition by tenant.

One tenant dominates.

Solutions:

```text
sub-shard hot tenant

adaptive partitioning

salting
```

Trade-off:

```text
more complex aggregation
```

---

# 375. Interview Problem — Global Model Routing

Need model locality plus load balance.

Potential:

```text
rendezvous hash to choose candidate replicas

pick least loaded healthy candidate
```

---

# 376. Algorithm Selection Framework

When solving coding/system problem ask:

```text
Do I need lookup?
-> hash map

ordered min/max?
-> heap

FIFO?
-> queue

recent window?
-> deque

dependency relationships?
-> graph

prefix lookup?
-> trie

connectivity?
-> union-find

sorted search?
-> binary search

top-K?
-> heap

approximate membership?
-> Bloom filter
```

---

# 377. Distributed-System Selection Framework

Ask:

```text
Need stable sharding?
-> consistent hashing

Need duplicate protection?
-> idempotency

Need global agreement?
-> consensus

Need one active owner?
-> lease + fencing

Need eventual dissemination?
-> gossip

Need cross-service workflow?
-> saga

Need DB + event consistency?
-> outbox
```

---

# 378. Correctness First

Before optimization define invariant.

Examples:

```text
No tenant exceeds quota.

No model executes before approval.

No task executes before dependencies succeed.
```

Then choose algorithm.

---

# 379. Invariant — Scheduler

```text
allocated GPUs
<=
physical available GPUs
```

must always hold.

---

# 380. Invariant — DAG Executor

A task begins only when:

```text
all required parents
succeeded
```

---

# 381. Invariant — Model Cache

Never return:

```text
partially loaded model
```

---

# 382. Invariant — Rate Limiter

For strict system:

```text
accepted usage
<=
defined allowance
```

for specified time semantics.

---

# 383. Invariant — Leader

At most one valid writer for resource at a given fencing epoch.

---

# 384. Liveness

Correctness is not enough.

System also needs progress.

Example:

```text
no quota violation
```

but scheduler never runs jobs.

Correct but useless.

---

# 385. Safety vs Liveness

Safety:

```text
bad thing never happens
```

Liveness:

```text
good thing eventually happens
```

---

# 386. Scheduler Safety

```text
never allocate same GPU twice
```

---

# 387. Scheduler Liveness

```text
eligible queued job eventually runs
```

assuming capacity.

---

# 388. Distributed Lock Safety

```text
two holders never act concurrently
```

---

# 389. Distributed Lock Liveness

```text
after holder dies,
someone else can eventually acquire
```

---

# 390. Fairness

A third dimension:

```text
which waiting party gets progress?
```

A scheduler can be safe/live yet unfair.

---

# 391. Availability

A strongly coordinated solution may preserve correctness but reject work during partitions.

That can be acceptable for some operations.

---

# 392. Performance

A theoretically elegant algorithm may have poor production characteristics due to:

```text
locks

cache misses

network chatter

serialization
```

Benchmark realistic workloads.

---

# 393. Space-Bounded Design

Every:

```text
queue

cache

dedup table

retry list

metrics label
```

must have bounded growth strategy.

---

# 394. Time-Bounded Design

Every:

```text
remote call

retry loop

lease

job

agent
```

should have meaningful time bounds.

---

# 395. Cardinality-Bounded Design

Every key dimension can explode.

Examples:

```text
per-user metrics

per-request locks

per-model caches
```

Ask:

```text
What happens at 100 million unique keys?
```

---

# 396. Production Big-O

Consider not only:

```text
n
```

but:

```text
number of nodes

number of network round trips

bytes transferred

durable writes
```

---

# 397. Distributed Complexity Example

Algorithm:

```text
O(log n)
```

but each step requires cross-region RPC.

10 steps × 100 ms:

```text
1 second
```

Network dominates.

---

# 398. Data Locality

A theoretically better algorithm can lose if it moves terabytes across network.

MLOps algorithms must consider where data lives.

---

# 399. Cache Locality

Sequential scans often perform well due to CPU/storage caching.

Pointer-heavy structures may have worse cache behavior.

This matters in performance-sensitive code.

---

# 400. Batch Complexity

One remote operation on 100 objects often beats 100 remote operations.

Batching transforms:

```text
network round-trip complexity
```

even if computational Big-O remains the same.

---

# 401. Interview Coding Framework

Use:

```text
1. Restate.

2. Clarify constraints.

3. Give simple solution.

4. Identify bottleneck.

5. Improve.

6. State complexity.

7. Implement.

8. Test.

9. Discuss production extension.
```

---

# 402. Example Interview Response

Problem:

> Find top K most expensive training jobs.

You might say:

```text
A full sort is O(n log n).

Because we only need K and K is small,
I'll maintain a min-heap of size K,
giving O(n log k) time
and O(k) extra space.
```

This is concise and strong.

---

# 403. Production Extension

Then add:

```text
If data no longer fits one machine,
I'd aggregate per partition,
produce local top-K,
then merge those K-sized results globally.
```

This moves from algorithms to distributed systems.

---

# 404. Local Top-K + Global Merge

Suppose 1,000 partitions.

Each computes:

```text
top 100
```

Global reducer sees:

```text
100,000 candidates
```

instead of billions of records.

---

# 405. Composable Algorithms Scale Better

Design local summaries that can merge.

Examples:

```text
top-K

histograms

counts

sketches
```

---

# 422. Retry Deadline Example

Overall:

```text
5 sec
```

Attempt 1:

```text
1 sec
```

```text
0.2 sec
```

Attempt 2 must use:

```text
remaining time
```

not another unlimited 5 sec.

# 423. Mock Coding Interview 10 — Sliding Feature Window

Need:

```text
transaction count
during previous 10 minutes
```

For one entity:

```text
deque timestamps
```

At scale:

```text
partitioned stream processor
with keyed state
```

---

# 424. From Local to Distributed

Memorize this transformation:

```text
Local Hash Map
    |
    v
Partitioned Key-Value Store

Local Queue
    |
    v
Durable Distributed Queue

Local Lock
    |
    v
Ownership / Consensus / Lease

Local Cache
    |
    v
Sharded Replicated Cache

Local Counter
    |
    v
Partitioned Aggregation
```

---

# 425. What Changes in Distributed Systems?

You gain:

```text
network failure

partial failure

duplicate messages

reordering

clock skew

independent crashes
```

---

# 426. Local Function Assumption

```text
call either returns
or throws
```

Distributed call may:

```text
succeed remotely
but response is lost
```

This is the source of many duplicate problems.

---

# 427. The Two Generals Intuition

Perfect certainty about distributed coordination over unreliable communication is impossible in some formulations.

Practical systems operate with bounded assumptions, retries, consensus, and idempotency.

---

# 428. FLP Intuition

In a fully asynchronous network with even one possible crash failure, deterministic consensus cannot guarantee termination in all executions.

You do not need to prove FLP.

Understand why:

```text
failure detection
and timing assumptions matter
```

---

# 429. Production Systems Use Partial Synchrony

Real systems assume things like:

```text
messages usually arrive within some bound

clocks are approximately synchronized

timeouts eventually become meaningful
```

after unstable periods.

---

# 430. Failure Model

Always state:

```text
crash failure?

network partition?

Byzantine behavior?

disk corruption?
```

Most enterprise MLOps control planes design primarily for:

```text
crash + network failures
```

not arbitrary Byzantine nodes.

---

# 431. Byzantine Failure

Node may behave arbitrarily or maliciously.

Requires much stronger protocols.

Usually outside ordinary internal ML platform control planes unless threat model demands it.

---

# 432. Durability

Once operation reports success:

```text
will it survive process/node failure?
```

That depends on:

```text
persistent storage

replication

fsync/commit semantics
```

---

# 433. Acknowledgement Semantics

Do not acknowledge:

```text
model registered
```

until required durable state is actually committed.

---

# 434. Write-Ahead Log

Persist intended changes before applying them to mutable structures.

Used in databases for crash recovery.

---

# 435. Log as Source of Truth

A durable append-only log enables:

```text
replay

rebuild

replication
```

---

# 436. Snapshot + Log

Common architecture:

```text
snapshot at T

+
events after T
```

reconstruct latest state.

---

# 437. Immutability

Immutable data simplifies concurrency.

Examples:

```text
model v31

dataset snapshot 812
```

No reader sees half-updated object.

---

# 438. Copy-on-Write

Instead of mutating shared state:

```text
create new version
```

then atomically switch reference.

Strong pattern for model/config deployment.

---

# 439. Atomic Pointer Swap

Traffic configuration may move:

```text
current -> v31
```

to:

```text
current -> v32
```

while artifacts remain immutable.

Rollback simply changes pointer back.

---

# 440. Compare-and-Swap

Update only if current version matches expected.

Example:

```text
UPDATE deployment
SET version = 13
WHERE version = 12
```

If zero rows updated:

```text
concurrent modification occurred
```

---

# 441. Optimistic Concurrency

Assume conflicts rare.

Detect version conflict and retry.

Good for metadata systems with relatively low contention.

---

# 442. Pessimistic Locking

Lock before modification.

Useful when conflicts frequent or invariant difficult.

Trade:

```text
blocking

deadlocks

reduced concurrency
```

---

# 443. Deadlock Prevention

Strategies:

```text
consistent lock order

short transactions

timeouts

avoid nested locks
```

---

# 444. Starvation vs Deadlock

Deadlock:

```text
nobody progresses
```

Starvation:

```text
some participant never progresses
```

---

# 445. Priority Inversion

Low-priority task holds resource required by high-priority task.

Relevant concept in schedulers and concurrency.

---

# 446. Distributed Priority Inversion

Low-priority training job may hold scarce GPU topology needed by urgent large job.

Preemption/checkpointing can mitigate.

---

# 447. Head-of-Line Blocking

First queued job cannot run.

Smaller jobs behind could run but are blocked.

---

# 448. Example

Queue:

```text
Job A: 512 GPUs

Job B: 1 GPU

Job C: 1 GPU
```

Only 100 GPUs free.

Strict FIFO means:

```text
B and C wait unnecessarily
```

---

# 449. Backfilling

Allow smaller jobs to use gaps while preserving future reservation for large job.

Improves utilization.

---

# 450. Backfill Risk

If runtime estimates wrong:

```text
small job runs too long
```

and delays reserved large job.

---

# 451. Reservation Scheduling

Reserve future capacity for large important workloads.

Trade:

```text
lower immediate utilization

better deadline predictability
```

---

# 452. Online vs Offline Algorithms

Online algorithm processes data as it arrives without seeing future.

Schedulers and stream processors are often online systems.

---

# 453. Competitive Thinking

An online scheduler cannot know future job arrivals.

Optimal decision with hindsight may be impossible online.

This explains why production scheduling is heuristic.

---

# 454. Deterministic vs Randomized Routing

Deterministic helps:

```text
reproducibility

cache locality
```

Randomization helps:

```text
avoid hotspots

load distribution
```

Hybrid strategies are common.

---

# 455. Stable Hashing and Tenant Isolation

Tenant assignment to cell can use deterministic hashing.

But high-risk tenants may override with explicit placement.

---

# 456. Capacity-Aware Hashing

If nodes have different capacities:

```text
weighted virtual nodes
```

or weighted rendezvous hashing can reflect this.

---

# 457. Failure-Aware Placement

Never replicate all copies into same:

```text
node

rack

zone
```

Placement algorithm must understand failure domains.

---

# 458. Anti-Affinity as Graph Constraint

Replicas have constraint:

```text
must not share failure domain
```

This is another scheduling/constraint-satisfaction problem.

---

# 459. Constraint Satisfaction

Scheduling may require:

```text
GPU type = X

region = Y

zone spread

tenant isolation

storage locality
```

Finding feasible placement precedes optimization.

---

# 460. Filter Then Score

Common scheduling architecture:

```text
1. Filter infeasible nodes.

2. Score feasible nodes.

3. Select best.
```

This simplifies complex constraints.

---

# 461. Filter Examples

Reject node if:

```text
not enough GPU

wrong region

wrong security tier

missing topology capability
```

---

# 462. Score Examples

Among remaining nodes prefer:

```text
best locality

lowest cost

best packing

lowest load
```

---

# 463. Hard vs Soft Constraints

Hard:

```text
must remain in EU
```

Soft:

```text
prefer cheaper zone
```

Do not mix them.

---

# 464. Lexicographic Optimization

First satisfy:

```text
safety/security
```

then optimize:

```text
cost/performance
```

A cheap but forbidden placement is not an option.

---

# 465. Multi-Objective Optimization

You may optimize:

```text
latency

cost

utilization

fairness
```

simultaneously.

Often convert to scoring function.

---

# 466. Scoring Function Risk

Example:

```text
score =
0.4 * cost
+
0.3 * locality
+
0.3 * utilization
```

Weights encode organizational policy.

Poor normalization can produce nonsense.

---

# 467. Explainability of Scheduling

At enterprise scale, users ask:

> Why is my job waiting?

Scheduler should surface reasons:

```text
quota exhausted

no matching GPU topology

higher-priority reservation

region capacity unavailable
```

Algorithm observability matters.

---

# 468. Algorithm Observability

Track:

```text
decision time

queue wait

rejected candidates

selected score

preemptions
```

without exploding telemetry cardinality.

---

# 469. Algorithm Correctness Testing

Test invariants using:

```text
unit tests

property-based tests

simulation
```

---

# 470. Scheduler Simulation

Generate synthetic workloads.

Measure:

```text
utilization

fairness

queue time

starvation

large-job completion
```

before production deployment.

---

# 471. Property Test Example

Invariant:

```text
allocated GPU count
never exceeds capacity
```

Generate thousands of random job arrival/completion sequences.

---

# 472. Deterministic Simulation

Use fixed seed to reproduce failures.

---

# 473. Chaos + Algorithm Testing

Simulate:

```text
node failures

slow workers

network partitions

stale state
```

and verify invariants remain.

---

# 474. Distributed Systems Anti-Pattern — Global Lock Everywhere

Creates:

```text
latency

single bottleneck

availability dependency
```

Use coordination only where invariant requires it.

---

# 475. Anti-Pattern — Exact Global Counter for Dashboard

Paying consensus cost per prediction just to display approximate traffic count is wasteful.

Use aggregation.

---

# 476. Anti-Pattern — Random Shard Key Without Query Analysis

Distribution may be great.

Queries may require scanning every shard.

---

# 477. Anti-Pattern — Tenant ID Only as Shard Key

One massive tenant can become hotspot.

---

# 478. Anti-Pattern — Global Ordering

Most event systems only need ordering by:

```text
entity

account

user
```

Global ordering destroys scalability.

---

# 479. Anti-Pattern — Clock Timestamp as Total Order

Clock skew makes distributed ordering unreliable.

---

# 480. Anti-Pattern — Lease Without Fencing

Old leader can resume after expiration and corrupt state.

---

# 481. Anti-Pattern — Retry Without Idempotency

Duplicate side effects.

---

# 482. Anti-Pattern — Unbounded Dedup Set

Memory grows forever.

Need:

```text
TTL

window

persistent compaction

probabilistic structure
```

---

# 483. Anti-Pattern — One Priority Queue for Multi-Tenant Fairness

Highest-priority tenant can monopolize queue.

Use hierarchical scheduling.

---

# 484. Anti-Pattern — Perfect Bin Packing

Spending seconds/minutes finding optimal placement in rapidly changing cluster may be worse than a fast good-enough heuristic.

---

# 485. Anti-Pattern — Cache Without Versioning

Model update occurs.

Old cached result remains.

Use version-aware keys/invalidation.

---

# 486. Anti-Pattern — Cache Without Stampede Protection

One hot expiry causes downstream outage.

---

# 487. Anti-Pattern — Consensus for Everything

Strong consensus has cost.

Use it for:

```text
critical coordinated state
```

not telemetry counters.

---

# 488. Anti-Pattern — Eventual Consistency for Critical Invariants

Do not use casually where:

```text
double allocation

double charge

unauthorized promotion
```

cannot be tolerated.

---

# 489. Anti-Pattern — Approximation Without Error Budget

If using sketch/sampling, define:

```text
acceptable error
```

Do not say "approximately correct" without quantified expectations.

---

# 490. Anti-Pattern — Algorithm Without Failure Semantics

A priority queue implementation is not a production scheduler.

You still need:

```text
durability

retries

ownership

recovery
```

---

# 524. The Architect Question

When choosing an algorithm ask:

> What happens when N becomes one million, one node fails, the request retries, and one tenant produces 80% of traffic?

That single question pushes a textbook algorithm toward production design.
