```text
"CI builds the Docker image
and CD deploys it."
```

to:

```text
"We can reproducibly promote code,
data references,
feature definitions,
models,
prompts,
policies,
runtime artifacts,
and infrastructure changes
through a cryptographically verifiable,
progressively delivered,
fully reversible enterprise release system."
```

That is the next layer of architecture depth.

# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 32 — CI/CD, GitOps, Release Engineering, and Software Supply Chain for ML Platforms

---

# 1. Why ML Release Engineering Is Harder Than Normal Software Delivery

Traditional software release often looks like:

```text
Source Code
    |
    v
Build
    |
    v
Test
    |
    v
Deploy
```

Production ML adds many independently changing artifacts:

```text
application code

training code

feature definitions

dataset references

model weights

tokenizer

runtime image

inference configuration

prompt templates

RAG index versions

policy bundles

infrastructure

GPU runtime

deployment routing
```

A production release may therefore be:

```text
Code
+
Data
+
Model
+
Runtime
+
Configuration
+
Policy
```

not simply:

```text
new Docker image
```

---

# 2. The Core Release Engineering Question

A Senior MLOps Architect must be able to answer:

> Exactly what changed between production version A and production version B?

If the answer is:

```text
"the latest model"
```

the release system is not mature enough.

A strong answer might be:

```text
Application commit:       83fa1c7
Training code:            12bd991
Training dataset:         ds-82911
Feature bundle:           fraud-features-v18
Model digest:             sha256:...
Runtime image digest:     sha256:...
Inference config:         serving-v42
Policy bundle:            policy-v11
Deployment manifest:      release-2026-08-23-04
```

---

# 3. The Immutable Release Unit

Conceptually define:

```text
ML Release
   |
   +-- Code
   +-- Data references
   +-- Features
   +-- Model
   +-- Runtime
   +-- Configuration
   +-- Policy
```

This becomes the reproducible unit promoted between environments.

---

# 4. Release Engineering Is About Controlling Change

The primary risk is not deployment itself.

The risk is uncontrolled change.

Enterprise release engineering answers:

```text
What changed?

Who changed it?

Was it tested?

Was it approved?

Was it signed?

Where is it running?

Can it be rolled back?

Can we prove all of that later?
```

---

# 5. CI vs CD

CI:

```text
Continuous Integration
```

focuses on integrating changes safely.

CD may mean:

```text
Continuous Delivery
```

or:

```text
Continuous Deployment
```

These are related but not identical.

---

# 6. Continuous Integration

Developers frequently merge changes into a shared mainline.

Automation validates:

```text
compile/build

unit tests

lint

security scans

contracts

integration tests
```

Goal:

```text
main branch remains releasable
```

---

# 7. Continuous Delivery

Every validated change can be deployed.

But production promotion may require:

```text
manual approval

change window

risk review
```

---

# 8. Continuous Deployment

Validated changes automatically reach production.

Suitable where:

```text
risk

testing maturity

rollback capability
```

support it.

---

# 9. Not Every ML Change Should Auto-Deploy

Possible examples:

```text
documentation change
-> automatic
```

```text
low-risk internal model
-> automatic canary
```

```text
high-risk lending model
-> approval required
```

Release process should be:

```text
risk-tier aware
```

---

# 10. Source Control Is the Beginning of Provenance

Important release inputs should live in controlled source repositories:

```text
training code

serving code

feature definitions

infrastructure code

policy code

prompt templates

deployment manifests
```

---

# 11. Git Commit as Identity

A Git commit is useful because it represents:

```text
immutable snapshot of repository state
```

Use:

```text
commit SHA
```

rather than:

```text
main
```

for reproducible references.

---

# 12. Branch Names Are Mutable

```text
main
```

today may point to:

```text
commit A
```

tomorrow:

```text
commit B
```

Do not use mutable references as release identities.

---

# 13. Tags Can Also Be Mutable

A Git tag can technically be moved unless protected.

Therefore production release systems should protect or verify tags.

---

# 14. Trunk-Based Development

Most engineers work from short-lived branches and merge frequently into:

```text
main/trunk
```

Advantages:

```text
small changes

frequent integration

less merge conflict

faster feedback
```

---

# 15. Long-Lived Feature Branch Risk

Branches diverge for weeks.

Results:

```text
integration pain

large risky merges

stale tests

slow delivery
```

---

# 16. Feature Flags

Incomplete functionality can merge into trunk while remaining disabled.

Example:

```text
new_model_router_enabled = false
```

This separates:

```text
code deployment
```

from:

```text
feature activation
```

---

# 17. Feature Flag Risk

Flags accumulate.

Eventually code contains:

```text
hundreds of stale branches
```

Every flag needs:

```text
owner

expiry

cleanup plan
```

---

# 18. Branch Protection

Production repositories should enforce:

```text
pull request review

required tests

signed commits where needed

no force push

CODEOWNERS-like review
```

---

# 19. Separation of Duties in Source Control

A change affecting:

```text
production policy
```

may require review from:

```text
security/governance owner
```

not just original author.

---

# 20. CI Pipeline Mental Model

```text
Commit
  |
  v
Checkout
  |
  v
Static Validation
  |
  v
Build
  |
  v
Unit Tests
  |
  v
Integration Tests
  |
  v
Security / Supply Chain
  |
  v
Package Artifact
  |
  v
Publish Immutable Artifact
```

---

# 21. Fast Feedback First

CI stages should roughly order:

```text
cheap + fast checks
before
expensive + slow checks
```

Example:

```text
syntax
lint
unit
integration
GPU tests
large-scale benchmarks
```

---

# 22. Why Pipeline Ordering Matters

If syntax error can be found in:

```text
10 seconds
```

do not first run:

```text
30-minute GPU evaluation
```

---

# 23. CI Parallelism

Independent tests can run simultaneously:

```text
Unit Tests

Security Scan

Static Analysis

Schema Validation
```

reducing wall-clock latency.

---

# 24. Critical Path of CI

Pipeline completion time depends on:

```text
longest dependency chain
```

Optimize critical path, not just total compute.

---

# 25. CI Queue Time

Even fast tests feel slow if runners wait:

```text
20 minutes
```

for capacity.

Track:

```text
queue delay

execution duration
```

separately.

---

# 26. CI Runner Isolation

CI executes:

```text
untrusted branch code
```

That is a serious security boundary.

Use:

```text
ephemeral workers

minimal privileges

network restrictions

short-lived credentials
```

---

# 27. Never Give Pull Requests Production Credentials

A malicious or compromised branch can exfiltrate them.

Instead:

```text
untrusted CI
```

should not have:

```text
production deploy access
```

---

# 28. Trusted Promotion Pipeline

Separate:

```text
build/test pipeline
```

from:

```text
production promotion identity
```

---

# 29. Ephemeral Runners

Create runner for one job.

Destroy afterward.

Benefits:

```text
reduced persistence

reduced cross-job contamination

clean environments
```

---

# 30. Persistent Runner Risk

Previous job may leave:

```text
credentials

artifacts

malware

cached secrets
```

for next job.

---

# 31. Reproducible Build

Given identical inputs:

```text
same source
same dependencies
same build configuration
```

build should produce equivalent artifact.

Ideal:

```text
same digest
```

where ecosystem allows.

---

# 32. Why Reproducibility Matters

If incident occurs:

```text
Can we rebuild exactly what ran?
```

If no:

```text
forensics become uncertain
```

---

# 33. Dependency Pinning

Bad:

```text
pip install package
```

Good:

```text
package==known-version
```

Better:

```text
locked dependency graph
+
verified hashes
```

---

# 34. Transitive Dependencies

You depend on:

```text
library A
```

which depends on:

```text
B
C
D
```

Supply-chain risk includes all of them.

---

# 35. Lockfile

Captures resolved dependency versions.

Helps avoid:

```text
build changed because dependency resolver changed
```

---

# 36. Base Image Pinning

Bad:

```text
FROM python:latest
```

Better:

```text
immutable image digest
```

---

# 37. Build Hermeticity

A hermetic build avoids uncontrolled dependence on:

```text
developer machine

ambient network

local package cache

current system clock
```

as much as practical.

---

# 38. Network-Dependent Build Risk

Build pulls arbitrary package from internet.

Tomorrow package changes/disappears.

Result:

```text
non-reproducible build
```

Use controlled dependency mirrors.

---

# 39. Internal Artifact Mirror

Mirror approved:

```text
packages

container bases

model dependencies
```

Benefits:

```text
availability

security scanning

reproducibility

policy enforcement
```

---

# 40. Build Artifact

Examples:

```text
container image

Python wheel

binary

Helm/package bundle

Terraform module

model runtime engine
```

Every published artifact should be:

```text
immutable
```

---

# 41. Artifact Repository

Stores build outputs.

Do not rebuild independently in each environment.

---

# 42. Build Once, Promote Many

Strong principle:

```text
BUILD ONCE
    |
    v
TEST
    |
    v
PROMOTE SAME DIGEST
    |
    +--> Dev
    +--> Staging
    +--> Production
```

---

# 43. Why Rebuilding per Environment Is Dangerous

Dev artifact:

```text
digest A
```

Production rebuild:

```text
digest B
```

Now production did not run what staging tested.

---

# 44. Artifact Immutability

A published digest should never change.

If fix needed:

```text
publish new artifact
```

---

# 45. Container Tags vs Digests

Tag:

```text
fraud-serving:v31
```

human-friendly.

Digest:

```text
sha256:...
```

immutable identity.

Production deployment should resolve to digest.

---

# 46. Model Artifact Immutability

Same principle applies to:

```text
weights

tokenizer

model config
```

Do not mutate:

```text
model:v31
```

in place.

---

# 47. Dataset Immutability

Training run should reference:

```text
dataset snapshot
```

not:

```text
latest dataset
```

---

# 48. Feature Definition Versioning

Model should bind to:

```text
fraud-feature-bundle-v18
```

not mutable feature names with changing semantics.

---

# 49. Prompt Versioning

Production prompt is code.

Version:

```text
system prompt

few-shot examples

tool instructions

response schema
```

---

# 50. RAG Release Unit

RAG behavior depends on:

```text
LLM

prompt

embedding model

chunker

retrieval config

reranker

index snapshot

document corpus

access policy
```

A meaningful RAG release must capture all of them.

---

# 51. Agent Release Unit

Agent behavior may depend on:

```text
base model

system prompt

tool registry

tool schemas

memory configuration

policy

workflow graph
```

Treat agent configuration as versioned software.

---

# 52. SBOM

Software Bill of Materials lists software components inside artifact.

Conceptually:

```text
Artifact
 |
 +-- Package A
 +-- Package B
 +-- Library C
```

---

# 53. Why SBOM Matters

When vulnerability discovered in library X:

```text
Which production artifacts contain X?
```

SBOM enables impact analysis.

---

# 54. Model BOM

ML systems may need analogous provenance:

```text
base model

adapter

tokenizer

runtime

training dataset

feature bundle
```

---

# 55. Artifact Provenance

Provenance answers:

```text
Who built it?

From which source?

Using which build system?

With which inputs?

When?

Under which policy?
```

---

# 56. Provenance Statement

Conceptually:

```text
artifact_digest
source_commit
builder_identity
build_definition
dependencies
timestamp
```

---

# 57. Trusted Builder

Production should trust:

```text
approved CI builder
```

not:

```text
developer laptop artifact
```

---

# 58. Signing

Artifact can be cryptographically signed.

Verifier checks:

```text
signature valid?

trusted signer?

expected provenance?
```

---

# 59. Signing Does Not Mean Secure

Signing proves:

```text
who approved/built artifact
```

It does not prove:

```text
artifact contains no vulnerability
```

Both security scans and provenance matter.

---

# 60. Signature Verification at Admission

Before workload runs:

```text
image signature valid?

artifact from approved builder?
```

If no:

```text
reject
```

for protected environments.

---

# 61. Provenance Policy

Example:

```text
Production images must:
- originate from approved repository
- be built by trusted CI
- pass critical vulnerability scan
- have valid signature
```

---

# 62. Supply-Chain Attack Surface

Possible compromise points:

```text
source repository

dependency registry

CI runner

build server

artifact registry

deployment system

runtime loader
```

---

# 63. Source Compromise

Attacker changes code.

Controls:

```text
review

branch protection

identity

audit
```

---

# 64. Dependency Compromise

Malicious dependency version enters build.

Controls:

```text
pinning

approved mirrors

scanning

provenance
```

---

# 65. CI Compromise

Attacker changes pipeline/build output.

Controls:

```text
isolated builders

signed provenance

minimal credentials
```

---

# 66. Registry Compromise

Attacker replaces artifact/tag.

Controls:

```text
immutability

digest pinning

signature verification
```

---

# 67. Deployment Compromise

Attacker changes production manifest.

Controls:

```text
Git review

policy gates

signed release manifests

audit
```

---

# 68. Runtime Artifact Verification

Model loader may verify:

```text
digest

signature

approved source
```

before loading model.

---

# 69. Vulnerability Scanning

Scan:

```text
OS packages

language packages

container layers
```

before promotion.

---

# 70. Vulnerability Severity Is Not Enough

A CVE may be:

```text
critical
```

but unreachable in your runtime.

Or:

```text
medium
```

but exposed on public endpoint.

Risk assessment needs context.

---

# 71. Vulnerability Gate

Example:

```text
block known exploitable critical vulnerabilities
```

Allow exception only through controlled waiver.

---

# 72. Security Waiver

A waiver should record:

```text
owner

reason

scope

expiration

mitigation
```

Waivers should expire automatically.

---

# 73. Static Application Security Testing

Analyze source code without executing.

Can find:

```text
unsafe functions

injection patterns

security mistakes
```

---

# 74. Secret Scanning

Detect:

```text
API keys

tokens

private keys
```

before merge.

---

# 75. Infrastructure-as-Code Scanning

Check:

```text
public buckets

open security groups

privileged workloads

unencrypted storage
```

in CI.

---

# 76. Policy-as-Code

Release rules can be executable policy.

Example:

```text
production deployment requires:
model approved
artifact signed
region allowed
security scan passed
```

---

# 77. Policy Evaluation in CI vs Admission

CI catches early.

Admission/runtime enforces final truth.

Use both:

```text
shift left
+
enforce at boundary
```

---

# 78. Never Trust CI Alone for Production Enforcement

CI could be bypassed.

Production environment should independently enforce critical policy.

---

# 79. Release Manifest

Define exact release composition:

```yaml
release:
  applicationImage: sha256:...
  modelArtifact: sha256:...
  featureBundle: fraud-features-v18
  policyBundle: policy-v11
  runtimeConfig: serving-v42
```

---

# 80. Release Manifest Digest

The release manifest itself can be hashed/signed.

Then production runs:

```text
Release R
```

as immutable configuration.

---

# 81. Promotion

Promotion means:

```text
same immutable artifact
```

moves to higher-trust environment.

It should not mean:

```text
rebuild from source again
```

---

# 82. Environment

Typical:

```text
Development

Integration

Staging

Production
```

But too many environments can slow delivery.

Use environments only when they represent meaningful validation boundaries.

---

# 83. Environment Parity

Staging should resemble production in:

```text
runtime

network policy

deployment mechanism

hardware class
```

where necessary.

Perfect scale parity is rarely economical.

---

# 84. Production-Like Does Not Mean Production-Sized

Staging may use:

```text
1 GPU
```

instead of:

```text
1000 GPUs
```

but should still validate:

```text
same runtime assumptions
```

---

# 85. Promotion Gate

A gate can check:

```text
tests passed

artifact signed

model evaluation passed

policy approval

performance benchmark

security scan
```

---

# 86. Automatic Gate

Example:

```text
accuracy >= baseline - tolerance
```

or:

```text
p99 <= 100 ms
```

---

# 87. Human Approval Gate

Useful for:

```text
high-risk production

irreversible change

regulatory review
```

But avoid unnecessary manual approvals everywhere.

---

# 88. Approval Fatigue

If reviewers approve hundreds of low-risk releases daily:

```text
approval becomes meaningless
```

Automate low-risk paths.

Reserve human judgment for genuine risk.

---

# 89. Risk-Based Release Tiers

Example:

```text
Tier 0
documentation
-> automatic

Tier 1
internal ML service
-> automated canary

Tier 2
customer-facing model
-> stronger evaluation

Tier 3
regulated decision model
-> formal approval
```

---

# 90. GitOps

Desired production state is stored declaratively in Git.

A reconciler ensures:

```text
cluster/runtime state
≈
Git desired state
```

---

# 91. GitOps Flow

```text
Change Request
     |
     v
Pull Request
     |
     v
Review + CI
     |
     v
Merge
     |
     v
GitOps Controller
     |
     v
Environment
```

---

# 92. GitOps Benefits

```text
audit trail

review

rollback

declarative state

drift detection
```

---

# 93. GitOps Is Not Just YAML

The important principles are:

```text
declarative desired state

versioned source

automated reconciliation

controlled promotion
```

---

# 94. GitOps Repository Design

Possible:

```text
application repos

platform config repo

environment config repo
```

Avoid one repository becoming impossible to manage.

---

# 95. Monorepo vs Multi-Repo

Monorepo advantages:

```text
atomic cross-component change

discoverability
```

Disadvantages:

```text
scale

permissions

CI complexity
```

Multi-repo advantages:

```text
ownership

independent lifecycle
```

Disadvantages:

```text
cross-repo coordination
```

No universal answer.

---

# 96. Environment Branches

Pattern:

```text
dev branch

staging branch

prod branch
```

can create merge drift.

Often stronger:

```text
one mainline
+
environment-specific overlays/refs
```

---

# 97. Promotion PR

Production promotion changes only:

```text
artifact digest
```

or:

```text
release manifest reference
```

Example:

```text
release-41 -> release-42
```

---

# 98. Why Small Promotion Diffs Matter

Reviewer should see:

```text
exact change
```

not:

```text
10,000 generated YAML lines
```

---

# 99. Configuration as Code

Store:

```text
replica limits

feature flags

routing weights

runtime settings
```

under review/versioning.

---

# 100. Secret Values Should Not Live in Git

Store:

```text
secret references
```

not plaintext secrets.

---

# 101. Secret Rotation

Release system should not require full application rebuild to rotate secret.

Secrets and artifacts have separate lifecycles.

---

# 102. Configuration Drift

Manual production edits create:

```text
Git says A

production says B
```

GitOps reconciler can detect/repair.

---

# 103. Intentional Emergency Change

During incident, direct change may be necessary.

Record:

```text
who

why

what

expiry
```

then reconcile back into source control.

---

# 104. Break-Glass Change

Should be:

```text
rare

audited

time-bounded

reviewed afterward
```

---

# 105. Progressive Delivery

Instead of moving:

```text
0% -> 100%
```

immediately, gradually increase exposure.

---

# 106. Canary

Example:

```text
1%
5%
25%
50%
100%
```

with health checks between steps.

---

# 107. Canary Is a Risk-Control Algorithm

At each step:

```text
observe candidate
compare baseline
decide continue/rollback
```

---

# 108. Canary Metrics

Software:

```text
errors

latency

resource usage
```

ML:

```text
prediction distribution

quality proxy

business outcome

fairness/safety metrics
```

---

# 109. Canary Window

Too short:

```text
not enough data
```

Too long:

```text
slow delivery
```

Choose based on:

```text
traffic

signal delay

risk
```

---

# 110. Delayed Labels

Model quality may only be known:

```text
hours/days later
```

Canary cannot rely only on immediate ground-truth metrics.

Use:

```text
proxy metrics

shadow comparison

business guardrails
```

---

# 111. Shadow Release

Candidate receives mirrored traffic.

Does not affect user response.

Useful for:

```text
performance

prediction comparison

resource sizing
```

---

# 112. Shadow Does Not Validate User Outcome

Because candidate response is not used.

It validates:

```text
behavior under real inputs
```

not full product effect.

---

# 113. Blue/Green

Maintain:

```text
Blue = current

Green = candidate
```

Switch routing.

Advantages:

```text
fast rollback

environment isolation
```

Costs:

```text
double capacity
```

---

# 114. Rolling Update

Replace replicas gradually.

Efficient.

But old/new versions coexist temporarily.

Need compatibility.

---

# 115. Compatibility During Rolling Deployment

New server may read/write data also accessed by old server.

Database/schema changes must support:

```text
mixed versions
```

---

# 116. A/B Experiment

Purpose:

```text
compare business outcomes
```

not simply release safety.

Canary and A/B should not be conflated.

---

# 117. Sticky Assignment

Same user should often remain in same experiment cohort.

Use stable hashing.

---

# 118. Traffic Splitting

Possible dimensions:

```text
percentage

tenant

region

user cohort

request attribute
```

---

# 119. Route Before Deploy?

No.

Candidate must be:

```text
loaded

ready

healthy
```

before traffic weight increases.

---

# 120. Readiness Gate

Promotion controller should verify:

```text
all required candidate replicas ready
```

before routing.

---

# 121. Rollback

A mature release system assumes:

```text
some releases will fail
```

Rollback should be:

```text
fast

safe

tested
```

---

# 122. Rollback Unit

Rollback release manifest:

```text
R42 -> R41
```

Better than trying to manually undo dozens of fields.

---

# 123. Rollback Is Easier With Immutable Artifacts

Old artifact still exists.

Switch references back.

---

# 124. Roll-Forward

Sometimes safer to:

```text
deploy fixed R43
```

than return to R41.

Especially after incompatible data migration.

---

# 125. Rollback Feasibility

Ask:

```text
Did schema change?

Did state mutate?

Did data format change?

Did irreversible external action occur?
```

Rollback may not always be possible.

---

# 126. Database Migration

One of the hardest release problems.

Bad pattern:

```text
deploy new app
and immediately make old schema unusable
```

---

# 127. Expand-Contract

Safer pattern:

```text
1. Add new schema.
2. Old code keeps working.
3. New code writes both/uses new.
4. Backfill.
5. Move readers.
6. Remove old later.
```

---

# 128. Backward Compatibility Window

During rolling deployment:

```text
old application
+
new application
```

must both function.

---

# 129. Database Migration Is a Distributed Protocol Upgrade

Multiple application versions coexist against one shared state.

Think:

```text
protocol compatibility
```

not merely:

```text
DDL
```

---

# 130. Online Schema Migration

Large table migration may take hours.

Do not lock production table for entire change if avoidable.

---

# 131. Migration Observability

Track:

```text
rows migrated

error count

replication lag

query latency

storage growth
```

---

# 132. Migration Rollback

If migration changes data irreversibly:

```text
rollback may require restore/reconciliation
```

Plan before launch.

---

# 133. Kubernetes CRD Migration

Changing CRD schema affects:

```text
stored objects

old controllers

new controllers

clients
```

---

# 134. CRD Version Evolution

Use compatible:

```text
v1alpha1
v1beta1
v1
```

with conversion when necessary.

---

# 135. Conversion Risk

Conversion webhook failure may affect:

```text
reads

writes

controllers
```

of CRD.

Keep conversion path highly reliable.

---

# 136. Operator Upgrade

New operator must tolerate existing resources.

Avoid requiring:

```text
delete and recreate every ML job
```

---

# 137. Controller Release

Controller changes can modify thousands of resources automatically.

Treat controller release as high-risk software.

---

# 138. Controller Canary

Deploy new controller against:

```text
small resource shard

test cell

shadow mode
```

before global rollout.

---

# 139. Shadow Controller

Candidate controller computes:

```text
planned actions
```

but does not apply.

Compare with production controller.

Excellent for:

```text
schedulers

autoscalers

policy engines
```

---

# 140. Scheduler Release

A scheduling policy change can alter:

```text
fairness

utilization

queue times

preemption
```

Test through simulation and shadow decisions.

---

# 141. GPU Driver Release

Traditional health check:

```text
node Ready?
```

is insufficient.

Need:

```text
training throughput

collective bandwidth

inference latency

GPU errors
```

performance canaries.

---

# 142. CUDA/Runtime Upgrade

May change:

```text
kernel performance

memory behavior

numerical output
```

Validate both:

```text
performance

model correctness
```

---

# 143. Model Runtime Engine Upgrade

New inference runtime might improve throughput but alter:

```text
numerics

token generation

batching behavior
```

Run golden and performance tests.

---

# 144. Quantization Release

A quantization change is both:

```text
performance change
```

and:

```text
model behavior change
```

Gate on:

```text
quality + latency + cost
```

---

# 145. Feature Release

Changing feature logic may require:

```text
historical backfill

online materialization

model compatibility
```

This is not just code deployment.

---

# 146. Feature Version Transition

Possible:

```text
feature-v18
-> shadow feature-v19
-> compare
-> backfill
-> deploy compatible model
-> promote
```

---

# 147. Data Pipeline Release

New pipeline version can corrupt enormous datasets.

Use:

```text
shadow output

quality checks

new namespace/version

atomic publication
```

---

# 148. Dataset Release

Dataset snapshot should be:

```text
immutable

validated

lineage-complete
```

before training consumption.

---

# 149. Training Code Release

Training code may only affect future model artifacts.

Therefore production serving release is indirect:

```text
training code
-> new model
-> evaluation
-> model promotion
```

---

# 150. Model Promotion Is Not Retraining

Training produces candidate.

Promotion changes lifecycle status:

```text
Candidate
-> Approved
-> Production eligible
```

Keep training and deployment separate.

---

# 151. Model Registry Stage

Possible:

```text
Experimental

Validated

Approved

Production

Retired
```

State machine should be governed.

---

# 152. Immutable Model Evidence

Promotion decision binds to exact model digest.

Not:

```text
model name = fraud-latest
```

---

# 153. Evaluation Artifact

Evaluation results should themselves be versioned.

Store:

```text
test dataset

metric code

metric values

environment

runtime
```

---

# 154. Baseline Comparison

Candidate should be compared against:

```text
current champion
```

not arbitrary threshold only.

---

# 155. Regression Gate

Example:

```text
accuracy degradation <= 0.2%

p99 improvement >= required

cost increase <= limit
```

---

# 156. Slice Evaluation

Global metric can hide degradation.

Evaluate important:

```text
regions

customer segments

device types

risk groups
```

as appropriate.

---

# 157. Statistical Uncertainty

Tiny metric difference may not be meaningful.

Release gates should consider:

```text
sample size

confidence

variance
```

where appropriate.

---

# 158. Model Performance Gate

Performance includes:

```text
latency

throughput

memory

startup time

cost
```

not just predictive quality.

---

# 159. Model Compatibility Gate

Check:

```text
feature versions

input schema

runtime version

tokenizer

hardware
```

---

# 160. Training Reproducibility Gate

Candidate should carry provenance:

```text
code commit

dataset snapshot

feature bundle

random seed/config

runtime image
```

---

# 161. LLM Evaluation Pipeline

Potential gates:

```text
task success

groundedness

toxicity/safety

format compliance

tool correctness

latency

tokens

cost
```

---

# 162. Prompt Regression Test

A prompt change can break:

```text
JSON output

tool selection

policy behavior
```

Treat prompt PR like code PR.

---

# 163. Golden Prompt Dataset

Maintain representative requests with expected constraints/outcomes.

---

# 164. LLM Non-Determinism

Exact output equality may be unrealistic.

Tests can assert:

```text
schema

semantic criteria

tool calls

safety constraints
```

instead.

---

# 165. RAG Evaluation

Test:

```text
retrieval recall

retrieval precision

grounded response

citation correctness

freshness

ACL enforcement
```

---

# 166. RAG Index Release

New index version should be built separately.

Then:

```text
validate
-> switch pointer
```

rather than update active index destructively.

---

# 167. Embedding Model Upgrade

Changing embedding model often requires:

```text
re-embedding corpus
```

because old/new vector spaces may not be compatible.

---

# 168. Dual-Index Migration

Build:

```text
Index A using embedding-v1

Index B using embedding-v2
```

shadow compare before switching.

---

# 169. Agent Tool Release

Changing tool schema can break agent behavior.

Need:

```text
backward compatibility

versioned tool contracts
```

---

# 170. Agent Policy Gate

Before release verify:

```text
allowed tools

scopes

max steps

max spend

confirmation requirements
```

---

# 171. Test Pyramid for ML Platform Services

```text
           E2E
          /   \
      Integration
       /       \
      Unit Tests
```

Most tests should be:

```text
fast + deterministic
```

---

# 172. Unit Tests

Validate:

```text
pure logic

state transitions

parsing

validation

scheduler scoring
```

---

# 173. Integration Tests

Validate:

```text
database

event bus

object storage

Kubernetes API

feature store
```

interaction.

---

# 174. Contract Tests

Ensure producer/consumer agree on:

```text
API schema

event schema

model signature

feature schema
```

---

# 175. End-to-End Tests

Validate full workflow:

```text
submit training
-> model produced
-> register
-> deploy
-> predict
```

Expensive, so keep focused.

---

# 176. Property-Based Tests

Excellent for:

```text
controllers

schedulers

resource allocation

serialization
```

Example invariant:

```text
allocated GPUs never exceed capacity
```

---

# 177. Fuzz Testing

Send malformed/randomized inputs.

Useful for:

```text
parsers

APIs

serialization

model input handlers
```

---

# 178. Concurrency Tests

Test:

```text
duplicate requests

simultaneous updates

race conditions
```

especially control-plane systems.

---

# 179. Failure Injection Tests

Simulate:

```text
DB unavailable

event duplicate

node crash

timeout

partial write
```

---

# 180. Deterministic Tests

Avoid relying on:

```text
wall-clock timing

random external data

uncontrolled network
```

for basic CI.

Flaky tests destroy trust.

---

# 181. Flaky Test Tax

If tests fail randomly:

```text
engineers rerun blindly
```

and eventually ignore failures.

Track flaky tests as production debt.

---

# 182. Quarantine Flaky Test

Temporary quarantine may keep pipeline usable.

But every quarantine needs:

```text
owner

expiry

fix tracking
```

---

# 183. ML Data Tests

Validate:

```text
schema

nulls

range

uniqueness

freshness

distribution
```

---

# 184. Feature Tests

Validate:

```text
definition semantics

point-in-time correctness

online/offline parity

missing values
```

---

# 185. Model API Contract Test

Send canonical inputs.

Ensure:

```text
accepted schema

output schema

error behavior
```

stable.

---

# 186. Model Golden Tests

For deterministic models:

```text
input X
-> output approximately Y
```

within tolerance.

---

# 187. Numerical Tolerance

GPU/runtime changes may produce small floating-point differences.

Test:

```text
acceptable tolerance
```

not exact bit equality unless required.

---

# 188. Performance Regression Test

Compare candidate:

```text
throughput

latency

memory
```

against baseline.

---

# 189. Performance Test Variance

Shared CI hardware creates noisy measurements.

Use:

```text
dedicated runners

multiple samples

statistical thresholds
```

for critical benchmarks.

---

# 190. GPU CI

Not every commit should consume expensive GPUs.

Use staged testing:

```text
CPU/unit
-> small GPU smoke
-> scheduled full benchmark
```

---

# 191. GPU Test Queue

Critical release validation should have priority over experimental benchmark jobs.

---

# 192. Hardware Matrix

Test only meaningful combinations.

Example:

```text
runtime x GPU-family x precision
```

Full combinatorial testing may be impossible.

---

# 193. Risk-Based Matrix

Prioritize:

```text
production hardware

largest traffic versions

new compatibility boundaries
```

---

# 194. Smoke Test

Immediately after deployment:

```text
process healthy?

model loads?

canonical prediction works?

dependencies reachable?
```

---

# 195. Synthetic Test

Continuously send known requests to production.

Detect:

```text
routing

certificate

feature-store

model-load
```

failures.

---

# 196. Production Verification

Deployment success is not:

```text
kubectl rollout completed
```

It is:

```text
new version healthy under real traffic
```

---

# 197. Release Observability

Every release should generate marker containing:

```text
release ID

artifact versions

time

actor

environment
```

---

# 198. Deployment Marker

Overlay release on dashboards.

Then incident at:

```text
14:05
```

can immediately show:

```text
release R42 at 14:02
```

---

# 199. Change Correlation

Track recent changes to:

```text
code

model

prompt

config

feature

infrastructure
```

during incident response.

---

# 200. DORA-Style Metrics

Useful software delivery signals include:

```text
deployment frequency

lead time

change failure rate

recovery time
```

Interpret carefully for ML.

---

# 201. Deployment Frequency

How often validated changes reach production.

Higher is not automatically better.

Goal:

```text
safe useful delivery
```

---

# 202. Lead Time

Time from change:

```text
commit/approval
```

to:

```text
production
```

Long lead times often indicate:

```text
slow tests

manual gates

queueing

environment bottlenecks
```

---

# 203. Change Failure Rate

Fraction of releases causing:

```text
rollback

incident

hotfix
```

---

# 204. Recovery Time

Time from release-related failure:

```text
to restored healthy service
```

---

# 205. ML Release Metrics

Additional:

```text
model promotion lead time

evaluation duration

GPU test queue time

dataset build time

canary duration

approval wait
```

---

# 206. Release Queue Time

A release may be technically ready but wait:

```text
6 hours for production window
```

Measure separately.

---

# 207. Approval Wait Time

If approval dominates delivery:

```text
automate evidence collection
```

rather than pressuring approvers to move faster blindly.

---

# 208. CI Cost

At large scale:

```text
build minutes

GPU benchmark hours

storage

artifact egress
```

become meaningful platform costs.

---

# 209. Test Selection

Run focused tests based on changed files.

But never skip critical global checks incorrectly.

---

# 210. Dependency Graph for CI

If:

```text
feature library A
```

changes, run downstream affected tests.

Dependency-aware CI can reduce cost significantly.

---

# 211. Build Cache

Reuse unchanged outputs.

Example:

```text
dependency layers
```

But cache key must include every relevant input.

---

# 212. Cache Poisoning

Untrusted branch should not be able to poison trusted production build cache.

Separate trust domains.

---

# 213. Remote Cache

Speeds large builds across runner fleet.

Need:

```text
integrity checks

tenant/trust isolation
```

---

# 214. Artifact Retention

Keep production artifacts long enough to support:

```text
rollback

audit

forensics
```

---

# 215. Temporary Build Artifact TTL

PR artifacts can expire quickly.

Production release artifacts may need much longer retention.

---

# 216. Artifact Garbage Collection

Before deleting:

```text
is any release still referencing artifact?
```

Use lineage/reference graph.

---

# 217. Model Retention

A retired model may still be required for:

```text
audit

reproduction

rollback
```

Retention follows governance, not only current traffic.

---

# 218. Release Graph

```text
Source
  |
  v
Build
  |
  v
Artifact
  |
  v
Release
  |
  v
Environment
```

For ML:

```text
Data ----+
Feature -+--> Model --> Release
Code ----+
```

---

# 219. Promotion Graph

```text
Candidate
   |
   v
Integration
   |
   v
Staging
   |
   v
Canary
   |
   v
Production
```

Each edge has gates.

---

# 220. Environment Promotion Should Be Monotonic in Trust

Moving higher means:

```text
more evidence

stronger policy

broader exposure
```

not simply copying files.

---

# 221. Release Policy

Example:

```text
Production requires:
- all mandatory CI tests
- signed image
- signed model
- approved dataset lineage
- model evaluation passed
- no blocking security issues
- rollout strategy defined
```

---

# 222. Release Risk Score

Could consider:

```text
changed components

traffic exposure

model risk tier

infrastructure scope

rollback difficulty
```

to choose pipeline path.

---

# 223. Change Classification

Example:

```text
prompt-only

model-only

runtime-only

infrastructure

database migration

security policy
```

Different change types need different tests.

---

# 224. Prompt-Only Change

May not require rebuilding runtime image.

But should run:

```text
LLM regression

safety

format tests
```

---

# 225. Model-Only Change

Need:

```text
quality

latency

compatibility

canary
```

Maybe no application rebuild.

---

# 226. Runtime-Only Change

Need:

```text
golden model correctness

performance

compatibility
```

across representative models.

---

# 227. Infrastructure Change

Need:

```text
plan validation

policy

canary environment/cell

rollback
```

---

# 228. Database Migration Change

Needs:

```text
expand-contract

mixed-version compatibility

backfill plan

rollback/roll-forward
```

---

# 229. Policy Change

Potentially affects:

```text
many deployments simultaneously
```

Release gradually.

---

# 230. Blast Radius Estimation

Before release ask:

```text
How many tenants?

How many clusters?

How many models?

How much traffic?
```

---

# 231. Progressive Infrastructure Rollout

Example:

```text
dev cluster
-> canary cell
-> 5% fleet
-> 25%
-> 50%
-> 100%
```

---

# 232. Fleet Release Waves

Useful for:

```text
GPU drivers

agents

operators

node images

CNI/CSI
```

---

# 233. Wave Health Gate

Do not proceed if:

```text
error rate rises

performance regresses

reconciliation backlog grows
```

---

# 234. Automatic Pause

Release controller should support:

```text
pause
```

without requiring full rollback immediately.

---

# 235. Resume

After investigation, continue from safe stage.

---

# 236. Abort

Stop future rollout and restore previous state where possible.

---

# 237. Kill Switch

For dangerous functionality:

```text
disable globally
```

without full software redeploy.

Use for:

```text
agent tool

model route

feature flag
```

---

# 238. Kill Switch Security

A kill switch is powerful.

Protect through:

```text
strong auth

audit

limited operators
```

---

# 239. Release Freeze

Temporary restriction during:

```text
major business event

incident

regulatory window
```

Allow emergency exceptions.

---

# 240. Freeze Abuse

Permanent freezes create:

```text
large batches of risky delayed changes
```

Release safety should not depend on avoiding change.

---

# 241. Deployment Windows

Useful where organizational/support constraints exist.

But automation and safe rollback may reduce need over time.

---

# 242. Environment-Specific Configuration

Avoid forking application source.

Use:

```text
same artifact

different controlled config
```

---

# 243. Configuration Validation

Before promotion validate:

```text
unknown fields

invalid ranges

missing secrets

incompatible model/runtime
```

---

# 244. Configuration Schema

Version config schema like API.

---

# 245. Default Value Risk

Changing a default can affect every resource that omitted field.

Treat default changes as behavioral changes.

---

# 246. Config Rollback

Versioned configuration enables:

```text
config-v42 -> config-v41
```

without rebuilding binary.

---

# 247. Dynamic Configuration

Some settings can update without restart.

Useful for:

```text
routing weights

rate limits

feature flags
```

---

# 248. Dynamic Config Risk

A bad update can affect entire fleet instantly.

Use:

```text
validation

versioning

progressive propagation
```

---

# 249. Configuration Distribution

Control plane may publish version:

```text
config generation 92
```

Regional agents apply progressively.

---

# 250. Last-Known-Good Config

Data plane should retain previous valid config.

If new config invalid:

```text
reject
```

and continue serving previous state.

---

# 251. CI/CD for Terraform-Style Infrastructure

Pipeline:

```text
format
-> validate
-> static policy
-> plan
-> review
-> apply
-> verify
```

---

# 252. Plan Is Evidence

Review should show:

```text
resources created

changed

destroyed
```

before apply.

---

# 253. Destructive Change Gate

If plan proposes:

```text
delete production database
```

require stronger confirmation/policy.

---

# 254. Infrastructure State Lock

Prevent concurrent conflicting applies.

---

# 255. Drift Detection

Scheduled plan can detect:

```text
manual infrastructure changes
```

---

# 256. Import Before Recreate

Existing manually created critical resource may need import into IaC state.

Never casually destroy/recreate.

---

# 257. Infrastructure Rollback Is Not Always Simple

Cloud APIs may not support perfect reversal.

Therefore:

```text
progressive rollout
```

is often safer than relying only on rollback.

---

# 258. Immutable Infrastructure

Prefer:

```text
replace node image
```

over:

```text
SSH and patch nodes
```

Improves consistency and rollback.

---

# 259. Node Image Release

Treat as versioned artifact.

Test:

```text
boot

drivers

GPU health

network

storage

performance
```

---

# 260. OS Patch Release

Security patch may change:

```text
kernel

driver interaction

network performance
```

Canary under realistic ML workloads.

---

# 261. CI/CD for Helm-Like Packages

Test:

```text
template rendering

schema

policy

upgrade

rollback

different values
```

---

# 262. Generated Manifest Validation

Render final manifests before apply.

Validate what environment actually receives.

---

# 263. Template Explosion

Overly complex templates become programming language.

Keep abstractions understandable.

---

# 264. CI/CD for Kubernetes Operators

Test:

```text
new install

upgrade

downgrade where supported

existing CRs

deletion/finalizers

leader failover
```

---

# 265. Operator Upgrade Compatibility

Existing CRs should continue reconciling across upgrade.

---

# 266. Finalizer Compatibility

Never remove controller logic required to clean old finalizers before migrating resources.

---

# 267. CRD Storage Migration

When changing stored version:

```text
convert existing objects
```

carefully.

---

# 268. CI/CD for Event Schemas

Producer change must be checked against consumers.

---

# 269. Backward-Compatible Event Change

Adding optional field generally safer.

---

# 270. Breaking Event Change

Changing field meaning/type may require:

```text
new event version/topic
```

or coordinated migration.

---

# 271. Consumer-Driven Contract Test

Consumers publish expectations.

Producer CI verifies compatibility.

---

# 272. CI/CD for APIs

Test:

```text
old client -> new server

new client -> old server
```

for supported compatibility windows.

---

# 273. API Deprecation Release

Before removal:

```text
measure usage

notify owners

provide migration

enforce deadline
```

---

# 274. Release Train

A scheduled group of changes moves together.

Useful for organizations requiring coordinated release windows.

---

# 275. Release Train Trade-Off

Pros:

```text
coordination

predictability
```

Cons:

```text
larger batches

slower feedback

bigger blast radius
```

---

# 276. Small Batch Principle

Smaller releases are easier to:

```text
understand

test

rollback

debug
```

---

# 277. Change Coupling

If ten services must deploy simultaneously:

```text
architecture may be too tightly coupled
```

Prefer backward-compatible protocols enabling independent rollout.

---

# 278. Expand-Contract Applies Beyond Databases

For APIs/events:

```text
add new capability

support old + new

migrate clients

remove old later
```

---

# 279. Compatibility Is a Release Feature

Backward compatibility increases:

```text
deployment independence

failure isolation

rollout flexibility
```

---

# 280. Release Dependency Graph

A release may depend on:

```text
new feature version
before
new model
before
new serving route
```

Control plane should encode dependencies explicitly.

---

# 281. Ordered Promotion

Example:

```text
1. Deploy feature-v19.
2. Verify freshness.
3. Deploy model-v42.
4. Shadow.
5. Increase traffic.
```

---

# 282. Dependency Failure

If feature-v19 fails:

```text
do not deploy model-v42
```

Gate automatically.

---

# 283. Transactional Release Is Rare

Global atomic release across:

```text
5 regions

100 clusters

multiple stores
```

is usually unrealistic.

Use:

```text
staged convergence
```

with compatible intermediate states.

---

# 284. Intermediate-State Safety

Every rollout stage should be valid.

This is a principal-level release design principle.

---

# 285. Example of Unsafe Intermediate State

New model requires feature-v19.

Traffic switched before feature-v19 available everywhere.

Result:

```text
production errors
```

---

# 286. Safe Strategy

First make:

```text
old + new features
```

available.

Then deploy:

```text
new model
```

Then retire old feature later.

---

# 287. Multi-Region Release

Do not deploy simultaneously everywhere by default.

Example:

```text
Region canary
-> 1 small region
-> 2 regions
-> global
```

---

# 288. Region Order

Consider:

```text
traffic size

risk

representativeness

local support
```

when selecting first region.

---

# 289. One Small Region Is Not Always Representative

Maybe it lacks:

```text
large tenants

GPU workload

special data
```

Use representative canary cells too.

---

# 290. Cell-Based Release

Roll candidate into:

```text
one control/serving cell
```

inside same region.

Limits blast radius while keeping realistic traffic.

---

# 291. Tenant Canary

Route internal or low-risk tenants first.

---

# 292. Hardware Canary

New GPU runtime should first run on:

```text
small hardware pool
```

before broad fleet.

---

# 293. Configuration Canary

Apply config to:

```text
1% replicas
```

even without binary change.

Configuration can break production too.

---

# 294. Policy Canary

Evaluate new policy in:

```text
shadow mode
```

to see what it would deny/allow before enforcement.

---

# 295. Shadow Policy

Log:

```text
would_allow

would_deny
```

without affecting request.

Excellent for safe policy migrations.

---

# 296. Release Controller

A dedicated controller can manage:

```text
stages

health gates

traffic

pause

rollback
```

---

# 297. Release State Machine

```text
PENDING
   |
   v
VALIDATING
   |
   v
DEPLOYING_CANARY
   |
   v
OBSERVING
   |
   +--> PROMOTING
   |       |
   |       v
   |     COMPLETE
   |
   +--> ROLLING_BACK
           |
           v
         FAILED
```

---

# 298. Release Status

Should expose:

```text
current stage

traffic percentage

health result

reason blocked

previous stable release
```

---

# 299. Promotion Decision

Can be:

```text
automatic
```

or:

```text
manual
```

depending on risk tier.

---

# 300. Release Timeout

No stage should wait forever.

Example:

```text
canary readiness deadline = 15 min
```

---

# 301. Rollback Deadline

Critical service may require:

```text
rollback completed < 5 min
```

Design architecture accordingly.

---

# 302. Release Lock

Prevent two conflicting production releases of same resource concurrently.

---

# 303. Serialized vs Parallel Releases

Different independent services can release in parallel.

Same service/model route may need serialized ownership.

---

# 304. Release Queues

High-risk environments may queue releases.

Track:

```text
oldest waiting release

approval state

dependency
```

---

# 305. CI/CD Failure — Green Pipeline, Broken Production

Possible because:

```text
tests incomplete

environment differs

traffic differs

dependency changed

data changed
```

This is why progressive delivery exists.

---

# 306. Failure — Staging Works, Production Fails

Investigate differences:

```text
config

traffic

hardware

network

data

permissions
```

Environment parity should be intentional.

---

# 307. Failure — New Model Quality Drops After One Day

Immediate canary metrics looked healthy.

Possible:

```text
delayed labels

segment shift

feedback loop
```

Model release monitoring must continue after deployment.

---

# 308. Failure — Rollback Fails

Potential causes:

```text
old image garbage-collected

old model deleted

database schema incompatible

feature removed
```

Test rollback readiness continuously.

---

# 309. Failure — CI Dependency Registry Down

Builds stop.

Mitigation:

```text
internal mirrors

cached approved dependencies
```

---

# 310. Failure — Artifact Registry Down

Existing workloads continue if images/artifacts cached.

New deploys may fail.

Design:

```text
regional mirrors

cache
```

for critical fleets.

---

# 311. Failure — Signing Service Down

Production releases may pause.

Existing production should continue.

This is acceptable if signing is control-plane-only dependency.

---

# 312. Failure — Vulnerability Scanner Down

Risk choice:

```text
fail closed for production promotion
```

or use:

```text
recent trusted scan evidence
```

for certain tiers.

Explicit policy required.

---

# 313. Failure — GitOps Controller Down

Existing workloads continue.

Desired changes stop reconciling.

This is a good control/data-plane separation.

---

# 314. Failure — Git Repository Down

Existing desired state should remain cached.

Do not delete production resources because Git temporarily unavailable.

---

# 315. Failure — Bad Git Commit Changes 10k Resources

Need:

```text
diff limits

blast-radius policy

staged rollout
```

---

# 316. Failure — Secret Rotated but App Does Not Reload

Secret lifecycle must define:

```text
reload

restart

dual credential window
```

---

# 317. Dual Credential Rotation

Safer:

```text
old + new accepted

deploy new credential

verify

disable old
```

---

# 318. Failure — Model Tag Was Mutated

Staging tested one model.

Production resolved same tag to another.

Solution:

```text
digest pinning
```

---

# 319. Failure — Feature Logic Updated In Place

Old model silently receives new semantics.

Solution:

```text
versioned features
```

---

# 320. Failure — Prompt Changed Outside Git

LLM behavior changes with no release record.

Solution:

```text
prompt configuration through governed release path
```

---

# 321. Failure — Index Updated Incrementally and Corrupted

Use:

```text
immutable index snapshot

shadow validation

atomic switch
```

---

# 322. Failure — Canary Looks Good Because Only Small Tenants Included

Canary sample not representative.

Use:

```text
stratified cohort

representative traffic
```

---

# 323. Failure — Performance Regression Hidden by Autoscaling

New version requires 2× replicas to meet SLO.

Latency appears healthy but cost doubles.

Canary should monitor:

```text
unit cost

resource efficiency
```

---

# 324. Failure — New Version Generates High-Cardinality Metrics

Observability costs explode.

Release tests should include telemetry behavior.

---

# 325. Failure — New Controller Causes Reconcile Storm

Canary control cell should measure:

```text
API calls

status writes

queue depth
```

before fleet rollout.

---

# 326. Failure — CNI Release Breaks Large Packets Only

Basic readiness works.

Distributed training fails.

Need workload-specific canaries.

---

# 327. Failure — GPU Driver Passes Health but Slows NCCL

Again:

```text
performance validation
```

is mandatory.

---

# 328. Release Anti-Pattern — Build in Production

Production should consume trusted immutable artifacts.

Do not compile from source on production host.

---

# 329. Anti-Pattern — Rebuild Every Environment

Breaks artifact identity.

---

# 330. Anti-Pattern — Mutable `latest`

Eliminates reproducibility.

---

# 331. Anti-Pattern — Manual SCP Deployment

No durable audit/provenance.

---

# 332. Anti-Pattern — One Giant CI Pipeline

Every repository change triggers:

```text
hours of unrelated tests
```

Use modular dependency-aware pipelines.

---

# 333. Anti-Pattern — Thousands of Tiny CI Jobs

Scheduler/orchestration overhead can dominate.

Balance parallelism.

---

# 334. Anti-Pattern — Shared Permanent CI Runner With Production Key

Huge supply-chain risk.

---

# 335. Anti-Pattern — Manual Security Checklist Only

Humans miss repetitive checks.

Automate policy.

---

# 336. Anti-Pattern — Sign Anything Built Anywhere

Signature trust is meaningless without trusted builder identity/provenance.

---

# 337. Anti-Pattern — SBOM Stored But Never Queried

Supply-chain metadata must support actual impact analysis.

---

# 338. Anti-Pattern — CI Says Passed, Therefore Production Is Safe

CI cannot reproduce every production condition.

Use progressive delivery.

---

# 339. Anti-Pattern — Canary Only HTTP Error Rate

ML behavior can be wrong while HTTP is perfect.

---

# 340. Anti-Pattern — Canary Only ML Accuracy

System could have:

```text
perfect accuracy

terrible p99

2× GPU cost
```

Need multidimensional gates.

---

# 341. Anti-Pattern — Manual Approval for Every Change

Creates bottlenecks and approval fatigue.

---

# 342. Anti-Pattern — No Approval for High-Risk Model

Automation should not erase governance requirements.

---

# 343. Anti-Pattern — In-Place Feature Change

Breaks reproducibility.

---

# 344. Anti-Pattern — In-Place Dataset Mutation

Historical model cannot be reproduced.

---

# 345. Anti-Pattern — Model Registry Stage Is Only a String

Promotion needs:

```text
policy

evidence

audit

state machine
```

not arbitrary field edit.

---

# 346. Anti-Pattern — Rollback Untested

An untested rollback is a hope, not a recovery strategy.

---

# 347. Anti-Pattern — Delete Old Artifact Immediately

Removes rollback capability.

---

# 348. Anti-Pattern — Production Database Migration First

Deploy compatibility before destructive schema removal.

---

# 349. Anti-Pattern — Cross-Service Big-Bang Deployment

Use protocol compatibility to decouple service releases.

---

# 350. Anti-Pattern — Global Fleet Upgrade Simultaneously

Blast radius too large.

---

# 351. Anti-Pattern — Config Change Bypasses Release System

Config is production behavior.

Treat it as releaseable artifact.

---

# 352. Anti-Pattern — Prompt Edits in Web UI Without Versioning

Creates untraceable behavioral changes.

---

# 353. Anti-Pattern — RAG Index `latest`

Same reproducibility problem as model `latest`.

---

# 354. Anti-Pattern — Agent Tool Schema Changes Without Versioning

Can silently break tool calls.

---

# 355. Anti-Pattern — Security Waiver With No Expiration

Temporary exception becomes permanent vulnerability.

---

Assume:

```text
10,000 engineers

2,000 ML teams

100,000 models

500 Kubernetes clusters

5 regions

regulated + non-regulated workloads
```

The organization needs one release platform.

# 366. Release Metadata Store

Tracks:

```yaml
  application: sha256:...
  model: sha256:...
```

Reconciles:

```text
desired release
```

against:

```text
model approved
```

```text
p99

prediction distribution
```

If healthy:

```text
1 -> 5 -> 25 -> 50 -> 100%
```

Each stage is explicit state.

# 372. Failure


```text
RolledBack
```

Evidence retained.

```text
-> Region A
-> Region B
-> Region C
```

Start with:

```text
representative but limited blast radius
```

not necessarily smallest possible environment.

# 381. Failure Domain in Release Systems

Different failures:

```text
CI failure

build failure

artifact publication failure

policy failure

deployment failure

runtime health failure

ML quality failure
```

Need separate statuses.

---

# 382. Do Not Collapse Every Failure Into "Pipeline Failed"

Users need precise reason.

---

# 383. Release SLO

Possible:

```text
99% of low-risk application releases
reach canary within 10 minutes
```

---

# 384. Promotion SLO

Model promotions may be slower because evaluation is expensive.

Track separately.

---

# 385. Rollback SLO

Critical serving:

```text
rollback initiation < 1 minute

traffic restoration < 5 minutes
```

example targets.

---

# 386. Release Platform Availability

If CD system is unavailable:

```text
existing production continues
```

New releases pause.

This is usually acceptable.

---

# 387. CI Availability

Temporary CI outage blocks new builds but should not affect running production.

---

# 388. Registry Availability

Existing running workloads may continue if cached.

New deployments may fail.

Use regional replication/cache for critical artifacts.

---

# 389. GitOps Controller Availability

Same principle:

```text
existing state remains
```

when controller unavailable.

---

# 390. Supply Chain Root of Trust

Ultimately production must trust:

```text
identity

source repository

builder

signing key

policy
```

These form the release trust chain.

---

# 391. Key Rotation

Signing keys must rotate.

Verifier should support:

```text
old valid keys

new keys
```

during transition.

---

# 392. Signing Key Compromise

Need ability to:

```text
revoke signer

identify affected artifacts

re-sign/rebuild trusted releases
```

Provenance graph enables blast-radius analysis.

---

# 393. Artifact Revocation

Sometimes an artifact must be globally disallowed.

Maintain:

```text
revocation list/policy
```

that deployment systems honor.

---

# 394. Emergency Model Revocation

If model found unsafe:

```text
stop new deployment

remove traffic

switch to last-known-good
```

without waiting for full normal release workflow.

---

# 395. Revocation vs Deletion

Do not immediately delete artifact.

You may need it for:

```text
audit

forensics
```

Mark unusable instead.

---

# 396. Release Governance

Govern:

```text
who can create release

who can approve

who can promote

who can override
```

---

# 397. Promotion Authority

Production promotion identity should be:

```text
narrowly scoped
```

not developer-wide permanent permission.

---

# 398. Short-Lived Deployment Credentials

CD system obtains temporary credentials for target environment.

---

# 399. Environment Boundary

Development credentials should never automatically imply:

```text
production credentials
```

---

# 400. Break-Glass Production Access

Emergency human access:

```text
JIT

time-limited

audited

strongly authenticated
```

---

# 401. Release Platform Observability

Metrics:

```text
CI queue time

build time

test failure rate

artifact publication latency

approval wait

canary duration

rollback count

change failure rate
```

---

# 402. Release Funnel

```text
Commits
  |
  v
CI Passed
  |
  v
Artifacts Built
  |
  v
Candidates
  |
  v
Approved
  |
  v
Canary
  |
  v
Production
```

Analyze drop-off/bottlenecks.

---

# 403. Common Bottleneck — Slow Integration Tests

Options:

```text
parallelize

reduce setup

reuse test environments safely

contract tests

test selection
```

---

# 404. Common Bottleneck — GPU Evaluation Queue

Options:

```text
prioritized release queue

smaller early test

scheduled full evaluation

hardware pool reservations
```

---

# 405. Common Bottleneck — Manual Approval

Automate evidence summary:

```text
quality

security

lineage

performance

diff
```

so reviewer focuses on judgment.

---

# 406. Common Bottleneck — Environment Drift

Use:

```text
declarative infra

immutable images

GitOps

conformance tests
```

---

# 407. Release Evidence Bundle

For high-risk change, generate one package containing:

```text
source diff

artifact provenance

SBOM

security results

model evaluation

data lineage

approvals

rollout plan
```

---

# 408. Evidence Graph

Approval should reference exact evidence IDs.

This allows:

```text
audit later
```

without reconstructing from scattered logs.

---

# 409. Release Diff

For ML, show:

```text
Model: v31 -> v32

Dataset: unchanged

Features: v18 -> v19

Prompt: unchanged

Runtime: shaA -> shaB

Traffic policy: unchanged
```

This is far better than generic "new release".

---

# 410. Semantic Diff

Raw YAML diff may be noisy.

Compute higher-level meaning:

```text
GPU replicas +4

context limit 8k -> 32k

model quantization FP16 -> INT8
```

---

# 411. Risk Diff

Highlight:

```text
new external network access

new sensitive dataset

new region

higher context limit

new tool permission
```

---

# 412. Release Review UX

Reviewers should see:

```text
what changed

why

risk

evidence

rollback
```

not hunt through ten systems.

---

# 413. Architect Scenario — Regulated Model Release

Model:

```text
credit-risk-v42
```

Release must include:

```text
dataset lineage

feature bundle

model card

evaluation

fairness analysis

approval

signed artifact
```

not model name.

unless policy explicitly allows equivalent rebuild.

Change:

```text
new scheduler scoring algorithm
```

Risk:

```text
all training placement changes
```

# 417. Controller Release Strategy

```text
offline simulation

historical replay

shadow scheduler

test cell

5% clusters

25%

100%
```

```text
queue wait

fairness

fragmentation

preemption

large-job completion
```

Flow:

```text
build node image

security scan

boot test

GPU diagnostic

training benchmark

inference benchmark

fleet waves
```

# 420. Driver Rollback

Keep previous node image available.

Replace affected nodes with old image if necessary.

Running jobs may need checkpoint/reschedule.

Need evaluate:

```text
cost
```

Cannot simply swap embedding model against old vectors.

Use:

```text
new corpus snapshot

new embeddings

new index

atomic route switch
```

Current version:

```text
R31
```

Candidate:

```text
R32
```

Strategy:

```text

-> Cell A1
-> Region A
-> Region B

```

---

# 424. Release Failure Matrix

| Failure                  | Expected behavior                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| CI outage                | new builds pause                                           |
| Artifact registry outage | running prod continues                                     |
| Git outage               | existing desired state continues                           |
| CD controller outage     | current release remains                                    |
| Canary failure           | promotion pauses/rolls back                                |
| Policy service outage    | high-risk promotions stop                                  |
| Observability outage     | risky automated promotion may pause                        |
| One region fails         | rollout to region pauses; current healthy regions continue |

---

# 425. Why Observability Is Part of CD

Automated promotion requires trustworthy health signals.

If metrics pipeline is broken:

```text
controller cannot know canary health
```

Safer response:

```text
pause
```

rather than blindly continue.

---

# 426. Health Signal Freshness

A canary metric from:

```text
20 minutes ago
```

should not approve current stage.

Release system needs:

```text
signal freshness
```

checks.

---

# 427. Missing Metric Semantics

Missing does not mean:

```text
zero errors
```

It may mean:

```text
telemetry broken
```

---

# 428. Canary Statistical Minimum

Do not promote from:

```text
3 requests
```

because zero failed.

Require sufficient:

```text
traffic/time/sample size
```

---

# 429. Low-Traffic Service Canary

If normal traffic is low:

```text
synthetic tests

shadow traffic

longer observation
```

may be required.

---

# 430. Automated Rollback Guardrail

Avoid flapping:

```text
promote
rollback
promote
rollback
```

Use hysteresis and terminal decision policy.

---

# 431. Rollback Safety Gate

Sometimes rollback also dangerous.

Example:

```text
database already migrated beyond old app compatibility
```

System should know:

```text
rollback not safe
```

and choose roll-forward.

---

# 432. Release Compatibility Matrix

Track:

```text
App v42 supports schema v18-v20

Model v31 requires features v17-v18

Agent v12 supports tool schema v3
```

---

# 433. Compatibility as Metadata

Do not rely on tribal knowledge.

Make machine-readable.

---

# 434. Release Planning Algorithm

Given desired candidate, controller can verify:

```text
all dependencies compatible?
```

before deployment.

---

# 435. Release Graph Cycle

If:

```text
A requires B2
B2 requires A2
```

careful migration planning needed.

Use expand-contract intermediate versions.

---

# 436. Principal-Level Release Question

Ask:

> What intermediate states are valid during the rollout?

This is often more important than final target state.

---

# 437. Another Principal Question

> Which artifact is authoritative if Git, registry metadata, and runtime disagree?

Define hierarchy.

Example:

```text
signed release manifest
```

may be authoritative desired state.

---

# 438. Another Principal Question

> Which systems must be available for current production to keep running?

Ideally not:

```text
CI

Git

model registry

approval service
```

on every request.

---

# 439. Another Principal Question

> What is the largest blast radius of one bad release?

Use:

```text
cells

waves

traffic percentages

tenant cohorts
```

to constrain it.

---

# 440. Another Principal Question

> Can the release platform prove that the artifact in production is the artifact that passed CI?

Need:

```text
digest

signature

provenance

deployment attestation
```

---

# 441. Deployment Attestation

Record:

```text
environment X
is running
release digest Y
```

at time T.

Useful for audit.

---

# 442. Runtime Verification

Periodically compare:

```text
desired signed release
```

vs:

```text
actual running digest
```

to detect drift.

---

# 443. Release Drift

If production Pod uses unexpected image:

```text
alert

quarantine

reconcile
```

depending on severity.

---
