```text
[ ] Durable workflow state

[ ] DAG validation

[ ] Task/attempt separation

[ ] Idempotency

[ ] At-least-once handling

[ ] Leases/heartbeats

[ ] Fencing

[ ] Retry policies

[ ] Timers

[ ] cancellation

[ ] cleanup

[ ] lineage

[ ] artifact references

[ ] multi-tenancy

[ ] HA
```

---

# 413. DAG Checklist

```text
[ ] Acyclic

[ ] dependencies explicit

[ ] fan-out bounded

[ ] branch semantics clear

[ ] failure semantics clear

[ ] skip semantics clear

[ ] dynamic expansion bounded
```

---

# 414. Task Execution Checklist

```text
[ ] Deterministic identity

[ ] Resource profile

[ ] Retry classification

[ ] Idempotency key

[ ] timeout

[ ] heartbeat

[ ] output commit protocol

[ ] cancellation

[ ] cleanup
```

---

# 415. Retry Checklist

```text
[ ] Retryable errors

[ ] max attempts

[ ] exponential backoff

[ ] jitter

[ ] retry budget

[ ] remaining deadline

[ ] checkpoint reuse

[ ] cost awareness
```

---

# 416. Backfill Checklist

```text
[ ] interval range

[ ] partitioning

[ ] concurrency limit

[ ] lower priority

[ ] dependency limits

[ ] checkpointing

[ ] lineage

[ ] progress reporting
```

---

# 417. Scheduler Checklist

```text
[ ] Sharded ownership

[ ] fairness

[ ] priorities

[ ] admission

[ ] queue backpressure

[ ] workload locality

[ ] recovery

[ ] no global leader bottleneck
```

---

# 418. Multi-Region Checklist

```text
[ ] Workflow home region

[ ] regional agents

[ ] artifact locality

[ ] data residency

[ ] partition behavior

[ ] fencing

[ ] DR ownership transfer

[ ] reconnect storm control
```

---

# 419. Architect Scenario — 50,000 Training Workflows per Day

Assume:

```text
50k workflows/day

20 tasks/workflow average
```

Tasks/day:

```text
1,000,000
```

Average:

```text
~11.6 tasks/sec
```

But scheduled bursts can be:

```text
thousands/sec
```

Architecture must be burst-aware.

---

# 420. Task Transition Volume

Suppose:

```text
6 durable transitions/task
```

Then:

```text
6 million state transitions/day
```

before heartbeats and retries.

Workflow DB must be designed accordingly.

---

# 421. High-Level Architecture

```text
                     WORKFLOW API
                         |
                         v
                  WORKFLOW METADATA DB
                         |
              +----------+----------+
              |                     |
              v                     v
        SCHEDULER SHARDS         TIMER SERVICE
              |
              v
         READY TASK QUEUES
              |
       +------+-------+
       |              |
       v              v
   CPU WORKERS     GPU LAUNCHERS
                      |
                      v
                ML PLATFORM API
                      |
                      v
                TRAINING CLUSTERS
```

---

# 422. Write Path

Workflow creation transaction:

```text
create run

create initial task state

write scheduling outbox

commit
```

---

# 423. Scheduler Path

```text
workflow event
->
scheduler shard
->
dependency evaluation
->
queue runnable task
```

---

# 424. Worker Path

```text
queue

claim attempt

launch execution

heartbeat

commit output

mark success

ack
```

---

# 425. Failure — Worker Dies

Lease expires.

Scheduler creates:

```text
new attempt
```

Old attempt result fenced.

---

# 426. Failure — Scheduler Dies

Another scheduler shard acquires workflow lease.

Reads durable state.

Continues.

---

# 427. Failure — Queue Message Lost

Reconciler detects:

```text
task = QUEUED
but no active delivery/execution
```

and republishes safely.

---

# 428. Failure — DB Commit Succeeds, Queue Publish Fails

Transactional outbox eventually publishes.

---

# 429. Failure — Queue Publish Succeeds Twice

Worker deduplicates by attempt identity.

---

# 430. Failure — Kubernetes Submission Times Out

Worker queries:

```text
deterministic external job ID
```

before creating another.

---

# 431. Failure — GPU Node Dies

Training operator marks task execution failed.

Workflow retries from checkpoint according to policy.

---

# 432. Failure — Artifact Publish Fails

Training computation may already be complete.

Retry:

```text
publish stage
```

not necessarily entire training.

This is why task decomposition matters.

---

# 433. Architect Scenario — Feature Backfill

Need recompute:

```text
365 days
×
100 feature groups
```

Potential:

```text
36,500 partitions
```

---

# 434. Naive Design

Launch all:

```text
36,500 tasks
```

immediately.

Potentially overwhelms:

```text
warehouse

feature store

scheduler
```

---

# 435. Better Design

```text
Backfill Controller
      |
      v
Partition Planner
      |
      v
Rate-Limited Ready Queue
      |
      v
Compute
```

Use:

```text
priority below fresh production

per-store concurrency limits
```

---

# 436. Dependency-Aware Throttling

If warehouse supports:

```text
500 concurrent queries
```

do not allow workflow system to launch:

```text
5000
```

Use downstream capacity tokens.

---

# 437. Resource Semaphore

Global logical semaphore:

```text
warehouse_query_slots = 400
```

Tasks acquire slot before running.

---

# 438. Semaphore Is Scheduling Capacity

Prefer scheduler admission token over worker sitting blocked while holding resources.

---

# 439. Hierarchical Limits

Example:

```text
global warehouse = 400

tenant max = 50

workflow max = 20
```

Protect both system and fairness.

---

# 440. Architect Scenario — Model Evaluation Workflow

```text
Candidate Model
      |
      +--> Accuracy Eval
      +--> Fairness Eval
      +--> Robustness Eval
      +--> Performance Eval
      +--> Security Eval
               |
               v
             Join
               |
               v
          Promotion Gate
```

---

# 441. Fan-Out Benefit

Independent evaluations run in parallel.

Workflow latency approximates:

```text
max(eval durations)
```

rather than sum.

---

# 442. Fail-Closed Evaluation

If mandatory evaluation fails due to infrastructure issue:

```text
do not interpret as model pass
```

Workflow should remain:

```text
evaluation incomplete
```

---

# 443. Architect Scenario — LLM Evaluation

Potential branches:

```text
quality

safety

tool correctness

RAG groundedness

cost

latency
```

Some use expensive external model calls.

Set:

```text
token/cost budget
```

per run.

---

# 444. Architect Scenario — Human Approval

After evaluations:

```text
WAITING_FOR_APPROVAL
```

No worker occupied.

Approval event resumes workflow.

---

# 445. Architect Scenario — Multi-Region Pipeline

Steps:

```text
EU dataset build

EU training

global evaluation metadata

EU deployment

US deployment
```

Policy may prevent raw EU data leaving region.

Only:

```text
model/evidence
```

moves globally.

---

# 446. Region-Constrained Task

Task metadata:

```text
allowed_regions = [EU]
```

Scheduler enforces.

---

# 447. Global vs Regional Workflow State

Global control may store:

```text
overall workflow
```

Regional systems manage:

```text
local task execution
```

Need clear ownership.

---

# 448. Architect Scenario — Million-Task DAG

Do not create one giant in-memory graph.

Use:

```text
partitioned task metadata

lazy expansion

incremental dependency tracking

sharded schedulers
```

---

# 449. Hierarchical DAG

```text
Workflow
   |
   +--> Partition Group 1
   |      +--> 10k tasks
   |
   +--> Partition Group 2
          +--> 10k tasks
```

Better operational locality.

---

# 450. Principal-Level Question

> Which state must be durable before a task can safely begin?

Answer should include:

```text
logical task identity

attempt identity

ownership/lease

inputs

retry state
```

---

# 451. Principal-Level Question

> What happens if the worker succeeds but the scheduler never hears about it?

Correct design:

```text
external result remains discoverable

worker/result update is idempotent

scheduler reconciles
```

---

# 452. Principal-Level Question

> What happens if a task runs twice?

You should be able to say:

```text
duplicate delivery is expected

logical side effect is idempotent/fenced

only one attempt becomes authoritative
```

---

# 453. Principal-Level Question

> What happens if the queue disappears?

Answer:

```text
rebuild pending work from durable workflow state
```

---

# 454. Principal-Level Question

> What happens if the scheduler database is unavailable?

Running tasks may continue.

Unsafe new scheduling stops.

Workers buffer/retry status where appropriate.

---

# 455. Principal-Level Question

> Why not put dependency evaluation inside workers?

Because:

```text
dependency state is orchestration control-plane concern
```

Workers should execute assigned work.

---

# 456. Principal-Level Question

> Why not model every training worker as a workflow task?

Because distributed training worker lifecycle belongs to:

```text
training scheduler/operator
```

Workflow engine should usually treat distributed training as one logical task.

---

# 457. Principal-Level Question

> What is the correct task granularity?

Large enough that:

```text
orchestration overhead is small
```

but small enough for:

```text
useful retry

parallelism

observability
```

---

129. How do approvals bind to workflow outputs?

130. Why is a workflow engine a Tier-0 service?

---

# 471. Principal-Level Questions

131. How would you design a workflow system processing 100M tasks/day?

132. Which state belongs in DB vs queue?

133. How do you guarantee no logical task is lost?

134. How do you handle duplicate execution safely?

135. How do you coordinate scheduler ownership without global locks?

136. How do you design for million-node dynamic DAGs?

137. How do you run global workflows with regional data residency?

138. How do you recover when queue and scheduler state disagree?

139. How do you determine ideal task granularity?

140. How would you prove workflow recovery after regional disaster?

# 472. Google-Style System Design Prompt

> Design a global ML workflow platform for 10,000 engineers, 50,000 workflows/day, millions of tasks/day, 10,000 GPUs, 500 clusters, and five regions.

Requirements:

```text
durable execution

DAG dependencies

dynamic fan-out

backfills

retries

GPU scheduling

regional data residency

fair multi-tenancy

workflow recovery

auditability
```

---

# 473. Step 1 — Functional Requirements

Support:

```text
create workflow

schedule

trigger by event

pause

resume

cancel

retry

backfill

inspect lineage
```

---

# 474. Step 2 — Nonfunctional Requirements

Define:

```text
scheduler availability

task-loss tolerance

queue latency

workflow throughput

RPO/RTO

tenant isolation
```

---

# 475. Step 3 — Data Model

Core entities:

```text
WorkflowDefinition

WorkflowRun

TaskInstance

TaskAttempt

Dependency

Timer

ArtifactReference
```

---

# 476. Step 4 — Source of Truth

Relational/workflow state store contains:

```text
logical workflow state
```

Task queues remain:

```text
delivery mechanism
```

not authoritative workflow truth.

---

# 477. Step 5 — Scheduler Shards

Partition workflows by:

```text
workflow_id
```

or cell ownership.

One active owner per workflow.

---

# 478. Step 6 — Transactional Scheduling

When task becomes ready:

```text
set task QUEUED

write queue outbox

commit
```

---

# 479. Step 7 — Queue

Partition by:

```text
region

resource type

priority
```

---

# 480. Step 8 — Workers

Workers:

```text
claim task

execute

heartbeat

publish immutable output

complete attempt
```

---

# 481. Step 9 — GPU Tasks

Workflow worker submits:

```text
TrainingJob
```

to ML compute platform.

It does not directly manage 1000 GPU Pods.

---

# 482. Step 10 — Timers

Use durable timer service for:

```text
retries

scheduled wakeups

approval deadlines

timeouts
```

---

# 483. Step 11 — Backfills

Separate low-priority queues.

Rate limit by downstream dependency.

---

# 484. Step 12 — Multi-Region

Global control owns workflow.

Regional agents launch local execution.

Sensitive tasks stay in allowed region.

---

# 485. Step 13 — DR

If queue lost:

```text
rebuild from state DB
```

If scheduler lost:

```text
reclaim workflow leases
```

If worker lost:

```text
lease expiry + retry
```

---

# 486. Step 14 — Observability

Track:

```text
scheduler latency

queue age

task attempts

retry rate

critical path

stuck runs

artifact publication
```

---

# 487. Failure Walkthrough — Scheduler Dies Mid-Decision

If decision not committed:

```text
new scheduler recomputes
```

If committed:

```text
outbox completes queue publication
```

---

# 488. Failure Walkthrough — Worker Dies After Output Written

New attempt checks:

```text
output manifest/idempotency record
```

and may adopt existing result rather than recompute.

---

# 489. Failure Walkthrough — Duplicate External Job

Deterministic external execution key allows:

```text
adoption

deduplication
```

---

# 490. Failure Walkthrough — Global Event Bus Outage

Workflow DB remains authoritative.

Scheduler can use:

```text
poll/reconcile degraded mode
```

or resume from durable state once event delivery returns.

---

# 491. Failure Walkthrough — Region Lost During Training

If checkpoint exists and policy allows:

```text
restart task in alternate region
```

Otherwise:

```text
wait/fail
```

according to residency and recovery requirements.

# 502. Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> The queue guarantees exactly once.

Ask:

```text
Exactly once delivery?

Exactly once execution?

Exactly once side effect?

Within what transactional boundary?
```

---

# 503. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> The worker timed out, so let's run it again.

Ask:

```text
Did the external job actually start?

Could the previous attempt still be running?

How is duplicate output fenced?
```

---

# 504. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> The scheduler crashed.

Ask:

```text
What durable state already exists?

Can another scheduler reconstruct the next decision?
```

---

# 505. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> We need a backfill for one year.

Ask:

```text
How many partitions?

How much compute?

Which downstream systems are capacity constrained?

What priority relative to current production?
```

---

# 506. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> Let's retry the entire training pipeline.

Ask:

```text
Which upstream outputs are still valid?

Can we recompute only the failed branch?
```

---

# 507. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> This workflow has one million tasks.

Ask:

```text
Must all tasks be materialized now?

Can the graph be hierarchical?

Can tasks be batched?

Is a DAG engine the correct abstraction?
```

---

# 508. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> We'll use a distributed lock so only one scheduler handles the job.

Ask:

```text
Can we shard workflow ownership?

What happens when the lock holder pauses?

Where is fencing enforced?
```

---

# 509. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> A task succeeded because the Kubernetes Job succeeded.

Ask:

```text
Was output published?

Was checksum validated?

Was metadata committed?

Is the business task actually complete?
```

# 510. What You Must Remember From Chapter 35

1. **Workflow orchestration is a distributed-state problem, not merely a cron or DAG-visualization problem.**

2. **A workflow engine must preserve execution intent across scheduler crashes, worker failures, duplicate delivery, retries, and infrastructure outages.**

3. **Workflow control state and task execution should remain separated: the scheduler coordinates; workers compute.**

4. **Workflow definitions and workflow runs are different objects; one describes reusable logic and the other one concrete execution.**

5. **Task identity and task-attempt identity must be separated because retries are first-class distributed-system events.**

6. **DAGs encode task dependencies, and cycle detection should reject impossible workflows before execution.**

7. **Topological ordering and indegree concepts provide the basis for efficient dependency scheduling.**

8. **Fan-out and fan-in make workflow parallelism explicit, but dynamic fan-out must always be bounded.**

9. **Workflow progress must be persisted durably so process memory is never the sole source of execution truth.**

10. **A robust scheduler should behave like a reconciler: derive required next actions from current durable workflow state.**

11. **Events should wake schedulers quickly, but lost events should not permanently block workflow progress.**

12. **Current workflow state and historical task-transition data often deserve separate storage paths.**

13. **Ready queues or incremental dependency tracking prevent schedulers from repeatedly scanning every blocked task.**

14. **Task queues should be treated as delivery infrastructure rather than the authoritative source of workflow intent.**

15. **At-least-once task delivery is a practical default; exactly-once logical effects come from transactions, idempotency, and fencing.**

16. **Acknowledging work before execution risks losing tasks, while acknowledging afterward creates duplicate-delivery scenarios that workers must tolerate.**

17. **Visibility timeouts and worker leases provide task failover but inevitably create the possibility of overlapping stale and replacement attempts.**

18. **Heartbeats should extend leases and report progress without flooding the primary workflow database.**

19. **A stale worker that continues after lease expiry is a fundamental distributed-systems case and must be handled through attempt generations or fencing.**

20. **Every retryable task should have a stable logical idempotency key.**

21. **Task outputs should be written to temporary locations and published atomically only after completion and validation.**

22. **Immutable artifact outputs dramatically simplify retries, lineage, caching, and partial recomputation.**

23. **Retry policies must classify transient vs permanent errors, set maximum attempts, use backoff and jitter, and respect total workflow deadlines.**

24. **Retry budgets are necessary because one failing downstream dependency can otherwise multiply platform workload dramatically.**

25. **Task retry and workflow retry are different operations; rerunning an entire workflow after one leaf failure wastes valid upstream work.**

26. **Partial recomputation is one of the highest-value optimizations in ML pipelines because expensive successful upstream artifacts can be reused.**

27. **Content-addressed task caching should include code, inputs, parameters, and relevant runtime versions in the cache key.**

28. **Only tasks whose outputs are sufficiently deterministic should be reused blindly from cache.**

29. **Backfills are first-class production workloads and should have explicit ranges, priorities, quotas, concurrency limits, and progress tracking.**

30. **Historical recomputation should usually not be allowed to violate freshness SLOs for current production data.**

31. **Workflow scheduling time and the data interval being processed are different concepts and must not be conflated.**

32. **Late-arriving data requires explicit watermark/reprocessing semantics rather than ad hoc reruns.**

33. **Blocking a worker for hours while waiting on an external condition is wasteful; durable waiting and timers should release compute capacity.**

34. **Long-running workflows require durable continuation because no process can safely remain alive for weeks or months.**

35. **Deterministic replay systems require external side effects, time, and randomness to be recorded rather than recomputed freely.**

36. **Long-running workflow instances must have defined compatibility semantics when workflow code changes.**

37. **Cancellation should stop new scheduling, signal current work, release resources, and run cleanup through durable state transitions.**

38. **Cleanup and compensation can fail and therefore deserve the same retry/idempotency rigor as primary work.**

39. **Task timeouts, queue-wait timeouts, heartbeat timeouts, and total workflow deadlines measure different failure modes.**

40. **Checkpoint intervals trade checkpoint overhead against expected lost compute after failure.**

41. **Specialized worker pools improve security and capacity isolation for GPU, database, and external-service task classes.**

42. **Task placement should account for data location, artifact caches, resource capability, and network cost when those dominate execution time.**

43. **Multi-tenant workflow scheduling needs fairness, quotas, borrowing, priorities, and aging—not strict priority alone.**

44. **Strict FIFO can produce head-of-line blocking when large jobs cannot fit, making backfilling and reservations useful scheduling techniques.**

45. **Deadline-aware scheduling requires estimates of remaining runtime and should account for uncertainty.**

46. **Spot/preemptible execution is valuable for checkpointable and lower-priority tasks but must be integrated with retry and checkpoint semantics.**

47. **Critical-path analysis reveals which tasks actually determine workflow completion time and therefore deserve optimization priority.**

48. **Queue wait, startup, execution, and output-commit times must be observed separately to identify the real bottleneck.**

49. **Scheduler ownership should be sharded across workflows instead of funneled through one global leader.**

50. **Single-writer ownership per workflow combined with horizontal ownership across workflows is a powerful scaling model.**

51. **Transactional outbox patterns prevent a scheduler from committing "task queued" state without eventually creating the corresponding queue message.**

52. **Queue messages can still be duplicated after outbox publication, so worker execution must remain idempotent.**

53. **Attempt-generation checks prevent stale task attempts from overwriting results produced by newer attempts.**

54. **Workflow engines should periodically reconcile database state, task queues, and external execution backends to repair partial failures.**

55. **Every externally launched job should have a deterministic identity so uncertain create calls can discover/adopt existing executions instead of creating duplicates.**

56. **A remote timeout means the outcome may be unknown—not necessarily that the operation failed.**

57. **Time-based, event-based, API-based, and data-arrival triggers all require explicit deduplication and overlap semantics.**

58. **Not every trigger should result in a distinct workflow; some desired-state workflows can safely coalesce intermediate changes.**

59. **Recurring workflows need an explicit policy for overlapping runs: allow, forbid, or replace/coalesce.**

60. **Publishing dataset partitions through immutable manifests/pointers provides strong exactly-once logical semantics under duplicate task execution.**

61. **Large artifacts should move through object/artifact storage, while the workflow database stores small references and lineage.**

62. **Cross-region workflow placement must account for data residency and data gravity rather than choosing compute solely by availability.**

63. **Regional execution agents allow local task execution to continue even when global workflow control connectivity is temporarily unavailable.**

64. **Global workflow failover requires ownership fencing so two regions cannot schedule the same workflow concurrently.**

65. **If a queue is lost but workflow state survives, queued work should be reconstructable from durable workflow state.**

66. **Recovery itself must be rate-limited because millions of workflows reconciling simultaneously can create a secondary outage.**

67. **Workflow history, task outputs, checkpoints, and audit data have different retention requirements and should not be deleted as one unit.**

68. **External resources created by workflows need ownership metadata and TTL/garbage-collection strategies to prevent orphaned infrastructure.**

69. **Per-task workload identity limits the blast radius of a compromised or buggy task.**

70. **Workflow lineage is one of the most important sources for reconstructing how datasets, features, evaluations, and models were produced.**

71. **Workflow cost should be attributable by task, run, team, and model so expensive retries and backfills are visible economically.**

72. **Human approval should be represented as durable waiting state rather than a blocked worker process.**

73. **Branch decisions should be persisted so replay does not reevaluate historical workflows against changed external state.**

74. **A generic workflow engine should orchestrate ML platform resources rather than duplicating Kubernetes scheduling or distributed-training operator logic.**

75. **Workflow scheduling, global resource scheduling, and local hardware scheduling are separate layers that answer separate questions.**

76. **Task granularity should make scheduling overhead small relative to useful work while preserving meaningful retry and parallelism boundaries.**

77. **Million-task graphs often require lazy expansion, hierarchy, batching, or subpartitioning rather than one massive flat in-memory DAG.**

78. **Workflow admission control should validate graph size, quota, security policy, and expected cost before allowing runaway work into the platform.**

79. **Backfills, retries, and recovery workloads should be lower priority than critical production repair unless business requirements say otherwise.**

80. **At Senior/Staff/Principal MLOps Architect level, workflow architecture means guaranteeing that distributed ML processes continue toward a correct durable outcome despite duplicate messages, worker crashes, scheduler restarts, partial external side effects, data lateness, resource scarcity, and regional failures.**

---


That is **workflow orchestration and distributed job-system design at Senior / Staff / Principal MLOps Architect depth**.

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 36 — High-Performance Model Serving and Inference Architecture: Dynamic Batching, Continuous Batching, Multi-Model Serving, KV Caches, Prefill/Decode, Quantization, Speculative Decoding, Routing, Autoscaling, and Global Inference

---

# 1. Why Inference Is Its Own Distributed-Systems Discipline

Training asks:

```text
How efficiently can we produce a model?
```

Inference asks:

```text
How reliably, quickly, and cheaply
can we execute that model
for real users
under unpredictable traffic?
```

Training can often tolerate:

```text
minutes of queueing
```

Interactive inference may have:

```text
50 ms
100 ms
500 ms
```

latency budgets.

That changes the entire architecture.

---

# 2. The Serving Optimization Problem

A production inference platform tries to optimize simultaneously:

```text
Latency

Throughput

Availability

Quality

Cost

Fairness
```

These objectives conflict.

Example:

```text
Larger batch
->
higher throughput

but often
->
higher queueing latency
```

---

# 3. The Core Serving Equation

Conceptually:

```text
Serving Efficiency
=
Useful Work
/
Allocated Compute
```

But useful work must satisfy:

```text
SLO
+
quality
+
reliability
```

A GPU at 99% utilization is not useful if:

```text
p99 latency violates the product SLO
```

---

# 4. Training vs Serving

Training:

```text
Throughput oriented

Large batches

Long jobs

Checkpointable

Often asynchronous
```

Serving:

```text
Latency sensitive

Bursty arrivals

Small unpredictable requests

Strict availability

Continuous operation
```

---

# 5. Main Inference Modes

```text
Batch inference

Online inference

Streaming inference

Interactive generative inference

Asynchronous inference
```

Each needs different architecture.

---

# 6. Batch Inference

Example:

```text
score 500 million customers overnight
```

Optimization priority:

```text
throughput
cost
```

Latency per individual record matters less.

---

# 7. Online Inference

Example:

```text
fraud decision during card payment
```

Priority:

```text
tail latency
availability
```

---

# 8. Streaming Inference

Example:

```text
continuous anomaly scoring
```

Architecture may resemble:

```text
stream processor
+
model runtime
```

with bounded event latency.

---

# 9. Generative Inference

LLMs introduce:

```text
variable context length

variable output length

long-lived requests

KV cache

token scheduling
```

The scheduler becomes far more complex.

---

# 10. Reference Request Path

```text
Client
  |
  v
Global Traffic Layer
  |
  v
Regional Gateway
  |
  v
Auth / Quota
  |
  v
Model Router
  |
  v
Admission Controller
  |
  v
Request Queue
  |
  v
Batch / Token Scheduler
  |
  v
Model Runtime
  |
  v
CPU / GPU
  |
  v
Postprocess
  |
  v
Response / Stream
```

---

# 11. Latency Decomposition

End-to-end latency:

```text
L_total =
L_network
+
L_gateway
+
L_queue
+
L_preprocess
+
L_model
+
L_postprocess
+
L_response
```

Architects should know which term dominates.

---

# 12. Queueing Is Often the Hidden p99 Killer

A model may execute in:

```text
20 ms
```

but the request waits:

```text
150 ms
```

in a saturated queue.

Optimization should target:

```text
queueing
```

not only faster kernels.

---

# 13. Little's Law

```text
L = λW
```

Where:

```text
L = average requests in system
λ = arrival rate
W = average time in system
```

Example:

```text
5000 RPS

average latency = 0.1 sec
```

Average in-flight:

```text
5000 × 0.1
=
500 requests
```

---

# 14. Utilization Near 100% Is Dangerous

As utilization approaches saturation:

```text
queueing delay rises nonlinearly
```

This is why inference fleets usually need headroom.

---

# 15. p50 vs p95 vs p99

p50:

```text
typical user
```

p99:

```text
worst 1%
```

Production systems often fail first at the tail.

---

# 16. Tail Amplification

If one product request fans out to:

```text
20 parallel services
```

the chance that at least one call experiences high tail latency increases.

---

# 17. SLO-Driven Design

Do not begin with:

```text
How many GPUs can we fit?
```

Begin with:

```text
What is the latency SLO?

What throughput?

What failure tolerance?

What traffic burst?
```

---

# 18. Model Server

A model server wraps a runtime with:

```text
network listener

request queue

batcher

preprocessing

model execution

postprocessing

metrics
```

---

# 19. Internal Model Server Architecture

```text
RPC Listener
    |
    v
Request Parser
    |
    v
Validation
    |
    v
Queue
    |
    v
Batch Scheduler
    |
    v
Runtime Worker
    |
    v
Accelerator
    |
    v
Response Serializer
```

---

# 20. Preprocessing

Examples:

```text
tokenization

normalization

image resize

feature assembly
```

Preprocessing may consume substantial CPU.

---

# 21. CPU Bottleneck Before GPU

A system may show:

```text
GPU utilization = 40%
```

because CPU tokenization cannot feed GPU fast enough.

The bottleneck is upstream.

---

# 22. Postprocessing

Examples:

```text
softmax

ranking

decoding

response formatting

business rules
```

May also dominate for small models.

---

# 23. CPU Serving

Best for:

```text
small tabular models

tree ensembles

lightweight neural networks

low throughput workloads
```

Benefits:

```text
cheap
simple
fast startup
```

---

# 24. CPU Concurrency

Potential models:

```text
one process per core

thread pool

async I/O

vectorized batch execution
```

Choice depends on runtime.

---

# 25. SIMD

CPU vector instructions allow processing multiple values per instruction.

Optimized numerical libraries can provide large speedups.

---

# 26. NUMA in CPU Serving

On multi-socket servers:

```text
CPU core
memory
NIC
```

locality matters.

Cross-NUMA memory access increases latency.

---

# 27. Process vs Thread Model

Threads:

```text
share memory
cheap communication
```

Processes:

```text
stronger isolation
higher memory cost
```

Runtime and language behavior matter.

---

# 28. GPU Serving

Best when:

```text
model computation large

parallelism high

throughput requirements high
```

But GPU serving introduces:

```text
HBM constraints

batch scheduling

kernel launch overhead

device transfer

model residency
```

---

# 29. GPU Request Path

```text
Client Request
    |
    v
CPU Preprocess
    |
    v
Pinned Host Buffer
    |
    v
Host -> GPU Transfer
    |
    v
GPU Kernels
    |
    v
GPU -> Host
    |
    v
Postprocess
```

---

# 30. HBM

GPU High Bandwidth Memory stores:

```text
model weights

activations

KV cache

temporary buffers
```

HBM is one of the most constrained resources in LLM serving.

---

# 31. GPU Memory Budget

Conceptually:

```text
HBM =
Weights
+
KV Cache
+
Activations
+
Runtime Workspace
+
Fragmentation
```

---

# 32. Model Weight Memory

Approximate:

```text
memory
=
parameter_count × bytes_per_parameter
```

Example:

```text
70B parameters

FP16 ≈ 2 bytes
```

≈:

```text
140 GB
```

before runtime overhead.

---

# 33. Why Quantization Matters

If weights become roughly:

```text
4 bits/parameter
```

weight footprint may drop dramatically.

But quality and kernel support matter.

---

# 34. Kernel Launch Overhead

For tiny GPU workloads:

```text
launch overhead
```

may dominate actual computation.

Batching amortizes this cost.

---

# 35. Static Batching

Requests are grouped before execution using predetermined batch.

Example:

```text
batch size = 32
```

Works well for batch/offline.

Less ideal for unpredictable interactive traffic.

---

# 36. Dynamic Batching

Requests arriving close together are combined dynamically.

Example:

```text
R1 arrives
R2 arrives 1 ms later
R3 arrives 2 ms later

batch = [R1,R2,R3]
```

---

# 37. Why Dynamic Batching Works

GPU executes:

```text
one larger operation
```

more efficiently than many tiny operations.

---

# 38. Dynamic Batch Parameters

Typical policy considers:

```text
maximum batch size

preferred batch sizes

maximum queue delay

shape compatibility
```

---

# 39. Maximum Queue Delay

The batcher may wait:

```text
2 ms
```

to collect more requests.

Trade:

```text
+ throughput

- latency
```

---

# 40. Throughput-Latency Curve

As batch size rises:

```text
throughput increases
```

until hardware saturation.

Latency may also rise because:

```text
queue wait
+
larger execution time
```

---

# 41. Batch Size Sweet Spot

Find the Pareto point:

```text
highest throughput
while meeting p99
```

Not simply maximum supported batch.

---

# 42. Shape Compatibility

Requests may differ by:

```text
image dimensions

sequence length

tensor shape
```

Batcher may only group compatible requests.

---

# 43. Padding

Variable-length sequences are padded to common length.

Example:

```text
100 tokens
100 tokens
100 tokens
4000 tokens
```

batch may effectively compute near:

```text
4 × 4000-token work
```

Huge waste.

---

# 44. Length Bucketing

Group similar lengths together:

```text
short

medium

long
```

to reduce padding.

---

# 45. Head-of-Line Blocking

One huge request waits at queue front.

Smaller requests behind may be delayed.

Queue discipline matters.

---

# 46. Multiple Queues

Separate:

```text
short requests

long requests
```

or:

```text
interactive

batch
```

to avoid interference.

---

# 47. Priority Queue

High-priority traffic may bypass lower-priority jobs.

But strict priority risks starvation.

---

# 48. Batching + Priority

A sophisticated scheduler tries to preserve:

```text
batch efficiency
```

while respecting:

```text
latency classes
```

---

# 49. Asynchronous Inference

Client submits:

```text
job
```

and later retrieves result.

Useful for:

```text
large media

slow models

batch scoring
```

---

# 50. Sync vs Async

Synchronous:

```text
simple client
low-latency expectation
```

Asynchronous:

```text
higher latency tolerance
better queue flexibility
```

---

# 51. Request Correlation

Async systems need:

```text
request_id
```

to retrieve result and trace execution.

---

# 52. Admission Control

Before accepting a request ask:

```text
Can we finish this within the SLO?
```

If not:

```text
reject

degrade

route elsewhere
```

instead of blindly queueing.

---

# 53. Unbounded Queue Is Dangerous

At overload:

```text
requests accumulate

latency rises

timeouts trigger retries

load increases further
```

This is overload collapse.

---

# 54. Queue Limit

Bound queue by:

```text
requests

tokens

bytes

estimated work
```

---

# 55. Backpressure

Signal upstream:

```text
slow down
```

through:

```text
429

503

flow control

reduced admission
```

---

# 56. Load Shedding

Prefer:

```text
reject 5%
```

while serving 95% within SLO

rather than:

```text
accept 100%
```

and violate SLO for everyone.

---

# 57. Retry-Aware Admission

If clients retry overloaded requests:

```text
rejection
```

can increase load.

Use:

```text
Retry-After

client backoff

retry budgets
```

---

# 58. Multi-Instance Serving

One GPU may run multiple runtime instances.

Useful when one model cannot fully utilize the GPU.

---

# 59. Instance Count

Too few:

```text
GPU underutilized
```

Too many:

```text
HBM pressure

context switching

cache contention
```

Benchmark.

---

# 60. Multi-Model Serving

One server/GPU hosts several models.

Advantages:

```text
higher utilization

less idle capacity
```

Challenges:

```text
memory

loading

eviction

isolation

routing
```

---

# 61. Resident Model

Weights already loaded in memory.

Request begins quickly.

---

# 62. Nonresident Model

Must be loaded first.

Cold load may take:

```text
seconds
or
minutes
```

for large models.

---

# 63. Model Residency Table

Track:

```text
model_id

GPU

memory_bytes

last_access

load_cost

pin_state

active_requests
```

---

# 64. Model Cache

GPU or host cache acts like weighted object cache.

Eviction should consider:

```text
size

frequency

reload cost

priority
```

---

# 65. Simple LRU Limitation

Model A:

```text
1 GB
```

Model B:

```text
80 GB
```

Treating both as one cache entry is naïve.

---

# 66. Weighted Eviction Score

Conceptually:

```text
eviction_score
=
low_frequency
+
old_age
+
large_size
-
high_reload_cost
```

Exact function depends on goals.

---

# 67. Pinning

Critical models may be:

```text
pinned
```

and not evicted.

---

# 68. Active-Reference Protection

Never evict a model while:

```text
active requests > 0
```

unless runtime explicitly supports safe migration.

---

# 69. Single-Flight Model Loading

If 100 requests arrive for cold model:

```text
one load
```

should occur.

Others wait.

Avoid 100 simultaneous loads.

---

# 70. Model Load State Machine

```text
ABSENT
  |
  v
LOADING
  |
  +--> READY
  |
  +--> FAILED
```

---

# 71. Model Repository

Stores:

```text
weights

tokenizer

config

runtime metadata
```

Use immutable versioned artifact identity.

---

# 72. Artifact Distribution

Large fleet should not download every model from one central origin.

Use:

```text
global origin

regional cache

node cache
```

---

# 73. Checksum

Every model artifact should verify:

```text
digest
```

before becoming READY.

---

# 74. Warmup

First inference may trigger:

```text
kernel compilation

memory allocation

runtime initialization

cache creation
```

Warmup before readiness.

---

# 75. Cold Start Decomposition

```text
Node provisioning
+
OS boot
+
driver init
+
container pull
+
model download
+
model load
+
JIT
+
warmup
```

Total can be large.

---

# 76. Scale-to-Zero

Good for:

```text
rare workloads
```

Bad for:

```text
strict low-latency SLO
```

if cold start is long.

---

# 77. Minimum Replicas

Maintain:

```text
baseline warm capacity
```

to absorb ordinary traffic immediately.

---

# 78. Warm Pools

Keep:

```text
ready nodes

ready GPUs

pre-pulled images
```

without necessarily loading every model.

---

# 79. Prewarming Popular Models

Forecast traffic and preload:

```text
likely hot models
```

before expected demand.

---

# 80. Inference Control Plane

Owns:

```text
desired deployment

model versions

replicas

routing

autoscaling policy
```

---

# 81. Inference Data Plane

Handles:

```text
actual prediction requests
```

Data plane should continue during temporary control-plane outage.

---

# 82. Declarative Serving Resource

Conceptually:

```yaml
model: fraud-v42
minReplicas: 20
maxReplicas: 200
latencySLO: 50ms
```

Controller reconciles toward desired deployment.

---

# 83. Gateway vs Model Server

Gateway:

```text
auth

quota

routing

policy
```

Model server:

```text
batching

runtime

accelerator execution
```

Keep responsibilities clear.

---

# 84. Version Resolution

Request may specify:

```text
model=fraud
```

Router resolves:

```text
fraud -> production version v42
```

using controlled version pointer.

---

# 85. Immutable Version Routing

Prefer:

```text
fraud:v42
```

for internal execution identity.

Mutable aliases are resolved before runtime.

---

# 86. Canary Routing

Traffic:

```text
v41 = 95%

v42 = 5%
```

Compare:

```text
errors

latency

quality

cost
```

---

# 87. Shadow Routing

Send mirrored request to candidate.

Do not use candidate response for user.

Excellent for:

```text
performance

prediction comparison
```

---

# 88. Champion-Challenger

Current champion:

```text
serves production
```

Challenger:

```text
evaluated in parallel
```

Promotion based on evidence.

---

# 89. A/B Testing

Purpose:

```text
business experiment
```

not just release safety.

Keep separate from canary.

---

# 90. Autoscaling

Goal:

```text
capacity follows demand
```

while avoiding:

```text
slow reaction

oscillation

cold-start failure
```

---

# 91. CPU Autoscaling Is Often Wrong for GPU Inference

CPU may stay low while:

```text
GPU queue grows
```

Use workload-relevant signals.

---

# 92. Useful Autoscaling Signals

```text
RPS

queue depth

queue age

concurrency

GPU utilization

GPU memory

tokens/sec

active sequences

KV cache pressure
```

---

# 93. Queue Depth

Good leading indicator.

But request sizes differ.

---

# 94. Queue Age

Often stronger:

```text
how long oldest request waits
```

Directly relates to SLO.

---

# 95. GPU Utilization

Useful but can be misleading.

High utilization may still have:

```text
excellent throughput
```

or:

```text
terrible queue latency
```

---

# 96. Memory Pressure

For LLMs:

```text
KV cache near full
```

may be the true capacity bottleneck.

---

# 97. Autoscaling Control Loop

```text
Measure
  |
  v
Estimate required capacity
  |
  v
Scale
  |
  v
Observe response
```

---

# 98. Reactive Scaling

Respond after traffic rises.

Simple.

Fails when:

```text
cold start > traffic spike duration
```

---

# 99. Predictive Scaling

Use:

```text
historical patterns

scheduled events

forecast
```

to prewarm.

---

# 100. Hybrid Scaling

```text
predict baseline
+
react to error
```

often strongest.

---

# 101. Scale-Up Formula

Conceptually:

```text
required_replicas
≈
peak_arrival_rate
/
safe_per_replica_throughput
```

then add:

```text
headroom
```

---

# 102. Capacity Example

Peak:

```text
100,000 RPS
```

safe replica:

```text
500 RPS
```

Base:

```text
200 replicas
```

With 30% headroom:

```text
~260 replicas
```

---

# 103. Safe Throughput

Do not use:

```text
maximum benchmark throughput
```

Use throughput at:

```text
target p99
```

---

# 104. Scale Hysteresis

Scale up quickly.

Scale down more slowly.

Avoid:

```text
replica flapping
```

---

# 105. Cooldown

After scaling:

```text
wait for system response
```

before another large adjustment.

---

# 106. Overshoot

Aggressive scale-up may create:

```text
artifact download storm

GPU allocation spike

registry pressure
```

Scale process itself needs rate limits.

---

# 107. Scale-Down Risk

Removing warm replicas can destroy:

```text
model cache

prefix cache

KV locality
```

Capacity is not purely stateless.

---

# 108. Cache-Aware Scale-Down

Prefer removing:

```text
cold

idle

low-value
```

replicas first.

---

# 109. LLM Serving Fundamentals

Autoregressive generation produces tokens sequentially:

```text
token 1

then token 2

then token 3
```

Each new token depends on previous context.

---

# 110. Two Major Phases

```text
Prefill

Decode
```

They have different compute characteristics.

---

# 111. Prefill

Processes prompt tokens.

Often:

```text
compute intensive

parallel across prompt positions
```

Long contexts can create large bursts.

---

# 112. Decode

Generates one/few new tokens per iteration.

Often:

```text
memory-bandwidth and KV-cache sensitive
```

and repeatedly executed.

---

# 113. Why Prefill and Decode Interfere

A huge prefill can occupy GPU and delay:

```text
decode tokens
```

for many active users.

That increases inter-token latency.

---

# 114. TTFT

Time To First Token:

```text
arrival
->
first generated token
```

Includes:

```text
queue

tokenization

prefill

first decode
```

---

# 115. TPOT

Time Per Output Token.

Represents:

```text
inter-token generation latency
```

after first token.

---

# 116. End-to-End Generation Latency

Approximate:

```text
TTFT
+
output_tokens × TPOT
```

More precisely decode behavior varies.

---

# 117. Tokens per Second

Important throughput metric.

Can measure:

```text
input tokens/sec

output tokens/sec

total tokens/sec
```

---

# 118. Request Count Is Misleading

Two requests:

```text
A: 100 input + 20 output

B: 100k input + 5k output
```

are not remotely equivalent.

---

# 119. Continuous Batching

Traditional dynamic batching processes full request batch together.

LLM continuous batching works at iteration/token level.

New requests can enter as others finish.

---

# 120. Iteration-Level Scheduler

At each decode step:

```text
choose active sequences

run one iteration

update state

admit new sequences
```

---

# 121. Benefit of Continuous Batching

Avoid waiting for all sequences in batch to complete.

Improves GPU utilization dramatically.

---

# 122. Sequence Completion Imbalance

Static batch:

```text
Request A ends after 20 tokens

Request B after 2000
```

GPU lanes for A may otherwise sit unused.

Continuous batching refills capacity.

---

# 123. KV Cache

Transformer attention reuses prior:

```text
keys

values
```

instead of recomputing all previous tokens at each decode step.

---

# 124. KV Cache Cost

KV memory grows roughly with:

```text
batch/sequence count

context length

number of layers

hidden/head dimensions

precision
```

---

# 125. Simplified KV Memory Intuition

Conceptually:

```text
KV bytes
∝
tokens
×
layers
×
KV heads
×
head dimension
×
bytes/value
×
2
```

The 2 represents:

```text
K + V
```

---

# 126. KV Cache Can Exceed Weight Memory Pressure

For many concurrent long sequences:

```text
KV
```

becomes the dominant dynamic memory consumer.

---

# 127. Admission Must Estimate KV

Before admitting request:

```text
prompt length

max output tokens

current KV usage
```

should influence decision.

---

# 128. Context Reservation

Naïve:

```text
reserve full max output KV
```

for every request.

Safe but wasteful.

---

# 129. Incremental KV Allocation

Allocate as tokens are generated.

Higher utilization.

Requires robust out-of-memory prevention.

---

# 130. Memory Fragmentation

Variable sequence lengths create:

```text
holes
```

in KV allocations.

A lot of free memory may exist but not in convenient contiguous layout.

---

# 131. Paged KV Concept

Manage KV cache in fixed-size blocks/pages.

Sequence maps logical tokens to physical blocks.

Benefits:

```text
less fragmentation

more flexible allocation
```

---

# 132. Paged Attention Concept

Attention kernels work with paged/noncontiguous KV representation.

This enables more efficient memory management.

---

# 133. Prefix Caching

If many requests share same prefix:

```text
system prompt

shared document context

conversation history prefix
```

cache precomputed KV for that prefix.

---

# 134. Prefix Cache Benefit

Avoid repeated prefill work.

Can improve:

```text
TTFT

GPU compute

cost
```

---

# 135. Prefix Cache Key

Must include all semantically relevant:

```text
model version

tokenizer

prompt tokens

adapter

runtime assumptions
```

---

# 136. Prefix Cache Security

Do not allow:

```text
tenant A
```

to reuse cache containing sensitive context from:

```text
tenant B
```

unless data is explicitly shareable.

---

# 137. Cache Tenant Isolation

Include:

```text
tenant/security domain
```

in cache key or isolation layer.

---

# 138. Chunked Prefill

Long prompts can be broken into chunks.

Allows scheduler to interleave:

```text
prefill chunks
```

with:

```text
decode iterations
```

---

# 139. Why Chunked Prefill Helps

Prevents one:

```text
100k-token prompt
```

from blocking all active decoders for too long.

---

# 140. Prefill Priority

Possible strategies:

```text
prefill first

decode first

balanced

deadline aware
```

---

# 141. Decode-First Bias

Improves:

```text
inter-token latency
```

for already active sessions.

But new requests may suffer TTFT.

---

# 142. Prefill-First Bias

Improves:

```text
new-request admission
```

but can harm ongoing streams.

---

# 143. Scheduler Trade-Off

Balance:

```text
TTFT
vs
TPOT
```

This is one of the central LLM-serving control problems.

---

# 144. Large Context Protection

One huge prompt should not monopolize GPU.

Possible:

```text
separate queue

context quota

chunked prefill

lower priority

admission limit
```

---

# 145. Max Sequence Length

Even if model supports:

```text
128k context
```

product may cap lower for:

```text
cost

latency

capacity
```

---

# 146. Token Admission

Rather than:

```text
max 100 requests
```

use:

```text
max estimated active token workload
```

---

# 147. Work Estimate

Could consider:

```text
prompt tokens

expected output tokens

model size

priority
```

---

# 148. Expected Output Length

Often unknown.

Use:

```text
historical distribution

client max_tokens

endpoint profile
```

---

# 149. Conservative Admission

Overestimate demand:

```text
safer SLO
lower utilization
```

---

# 150. Aggressive Admission

Underestimate:

```text
higher utilization
higher OOM/latency risk
```

---

# 151. Sequence Scheduler

Potential scheduling policies:

```text
FCFS

shortest predicted job

priority

deadline

token-aware fair queue
```

---

# 152. FCFS

Simple and predictable.

Bad for mixed:

```text
tiny

huge
```

requests.

---

# 153. Shortest-Job-Like Scheduling

Serve short requests first.

Can reduce average latency.

Risk:

```text
long request starvation
```

---

# 154. Aging

Increase priority of long-waiting requests.

Protects against starvation.

---

# 155. Deadline-Aware Scheduling

Prioritize based on:

```text
remaining SLO budget
```

---

# 156. Tenant Fairness

One tenant sending huge prompts should not consume entire GPU fleet.

---

# 157. Request-Based Fairness Is Weak for LLMs

100 short requests may consume less than:

```text
1 gigantic request
```

Fairness should consider:

```text
tokens

GPU time

KV memory
```

---

# 158. Token-Weighted Fairness

Tenant gets entitlement measured in:

```text
processed tokens/sec

GPU-seconds

KV allocation
```

depending on platform.

---

# 159. Streaming

LLM response often streams tokens to client.

Protocols may use:

```text
HTTP streaming

SSE

WebSocket

gRPC streaming
```

---

# 160. Streaming Backpressure

Client reads slowly.

Server must avoid buffering unlimited tokens.

---

# 161. Slow Client

Options:

```text
bounded buffer

pause generation if possible

disconnect

drop low-priority stream
```

---

# 162. Client Cancellation

If user closes connection:

```text
cancel generation
```

to avoid wasting GPU.

---

# 163. Cancellation Propagation

```text
Client disconnect
  |
  v
Gateway
  |
  v
Model router
  |
  v
Scheduler
  |
  v
Runtime sequence removed
```

---

# 164. Cancellation Delay

If GPU batch already executing:

```text
cancellation may take effect next scheduling boundary
```

---

# 165. Zombie Generation

Client gone.

Runtime keeps decoding.

Pure wasted tokens and GPU.

Monitor:

```text
cancel propagation latency
```

---

# 166. Tensor Parallelism

Split model tensors across GPUs.

Used when:

```text
model does not fit one GPU

or throughput requires multiple GPUs
```

---

# 167. Tensor Parallel Cost

Requires communication each layer/operation.

Benefits only if GPUs have:

```text
fast interconnect
```

---

# 168. Tensor Parallel Placement

Prefer GPUs within:

```text
same NVLink/NVSwitch domain
```

where possible.

---

# 169. Pipeline Parallelism

Split layers across stages.

Requests flow through stages.

---

# 170. Pipeline Bubble

If stages are uneven or microbatching poor:

```text
some GPUs idle
```

---

# 171. Data Parallel Serving

Multiple identical model replicas.

Requests distributed between them.

Simplest scale-out pattern.

---

# 172. Hybrid Parallelism

Large model may use:

```text
tensor parallel within replica
```

and:

```text
data-parallel replica groups across fleet
```

---

# 173. Replica Group

Example:

```text
8 GPUs
=
one LLM serving replica
```

Global router chooses among replica groups.

---

# 174. Replica-Level Capacity

Capacity should be measured per:

```text
replica group
```

not individual GPU if request requires all 8.

---

# 175. Topology Fragmentation

Fleet may have:

```text
80 free GPUs
```

but no contiguous:

```text
8-GPU high-speed group
```

for another replica.

---

# 176. Disaggregated Prefill/Decode

Separate hardware pools:

```text
prefill workers

decode workers
```

because their compute characteristics differ.

---

# 177. Disaggregation Benefit

Tune:

```text
prefill hardware/capacity
```

separately from:

```text
decode hardware/capacity
```

---

# 178. Disaggregation Cost

Need transfer of:

```text
KV state
```

between phases.

This can be expensive.

---

# 179. Network Requirement

Prefill/decode split only works if:

```text
KV transfer latency + bandwidth
```

is acceptable.

---

# 180. When Disaggregation Helps

Potentially with:

```text
very long prompts

high scale

very different prefill/decode bottlenecks
```

Not automatically beneficial.

---

# 181. Quantization

Represent weights/activations with lower precision.

Examples conceptually:

```text
FP16

BF16

FP8

INT8

INT4
```

---

# 182. Quantization Benefits

```text
less HBM

less memory bandwidth

potentially higher throughput
```

---

# 183. Quantization Costs

Potential:

```text
quality loss

calibration complexity

kernel restrictions

numerical instability
```

---

# 184. Weight-Only Quantization

Weights lower precision.

Activations may remain higher precision.

Common way to reduce weight memory.

---

# 185. Activation Quantization

Can further accelerate compute.

May require more careful calibration.

---

# 186. KV Quantization

Reduce precision of KV cache.

Can significantly increase concurrent sequence capacity.

Must validate quality.

---

# 187. Quantization Is a Product Decision

Evaluate:

```text
quality

latency

throughput

memory

cost
```

together.

---

# 188. Speculative Decoding

Use smaller/faster:

```text
draft model
```

to propose tokens.

Main model verifies them in groups.

---

# 189. Speculative Flow

```text
Draft proposes:
A B C D

Main model verifies

Accept:
A B C

Reject:
D
```

Multiple tokens may be committed per expensive main-model step.

---

# 190. Why It Can Help

If draft model predictions often agree:

```text
fewer main-model decode iterations
```

---

# 191. Acceptance Rate

A key metric.

Low acceptance:

```text
draft work wasted
```

---

# 192. Speculative Decoding Trade-Off

Extra:

```text
draft model compute

memory

complexity
```

versus reduced main model work.

---

# 193. When Speculation Helps

Usually when:

```text
draft is cheap

acceptance high

main decode expensive
```

---

# 194. When It Doesn't

If:

```text
draft is poor

main model already fast

network/runtime overhead high
```

benefit may disappear.

---

# 195. Distillation

Train smaller model to approximate larger model.

Can reduce inference cost dramatically.

---

# 196. Model Cascade

Try cheap model first.

Escalate hard requests to expensive model.

```text
small model
   |
confident?
   |
yes -> respond
no  -> large model
```

---

# 197. Cascade Benefit

Average cost falls if many requests are easy.

---

# 198. Cascade Risk

Need reliable:

```text
confidence/gating signal
```

Poor gating reduces quality.

---

# 199. Model Routing

Choose model based on:

```text
tenant

task

quality requirement

latency

cost
```

---

# 200. Quality-Cost Frontier

Different models occupy different points:

```text
cheap / lower quality

expensive / higher quality
```

Routing can optimize per request.

---

# 201. LoRA / Adapter Serving

Base model shared.

Tenant/task-specific adapters loaded dynamically.

---

# 202. Adapter Benefit

Avoid storing full duplicate model per customization.

---

# 203. Adapter Scheduling

Need manage:

```text
adapter residency

load time

tenant isolation

batch compatibility
```

---

# 204. Adapter Batching

Requests using different adapters may not batch efficiently depending on runtime.

Serving scheduler may cluster by adapter.

---

# 205. MoE Serving

Mixture-of-Experts models activate subset of experts per token.

Challenges:

```text
expert placement

network communication

load imbalance
```

---

# 206. Hot Experts

Some experts receive more tokens.

Can create:

```text
stragglers

network hotspots
```

---

# 207. Expert Parallelism

Experts distributed across GPUs/nodes.

All-to-all communication becomes critical.

---

# 208. RAG Serving Path

```text
User
  |
  v
Embedding
  |
  v
Retrieval
  |
  v
Rerank
  |
  v
Prompt Build
  |
  v
LLM
```

---

# 209. RAG Latency Budget

Example:

```text
Embedding       10 ms

Retrieval       20 ms

Rerank          25 ms

Prompt build     5 ms

TTFT            150 ms
```

Each stage matters.

---

# 210. RAG Top-K

Higher top-K:

```text
better recall
```

potentially.

But increases:

```text
retrieval cost

reranking cost

prompt tokens
```

---

# 211. Context Inflation

Adding excessive documents raises:

```text
prefill time

KV memory

token cost
```

RAG architecture directly affects serving capacity.

---

# 212. RAG Degradation Strategy

During overload:

```text
reduce top-K

skip expensive reranker

use smaller model
```

if product allows.

---

# 213. Agent Serving

Agent request may involve:

```text
LLM

tool calls

retrieval

loops

memory
```

End-to-end runtime may be seconds/minutes.

---

# 214. Agent Execution Is Not Simple Inference

Architecture may need:

```text
durable workflow

async execution

budgets

tool deadlines
```

---

# 215. Tool Timeout

Each tool call needs:

```text
deadline
```

within overall agent budget.

---

# 216. Agent Retry

Tool may be non-idempotent.

Do not automatically retry:

```text
send payment

send email

modify resource
```

without idempotency.

---

# 217. Agent Cost Budget

Limit:

```text
tokens

tool calls

wall-clock

external API spend
```

---

# 218. Serving SLOs

Possible:

```text
availability

p99 latency

TTFT

TPOT

model freshness

error rate

quality floor
```

---

# 219. LLM SLO Example

```text
99% TTFT < 1.5 sec

99% TPOT < 80 ms

99.9% request success

99.99% routing availability
```

Targets depend on product.

---

# 220. Quality SLO

Serving can be technically healthy but behaviorally wrong.

Monitor:

```text
model quality proxy

safety rate

business success
```

---

# 221. Model Freshness SLO

Example:

```text
approved model release
-> production everywhere
within 30 min
```

---

# 222. Observability Layers

Track:

```text
gateway

router

queue

batcher

runtime

GPU

model

tenant
```

---

# 223. RED Metrics

```text
Rate

Errors

Duration
```

Useful baseline.

---

# 224. Batching Metrics

```text
batch size distribution

queue delay

batch fill ratio

padding ratio
```

---

# 225. GPU Metrics

```text
SM utilization

HBM usage

memory bandwidth

power

temperature

errors
```

---

# 226. LLM Metrics

```text
TTFT

TPOT

tokens/sec

prompt tokens

generated tokens

active sequences

KV usage

prefix-cache hit
```

# 227. Model Load Metrics

```text
load latency

load failures

evictions

cache hit rate
```

```text
desired replicas

actual replicas

scale lag

pending capacity

cold-start time
```

---

# 229. Cardinality Risk

Do not put raw:

```text
user_id

request_id
```

as metrics labels.

Use logs/traces for high-cardinality identity.

---

# 230. Per-Model Metrics

At 100k models:

```text
model_id
```

itself may create huge cardinality.

Use:

```text
top models

aggregated classes

sampled diagnostics
```

---

# 231. Distributed Tracing

Useful for:

```text
gateway
-> router
-> model
-> vector store
```

latency decomposition.

---

# 232. Benchmarking

A serving benchmark must specify:

```text
hardware

model

precision

request distribution

concurrency

arrival pattern

warm/cold state
```

---

# 233. Closed-Loop Benchmark

Each client waits for response before sending next.

Problem:

```text
offered load decreases
when server slows
```

Can hide overload.

---

# 234. Open-Loop Benchmark

Requests arrive according to independent schedule.

Better for measuring:

```text
overload

queueing

tail latency
```

---

# 235. Concurrency Sweep

Test:

```text
1

2

4

8

16

...
```

concurrent requests.

Plot:

```text
throughput
vs
p99
```

---

# 236. Pareto Frontier

Choose configuration where no improvement in one objective is possible without worsening another.

Example:

```text
throughput vs latency
```

---

# 237. Warm Benchmark

Model already loaded.

Caches warm.

Measures steady-state performance.

---

# 238. Cold Benchmark

Includes:

```text
container start

model load

JIT
```

Useful for autoscaling design.

---

# 239. Realistic Request Distribution

Do not benchmark only:

```text
fixed 512-token prompt
```

if production includes:

```text
10 tokens to 100k tokens
```

Use real histograms.

---

# 240. Request Mix

Benchmark:

```text
short/long

small/large model

tenant classes

streaming/non-streaming
```

---

# 241. Tail Latency Under Saturation

The most important curve often appears around:

```text
70%
80%
90%
95%
```

safe capacity.

---

# 242. Performance Tuning Hierarchy

Optimize in this order:

```text
1. Model / algorithm

2. Request shaping

3. Batching

4. Runtime

5. Kernel

6. Memory

7. Routing

8. Capacity
```

Do not begin with exotic kernel tuning if architecture wastes 80% of work.

---

# 243. Model Optimization

Possible:

```text
distillation

pruning

quantization

smaller architecture
```

may yield larger gains than infrastructure changes.

---

# 244. Input Optimization

Reduce:

```text
unnecessary context

duplicate features

oversized images
```

before serving.

---

# 245. Runtime Optimization

Examples:

```text
kernel fusion

graph capture

memory pooling

optimized attention
```

---

# 246. Memory Pooling

Reuse buffers.

Avoid repeated allocate/free on hot path.

---

# 247. Kernel Fusion

Combine operations to reduce:

```text
memory traffic

launch overhead
```

---

# 248. CUDA Graph-Like Execution

Capture recurring operation sequence.

Reduce launch overhead for stable shapes.

---

# 249. Shape Polymorphism Cost

Highly variable tensor shapes may prevent certain optimizations.

Bucketing can help.

---

# 250. Classical ML Serving

A tabular model may need:

```text
feature fetch
+
CPU prediction
```

The feature store may dominate latency.

Do not use GPU just because platform has GPUs.

---

# 251. Tree Model Serving

Often CPU-efficient.

Can vectorize batches.

Memory locality matters.

---

# 252. Recommendation Serving

Often multi-stage:

```text
candidate generation

filtering

ranking

reranking
```

Different stages may use different models/hardware.

---

# 253. Recommender Latency

Parallelize candidate sources where possible.

Avoid serial dependency chain.

---

# 254. CV Serving

Large images create:

```text
network cost

decode cost

preprocess cost
```

GPU inference may not dominate.

---

# 255. CV Batching

Image shape bucketing reduces padding/resizing waste.

---

# 256. Failure Engineering

Inference systems must assume:

```text
model server crash

GPU failure

node failure

artifact outage

router failure

control-plane outage

region loss
```

---

# 257. Model Server Crash

Load balancer removes endpoint.

Requests:

```text
retry elsewhere
```

if safe and deadline allows.

---

# 258. GPU Failure

Could be:

```text
ECC error

driver reset

device lost
```

Node should be quarantined.

---

# 259. Driver Crash

May kill all models on one node.

This is a larger failure domain than one process.

---

# 260. Artifact Store Outage

Existing resident models should continue serving.

New model loads may fail.

This is why:

```text
data plane
```

should not depend on registry/object store per request.

---

# 261. Router Failure

Run:

```text
redundant stateless router replicas
```

with cached route tables.

---

# 262. Control Plane Failure

Existing data plane should continue with:

```text
last-known-good desired state
```

New deployments/autoscaling may degrade.

---

# 263. Region Loss

Global traffic manager shifts eligible traffic.

Destination regions need:

```text
capacity

model artifacts

data

policy permission
```

---

# 264. Failover Headroom

If every region runs at:

```text
95%
```

capacity, region failover is mostly fictional.

---

# 265. N+1 Capacity

Design to survive:

```text
one failure domain
```

while maintaining required SLO.

---

# 266. Graceful Degradation

Possible:

```text
smaller model

lower max output

lower top-K

disable reranking

lower priority admission

cached response
```

---

# 267. Fallback Model

If premium model unavailable:

```text
use smaller model
```

only if:

```text
quality/product policy allows
```

---

# 268. Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed

Safety-critical policy:

```text
fail closed
```

Optional enrichment:

```text
possibly fail open
```

depending on product.

---

# 269. Circuit Breaker

If a model/backend repeatedly fails:

```text
stop sending traffic briefly
```

to prevent cascading load.

---

# 270. Bulkhead

Separate capacity for:

```text
critical tenant

batch traffic

internal evaluation
```

so one class cannot consume everything.

---

# 271. Recovery Storm

1000 replicas restart and all download:

```text
50 GB model
```

Potential:

```text
50 TB transfer
```

Throttle recovery.

---

# 272. Staged Recovery

Priority:

```text
critical models first

popular models

low-priority tail models later
```

---

# 273. Prewarm Throttling

Limit concurrent:

```text
model loads

image pulls

GPU allocations
```

to protect infrastructure.

---

# 274. Multi-Region Serving

Each region should ideally be autonomous for:

```text
request routing

model execution

feature access
```

---

# 275. Global Routing

Choose region based on:

```text
latency

health

capacity

residency

model availability
```

---

# 276. Model Availability Map

Global router knows:

```text
which model versions
exist in which regions
```

---

# 277. Regional Model Pinning

Some regulated models may only run:

```text
specific regions
```

Routing must enforce.

---

# 278. Session Affinity Across Regions

For conversational systems, keeping session in same region may improve:

```text
cache locality

memory locality
```

But reduces failover flexibility.

---

# 279. Externalized Session State

Store durable conversation state outside a single serving Pod.

Allows replica replacement.

---

# 280. Regional Session State

Keep low-latency state regional.

Cross-region replication depends on failover requirements.

---

# 281. Global Serving Cells

```text
Global Edge
   |
   +--> Region A
   |      +--> Cell A1
   |      +--> Cell A2
   |
   +--> Region B
          +--> Cell B1
          +--> Cell B2
```

---

# 282. Cell Advantage

Limits impact of:

```text
bad rollout

driver issue

router bug

GPU pool failure
```

---

# 283. Cell Capacity

Route traffic to cells based on:

```text
health

available capacity

model availability
```

---

# 284. Traffic Spillover

If preferred cell full:

```text
spill
```

to another compatible cell.

Avoid overflow chain causing fleet-wide collapse.

---

# 285. Global Admission

For scarce premium models:

```text
global quota
```

may exist.

But per-request global coordination can add latency.

Use:

```text
regional entitlement allocation
```

where possible.

---

# 286. Cost per Prediction

Conceptually:

```text
inference infrastructure cost
/
successful predictions
```

---

# 287. Cost per Token

For LLM:

```text
GPU cost
+
CPU
+
network
+
storage
```

divided by:

```text
useful tokens
```

---

# 288. Useful Tokens

Not all generated tokens create user value.

Cancelled or discarded tokens:

```text
waste
```

Track separately.

---

# 289. Cost Drivers

```text
idle GPU

low batching

long context

large output

cold starts

cross-region traffic

cache misses
```

---

# 290. Idle Capacity vs SLO

Low utilization may be rational if it buys:

```text
burst tolerance

failover

latency
```

This is reliability capacity.

---

# 291. Shared vs Dedicated Serving

Shared fleet:

```text
better utilization
```

Dedicated fleet:

```text
better isolation

predictability
```

---

# 292. Tenant-Specific Dedicated Capacity

Use for:

```text
large customer

regulatory isolation

strict SLO
```

---

# 293. Shared Tail Models

Rarely used models can share:

```text
multi-model serving pool
```

to avoid one idle GPU per model.

---

# 294. Hot Models

Popular models may deserve:

```text
dedicated resident replicas
```

---

# 295. Hybrid Fleet

A common architecture:

```text
dedicated hot-model pools
+
shared long-tail pool
```

---

# 296. Model Placement

Global serving scheduler decides:

```text
where should model replicas live?
```

based on:

```text
traffic

GPU type

memory

locality

cost
```

---

# 297. Request Routing vs Model Placement

Placement is slower-timescale:

```text
minutes
```

Routing is fast-timescale:

```text
milliseconds
```

Different control loops.

---

# 298. Avoid Coupled Oscillation

If router shifts traffic every second and autoscaler reacts aggressively:

```text
system can oscillate
```

Control loops need different time constants.

---

# 299. Fast Loop

Request routing:

```text
milliseconds-seconds
```

---

# 300. Medium Loop

Replica autoscaling:

```text
seconds-minutes
```

---

# 301. Slow Loop

Fleet placement/capacity planning:

```text
minutes-hours
```

---

# 302. Control-Theory Principle

Fast loops react locally.

Slow loops adjust structural capacity.

Do not let every layer independently chase the same signal.

---

# 303. Benchmark Before Autoscaling

Autoscaler needs empirical:

```text
capacity curves
```

for each:

```text
model

hardware

precision

batching config
```

---

# 304. Capacity Profile

Example:

```text
model=v42
gpu=H
precision=FP8

safe throughput at p99 target:
12k tokens/sec
```

---

# 305. Hardware Heterogeneity

Same model may run differently on:

```text
GPU family A

GPU family B
```

Global scheduler needs per-profile performance data.

---

# 306. Performance per Dollar

Compare:

```text
throughput / cost
```

not just raw speed.

---

# 307. Performance per Watt

Important for:

```text
power-constrained data centers
```

---

# 308. Energy as Capacity Constraint

Large GPU cluster may hit:

```text
power/cooling limit
```

before physical rack slots.

---

# 309. Kubernetes Serving Pattern

Kubernetes can manage:

```text
replicas

health

placement

rollouts
```

while inference-specific runtime manages:

```text
batching

KV

token scheduling
```

---

# 310. Kubernetes Requests/Limits

Set CPU/memory requests accurately.

GPU allocation should reflect:

```text
replica topology
```

---

# 311. Startup Probe

Use for long:

```text
model load
```

so system doesn't kill container prematurely.

---

# 312. Readiness Probe

True only when:

```text
runtime can serve
```

---

# 313. Liveness Probe

Should detect:

```text
deadlocked/unrecoverable process
```

not temporary dependency slowness.

---

# 314. Graceful Shutdown

On termination:

```text
mark unready

stop new requests

drain streams

cancel after deadline

exit
```

---

# 315. PDB

Protect minimum serving capacity during voluntary maintenance.

---

# 316. Topology Spread

Spread independent replica groups across:

```text
nodes

zones

cells
```

---

# 317. Intra-Replica Packing

Within tensor-parallel group:

```text
pack tightly
```

Across groups:

```text
spread widely
```

This is a key placement principle.

---

# 318. Dedicated Inference Clusters

Advantages:

```text
predictable upgrades

capacity protection

security

network tuning
```

---

# 319. Shared Training + Serving Cluster

Potentially higher utilization.

Risk:

```text
training starves serving

driver upgrade coupling

blast radius
```

---

# 320. Serving Cluster Isolation

Tier-0 inference often deserves:

```text
dedicated cell/pool
```

even in shared organization.

---

# 321. Release Engineering

Build runtime once.

Promote same:

```text
image digest

model digest

config
```

through staging/canary/prod.

---

# 322. Model Rollout

```text
deploy candidate

warm

shadow

canary

expand traffic
```

---

# 323. Model Rollback

Keep previous:

```text
weights

runtime

config
```

available and warm enough for fast restoration where required.

---

# 324. Runtime Compatibility

Model may require:

```text
specific runtime version

custom kernel

tokenizer
```

Capture in release metadata.

---

# 325. Version Skew

During rollout:

```text
old router

new router

old server

new server
```

may coexist.

Protocols must remain compatible.

---

# 326. Serving Anti-Pattern — Scale on CPU Only

GPU queue can collapse while CPU looks healthy.

---

# 327. Anti-Pattern — Maximize GPU Utilization Blindly

Tail latency explodes near saturation.

---

# 328. Anti-Pattern — One Queue for All Request Sizes

Large requests create HoL blocking.

---

# 329. Anti-Pattern — Dynamic Batching Without Queue Deadline

Throughput wins while SLO silently dies.

---

# 330. Anti-Pattern — Batch by Request Count Only

Variable sequence lengths cause massive padding waste.

---

# 331. Anti-Pattern — One GPU per Long-Tail Model

Huge idle cost.

---

# 332. Anti-Pattern — Multi-Model Serving Without Memory Accounting

Runtime OOM and eviction storms.

---

# 333. Anti-Pattern — LRU Eviction Ignoring Model Size

Large model reload cost ignored.

---

# 334. Anti-Pattern — Multiple Requests Trigger Same Cold Model Load

Use single-flight.

---

# 335. Anti-Pattern — Readiness Before Model Warmup

First users pay cold-start penalty or see failures.

---

# 336. Anti-Pattern — Scale-to-Zero for Strict SLO

Cold start makes target impossible.

---

# 337. Anti-Pattern — Autoscale on Average GPU Utilization

Misses:

```text
queue age

KV pressure

burst
```

---

# 338. Anti-Pattern — LLM Routing by Request Count

Tokens determine work.

---

# 339. Anti-Pattern — Reserve Maximum Context for Every LLM Request

Safe but wastes enormous KV capacity.

---

# 340. Anti-Pattern — No Large-Context Isolation

One request hurts every active stream.

---

# 341. Anti-Pattern — Prefix Cache Without Tenant Isolation

Potential information leak.

---

# 342. Anti-Pattern — Decode Scheduler Ignores TTFT

Existing users are fast while new users wait forever.

---

# 343. Anti-Pattern — Prefill Scheduler Ignores TPOT

New users start fast while active streams stutter.

---

# 344. Anti-Pattern — Tensor Parallel Across Slow Network

Communication dominates computation.

---

# 345. Anti-Pattern — Disaggregated Prefill/Decode Without KV Transfer Math

Network becomes bottleneck.

---

# 346. Anti-Pattern — Quantize Based Only on Memory

Quality regression may make optimization worthless.

---

# 347. Anti-Pattern — Speculative Decoding Without Acceptance Metrics

Draft model consumes compute without benefit.

---

# 348. Anti-Pattern — RAG top-K Unlimited

Context and latency explode.

---

# 349. Anti-Pattern — Ignore Client Cancellation

Zombie generation wastes GPU.

---

# 350. Anti-Pattern — Retry Long Generations Blindly

A nearly complete request may restart and double GPU cost.

---

# 351. Anti-Pattern — Region Failover Without Spare GPU Capacity

Routing exists, serving does not.

---

# 352. Anti-Pattern — Data Plane Reads Registry on Every Request

Control-plane outage becomes serving outage.

---

# 353. Anti-Pattern — All Regions Depend on One Central Router DB

Regional autonomy lost.

---

# 354. Anti-Pattern — Benchmark Fixed Synthetic Inputs Only

Results do not predict production.

---

# 355. Anti-Pattern — Closed-Loop Load Test Only

Can hide overload.

---

# 356. Anti-Pattern — Report Average Latency Only

Tail behavior remains invisible.

---

# 357. Anti-Pattern — Cost Excludes Failed/Cancelled Tokens

Understates true serving economics.

---

```text
50 replicas
```

```text
separate queue
```

# 386. Failure Walkthrough — Prefix Cache Leak

Fix:

```text
security-domain-aware cache key
```

# 387. Failure Walkthrough — Model Eviction Storm

```text
A evicted for B

B evicted for A

A reloaded

B reloaded
```

Use:

```text
admission

pinning

hysteresis

frequency-aware eviction
```

```text
warm headroom

predictive scaling
```

# 389. Failure Walkthrough — Scale-Up Artifact Storm

```text
pre-pull

staged scale
```

# 390. Failure Walkthrough — Regional Brownout

```text
reduce traffic gradually
```

without instantly overloading another region.

# 391. Failure Walkthrough — Router Stale Model Map

and route only to confirmed serving endpoints.

of waste.

Throughput worsens.

```text
speculative benefit < 0
```

and disable.
