# MLOps Architect Handbook

## From DevOps Engineer to Senior MLOps / ML Platform Architect

### Volume 1 — Foundations

# Chapter 39 — Kubernetes Operators and ML Platform Controllers: CRDs, Reconciliation, Informers, Work Queues, Finalizers, Admission, Scheduling Integration, and Production Operator Design

---

# 1. Why ML Platforms Need Operators

A basic Kubernetes deployment says:

```text
Run this container.
Keep N replicas alive.
```

A production ML platform needs higher-level semantics:

```text
Train this model.

Use 64 GPUs.

Wait until all workers can start together.

Retry from checkpoint on recoverable failure.

Register the resulting model.

Deploy it gradually.

Maintain feature compatibility.

Retire resources safely.
```

These are not ordinary Pod semantics.

They require:

```text
domain-specific APIs

state machines

controllers

reconciliation

policy
```

That is the purpose of ML operators.

---

# 2. The Core Operator Mental Model

An operator is:

```text
Domain API
+
Controller
+
Operational Knowledge
```

It converts high-level intent into lower-level Kubernetes resources and external actions.

Example:

```text
TrainingJob
    |
    v
Training Controller
    |
    +--> Pods
    +--> Services
    +--> ConfigMaps
    +--> PVCs
    +--> GPU reservations
```

---

# 3. Kubernetes Is a Desired-State System

The user declares:

```text
I want X.
```

The controller observes:

```text
What currently exists?
```

Then repeatedly tries to make:

```text
actual state
```

converge toward:

```text
desired state
```

---

# 4. Reconciliation

The core function conceptually is:

```text
reconcile(desired, observed)
    -> actions
```

It should be safe to run:

```text
once

twice

100 times
```

against the same logical state.

---

# 5. Operator Architecture

```text
                 KUBERNETES API SERVER
                         |
                         v
                    CUSTOM RESOURCE
                         |
                         v
                      WATCH
                         |
                         v
                    INFORMER CACHE
                         |
                         v
                     WORK QUEUE
                         |
                         v
                     RECONCILER
                         |
          +--------------+--------------+
          |              |              |
          v              v              v
       PODS           SERVICES      EXTERNAL APIs
```

---

# 6. Custom Resource

A custom resource lets Kubernetes represent a domain object.

Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: ml.platform/v1
kind: TrainingJob
metadata:
  name: fraud-v42
spec:
  image: trainer@sha256:...
  workers: 64
  gpusPerWorker: 8
  checkpointUri: ...
```

---

# 7. CRD

A CustomResourceDefinition tells Kubernetes:

```text
this new resource type exists
```

and describes:

```text
schema

versions

validation

subresources
```

---

# 8. Why CRD Design Is API Design

Once thousands of teams create:

```text
TrainingJob
```

resources, the CRD becomes:

```text
a public platform contract
```

Changing it casually becomes expensive.

---

# 9. Start From User Intent

Bad CRD:

```yaml
spec:
  podTemplate:
    ...
```

for everything.

This exposes raw infrastructure.

Better:

```yaml
spec:
  workloadProfile: distributed-gpu-large
  workers: 64
  retryPolicy: checkpoint
```

The platform translates intent into infrastructure.

---

# 10. Abstraction Boundary

A good CRD hides:

```text
implementation details
```

but exposes:

```text
meaningful workload intent
```

---

# 11. Thin vs Thick Abstraction

Thin:

```text
mostly Kubernetes fields
```

Pros:

```text
flexible
```

Cons:

```text
low platform leverage
```

Thick:

```text
high-level ML semantics
```

Pros:

```text
strong golden path
policy
portability
```

Cons:

```text
more controller responsibility
```

---

# 12. CRD Example

```yaml
apiVersion: ml.company.io/v1
kind: ModelDeployment
metadata:
  name: fraud-prod
spec:
  modelRef: model://fraud/v42
  replicas:
    min: 10
    max: 100
  hardwareProfile: gpu-small
  rollout:
    strategy: canary
    canaryPercent: 5
```

---

# 13. metadata/spec/status

Canonical shape:

```text
metadata
spec
status
```

---

# 14. metadata

Contains Kubernetes-managed identity:

```text
name

namespace

uid

generation

resourceVersion

labels

annotations
```

---

# 15. spec

Represents:

```text
desired state
```

What the user wants.

---

# 16. status

Represents:

```text
observed state
```

What the controller knows about reality.

---

# 17. Never Put Controller-Owned Fields in spec

Bad:

```yaml
spec:
  podName: trainer-abc
  currentPhase: Running
```

These are observed/runtime state.

They belong in:

```text
status
```

---

# 18. Never Let Users Mutate Controller Status

Status should usually use the:

```text
/status
```

subresource.

This separates intent from observation.

---

# 19. generation

Whenever desired spec changes:

```text
metadata.generation
```

typically advances.

This helps controllers determine whether status reflects the newest spec.

---

# 20. observedGeneration

Controller can record:

```text
status.observedGeneration
```

Meaning:

```text
I have processed spec generation N.
```

---

# 21. Why observedGeneration Matters

Suppose:

```text
generation = 12
observedGeneration = 10
```

Then status may be stale relative to current user intent.

---

# 22. Resource Version

```text
resourceVersion
```

represents API object concurrency/version state.

Useful for:

```text
optimistic concurrency

watch continuation
```

Do not treat it as business version.

---

# 23. generation vs resourceVersion

generation:

```text
desired-spec evolution
```

resourceVersion:

```text
storage/API mutation version
```

They solve different problems.

---

# 24. Conditions

A robust status often uses conditions.

Example:

```text
Ready

Scheduled

Running

Succeeded

Degraded
```

---

# 25. Condition Structure

Conceptually:

```yaml
type: Ready
status: "False"
reason: WaitingForGPUs
message: "64 matching GPUs are not yet available"
observedGeneration: 12
```

---

# 26. Why Conditions Beat One Phase String

A single phase:

```text
Running
```

cannot express:

```text
Running = true
Degraded = true
CheckpointHealthy = false
```

Conditions allow multidimensional state.

---

# 27. Phase Still Has Value

A high-level lifecycle field can help:

```text
Pending

Running

Succeeded

Failed
```

But conditions provide richer diagnostics.

---

# 28. Status Should Be Bounded

Bad:

```text
status.logs = 10 MB
```

API server and etcd are not log storage.

Store:

```text
small summaries

references
```

---

# 29. High-Frequency Status Updates Are Dangerous

If 100k objects update every second:

```text
100k writes/sec
```

to Kubernetes control plane.

This can overwhelm:

```text
API server

etcd

watchers
```

---

# 30. Status Update Rule

Update when:

```text
meaningful state changes
```

not every heartbeat.

---

# 31. Controller Loop

Canonical model:

```text
watch object changes

enqueue resource key

reconcile key

requeue if necessary
```

---

# 32. Resource Key

Usually:

```text
namespace/name
```

not full object serialized into queue.

---

# 33. Why Queue Keys

By the time worker processes event:

```text
object may have changed again
```

The reconciler should fetch:

```text
latest desired state
```

---

# 34. Edge-Triggered vs Level-Triggered

Edge-triggered:

```text
event happened
```

Level-triggered:

```text
current state is X
```

Kubernetes controllers should primarily be:

```text
level-driven
```

---

# 35. Events Are Hints

A watch event says:

```text
you should reconcile
```

It should not be the only source of correctness.

---

# 36. Lost Event

If one event disappears:

```text
periodic resync/reconciliation
```

should still converge the system.

---

# 37. Idempotent Reconcile

Suppose desired deployment already exists.

Reconcile should detect:

```text
nothing to do
```

rather than create duplicate deployments.

---

# 38. Desired Child Naming

Use deterministic child names:

```text
trainingjob-123-worker-0
```

rather than random names on every reconcile.

---

# 39. Deterministic Identity

This converts:

```text
create
```

into:

```text
ensure exists
```

which is easier to make idempotent.

---

# 40. Reconcile Skeleton

Conceptually:

```text
1. Read resource.

2. If deleting:
      finalize.

3. Validate dependencies.

4. Observe children/external state.

5. Compute desired child state.

6. Apply changes.

7. Update status.

8. Requeue if needed.
```

---

# 41. Informer

An informer watches Kubernetes resources and maintains local cache.

Instead of every reconcile doing:

```text
API GET
```

controllers often read:

```text
local informer cache
```

---

# 42. Informer Architecture

```text
API Server
   |
   v
LIST + WATCH
   |
   v
Local Store
   |
   v
Event Handlers
   |
   v
Work Queue
```

---

# 43. Why Informers Matter

Without caches:

```text
thousands of controllers
```

could bombard API server with repeated GET/LIST calls.

---

# 44. List-Watch

Initial:

```text
LIST
```

obtains current objects.

Then:

```text
WATCH
```

streams future changes.

---

# 45. Watch Compaction

If controller falls too far behind:

```text
old resource versions may no longer be available
```

It must:

```text
re-list
```

and resume watch.

---

# 46. Relist Storm

If many controllers simultaneously lose watches:

```text
every controller lists millions of objects
```

API server may overload.

Use:

```text
jitter

shared informers

backoff

priority
```

---

# 47. Informer Cache Staleness

Cache may lag API server slightly.

Reconciler logic should tolerate:

```text
eventual observation
```

---

# 48. Direct Read When Strong Freshness Needed

Certain conflict-sensitive operations may need:

```text
uncached/direct API read
```

But use sparingly.

---

# 49. Shared Informer

Multiple controllers watching same resource type should avoid independent redundant watch streams where frameworks support sharing.

---

# 50. Work Queue

Decouples:

```text
event arrival
```

from:

```text
reconciliation execution
```

---

# 51. Queue Coalescing

If resource receives 100 updates rapidly:

```text
one key
```

can often represent the need:

```text
reconcile latest state
```

No need to process all 100 events individually.

---

# 52. Queue Deduplication

A resource already queued need not be queued repeatedly.

---

# 53. Rate-Limiting Queue

Failed resources should not immediately retry in tight loop.

Use:

```text
exponential backoff

jitter

max delay
```

---

# 54. Hot Loop

Bad reconciler:

```text
error
-> requeue immediately
-> error
-> requeue immediately
```

Can generate:

```text
thousands of API calls/sec
```

for one resource.

---

# 55. Requeue After

Useful for:

```text
poll external state in 30s
```

But prefer event-driven updates where available.

---

# 56. Polling External APIs

If external provider lacks watches:

```text
controller may poll
```

Need:

```text
bounded frequency

backoff

global rate limit
```

---

# 57. Per-Resource Backoff

One bad resource should not consume all controller workers.

---

# 58. Global External API Budget

Cloud API may allow:

```text
100 requests/sec
```

Controller fleet must coordinate within that limit.

---

# 59. Bulkhead

Separate queues/workers for:

```text
critical reconciliation

slow external APIs
```

so one dependency does not block everything.

---

# 60. Worker Concurrency

Controller often runs:

```text
N reconcile workers
```

Higher N:

```text
higher throughput
```

but also:

```text
more API concurrency

more external pressure
```

---

# 61. Concurrency Sizing

Estimate using:

```text
arrival rate

reconcile latency

dependency limits
```

Little's Law applies conceptually.

---

# 62. Reconcile Latency

If:

```text
100 reconciles/sec arrive
```

and each averages:

```text
0.2 sec
```

average active work:

```text
20 concurrent reconciles
```

before headroom.

---

# 63. Single Writer per Resource

A valuable logical invariant:

```text
one active reconcile path
for a resource key
```

reduces race complexity.

---

# 64. Parallel Resources

Different resource keys can reconcile concurrently.

---

# 65. Leader Election

Multiple controller replicas may run.

Leader election can ensure:

```text
one active controller instance
```

for some workloads.

---

# 66. Leader Election Does Not Scale Reconciliation by Itself

If only one replica is active:

```text
HA
```

but not necessarily:

```text
horizontal throughput
```

---

# 67. Active-Active Sharded Controllers

For very large scale:

```text
partition resource ownership
```

across controller replicas.

---

# 68. Shard Key

Possible:

```text
namespace

tenant

resource UID hash

cluster
```

---

# 69. Rendezvous Hashing

Useful to reduce movement when controller replicas change.

---

# 70. Ownership Lease

Alternative:

```text
resource/shard lease
```

with fencing if external side effects require it.

---

# 71. CRD Validation

Schema should reject invalid objects before reconciliation.

Examples:

```text
workers < 1

negative GPU count

unknown rollout strategy
```

---

# 72. OpenAPI Schema

CRD schema can enforce:

```text
types

required fields

patterns

ranges

enums
```

---

# 73. Structural Schema

Helps Kubernetes:

```text
prune unknown fields

support version conversion

apply management
```

---

# 74. Validation Principle

Reject invalid intent:

```text
as early as possible
```

Prefer:

```text
API admission
```

over failing hours later in controller.

---

# 75. Cross-Field Validation

Example:

```text
if strategy = canary
then canaryPercent must exist
```

May require richer validation logic.

---

# 76. Admission Webhook

Runs during API request admission.

Can:

```text
validate

mutate
```

before object is persisted.

---

# 77. Validating Webhook

Rejects:

```text
invalid

unsafe

policy-violating
```

resources.

---

# 78. Mutating Webhook

Can apply:

```text
defaults

injected fields

required labels
```

---

# 79. Mutation Risk

Users submit:

```text
A
```

but stored object becomes:

```text
A + hidden mutation
```

Too much mutation hurts debuggability.

---

# 80. Defaulting

Prefer deterministic documented defaults.

Example:

```text
retryPolicy = Never
```

if omitted.

---

# 81. Default Evolution Problem

Suppose old default:

```text
gpuProfile = A
```

new default:

```text
gpuProfile = B
```

Reapplying old manifests might change behavior.

Persist defaults or version behavior carefully.

---

# 82. Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed Admission

Security-critical validation:

```text
usually fail closed
```

Optional metadata mutation:

```text
may fail open
```

depending on risk.

---

# 83. Admission Webhook Outage

If every Pod creation depends on unavailable webhook:

```text
cluster operations can freeze
```

Therefore webhook availability is Tier-0.

---

# 84. Webhook Latency

Admission sits on:

```text
API request critical path
```

Keep it:

```text
fast

highly available

dependency-light
```

---

# 85. Webhook Anti-Pattern

Admission webhook calls:

```text
external SaaS API
```

for every resource.

Now external SaaS latency can block Kubernetes API.

---

# 86. Cache Policy Data Locally

If admission requires policy:

```text
replicate/cache policy
```

inside cluster.

---

# 87. Admission vs Controller Validation

Admission:

```text
is this intent allowed?
```

Controller:

```text
can this intent be realized right now?
```

Do not confuse.

---

# 88. Scheduling Feasibility

A request for:

```text
1024 GPUs
```

may be valid but currently unschedulable.

Admission should not necessarily reject.

Controller can report:

```text
WaitingForCapacity
```

---

# 89. Hard Constraint vs Temporary Condition

Hard:

```text
unsupported GPU type
```

Reject.

Temporary:

```text
no GPUs available now
```

Queue/wait.

---

# 90. Finalizer

A finalizer prevents Kubernetes from fully deleting a resource until cleanup occurs.

---

# 91. Deletion Lifecycle

User deletes object.

Kubernetes sets:

```text
deletionTimestamp
```

Object remains until finalizers removed.

---

# 92. Why Finalizers Matter

TrainingJob may own:

```text
cloud reservation

external checkpoint

remote scheduler allocation
```

These must be cleaned before object disappears.

---

# 93. Finalizer Reconcile

```text
if deletionTimestamp set:
    cleanup external state
    remove finalizer
```

---

# 94. Finalizer Must Be Idempotent

Cleanup can run multiple times.

Example:

```text
delete reservation
```

should succeed logically even if already deleted.

---

# 95. Stuck Terminating

If finalizer controller is broken:

```text
resource never disappears
```

This is a common production failure.

---

# 96. Finalizer Escape Procedure

Need controlled operator path to:

```text
inspect

manually remediate

remove finalizer
```

with audit.

---

# 97. Never Blindly Remove Finalizers

You may leak:

```text
GPU reservation

cloud load balancer

storage volume

security policy
```

---

# 98. Owner References

Kubernetes can establish ownership:

```text
TrainingJob
   |
   +--> Pod A
   +--> Pod B
```

---

# 99. Garbage Collection

When owner disappears:

```text
owned dependents can be deleted
```

automatically.

---

# 100. Owner Reference Limit

Only suitable for Kubernetes-owned resources with valid ownership relationships.

External cloud objects still need finalizers/controllers.

---

# 101. Controller-Owned Children

Set:

```text
ownerReference
```

where appropriate.

Then watches on children can enqueue parent.

---

# 102. Child-to-Parent Watch

Pod changes:

```text
worker failed
```

Controller maps child event back to:

```text
TrainingJob
```

and reconciles.

---

# 103. Do Not Put Business Logic in Event Handler

Event handler should usually:

```text
enqueue key
```

Reconciler owns logic.

---

# 104. External Side Effects

Operators often call:

```text
cloud APIs

model registry

scheduler

DNS

storage
```

These calls are not transactionally coupled to Kubernetes API.

---

# 105. The Partial-Failure Problem

Controller:

```text
creates cloud resource
```

then crashes before recording:

```text
external ID
```

On restart it might create another.

---

# 106. Deterministic External Identity

Use:

```text
resource UID
```

to derive external idempotency key.

---

# 107. Example

```text
reservation name =
trainingjob-<UID>
```

After timeout/crash:

```text
lookup by deterministic name
```

before creating again.

---

# 108. Remote Timeout Is Ambiguous

If cloud API times out:

```text
request may have succeeded
```

Never assume:

```text
timeout = no resource created
```

---

# 109. Adopt Existing External Resource

On reconcile:

```text
find external resource by ownership key
```

If exists:

```text
adopt
```

rather than recreate.

---

# 110. External Resource Tagging

Tag:

```text
k8s_uid

namespace

resource_name

controller
```

for adoption and cleanup.

---

# 111. Fencing External Actions

If stale controller ownership is possible, include:

```text
generation/epoch
```

so older actor cannot overwrite newer state.

---

# 112. Desired External State

Controller should model:

```text
ensure reservation exists with spec X
```

not:

```text
call CreateReservation once
```

---

# 113. Saga-Like Cleanup

Multi-step external workflow:

```text
create reservation

create endpoint

update DNS
```

can partially fail.

Controller repeatedly reconciles until desired state or cleanup is reached.

---

# 114. Kubernetes as Durable Intent Store

CRD contains:

```text
desired state
```

Controller derives actions repeatedly.

This reduces need for ad hoc workflow state in controller memory.

---

# 115. But Kubernetes Is Not Unlimited Workflow Storage

Do not store:

```text
massive event histories

large logs

GB artifacts
```

inside CRDs.

---

# 116. TrainingJob Operator

High-level resource:

```yaml
kind: TrainingJob
spec:
  workers: 128
  gpusPerWorker: 8
  checkpointPolicy: periodic
```

---

# 117. Training Controller Responsibilities

```text
validate

admit resources

create distributed job

monitor ranks

handle retries

report checkpoints

finalize
```

---

# 118. Whole-Job Semantics

Distributed training often needs:

```text
all workers available together
```

Default Pod-by-Pod scheduling may be insufficient.

---

# 119. Gang Scheduling Integration

Controller can create:

```text
workload/pod group
```

describing:

```text
all-or-nothing resource demand
```

for external scheduler/admission layer.

---

# 120. Workload Admission Before Pod Explosion

Bad pattern:

```text
create 1024 Pods immediately
```

with no cluster capacity.

This floods scheduler/API.

Better:

```text
admit logical workload first
```

then instantiate Pods after capacity granted.

---

# 121. TrainingJob State

Example:

```text
Pending

Admitted

Starting

Running

Checkpointing

Succeeded

Failed
```

---

# 122. Training Conditions

Examples:

```text
ResourcesReserved

WorkersReady

CheckpointAvailable

Degraded
```

---

# 123. Rank Identity

Distributed training may require stable:

```text
rank 0

rank 1

...
```

Controller/operator should preserve deterministic role assignment.

---

# 124. Rendezvous Service

Operator may create:

```text
Service

ConfigMap

endpoint
```

for distributed workers to discover one another.

---

# 125. Master/Coordinator Failure

Need defined semantics:

```text
restart entire gang?

restart leader only?

resume checkpoint?
```

Depends on training framework.

---

# 126. Worker Failure Policy

Possible:

```text
FailFast

RestartWorker

RestartGroup

ResumeCheckpoint
```

---

# 127. Checkpoint-Aware Retry

Controller status can include:

```text
latestCheckpointRef
```

Then replacement job resumes.

---

# 128. Spot/Preemptible Nodes

Training operator can classify node loss:

```text
infrastructure retryable
```

rather than:

```text
application failure
```

---

# 129. Failure Classification

Important categories:

```text
user code

data

capacity

node

GPU

network

platform
```

Retry policy should differ.

---

# 130. ModelDeployment Operator

Higher-level deployment semantics include:

```text
model artifact

runtime

autoscaling

canary

traffic routing

rollback
```

---

# 131. ModelDeployment Controller

May create:

```text
Deployment/StatefulSet

Service

autoscaler

routing resource

configuration
```

---

# 132. Artifact Readiness

Do not mark:

```text
Ready
```

until model:

```text
loaded

verified

warmed
```

and endpoint passes readiness.

---

# 133. Canary Rollout

Controller can represent:

```text
desired traffic:
95% old
5% new
```

and advance only if metrics pass.

---

# 134. External Metrics Dependency

Canary controller may depend on observability system.

If metrics unavailable:

```text
pause rollout
```

rather than assume success.

---

# 135. Rollback

Desired state can move:

```text
production -> previous release
```

Controller reconciles infrastructure.

---

# 136. DatasetBuild Operator

Could represent:

```text
build immutable dataset snapshot
```

with:

```text
inputs

transform version

output manifest
```

---

# 137. DatasetBuild Status

```text
Planning

Running

Validating

Published

Failed
```

---

# 138. Dataset Outputs

Store:

```text
artifact references
```

not actual dataset bytes in CRD.

---

# 139. FeatureMaterialization Operator

Could manage:

```text
offline-to-online backfill

streaming bootstrap

validation

promotion
```

---

# 140. Notebook Operator

Can create:

```text
workspace

PVC

identity

network policy

idle timeout
```

from high-level notebook resource.

---

# 141. Notebook Security

Controller should enforce:

```text
resource limits

service account

egress policy

runtime image policy
```

---

# 142. GPUReservation Resource

Logical resource:

```text
reserve N GPUs
```

with:

```text
profile

duration

tenant

priority
```

Controller integrates with scheduler/capacity service.

---

# 143. Reservation Expiry

Use:

```text
lease/TTL
```

to prevent abandoned reservations.

---

# 144. Capacity as Separate Resource

Instead of embedding everything inside TrainingJob:

```text
TrainingJob
   |
   v
Workload/Reservation
```

separation can improve scheduler integration.

---

# 145. Scheduler Architecture Integration

The operator should not implement:

```text
low-level node selection
```

if scheduler already owns that responsibility.

---

# 146. Layering

```text
ML Operator
    |
    v
Workload Admission
    |
    v
Kubernetes Scheduler
    |
    v
Node
```

---

# 147. Operator Responsibility

Answer:

```text
what workload should exist?
```

Scheduler answers:

```text
where should its Pods run?
```

---

# 148. Hardware Profiles

Expose:

```text
gpu-large

gpu-high-memory

cpu-high-memory
```

instead of hardcoded node labels to most users.

---

# 149. Profile Resolution

Controller/scheduler translates profile into:

```text
resource requests

node selectors

topology constraints

runtime class
```

---

# 150. Profile Versioning

If hardware profile changes:

```text
existing workloads
```

should not silently mutate unexpectedly.

Use versioned policy or resolved status.

---

# 151. Taints and Tolerations

Operator can attach required tolerations for:

```text
dedicated GPU pools
```

without requiring every ML engineer to understand raw cluster internals.

---

# 152. Affinity

Generated placement may include:

```text
node affinity

pod anti-affinity

topology spread
```

based on platform policy.

---

# 153. Topology-Aware Training

For multi-GPU jobs, operator/scheduler may request:

```text
same rack

same network fabric

same NVSwitch domain
```

depending on parallelism.

---

# 154. Do Not Encode Topology in User API Too Literally

Prefer:

```text
communicationProfile: high-bandwidth
```

over exposing internal rack labels.

---

# 155. Device Plugins

Kubernetes exposes devices through plugin mechanisms.

Operator generally requests logical resources:

```text
vendor.com/gpu: 8
```

or higher-level profile abstraction.

---

# 156. GPU Sharing

If platform supports:

```text
MIG

time slicing

shared accelerator
```

CRD should expose semantics such as:

```text
isolation class
```

rather than implementation if possible.

---

# 157. Multi-Cluster Operator Pattern

Global control plane cannot directly rely on one cluster.

Use:

```text
Global Resource
      |
      v
Placement Controller
      |
      v
Cluster Agent
      |
      v
Local Kubernetes
```

---

# 158. Cluster Agent

Runs close to cluster and:

```text
receives desired work

creates local resources

reports status

buffers during disconnect
```

---

# 159. Pull Model

Agent pulls:

```text
desired assignments
```

from global control plane.

Security advantage:

```text
cluster needs outbound connection only
```

---

# 160. Push Model

Global control plane writes directly into remote cluster API.

Simpler initially.

Harder for:

```text
networking

credentials

large fleet isolation
```

---

# 161. Agent Offline

During WAN partition:

```text
existing workloads continue
```

Agent uses last-known-good desired state.

---

# 162. New Work During Partition

May:

```text
pause
```

or allow bounded local autonomy.

Policy must be explicit.

---

# 163. Cluster Capability Advertisement

Agent reports:

```text
GPU types

available capacity

runtime versions

region

network fabric
```

to placement layer.

---

# 164. Stale Inventory

Global scheduler must know:

```text
inventory age
```

because stale cluster capacity can cause bad placement.

---

# 165. Assignment Generation

Global assignment should include:

```text
generation
```

so agent ignores stale updates.

---

# 166. Multi-Cluster Failover

If cluster dies:

```text
placement controller
```

can assign workload elsewhere if policy permits.

---

# 167. External Stateful Jobs

For training with checkpoints:

```text
new cluster
```

can resume from shared checkpoint.

---

# 168. CRD Versioning

Eventually:

```text
v1alpha1

v1beta1

v1
```

or equivalent lifecycle.

Do not treat version naming as cosmetic.

---

# 169. API Version Represents Contract

Different versions may expose:

```text
different field shapes
```

while mapping to one storage representation.

---

# 170. Storage Version

Kubernetes persists one preferred version internally.

Older/newer API versions can be converted.

---

# 171. Conversion Webhook

Converts:

```text
v1beta1 <-> v1
```

when schemas differ materially.

---

# 172. Conversion Must Preserve Meaning

If old field:

```text
gpuType: a100
```

becomes:

```text
hardwareProfile: gpu-a100-standard
```

conversion must preserve semantics.

---

# 173. Round-Trip Safety

Ideal:

```text
old -> new -> old
```

does not lose meaningful data.

---

# 174. Hub-and-Spoke Conversion

Choose one canonical/internal version.

Convert:

```text
all versions <-> hub
```

rather than every pair.

---

# 175. Dropping Fields

If new API cannot represent old field:

```text
migration is breaking
```

and needs explicit strategy.

---

# 176. API Deprecation

Before removing version:

```text
measure usage

notify users

provide migration

block new use gradually
```

---

# 177. Stored Objects May Outlive API Version

You must migrate persisted storage before removing conversion support.

---

# 178. Controller Version Skew

During rollout:

```text
old controller

new CRD

new controller

old webhook
```

may briefly coexist.

Plan compatibility.

---

# 179. Upgrade Order

Often safer:

```text
1. Add new compatible CRD/schema.

2. Deploy compatible controller.

3. Migrate resources.

4. Remove old behavior later.
```

---

# 180. CRD Schema Change Risk

Tightening validation can cause existing objects to become:

```text
invalid under new rules
```

even though already stored.

Test fleet data before rollout.

---

# 181. Controller Upgrade

Reconciliation is continuous.

New controller must be able to observe:

```text
resources created by old controller
```

and adopt them safely.

---

# 182. Child Resource Versioning

Label children with:

```text
controller version

template hash

parent UID
```

for migration/debugging.

---

# 183. Template Hash

If desired Pod template changes:

```text
hash changes
```

controller can trigger controlled replacement.

---

# 184. Immutable vs Mutable Child Update

Some child fields can update in place.

Others require:

```text
recreate
```

Controller must understand Kubernetes semantics.

---

# 185. Rollout Strategy

For serving:

```text
rolling

canary

blue-green
```

For training:

```text
usually immutable job execution
```

Do not apply web-service rollout semantics blindly.

---

# 186. Controller Testing Pyramid

```text
unit

reconcile tests

fake API tests

integration

envtest-like API tests

real cluster tests

failure tests
```

---

# 187. Pure Reconcile Logic

Where possible separate:

```text
decision logic
```

from:

```text
API side effects
```

for easier testing.

---

# 188. State-Transition Test

Verify:

```text
Pending -> Running

Running -> Succeeded

Running -> Failed

Deleting -> Finalized
```

---

# 189. Idempotency Test

Run reconcile twice.

Second reconcile should not create duplicate side effects.

---

# 190. Crash-Boundary Test

Inject crash:

```text
after child create

before status write

after external create

before finalizer removal
```

---

# 191. Duplicate Event Test

Send same watch event repeatedly.

Final state should remain correct.

---

# 192. Out-of-Order Event Test

Child updates may be observed in different order.

Reconciler should derive truth from current state.

---

# 193. Stale Cache Test

Informer cache may briefly show old object.

Ensure controller eventually converges.

---

# 194. API Conflict Test

Two writers update same object.

Controller should:

```text
retry on conflict
```

without overwriting unrelated fields.

---

# 195. Status Patch

Prefer minimal status patch/update.

Avoid replacing whole object unnecessarily.

---

# 196. Server-Side Apply Concept

Multiple actors can own different fields.

Useful for declarative configuration.

But field ownership must be understood.

---

# 197. Field Ownership Conflict

Two controllers manage same field:

```text
oscillation
```

or apply conflict.

Establish one owner per field.

---

# 198. One Controller, One Responsibility

Avoid mega-controller that owns:

```text
training

serving

networking

billing

governance
```

Separate domains while coordinating via APIs.

---

# 199. Controller Choreography

Example:

```text
TrainingJob Controller
       |
       v
Model Registry Resource
       |
       v
ModelDeployment Controller
```

Each controller owns one domain.

---

# 200. Avoid Tight Controller Call Chains

Controller A should not synchronously call controller B's internal API.

Prefer:

```text
durable resource creation
```

and reconciliation.

---

# 201. Resource-Oriented Choreography

```text
Controller A creates Resource B

Controller B reconciles B

Controller A observes B status
```

This creates durable loose coupling.

---

# 202. Backpressure Between Controllers

If downstream controller overloaded:

```text
upstream should not create unlimited resources
```

Use admission/quotas.

---

# 203. API Server as Shared Bottleneck

Every custom controller contributes:

```text
LIST

WATCH

GET

PATCH

UPDATE

CREATE
```

load.

At fleet scale this matters enormously.

---

# 204. QPS/Burst Limits

Controller clients should use:

```text
bounded QPS

bounded burst
```

rather than unlimited API traffic.

---

# 205. Informer Selectors

If controller only cares about:

```text
specific labels/namespaces
```

scope watch where possible.

---

# 206. Namespace Scoping

A controller per tenant namespace can improve isolation.

But thousands of controller instances may increase overhead.

Trade carefully.

---

# 207. Cluster-Scoped Controller

More efficient globally.

But blast radius is larger.

---

# 208. Cell-Scoped Controller

Operate one controller fleet per:

```text
cluster/cell
```

Strong compromise for large platforms.

---

# 209. Etcd Pressure

CRDs are persisted in etcd.

Problems:

```text
large objects

high write churn

massive object counts
```

increase pressure.

---

# 210. CRD Object Size

Keep:

```text
small

bounded

operational
```

Store bulky details externally.

---

# 211. Status History Anti-Pattern

Do not append:

```text
every state transition
```

inside status array forever.

Use external event/history store.

---

# 212. Kubernetes Events

Useful for:

```text
human diagnostics
```

but not durable long-term audit.

---

# 213. Event Spam

Repeated warning every reconcile:

```text
millions of events
```

Can overload event storage/logging.

Rate-limit/deduplicate.

---

# 214. API Priority and Fairness

Critical Kubernetes components should remain responsive even when custom controllers generate high load.

Platform must protect:

```text
system control traffic
```

from custom workload storms.

---

# 215. Controller Storm Scenario

A global ConfigMap change triggers:

```text
100k TrainingJobs
```

to reconcile.

If each performs:

```text
10 API calls
```

that's:

```text
1M API operations
```

potentially at once.

---

# 216. Storm Mitigation

Use:

```text
queue rate limits

jitter

priority

batching

dependency version tracking
```

---

# 217. Dependency Version Tracking

Instead of all resources polling policy:

```text
record policy generation
```

and reconcile only when relevant version changes.

---

# 218. Resync

Periodic reconciliation can catch drift.

But full resync of millions of objects at once is dangerous.

Use:

```text
staggered resync

jitter
```

---

# 219. Reconcile Budget

One reconcile should have:

```text
time bound

API call bound

external-call bound
```

Avoid one object monopolizing worker for minutes.

---

# 220. Long External Operation

Do not block worker:

```text
30 minutes waiting for cluster creation
```

Persist state and requeue later.

---

# 221. Async External Operation

External create returns:

```text
operation ID
```

Controller stores reference.

Later reconcile polls/observes completion.

---

# 222. Controller Should Be Restartable Anytime

No critical state should exist only in:

```text
goroutine

thread

process memory
```

---

# 223. Caches Are Rebuildable

Informer cache loss:

```text
re-list
```

and resume.

---

# 224. Work Queue Is Rebuildable

If queue state lost:

```text
watch/resync/current resources
```

should recreate needed reconciliations.

---

# 225. External IDs Must Be Durable

If controller creates remote resource:

```text
persist identity in status/spec/metadata
```

or derive deterministically.

---

# 226. Status as Operational Pointer

Example:

```yaml
status:
  externalReservationId: res-8821
```

bounded and useful.

---

# 227. Status Is Not Secret Storage

Do not store:

```text
cloud credentials

tokens
```

in CRD status.

---

# 228. Secrets

Reference:

```text
Secret object
```

or external secret identity.

Do not duplicate values into CRD.

---

# 229. RBAC

Controller service account should receive only required verbs/resources.

---

# 230. Least-Privilege Controller

Training operator may need:

```text
get/list/watch TrainingJobs

create/update Pods

create Services
```

It should not necessarily:

```text
delete arbitrary Secrets cluster-wide
```

---

# 231. Namespace Boundary

If controller manages many namespaces:

```text
cluster-wide privileges
```

increase blast radius.

Consider scoped roles and admission guardrails.

---

# 232. Impersonation

Avoid unnecessary controller ability to impersonate users.

Use explicit workload identity/proxy flows.

---

# 233. Privilege Escalation Through CRD

Suppose user controls:

```yaml
spec:
  serviceAccountName: cluster-admin
```

Operator creates Pod with that service account.

This becomes a privilege escalation bug.

---

# 234. Validate Security-Sensitive Fields

Fields such as:

```text
service account

hostPath

privileged

hostNetwork

runtime class

node selector
```

must be policy-controlled.

---

# 235. Pod Security

Operator should generate secure defaults:

```text
non-root

drop capabilities

read-only root where possible

seccomp

resource limits
```

---

# 236. Image Policy

Only permit:

```text
approved registries

signed images

immutable digests
```

for high-trust workloads.

---

# 237. Model Artifact Policy

Similarly verify:

```text
digest

signature/provenance

approved registry state
```

before deployment.

---

# 238. Network Policy

Operator can generate workload-specific:

```text
ingress/egress rules
```

from high-level access intent.

---

# 239. Workload Identity

TrainingJob may specify:

```text
dataAccessProfile
```

Platform resolves to safe workload identity.

---

# 240. Avoid User-Provided Cloud Credentials

Prefer:

```text
short-lived identity
```

bound to workload.

---

# 241. Multi-Tenant Controller Isolation

Options:

```text
shared controller

controller per tenant

controller per cell

dedicated cluster
```

Choose by:

```text
trust

scale

blast radius
```

---

# 242. Noisy Tenant

One tenant creates:

```text
1M broken resources
```

Shared controller queue may starve everyone.

---

# 243. Tenant Fairness

Queue can enforce:

```text
per-tenant concurrency

rate limits

weighted fairness
```

---

# 244. Priority

Production deployment repairs may outrank:

```text
experimental notebook provisioning
```

---

# 245. Reconcile Priority Classes

Possible:

```text
P0:
security/failure recovery

P1:
production serving

P2:
training

P3:
experiments
```

---

# 246. Starvation

Priority-only scheduling can starve lower classes.

Use quotas/fair-share.

---

# 247. Controller Metrics

Track:

```text
reconcile rate

reconcile duration

errors

queue depth

queue age

retries
```

---

# 248. Per-Resource Metrics

Useful but high cardinality.

Do not label Prometheus metrics with:

```text
every resource UID
```

at huge scale.

---

# 249. Logs

Structured reconcile logs should include:

```text
resource

generation

request ID

controller version

result
```

---

# 250. Correlation ID

Useful across:

```text
API admission

controller

scheduler

external cloud API
```

---

# 251. Reconcile Trace

Distributed trace can show:

```text
TrainingJob reconcile
 -> scheduler reservation
 -> Kubernetes child create
```

---

# 252. Error Classification

Metrics should distinguish:

```text
user error

transient external error

API conflict

rate limit

controller bug
```

---

# 253. Condition Reasons

Expose stable machine-readable reasons:

```text
InsufficientCapacity

ArtifactUnavailable

PolicyDenied

CheckpointMissing
```

---

# 254. Human-Friendly Message

Condition message gives details.

But automation should rely on:

```text
reason code
```

not parse free text.

---

# 255. Stuck Reconciliation

Detect resources whose:

```text
generation not observed for too long
```

---

# 256. Status Freshness

Metrics:

```text
now - last successful reconcile
```

per class/aggregate.

---

# 257. Queue Age

Often more important than queue depth.

A queue of 10k fast-moving items may be healthy.

One resource waiting 30 minutes may not.

---

# 258. Reconcile SLO

Example:

```text
99% of spec changes
observed by controller < 30 sec
```

---

# 259. Provisioning SLO

Separate:

```text
controller response time
```

from:

```text
actual infrastructure provisioning time
```

---

# 260. Condition-Based SLO

Example:

```text
TrainingJob generation accepted
-> Scheduled condition
< 2 min
```

---

# 261. Controller Availability

Multiple replicas plus:

```text
leader/shard failover
```

provide HA.

---

# 262. Failover Time

Depends on:

```text
leader lease

watch rebuild

cache sync

queue reconstruction
```

---

# 263. Cache Sync

Controller should not act prematurely before initial informer cache is synchronized.

---

# 264. Startup Thundering Herd

After restart, controller may see:

```text
500k resources
```

and enqueue all.

Rate-limit startup.

---

# 265. Warm Restart

Persisting certain checkpoints outside process can reduce rebuild time.

But correctness should not depend solely on them.

---

# 266. Cluster Upgrade

During API server/network disruption:

```text
watch disconnects

reconnects

relist may occur
```

Controller must tolerate.

---

# 267. Node Upgrade

Operator may observe workers evicted.

Training policy decides:

```text
retry

resume checkpoint

fail
```

---

# 268. Driver Upgrade

GPU jobs may be interrupted.

Operator should classify:

```text
planned infrastructure disruption
```

differently from user-code error.

---

# 269. Pod Eviction

Do not assume:

```text
Pod failed
=
user code failed
```

Read termination/eviction reasons.

---

# 270. OOMKilled

Could indicate:

```text
bad resource sizing

data spike

application leak
```

Retrying indefinitely is unsafe.

---

# 271. GPU Device Error

May require:

```text
node quarantine
```

rather than simply restart Pod on same node.

---

# 272. Node Health Integration

Operator/scheduler can consume:

```text
node health signals
```

to avoid repeatedly placing workload on bad hardware.

---

# 273. DNS Failure

Distributed training may fail even with healthy Pods.

Operator diagnostics should include:

```text
rendezvous/DNS/service state
```

---

# 274. CNI Failure

Pod network not ready.

Classify as:

```text
platform/infrastructure
```

---

# 275. CSI Failure

Checkpoint volume fails to mount.

Operator should expose:

```text
StorageUnavailable
```

rather than generic Failed.

---

# 276. Image Pull Failure

Could be:

```text
bad image reference

registry outage

auth failure
```

Different remediation.

---

# 277. Scheduling Failure

Pod pending because:

```text
GPU unavailable

affinity impossible

taint mismatch

quota
```

Expose scheduler reason in higher-level status.

---

# 278. Operator Status Should Translate Infrastructure

Users should see:

```text
WaitingFor8GPUNode
```

not only:

```text
0/500 nodes available...
```

Platform abstraction adds value.

---

# 279. Preserve Raw Diagnostic Reference

Still retain link/reference to lower-level details for experts.

---

# 280. Failure — Admission Webhook Down

Symptoms:

```text
create requests timeout/fail
```

Mitigation:

```text
HA webhook

local dependencies

monitor p99

emergency bypass policy
```

---

# 281. Failure — Controller Hot Loop

One malformed resource causes:

```text
100k reconciles/min
```

Mitigation:

```text
per-key backoff

circuit breaker

dead-letter/paused condition
```

---

# 282. Failure — Finalizer Deadlock

Resource deletion blocked because dependency already disappeared.

Finalizer must handle:

```text
not found = cleaned
```

idempotently.

---

# 283. Failure — External Resource Created Twice

Usually due to:

```text
timeout/crash
```

without deterministic identity.

Fix:

```text
idempotency/adoption
```

---

# 284. Failure — Child Deleted Manually

Reconciler observes child missing.

If parent still desires it:

```text
recreate
```

This is self-healing.

---

# 285. Failure — User Manually Edits Child

Controller should decide:

```text
revert

adopt

mark drift
```

according to ownership.

---

# 286. Drift

Actual child differs from desired child.

Reconciler repairs.

---

# 287. Escape Hatch Ownership

If users are allowed to edit certain child fields:

```text
controller must not overwrite them
```

Define field ownership clearly.

---

# 288. Failure — Child Has Same Name but Wrong Owner

Never adopt blindly.

Verify:

```text
owner UID

labels

identity
```

before mutation.

---

# 289. UID Matters

Kubernetes object name can be reused after deletion.

UID distinguishes:

```text
old object

new object with same name
```

---

# 290. Finalizer + UID

External resource ownership should bind to:

```text
UID
```

not only namespace/name.

---

# 291. Failure — Stale Controller Writes Status

Optimistic concurrency should reject stale update.

Retry against newest resource.

---

# 292. Failure — Status Update Causes Reconcile Loop

Controller updates status.

Watch sees update.

Controller reconciles and writes same status again.

Infinite loop.

---

# 293. Avoid No-Op Status Writes

Compare desired status with current.

Write only on meaningful change.

---

# 294. Predicate Filtering

Controller can ignore changes that do not affect desired reconciliation.

Example:

```text
status-only update
```

for some watches.

Use carefully so important transitions are not missed.

---

# 295. Generation Predicate

A common pattern:

```text
reconcile primary object
when generation changes
```

but child events and deletion still matter.

---

# 296. Failure — Massive Label Update

Organization changes label on 1M objects.

Controllers watching all metadata changes may storm.

Use predicates and queue controls.

---

# 297. Failure — CRD Size Explosion

User embeds:

```text
1 MB training config
```

across 100k resources.

etcd pressure explodes.

Store large configs externally and reference them.

---

# 298. Failure — Conversion Webhook Down

Old/new API version reads may fail.

Conversion webhook is another Tier-0 API dependency.

---

# 299. Conversion Availability

Keep:

```text
fast

HA

dependency-light
```

like admission webhooks.

---

# 300. Failure — Version Conversion Loses Fields

User reads v1 and writes back.

Old-only field disappears.

This is a serious compatibility bug.

---

# 301. Conversion Property Testing

Generate objects across versions.

Test:

```text
old -> hub -> old
```

for semantic preservation.

---

# 302. Failure — Old Controller With New Schema

Can ignore new fields and accidentally revert behavior.

Use:

```text
compatibility gates

version-aware reconciliation
```

---

# 303. Controller Capability

Status may report:

```text
controllerVersion

supportedFeatures
```

for debugging, though avoid excessive status churn.

---

# 304. Feature Gates

Roll out new behavior gradually.

Example:

```text
newCheckpointController = enabled
```

per tenant/cell.

---

# 305. Feature-Gate Maturity

Support:

```text
off

canary

partial

default-on

removed
```

with cleanup plan.

---

# 306. Multi-Cell Upgrade

Upgrade:

```text
cell A canary

cell B

cell C
```

instead of global simultaneous operator replacement.

---

# 307. Operator Release Observability

Compare:

```text
reconcile errors

queue latency

API QPS

resource success rate
```

between old/new controller versions.

---

# 308. Canary Controller

Route subset of resources to new controller shard.

Requires:

```text
non-overlapping ownership
```

to avoid dual writers.

---

# 309. Ownership Selector

Example:

```text
label controller-ring=canary
```

or deterministic shard assignment.

---

# 310. Controller Rollback

New version fails.

Old controller must be able to:

```text
adopt existing resources
```

unless schema migration made it impossible.

Thus backward compatibility matters.

---

# 311. CRD Deletion

Deleting CRD can delete all custom resources.

This is extremely dangerous.

Protect with:

```text
RBAC

change controls

backup
```

---

# 312. CRD Backup

Back up:

```text
custom resource data
```

and conversion/schema definitions needed to interpret it.

---

# 313. Restore

Restoring resources can trigger:

```text
controllers recreating external side effects
```

Need adoption/idempotency before bulk restore.

---

# 314. Disaster Recovery Storm

Restored cluster gets:

```text
100k TrainingJobs
```

Controllers may try to recreate everything.

Use:

```text
paused restore mode

rate-limited reconciliation

ownership verification
```

---

# 315. Restore Semantics

Some old workloads should not restart.

Example:

```text
historical completed training jobs
```

Controller must understand terminal state.

---

# 316. Completed Resource Reconcile

A completed TrainingJob should not:

```text
recreate missing worker Pods
```

unless retention policy explicitly wants them.

---

# 317. Terminal State

Terminal resources should generally:

```text
stop active reconciliation
```

except:

```text
retention

cleanup

drift checks
```

as needed.

---

# 318. Status Conditions as User API

Conditions should remain:

```text
stable

documented

machine-readable
```

because automation may depend on them.

---

# 319. Reason Codes Are API

Changing:

```text
InsufficientGPU
```

to:

```text
NoCapacity
```

can break automation.

Version carefully.

---

# 320. Error Messages Are Not Stable API

Humans can read free-text message.

Machines should use structured fields.

---

# 321. Observed State Snapshot

Status should summarize:

```text
important reality
```

not mirror every child object field.

---

# 322. Child Count

Useful:

```text
desiredWorkers: 64
readyWorkers: 61
failedWorkers: 2
```

rather than embedding every worker Pod.

---

# 323. External Reference

Useful:

```text
schedulerWorkloadRef
```

for debugging.

---

# 324. Status Truncation

If thousands of failures exist:

```text
store summary + external report URI
```

---

# 325. Operator API Design Principle

User CRD should expose:

```text
what
```

and:

```text
policy intent
```

not:

```text
exact low-level mechanism
```

unless needed.

---

# 326. Example — Bad API

```yaml
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    rack-id: rack-27
```

---

# 327. Better API

```yaml
spec:
  topologyProfile: low-latency-gpu
```

Platform can evolve physical racks without breaking users.

---

# 328. But Avoid Over-Abstraction

If every advanced need requires:

```text
new API field
```

teams become blocked.

Provide controlled escape hatches.

---

# 329. Escape Hatch Governance

Allow:

```text
podTemplatePatch
```

only for approved teams or limited safe fields.

---

# 330. Escape Hatch Metrics

Measure how often users bypass golden path.

High rate indicates abstraction gaps.

---

# 331. Operator Product Thinking

An operator is a product API for engineers.

Measure:

```text
adoption

success rate

time-to-ready

support tickets

escape-hatch usage
```

---

# 332. API Error UX

Instead of:

```text
admission denied
```

return:

```text
Requested hardware profile gpu-x is not permitted for project P.
Allowed profiles: gpu-small, gpu-large.
```

---

# 333. Explainability

For Pending workload, explain:

```text
waiting for quota

waiting for topology

waiting for artifact

waiting for policy approval
```

---

# 334. Scheduling Explainability

Users should know why:

```text
job has waited 3 hours
```

without cluster-admin access.

---

# 335. Desired State Ownership

One field:

```text
one authoritative owner
```

prevents controllers fighting.

---

# 336. Controller Oscillation

Controller A sets:

```text
replicas=10
```

Controller B sets:

```text
replicas=20
```

Endless updates.

Avoid shared ownership.

---

# 337. Cross-Controller Contract

If autoscaler owns replicas:

```text
deployment controller
```

should not constantly overwrite replica count.

---

# 338. Parent/Child API Boundary

Parent owns:

```text
high-level policy
```

Child controller owns:

```text
derived low-level state
```

---

# 339. Example

```text
ModelDeployment
   |
   v
ServingWorkload
   |
   v
Deployment
```

Each layer has one owner.

---

# 340. Why Layered Resources Help

They create:

```text
stable seams

testable contracts

clear ownership
```

---

# 341. Too Many Layers

Can also make:

```text
debugging

latency

failure tracing
```

hard.

Use layers only when responsibilities differ materially.

---

# 342. Operator Design Review Questions

Ask:

```text
What is desired state?

What is observed state?

What is authoritative?

Can reconcile run twice?

What if event is lost?

What if external call times out?

What if controller crashes after success?

What if deletion occurs mid-operation?

What if API changes next year?
```

---

# 343. Reconcile Invariant

After each successful reconcile:

```text
system moves closer
to desired state
```

or remains safely converged.

---

# 344. Safety vs Liveness

Safety:

```text
never create two conflicting production endpoints
```

Liveness:

```text
eventually create the desired endpoint
```

Both matter.

---

# 345. Example Safety Invariant

```text
only one active production pointer
per model/environment
```

---

# 346. Example Liveness Invariant

```text
if capacity exists and dependencies healthy,
an admitted TrainingJob eventually starts
```

---

# 347. Controller Correctness Is Invariant Engineering

Do not think only:

```text
does code execute?
```

Think:

```text
what must never happen?

what must eventually happen?
```

---

# 348. Property-Based Testing

Generate random:

```text
spec changes

failures

reconcile order
```

and verify invariants.

---

# 349. Chaos Reconciliation

Inject:

```text
API conflicts

timeouts

worker crashes

duplicate child resources

lost watches
```

---

# 350. State-Space Testing

For lifecycle:

```text
create

update

delete

retry

restore
```

test all relevant transitions.

---

# 351. Failure Injection — Create Child Then Crash

Expected:

```text
next reconcile adopts existing child
```

---

# 352. Failure Injection — Delete Child Then API Error

Expected:

```text
next reconcile verifies deletion
```

before retrying side effect.

---

# 353. Failure Injection — External API Returns 500

Expected:

```text
bounded retry

condition update

no tight loop
```

---

# 354. Failure Injection — API Conflict

Expected:

```text
refetch

recompute

retry
```

---

# 355. Failure Injection — Stale Generation

Expected:

```text
do not publish Ready
for old spec
```

---

# 356. Failure Injection — Deletion During Provisioning

Controller must transition to:

```text
cleanup
```

not finish creating resources indefinitely.

---

# 357. Failure Injection — Finalizer Controller Unavailable

Observe:

```text
Terminating backlog
```

and alert.

---

# 358. Failure Injection — Admission Latency 5s

Measure:

```text
API server request backlog
```

and cluster impact.

---

# 359. Failure Injection — Relist Storm

Restart controllers simultaneously.

Verify:

```text
API server survives
```

---

# 360. Failure Injection — 100k Spec Changes

Measure:

```text
queue age

reconcile SLO

API QPS

etcd latency
```

---

# 361. Capacity Math — Controller

Suppose:

```text
1M resources
```

and 1% change each minute:

```text
10k reconciles/min
≈ 167/sec
```

If average reconcile:

```text
100 ms
```

theoretical concurrency:

```text
~17
```

before headroom and retries.

---

# 362. API Call Math

If each reconcile makes:

```text
8 API calls
```

then:

```text
167 × 8
≈ 1336 API calls/sec
```

one controller alone.

---

# 363. Status Write Math

If every reconcile writes status:

```text
167 status writes/sec
```

even when nothing changed.

Avoid no-op writes.

---

# 364. Watch Fanout

One object update may be delivered to:

```text
many controllers
```

so global write cost is larger than one etcd write.

---

# 365. API Object Count

Millions of small objects can still create:

```text
list latency

memory pressure

watch load
```

even if each object is small.

---

# 366. Namespace Strategy

Too many objects in one namespace can affect:

```text
listing

operational blast radius
```

but excessive namespaces also add management complexity.

---

# 367. CRD Cardinality Review

Before creating one CR per:

```text
prediction

token

metric point
```

stop.

Kubernetes is not a general event database.

---

# 368. Good CRD Granularity

Use CRDs for:

```text
durable operational resources
```

with lifecycles measured in:

```text
minutes/hours/days
```

not millions of ephemeral events/sec.

---

# 369. TrainingJob Good Fit

Durable resource:

```text
one logical training execution
```

---

# 370. PredictionRequest Bad Fit

# 404. Failure Walkthrough — Controller Crashes After Child Create

1. Child exists.

2. Status may not yet mention it.

3. Controller restarts.

4. Informer discovers child.

5. Reconcile verifies owner UID.

6. Adopts child.

7. Continues.

No duplicate child.

---

# 405. Failure Walkthrough — External Reservation Timeout

1. Create request times out.

2. Outcome is unknown.

3. Controller requeues.

4. Next reconcile looks up reservation by deterministic parent UID.

5. If found, adopt.

6. If absent, retry create.

---

# 406. Failure Walkthrough — API Server Brownout

1. Watches disconnect.

2. Controllers back off.

3. Existing workloads continue.

4. API recovers.

5. Informers relist with jitter.

6. Queues refill gradually.

---

# 407. Failure Walkthrough — Admission Webhook Outage

1. New resource requests fail or time out according to failure policy.

2. Existing workloads continue.

3. Alert immediately.

4. Recover webhook.

5. Avoid bypass unless documented emergency path exists.

---

# 408. Failure Walkthrough — Finalizer Stuck

1. Resource remains Terminating.

2. Controller exposes cleanup error.

3. Operator repairs external dependency.

4. Reconcile confirms cleanup.

5. Finalizer removed.

---

# 409. Failure Walkthrough — 100k Jobs Reconcile at Once

1. Queue grows.

2. Per-tenant and global limits apply.

3. Production repairs prioritized.

4. API QPS constrained.

5. Queue drains gradually.

6. Reconcile SLO monitored.

---

# 410. Failure Walkthrough — Multi-Cluster Partition

1. Global plane cannot reach cluster agent.

2. Existing local workloads continue.

3. Assignment state marked stale.

4. Global scheduler avoids assigning new work unless autonomy policy permits.

5. On reconnect, generations reconcile.

---

# 411. Failure Walkthrough — Bad Controller Release

1. Canary cell shows error spike.

2. Stop rollout.

3. Restore previous controller.

4. Previous version adopts current resources.

5. No CRD rollback required because schema was backward-compatible.

---

# 412. Failure Walkthrough — CRD Restore After Disaster

1. Restore CRDs and schemas.

2. Restore custom resources.

3. Controllers start in rate-limited mode.

4. Existing external resources are discovered/adopted.

5. Terminal workloads remain terminal.

6. Active workloads reconcile gradually.

# 418. Senior Architect Thought Process

When someone says:

> The controller got the event, so it should work.

Ask:

```text
What if the event is lost?

Can the desired state be reconstructed from the API object?
```

---

# 419. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> The external API timed out, so we'll call create again.

Ask:

```text
Could the first create have succeeded?

What deterministic identity lets us discover it?
```

---

# 420. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> We'll store every worker state in TrainingJob.status.

Ask:

```text
How many workers?

How often does status change?

What does that do to etcd and watch fanout?
```

---

# 421. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> We'll solve HA with leader election.

Ask:

```text
Does that provide only failover,
or enough reconciliation throughput?
```

---

# 422. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> The webhook can query our central policy service.

Ask:

```text
What happens to the Kubernetes API
when that service is slow or unavailable?
```

---

# 423. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> Just remove the finalizer.

Ask:

```text
Which external resources still exist?

What would leak if we bypass cleanup?
```

---

# 424. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> We need to expose node selectors in the CRD.

Ask:

```text
Is that durable user intent,
or an implementation detail
that should be hidden behind a hardware/topology profile?
```

---

# 425. Another Thought Process

When someone says:

> New controller code is backward compatible.

Ask:

```text
Can it adopt children created by the old version?

Can the old version safely roll back after new resources exist?
```

# 426. What You Must Remember From Chapter 39

1. **A Kubernetes operator is a domain API plus controller plus operational knowledge encoded as reconciliation.**

2. **ML operators exist because training, serving, feature, dataset, and GPU workflows require semantics beyond ordinary Pods and Deployments.**

3. **Kubernetes is fundamentally a desired-state system: users declare intent and controllers continuously converge reality toward it.**

4. **CRD design is public API design and should be treated with the same rigor as any long-lived platform contract.**

5. **A strong ML CRD exposes workload intent and policy, not raw infrastructure details by default.**

6. **metadata/spec/status should remain conceptually distinct: identity, desired state, and observed state.**

7. **Controller-generated operational state belongs in status rather than user-owned spec.**

8. **generation represents desired-spec evolution, while resourceVersion represents API/storage concurrency state.**

9. **observedGeneration lets users know whether status reflects the newest desired specification.**

10. **Conditions are more expressive than one phase string because a resource can be simultaneously Running, Degraded, and not Ready.**

11. **Status must remain small and bounded because API server and etcd are not telemetry, log, or history databases.**

12. **High-frequency status updates can become one of the largest sources of Kubernetes control-plane write amplification.**

13. **Reconciliation should be level-based and derive actions from current state rather than depend on exact event sequences.**

14. **Watch events are hints to reconcile; they should not be the only record of what must happen.**

15. **A good reconciler is idempotent: running it repeatedly against the same state does not create duplicate logical effects.**

16. **Deterministic child names and ownership make "ensure resource exists" much safer than repeated create calls.**

17. **Informers reduce API-server load by maintaining local caches through list-watch.**

18. **Informer caches can be stale, so reconciliation must tolerate eventual observation.**

19. **Watch compaction and reconnects can trigger expensive relists, making relist storms a first-class reliability concern.**

20. **Work queues decouple event arrival from reconcile execution and support coalescing, deduplication, retry, and backpressure.**

21. **One resource can receive thousands of events while requiring only one reconciliation of its latest state.**

22. **Rate-limited queues prevent broken resources from creating tight retry loops and control-plane denial of service.**

23. **Controller concurrency should be sized from reconcile latency, event rate, API limits, and external-service capacity—not maximized blindly.**

24. **Leader election provides HA but does not automatically provide horizontal reconciliation throughput.**

25. **High-scale controller fleets often require sharded active ownership rather than one globally active leader.**

26. **Schema validation should reject structurally invalid or permanently unsupported user intent before reconciliation begins.**

27. **Admission should separate hard invalidity from temporary lack of capacity.**

28. **Admission webhooks are on the Kubernetes API critical path and therefore must be fast, highly available, and dependency-light.**

29. **Security-critical webhooks usually fail closed; optional mutation may have different failure semantics.**

30. **Calling remote internet/SaaS services synchronously from admission is a dangerous architecture because it can freeze cluster control operations.**

31. **Defaulting is API behavior; changing defaults can silently change workloads and therefore requires versioning discipline.**

32. **Finalizers protect cleanup of resources that Kubernetes garbage collection cannot safely remove automatically.**

33. **Finalizer cleanup must be idempotent because deletion reconciliation can run repeatedly.**

34. **Stuck finalizers are a common operator failure and require observability plus controlled manual remediation.**

35. **Blindly removing finalizers can leak cloud, GPU, storage, networking, or security resources.**

36. **Owner references are excellent for Kubernetes child resources but do not replace cleanup of external systems.**

37. **Child events should enqueue the parent resource instead of executing business logic inside watch callbacks.**

38. **External side effects are dangerous because Kubernetes state and remote APIs do not share one transaction.**

39. **A remote timeout has an unknown outcome; the external operation may have succeeded.**

40. **External resources should use deterministic idempotency identities derived from stable Kubernetes resource identity such as UID.**

41. **Controllers should discover and adopt already-created external resources rather than recreate them after uncertain outcomes.**

42. **Fencing or generation tokens may be required when stale owners can still mutate external state.**

43. **Kubernetes is an excellent durable intent store, but it should not be abused as a large workflow history or telemetry database.**

44. **Distributed TrainingJob operators should model logical training jobs rather than force every user to manage individual worker Pods.**

45. **Large distributed training needs workload-level admission and gang/co-scheduling semantics, not only independent Pod scheduling.**

46. **Creating thousands of unschedulable Pods before logical workload admission wastes API-server and scheduler capacity.**

47. **Training operators should classify failures into user, data, capacity, node, GPU, network, and platform categories so retry policy is meaningful.**

48. **Checkpoint-aware retries allow long expensive training runs to recover from infrastructure loss without restarting from zero.**

49. **ModelDeployment operators should treat model loading and warmup as part of readiness, not merely process startup.**

50. **Canary controllers should pause rather than assume success when required evaluation or observability signals are unavailable.**

51. **Operators should orchestrate higher-level resources and leave low-level node selection and topology optimization to scheduling layers designed for that purpose.**

52. **Hardware and topology profiles provide a more stable user API than exposing internal node labels, racks, or GPU implementation details.**

53. **Multi-cluster ML platforms benefit from cluster agents that translate global assignments into local Kubernetes resources.**

54. **Pull-based cluster agents reduce inbound connectivity and credential-management complexity in large fleets.**

55. **Regional/cluster agents should allow existing workloads to continue through temporary global-control-plane disconnection.**

56. **Cluster capacity advertisements need freshness metadata because stale inventory causes poor placement decisions.**

57. **Assignment generations prevent agents from applying stale desired state after reconnects.**

58. **CRD versions represent API contracts and must evolve through explicit compatibility and conversion mechanisms.**

59. **Conversion webhooks are Tier-0 dependencies when multiple CRD versions coexist.**

60. **Round-trip conversion should preserve semantically meaningful data across API versions.**

61. **Hub-and-spoke conversion simplifies multi-version evolution compared with implementing every pairwise converter.**

62. **Controller upgrades must be compatible with resources and child objects created by earlier versions.**

63. **Safe CRD evolution usually follows expand-contract: add compatibility, migrate, then remove old behavior later.**

64. **Tightening validation can unexpectedly invalidate already-existing fleet objects and must be tested against real stored data.**

65. **Control-plane scale is often limited by API-server, etcd, watch fanout, status churn, and list operations rather than controller CPU.**

66. **Every custom controller shares the Kubernetes API server with critical built-in control-plane components.**

67. **Controller clients need bounded QPS and burst limits to avoid becoming cluster-wide noisy neighbors.**

68. **Large resync or relist operations should be staggered and jittered to avoid synchronized control-plane storms.**

69. **One reconcile should be bounded; long external operations should be represented as asynchronous state and revisited later.**

70. **Any controller should be restartable at arbitrary points without losing the information necessary to continue correctly.**

71. **Informer caches and work queues should be reconstructable rather than treated as permanent truth.**

72. **Critical external IDs must be deterministic or durably recorded so resources can be adopted after restart.**

73. **RBAC for controllers should follow least privilege because operators frequently have powerful cross-resource capabilities.**

74. **CRD fields can become privilege-escalation vectors if users can choose unrestricted service accounts, host paths, privileged modes, or network settings.**

75. **Operators should generate secure workload defaults including non-root execution, reduced capabilities, approved images, and policy-controlled networking.**

76. **Workload identity should replace long-lived user-provided cloud credentials in ML job specifications.**

77. **Multi-tenant shared controllers need tenant-aware queue fairness, rate limits, and priority so one broken tenant cannot starve others.**

78. **Reconcile metrics should include rate, duration, error class, retry count, queue depth, and especially queue age.**

79. **Condition reason codes are part of the machine-readable platform API and should be stable.**

80. **Free-form human messages should explain problems but should not be parsed as structured automation contracts.**

81. **Controller SLOs should distinguish how quickly the controller processes intent from how long infrastructure itself takes to provision.**

82. **Startup after controller or cluster recovery can cause a thundering herd when hundreds of thousands of resources are rediscovered.**

83. **Recovery reconciliation must be rate-limited and prioritized just like ordinary production traffic.**

84. **Pod failures must be classified correctly; eviction, CNI, CSI, image-pull, GPU, OOM, and user-code failures have different remediation.**

85. **A platform operator should translate raw infrastructure errors into domain-specific conditions that ML users can understand.**

86. **Status writes can themselves trigger watch events and reconcile loops, so no-op status updates should be eliminated.**

87. **Predicates can suppress irrelevant events but must be designed carefully so meaningful child/deletion events are not lost.**

88. **Kubernetes CRDs should represent durable operational resources, not per-request telemetry or millions of extremely short-lived events.**

89. **Resource granularity is architectural: TrainingJob is a good CRD; PredictionRequest at 1M RPS is not.**

90. **Operators should expose controlled escape hatches because abstractions that hide everything can become inflexible.**

91. **Escape-hatch usage should be measured; high usage often signals weaknesses in the platform's golden path.**

92. **Operators are platform products, so adoption, user success, time-to-ready, support tickets, and explainability matter alongside technical correctness.**

93. **Multiple controllers should never fight over the same field; desired-state ownership must be explicit.**

94. **Resource-oriented choreography—controller A creates resource B and controller B reconciles it—is often safer than direct synchronous controller-to-controller calls.**

95. **Safety invariants describe what must never happen; liveness invariants describe what must eventually happen.**

96. **Controller correctness should be designed around these invariants rather than merely unit-testing happy-path functions.**

97. **Property-based and failure-injection testing can expose duplicate-event, stale-cache, timeout, conflict, and crash-boundary bugs that ordinary tests miss.**

98. **Disaster restoration of custom resources can itself recreate external resources, so restore procedures require adoption, terminal-state awareness, and rate limiting.**

99. **Completed resources should not accidentally restart simply because their child Pods are missing after restoration or cleanup.**

100. **At Senior/Staff/Principal MLOps Architect level, Kubernetes operator design means building durable APIs and reconciliers that preserve invariants across duplicate events, stale caches, API conflicts, controller crashes, external side effects, deletion races, version upgrades, multi-cluster partitions, and large-scale recovery storms.**

A Senior MLOps Architect should no longer ask only:

```text
Did the controller create the Pod?
```

They should ask:

```text
Is the CRD a stable user contract?

Who owns each field?

Can reconciliation execute repeatedly?

What if the watch event is lost?

What if the cache is stale?

What if the API write conflicts?

What if the external create timed out after succeeding?

Can the controller adopt the resource?

How is deletion finalized?

What happens if the finalizer controller is down?

Will 100k simultaneous updates overload the API server?

Can the controller shard horizontally?

Can v1 and v2 coexist?

Can we roll the controller back?

What happens during a multi-cluster partition?

Can the entire system reconstruct itself after a disaster?
```

That is **Kubernetes operator and ML controller engineering at Senior / Staff / Principal depth**.
